title: Working with S3 Object Tags in Buckets: SET, MERGE and CLEAR
description:
A practical walkthrough for keeping Amazon S3 objects organized without changing what is inside the files.

Object tags are easy to overlook when you are busy uploading and moving files around S3. But once a bucket starts filling up, a few consistent labels can make objects easier to organize and manage. The part that matters is how you update them: replacing a tag set is not the same as adding a tag to what is already there.

I used Buckets by Serverless Creed to explore three useful actions—SET, MERGE and CLEAR—and checked the results in the AWS S3 console. I also compared the downloaded files with their original SHA-256 hashes to make sure the contents stayed exactly the same.

A quick look at object tags

An S3 object tag is a key-value pair attached to an object. For example, env=test, team=intern or phase=review can describe where a file belongs or how it is used. These are separate from the file itself and from ordinary user-defined object metadata. S3 allows up to ten tags per object.

Tags can be useful for organizing data and for AWS features that are configured to use them, including lifecycle rules and some access-control policies. That is why updating tags deserves a little more care than simply changing a filename.

Start with a small sample folder

I worked with a handful of harmless text files in a private S3 bucket:

  docs/readme.txt
  b.txt
  c.txt
  control.txt

The files were small enough to inspect easily. The bulk operations shown below target only b.txt and c.txt. I left control.txt with a separate control=keep tag so there was always an object to compare against the ones being updated.

The sample files as they appear in the Buckets object browser.

SET: replace the existing tags

SET is the option to choose when an object needs a completely new tag set. In Buckets, select the files, open the bulk tagging action and choose Set (replace). For this example, I entered team=intern.

The important word is replace: tags that were on the object before, but are not included in the new set, will be removed. Before applying the change, the dialog shows the exact object keys being updated. It is worth reading that list rather than assuming every visible folder or file is included.

SET preview in Buckets, with the new team tag and the exact object list.

The operation completes and Buckets displays the update result.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for SET.

I then opened the object details in AWS. The tag panel showed one tag, team=intern, which is the state I expected after a replacement.

AWS S3 shows the new tag set after SET.

MERGE: add a tag without losing the others

MERGE is more useful when the existing labels should stay. I kept team=intern, switched to Merge, and entered a new tag: phase=review. I left the remove-keys field empty.

That should leave both tags on the objects. If a tag key already exists, MERGE updates that key; keys not mentioned are preserved. This is usually a safer option for incremental changes than rebuilding the full tag list by hand.

MERGE adds phase=review while preserving the other tag keys.

The MERGE action completes successfully.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for MERGE.

The AWS object details now displayed both team=intern and phase=review. Checking the entire tag list is useful here: seeing only the new key would not prove that the earlier one survived.

Both team and phase are visible in the AWS object-tag panel.

CLEAR: remove tags, not the object

CLEAR does exactly what the name suggests: it removes the object’s tag set. In Buckets, choose Clear all after selecting the intended files. The confirmation makes the scope explicit and warns that tag-dependent lifecycle rules or policies may no longer match.

This is the step where I would be most careful in a real bucket. Clearing tags does not delete a file, but tags may be used by other AWS configurations. Always check the objects listed in the confirmation before proceeding.

CLEAR warns about removing all tags and shows the affected object keys.

Buckets confirms that the tag-removal operation completed.

Buckets reported Updated: 2, Failed: 0 for CLEAR.

Afterward, the AWS object details showed Tags (0). The AWS object details still identified b.txt; the wider Buckets capture also shows readme.txt remaining in the browser after tag removal. That distinction is important: removing tags is not the same thing as deleting objects.

The S3 tag section is empty after CLEAR.

A wider view of the Buckets object browser after tag removal.

The AWS object details page still shows the file and its empty tag set.

Independent verification and SHA-256 integrity checking

I kept control.txt out of the tagging changes. Its control=keep tag was still there at the end, which was a quick check that the untouched object had retained its original tag.

The control object keeps its original tag.

For file contents, I recorded SHA-256 hashes of the original text files before uploading them. After the tagging sequence, I downloaded the S3 objects into a separate folder and compared them with that original hash list. Run the check from the download folder, with the original hash list one directory above it:

shasum -a 256 -c ../original-hashes.txt

All four downloaded files match their original SHA-256 hashes.

The output was:

docs/readme.txt: OK
b.txt: OK
c.txt: OK
control.txt: OK

The AWS Console screenshot lists CRC64NVME as its stored checksum function. The SHA-256 verification here is a separate local comparison of the downloaded bytes against the original files.

All four checks returned OK. That gives two independent views of the outcome: the AWS Console shows how the tags changed, and the hash check shows that the downloaded file bytes matched the originals.

A few habits worth keeping

Three things made this workflow straightforward. First, use SET only when replacing the full tag set is intentional; use MERGE when existing labels should remain. Second, review the exact object list before any bulk operation, especially when folders and nested files are involved. Third, check the resulting tags in S3 rather than relying on a success message alone.

For a small example like this, the difference between SET, MERGE and CLEAR is easy to see. On a busy bucket, choosing the right operation—and verifying the final state—can save a lot of confusion later.

title: Simplified onboarding for deepsec
description:
deepsec, the open-source security review harness from Vercel, now lets you set up a repository and run its first security review with a single command.

The init command now automates the standard setup process:

  • creates the isolated .deepsec/ workspace, the only thing added to your repository, and installs its dependencies

  • configures model access, through Vercel AI Gateway or your own provider keys

  • generates a description of the codebase and its attack surface that every later review depends on

  • runs a pattern scan, generating extra scan patterns where the built-in set leaves coverage gaps

  • starts the AI review of the flagged files

Setup is checkpointed after each step. If a run stops, whether from closing the process, a failed step, or a hit cost or duration limit, re-running init resumes from the last completed step.

Run npx deepsec init to start your first scan, or read the docs to learn more.

title: Hono vs Express vs Fastify (and NestJS) in 2026: Real Benchmarks on Node 24, Node 26 and Bun
description:
I ran these benchmarks myself, and every number below comes from those runs. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

Hono vs Express in 2026 is a closer race than the benchmark charts you've seen suggest. On Node.js 24, Hono served 1.44× as many JSON requests per second as Express 5 in my tests, and Fastify was right next to it. But Fastify beat Hono on route parameters and POST bodies, and NestJS added 21 to 23% overhead on top of whichever engine it ran on. The biggest jump didn't come from the framework at all: moving Hono from Node to Bun gave another 1.6×.

I benchmarked seven setups (raw node:http, Hono, Express, Fastify with and without response schemas, and NestJS 12 on both its Express and Fastify adapters) across three workloads, two Node versions and Bun. Here's every number, how I got it, and which framework I'd pick for which job.

TL;DR: Hono vs Express vs Fastify, which is fastest?

On Node, Hono and Fastify are tied for first, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express. Hono won the plain JSON test, Fastify won route parameters and POST bodies. Express 5 is the slowest of the three but still served 50,000 requests per second on two CPU cores, which is more than most APIs will ever see. On Bun, Hono pulls clearly ahead at 118,000 requests per second.

Node 24.22, 2 cores, requests/s (median) JSON Route param POST JSON body Startup to first response Install size
node:http (no framework) 78,870 73,049 41,917 76 ms none
Hono 4.13.13 73,067 70,128 36,553 94 ms 3.9 MB, 2 packages
Fastify 5.12.7 71,786 76,746 38,936 153 ms 14.4 MB, 48 packages
Express 5.3.0 50,744 48,335 28,569 116 ms 4.3 MB, 65 packages
NestJS 12.1.3 + Fastify 56,434 59,499 33,418 425 ms n/a
NestJS 12.1.3 + Express 38,893 35,829 23,011 320 ms 22.4 MB, 98 packages

My pick: Hono for new APIs, especially anything that might run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or another edge runtime. Fastify for Node-only services where you want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express when the team and middleware already exist, because it's fast enough. NestJS when the codebase is big enough that structure matters more than 20% of throughput, and then put it on the Fastify adapter.

What are Hono, Express and Fastify?

All three are HTTP frameworks for JavaScript and TypeScript, and they come from different eras.

  • Express is the 2010 original and still the default. Express 5 finally shipped native promise support in route handlers and dropped a lot of legacy API. It has the largest middleware ecosystem by far: 145 million npm downloads in the week of October 6 to 12, 2026.
  • Fastify was built for speed on Node. It compiles JSON schemas into fast serializers and validators, has a strict plugin system with encapsulation, and logs with Pino by default. 15.4 million downloads that week.
  • Hono is built on web standards: handlers take a Request-like context and return a Response. The same app runs on Node, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel. It's tiny and has zero dependencies. 74 million downloads that week, partly because other tools bundle it.
  • NestJS isn't a fourth HTTP engine. It's an application framework with modules, dependency injection and decorators that runs on top of Express (the default) or Fastify. I covered the latest release in my NestJS 12 upgrade guide.

The code looks similar for a simple route. Here are the three handlers I benchmarked:

// Hono
app.get('/users/:id', c => c.json({ id: c.req.param('id'), fields: c.req.query('fields') ?? null }))

// Express 5
app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

// Fastify 5
app.get('/users/:id', async req => ({ id: req.params.id, fields: req.query.fields ?? null }))

How I benchmarked them

Benchmarks of web frameworks are easy to get wrong, so here's exactly what I ran.

  1. Machine. An 8 vCPU Intel Xeon VM with 15 GB of RAM. Each server was pinned to 2 cores with taskset. The load generator, oha 1.16.0, ran on the other 6 cores with 64 connections.
  2. Runtimes. Node.js 24.22.0, Node.js 26.12.0 and Bun 1.4.3.
  3. Versions. Hono 4.13.13 with @hono/node-server 2.1.5, Express 5.3.0, Fastify 5.12.7, and NestJS 12.1.3 with @nestjs/platform-express and @nestjs/platform-fastify. These were the latest npm releases on October 17, 2026.
  4. Workloads. GET /json returns {"message":"Hello, World!"}. GET /users/42?fields=name reads a route parameter and a query string. POST /echo parses a 907-byte JSON body and returns a count.
  5. Fair settings. No logging. ETags off in Express and in NestJS on Express, and x-powered-by off in Express. Fastify ran twice, once without schemas and once with response schemas. Every app returns the same JSON.
  6. Method. Each run started a fresh server, warmed it up for 4 seconds, then measured for 10 seconds. I ran 3 rounds per setup and report the median. Four setups had one noisy round, so I re-ran those with 5 rounds. That's 32 setups and more than 65 million measured requests, with a 100% success rate.

Absolute numbers depend on hardware. The ratios between frameworks are what transfer to your servers.

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. On Node 24, Hono handled 1.44× Express's throughput on plain JSON (73,067 vs 50,744 requests per second), 1.45× on route parameters and 1.28× on POST bodies. Latency followed: p99 on the JSON test was 1.50 ms for Hono against 2.12 ms for Express.

Two details matter more than the headline:

  • Hono came within 8% of raw node:http on the JSON test. There's very little left to optimize in the framework itself.
  • Hono's lead shrinks on POST. On Node, Hono goes through @hono/node-server, which turns Node's request into a web-standard Request before your handler sees it. Parsing a body through that layer costs more than Fastify's native parser. On Bun, where Request is native, the same Hono app did 80,749 POST requests per second, 2.2× its Node result.

Express 5 pays for its flexible middleware pipeline and the extra properties it adds to every request and response. It's still not slow. Fifty thousand requests per second on two cores is about 4 billion requests a day. Your database will give out long before Express does.

Hono vs Fastify: which is faster?

It depends on the route. On Node 24:

Requests/s, Node 24 Hono Fastify Fastify + response schema Winner
JSON 73,067 71,786 74,567 tie (within 4%)
Route param + query 70,128 76,746 75,526 Fastify, +9%
POST JSON body 36,553 38,936 39,045 Fastify, +7%

Fastify's router is a radix tree (find-my-way), and it beat even my hand-written node:http router on the route parameter test (76,746 vs 73,049), because my raw version builds a URL object per request. Adding response schemas, which Fastify compiles into a serializer with fast-json-stringify, was worth only about 4% on these small responses. The bigger value of schemas is validation and documentation, not speed.

So on Node, call it a draw. Pick between them on design: web standards and portability (Hono), or schemas, plugins and Node depth (Fastify).

Fastify vs Express: is it worth switching in 2026?

On raw speed, Fastify was 1.41× faster on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST. Its p99 latency was 25 to 40% lower too.

Whether that justifies a rewrite depends on where your time goes. If a typical request spends 20 ms in Postgres and 0.3 ms in the framework, cutting the framework's share in half changes nothing a user can feel. Switch when profiling shows the framework near the top, when you want schema validation built in, or when you're starting fresh anyway. Don't switch because of a chart, including this one.

How much overhead does NestJS add?

NestJS adds a layer of decorators, guards, pipes and interceptors on top of the engine. In my tests that cost 23% of Express's throughput (38,893 vs 50,744 on JSON) and 21% of Fastify's (56,434 vs 71,786). It also used more memory: about 100 MB idle versus 65 MB for plain Express.

The fix is easy and well documented in the NestJS performance guide: NestJS on Fastify was 1.45× faster than NestJS on Express on JSON and POST, and 1.66× faster on route parameters. It was also faster than plain Express on every test. If you use NestJS and none of your middleware is Express-specific, the Fastify adapter is the cheapest performance win available.

Do Node 26 and Bun change the ranking?

Node 26 made every framework faster without code changes. On the JSON test, Express and Fastify gained about 12%, NestJS 10%, Hono 6% and raw node:http 7%.

JSON requests/s Node 24.22 Node 26.12 Bun 1.4.3
Hono 73,067 77,454 118,432
Fastify 71,786 80,220 86,269
Express 50,744 56,627 72,479
NestJS + Express 38,893 42,923 not tested

On Bun, the ranking changes. Hono uses Bun's native server directly, so it ran 1.62× faster than on Node 24 and opened a 37% lead over Fastify. Express and Fastify also got faster on Bun (1.43× and 1.20×) but they run through Bun's node:http compatibility layer instead of calling Bun.serve directly. If you plan to run on Bun, Hono is the obvious choice. I compared the runtimes themselves in Bun vs Node.js in 2026.

Memory, startup time and install size

Throughput isn't the only cost. Startup matters for serverless and autoscaling, and install size matters for container images and cold deploys.

Node 24 Startup to first 200 Peak RSS at startup RSS idle Peak RSS under JSON load
node:http 76 ms 62 MB 58 MB 97 MB
Hono 94 ms 67 MB 63 MB 104 MB
Express 116 ms 75 MB 65 MB 97 MB
Fastify 153 ms 78 MB 72 MB 105 MB
NestJS + Express 320 ms 100 MB 98 MB 143 MB
NestJS + Fastify 425 ms 109 MB 106 MB 138 MB
Hono on Bun 14 ms 24 MB 20 MB 43 MB

Startup is the time from launching the process to the first successful response, measured with hyperfine over 20 runs. Hono on Bun was ready in 14 ms, which is why it's popular for serverless functions. NestJS needed about 2.8 times as long as the plain framework underneath it, because it scans modules and builds its dependency graph at boot.

Install size, measured in a fresh folder with npm: Hono plus its Node adapter is 2 packages and 3.9 MB. Express 5 is 65 packages but only 4.3 MB. Fastify is 48 packages and 14.4 MB. A minimal NestJS app on Express (core, common, platform-express, reflect-metadata, rxjs) is 98 packages and 22.4 MB. If you ship Docker images, my Next.js Dockerfile guide has the same multi-stage tricks that keep a Node API image small.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

If you need... Pick Why
A new API with the fewest moving parts Hono Within 8% of raw Node, zero dependencies, web-standard code
To run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda Hono Same app everywhere; 118k req/s on Bun
The best Node throughput on real routes Fastify Won route params and POST; schemas and plugins built in
An existing team and Express middleware Express 5 50k req/s is plenty; huge ecosystem; easy hiring
Structure for a large team (modules, DI) NestJS on Fastify 1.45 to 1.66× faster than NestJS on Express
End-to-end typed clients Hono (RPC) or Fastify with TypeBox Types flow from routes to clients

Two more points rarely show up in benchmark posts:

  • Ecosystem. Express still has the most middleware, tutorials and Stack Overflow answers. Fastify's plugin ecosystem covers most production needs. Hono's middleware set is smaller but growing, and anything built on web standards tends to just work.
  • Typed clients. Hono's RPC mode lets a frontend import the API's types directly. If your frontend is Next.js, also check whether you need a separate API at all; I covered that in Server Actions vs Route Handlers.

How do I migrate from Express to Hono or Fastify?

You don't need a big-bang rewrite. Both frameworks can sit next to Express while you move routes.

// Fastify: run existing Express middleware during a migration
import Fastify from 'fastify'
import expressPlugin from '@fastify/express'
const app = Fastify()
await app.register(expressPlugin)
app.use(legacyExpressMiddleware)

// Hono: same handler shape on every runtime
import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()
app.get('/health', c => c.json({ ok: true }))
export default app // Bun, Workers, Deno; use @hono/node-server on Node

A safe order: move health checks and read-only routes first, measure them in production, then move the routes that write data. Keep the request and response shapes identical so clients never notice. Watch for Express habits that don't carry over: mutating req from middleware, res.locals, and error handlers with four arguments.

Common mistakes when benchmarking web frameworks

  • Running the load generator on the server's cores. Pin them apart, or you measure contention.
  • Benchmarking only /hello. Hono won plain JSON, Fastify won routes with parameters and bodies. One endpoint gives you one answer.
  • Leaving logging on. Fastify with a logger and Express with morgan are both much slower. Compare like with like.
  • Trusting a single run. Four of my 32 setups had one round 10 to 20% below the others. Take the median of several runs.
  • Comparing frameworks on different runtimes. "Hono is 2× faster than Express" is often Hono on Bun versus Express on Node.
  • Ignoring where time actually goes. Profile one real request. The framework is rarely the bottleneck.

Related: if your API is meant for AI agents, read MCP vs API before choosing a framework, because the protocol choice changes more than the framework does.

Key takeaways

  • On Node 24, Hono (73,067 req/s) and Fastify (71,786) are tied on JSON, and both are about 1.4× faster than Express 5 (50,744).
  • Fastify won route parameters (+9% over Hono) and POST bodies (+7%). Hono won plain JSON and came within 8% of raw node:http.
  • NestJS costs about 21 to 23% throughput and about 2.8× the startup time. On the Fastify adapter it's 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express.
  • Node 26 sped every framework up by 6 to 12% with no code changes.
  • On Bun, Hono jumped to 118,432 req/s, 1.62× its Node result, with 14 ms startup and 43 MB under load.
  • Hono installs as 2 packages (3.9 MB). Express is 65 packages (4.3 MB), Fastify 48 (14.4 MB), and NestJS 98 (22.4 MB).
  • Even Express handled 50,000 requests per second on 2 cores. Pick on design and ecosystem first; the framework is rarely your bottleneck.

FAQ

Is Hono faster than Express?

Yes. In my October 2026 benchmark on Node 24, Hono 4.13.13 served 73,067 JSON requests per second against 50,744 for Express 5.3.0, which is 1.44× faster. It was 1.45× faster on route parameters and 1.28× faster on POST bodies, with lower p99 latency.

Is Hono faster than Fastify?

On Node they're tied. Hono won plain JSON by 2%, but Fastify won route parameters by 9% and POST bodies by 7%. On Bun, Hono pulls ahead: 118,432 requests per second versus 86,269 for Fastify, because Hono uses Bun's native server directly.

Is Fastify faster than Express in 2026?

Yes. Fastify 5.12.7 was 1.41× faster than Express 5.3.0 on JSON, 1.59× on route parameters and 1.36× on POST bodies, with 25 to 40% lower p99 latency. Express still handled about 50,000 requests per second on two cores, which is enough for most APIs.

How much slower is NestJS than Express or Fastify?

NestJS 12.1.3 cost about 23% of Express's throughput and 21% of Fastify's on the JSON test, used about 100 MB of memory at idle, and took about 2.8× as long to start. Using the Fastify adapter made NestJS 1.45 to 1.66× faster than on Express, and faster than plain Express on every test.

Should I switch from Express to Hono or Fastify?

Only if you have a reason beyond a benchmark. Switch when profiling shows the framework is a real cost, when you want built-in schema validation (Fastify), or when you need to run on Bun, Cloudflare Workers or other runtimes (Hono). If most request time is spent in the database, a faster framework won't be noticeable.

Which Node.js framework should I use in 2026?

Hono for new APIs and anything that may run on Bun, Workers, Deno or Lambda. Fastify for Node-only services that want schemas, plugins and the best throughput on real routes. Express 5 for teams with existing middleware and experience. NestJS on the Fastify adapter for large codebases that need modules and dependency injection.

Does Node 26 make Express, Fastify and Hono faster?

Yes. With no code changes, Node 26.12 improved JSON throughput over Node 24.22 by about 12% for Express and Fastify, 10% for NestJS, 7% for raw node:http and 6% for Hono.

How did you benchmark Hono, Express and Fastify?

Each server ran on 2 pinned CPU cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM, with oha 1.16.0 on the other cores at 64 connections. Every run started a fresh server, warmed up for 4 seconds and measured for 10 seconds. I report the median of 3 rounds, or 5 rounds for setups with a noisy round, across 32 setups on Node 24.22, Node 26.12 and Bun 1.4.3.

title: Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis
description:
title: "Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-11T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [nodejs, redis, backend, architecture]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Producers And Consumers: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Delayed And Recurring Jobs: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Concurrency Control: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Exponential Backoff Retries: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Building a Background Job Processing System in Node.js Using BullMQ and Redis functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: Producers and consumers, delayed and recurring jobs, concurrency control, exponential backoff retries, and monitoring queue health with Arena."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Enforcing Accessibility Gates in Component Libraries: plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Review
description:
The Problem: LLMs Generate Plausible Garbage

When you ask Claude or GPT to build a modal dialog with "proper accessibility," you'll get role="dialog" and aria-labelledby attributes. Ship it to production and discover VoiceOver users are trapped inside the modal because focus management is broken.

The root cause: code generation optimizes for syntactic correctness, not runtime behavior. Most component skills teach the model ARIA vocabulary without enforcing the invariants that make it work.

What plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills Does Differently

This repository packages 52 production-grade component patterns (modals, dropdowns, tabs, carousels) with 50 objective verification gates that fail your build if the output violates WCAG 2.2 AA/AAA requirements.

Key architectural decisions:

  1. DTCG token contracts first: Design tokens follow the W3C Design Token Community Group spec, so Tailwind utility classes map to semantic color/spacing/typography tokens that survive theme switches.

  2. Framework-agnostic primitives: The skill set teaches Claude to reason about accessible state machines (disclosure widgets, comboboxes) independent of React/Vue/Svelte, then emit framework-specific bindings.

  3. Objective gates over subjective prompts: Instead of "make sure focus is managed," the skill includes executable tests (using tools like axe-core + Playwright) that physically verify focus trap behavior and keyboard navigation sequences.

Integration Example: Dropdown with Live Region Announcements

When I integrated this into our design system migration, the skill generated a Radix Primitives dropdown that handles an edge case our team missed:

import * as DropdownMenu from '@radix-ui/react-dropdown-menu';
import { VisuallyHidden } from '@radix-ui/react-visually-hidden';

export function AccessibleDropdown({ items, onSelect }) {
  const [announcement, setAnnouncement] = React.useState('');

  return (
    <>
      <DropdownMenu.Root>
        <DropdownMenu.Trigger className="px-4 py-2 bg-primary-600 text-white rounded-md">
          Options
        </DropdownMenu.Trigger>

        <DropdownMenu.Portal>
          <DropdownMenu.Content
            className="min-w-[220px] bg-white rounded-md shadow-lg p-1"
            onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()}
          >
            {items.map((item) => (
              <DropdownMenu.Item
                key={item.id}
                className="px-3 py-2 rounded hover:bg-gray-100 focus:bg-gray-100 outline-none cursor-pointer"
                onSelect={() => {
                  onSelect(item);
                  setAnnouncement(`${item.label} selected`);
                }}
              >
                {item.label}
              </DropdownMenu.Item>
            ))}
          </DropdownMenu.Content>
        </DropdownMenu.Portal>
      </DropdownMenu.Root>

      <VisuallyHidden role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-atomic="true">
        {announcement}
      </VisuallyHidden>
    </>
  );
}

Why this matters: The live region announces selection changes to screen reader users without visual flash. Most component libraries skip this because sighted QA never catches it.

The Build Gate That Saved Us

Our CI pipeline now runs:

npx playwright test --grep @a11y

One of the generated tests physically verifies focus behavior:

test('dropdown focus trap @a11y', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/dropdown-demo');
  await page.click('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]');

  // Verify focus enters the menu
  await page.keyboard.press('Tab');
  const firstItem = page.locator('[role="menuitem"]').first();
  await expect(firstItem).toBeFocused();

  // Verify Escape closes and returns focus
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(page.locator('[data-testid="dropdown-trigger"]')).toBeFocused();
});

This caught a regression where a junior dev removed onCloseAutoFocus={(e) => e.preventDefault()} during a refactor, breaking keyboard navigation for 8% of our user base.

TailwindCSS Integration: Container Queries for Responsive Components

The skill set includes a micro-interaction pattern leveraging Tailwind v4's native container query support:

@layer components {
  .adaptive-card {
    container-type: inline-size;
    @apply bg-white rounded-lg shadow;
  }

  .adaptive-card__title {
    @apply text-lg font-semibold;
  }

  @container (min-width: 400px) {
    .adaptive-card__title {
      @apply text-2xl;
    }
    .adaptive-card__content {
      @apply grid grid-cols-2 gap-4;
    }
  }
}

This eliminates layout thrashing from JavaScript-based resize observers. Our Lighthouse performance score jumped from 78 to 94 after migrating 23 card components to this pattern.

When to Use This vs. shadcn/ui Directly

If you're building a standard CRUD app, shadcn/ui's pre-built components are faster. Use plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills when:

  1. You need to teach an LLM your design system's accessibility requirements
  2. You're migrating legacy components and want automated compliance checks
  3. You're in a regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government) where WCAG violations carry legal risk

The 138 design system references (Material, Spectrum, Carbon, etc.) help Claude generate components that match your existing visual language without manual token mapping.

Limitations I Hit

No visual regression testing: The gates verify semantic HTML and ARIA, but won't catch a button that's visually 2px too small for WCAG 2.2's 24×24 touch target requirement. You still need Percy or Chromatic.

Learning curve for custom components: The DTCG token structure assumes you've already defined semantic design tokens. If you're still using raw Tailwind utilities everywhere, the initial setup takes 2-3 hours.

Conclusion

After three weeks using plugin87/ux-ui-agent-skills on a client project (migrating a React component library to Radix + Tailwind v4), the build gates caught 14 accessibility regressions that our manual QA process missed.

The killer feature isn't the 52 component patterns—it's the shift from "Claude, make this accessible" (subjective, unverifiable) to "the build fails if focus order is wrong" (objective, enforceable).

If you're tired of shipping ARIA soup that looks correct in the inspector but breaks for real users, this skill set forces the issue at merge time instead of in production.

title: Postgres Logical Replication: Slots, DDL, and Failover
description:
At 2 a.m. on a Tuesday, a client's reporting replica silently stopped applying changes. The publisher kept accepting writes. The replica kept answering read queries. And a logical replication slot sat inactive for six hours, pinning WAL files until the disk hit 96 percent. Nobody got paged because "replication is running" was a monitoring lie I had set up myself: a check for the slot's existence, not its health. That night taught me that logical replication is not a feature you turn on. It is a pipeline you operate.

This is the guide I wish I had that night. It covers what logical replication is actually good for, how to watch replication slots so they do not eat your disk, why schema changes are the quiet killer, and what happens when the primary fails.

What logical replication is (and is not)

Logical replication in PostgreSQL replicates data changes at the level of rows and transactions, not disk blocks. A publisher marks tables in a publication. A subscriber creates a subscription, and the publisher streams decoded write-ahead log (WAL) entries through an output plugin, pgoutput by default, as a replication protocol stream. Subscribers apply those changes with normal SQL, which means the data arrives through ordinary tables, triggers, and constraints.

That design choice is the source of both its power and its traps:

Aspect Logical replication Physical (streaming) replication
Unit of replication Row changes, per table Whole database cluster, block level
Target Any Postgres instance, any major version within reason Same major version, same architecture
Selectivity Per table, per row, per column All or nothing
DDL (schema changes) Not replicated Replicated
Writes on subscriber Allowed Not allowed
Conflict detection Minimal, async only None needed

The official logical replication documentation is the primary reference, and the restrictions section is required reading; every claim about defaults in this post traces back to them.

For a small business, the practical meaning is this: logical replication is the right tool when you want a subset of data somewhere else, on infrastructure you do not fully control, or in a version you cannot upgrade in lockstep. It is the wrong tool when you want a byte-for-byte standby for disaster recovery. Use physical replication for that.

Use cases that justify the operational cost

I only recommend logical replication when one of these is true. Each one I have run in production.

Reporting and analytics offloading

Point your BI tool at a subscriber that holds only the tables analytics needs, optionally with row filters and column lists (available since PostgreSQL 15). Writers keep their I/O profile; readers stop hammering the OLTP primary. This is the most common and the most forgiving use case.

Zero-downtime major version upgrades

Upgrade the replica to the newer Postgres major version, subscribe it to the old primary, let it catch up, flip a connection string, and drop the old node. Logical replication works across major versions in the direction old-to-new. This is the standard escape hatch when pg_upgrade's downtime window is unacceptable.

Cross-region read scaling and consolidation

A subscriber in another region serves local reads, or pulls data from several publishers into one warehouse-shaped database. Because replication is per-table, you can consolidate five regional databases into one reporting node without shipping every byte. For teams evaluating multi-datacenter latency, our analysis of multi-region architecture maps out routing tradeoffs and read-replica replication lag.

Selective data sharing

Expose a subset of rows to a partner, a contractor, or a staging environment without granting anyone access to the full primary. Row filters make this defensible; you are not copy-pasting exports that go stale.

If your need is "a copy of everything, fast, automatically," use streaming replication and stop reading. If your team is still choosing a database stack, our breakdown of building a small business tech stack from scratch covers where Postgres fits among managed and self-hosted options.

Replication slots: the part that bites you

Every logical subscription consumes a replication slot on the publisher. The slot's job is to guarantee that the WAL the subscriber has not consumed yet is not recycled. That guarantee is unconditional. If the subscriber falls behind or dies, the slot holds WAL, and WAL accumulates on disk until either the subscriber catches up or the disk fills.

PostgreSQL exposes everything you need in the pg_replication_slots view. These are the columns I alert on:

  • active: false for more than a few minutes means the consumer is down or stuck.
  • inactive_since: tells you exactly when the slot went quiet.
  • wal_status: anything other than reserved means trouble. unreserved means WAL is about to be removed; lost means the slot is dead and the replica needs a rebuild.
  • restart_lsn and confirmed_flush_lsn: the gap between current LSN and these values is your disk-usage clock.
  • conflicting and invalidation_reason: if invalidation_reason is set, the slot has already failed and the reason tells you which protection (max_slot_wal_keep_size, idle_replication_slot_timeout) killed it.

One short query covers a morning health check:

SELECT slot_name, active, inactive_since, wal_status,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots WHERE slot_type = 'logical';

Set max_slot_wal_keep_size to a value your disk can survive (a few GB, not -1) so a runaway slot errors instead of filling the volume. Pair it with idle_replication_slot_timeout for slots from decommissioned environments. Yes, a slot that overruns its budget invalidates and forces a resync of that subscriber. That is the correct trade. An invalidated slot is a bad afternoon. A full disk is a bad week.

WAL retention pressure is only one flavor of the resource problem. If you are also scaling write capacity across database clusters, our database sharding for Postgres SaaS guide breaks down partitioning, replication boundaries, and horizontal distribution patterns.

Schema changes: the quiet killer

Logical replication does not replicate DDL. Add a column on the publisher and nothing breaks immediately, because the subscriber simply never sees the new column. Rename a column and the subscriber starts erroring on apply, the subscription halts, and the slot begins retaining WAL while your on-call rotation sleeps.

The failure pattern I see most often: a migration framework (Flyway, Alembic, a hand-rolled migration directory) deploys schema changes to the primary without any awareness of subscribers. The team finds out at 9 a.m. from a disk alert.

The playbook that works:

  1. Additive changes only, subscriber first: add new columns and new tables to the subscriber before the publisher, never the reverse. Dropping is the dangerous direction.
  2. Treat renames and type changes as two-step operations: add the new column, backfill, switch writes, then drop the old one later.
  3. Expand and contract: write code that tolerates both schemas during the transition window.
  4. Wire migrations into deployment order: subscribers get DDL before publishers, enforced by your pipeline, not by memory.
  5. After any migration, check pg_stat_subscription_stats on the subscriber for apply errors before you call it done.

Column lists and row filters (publication options, PostgreSQL 15 and later) make some of this easier: if the subscriber declares a column list that matches its local schema, publisher-side additions do not break apply. Row filters deserve the same care, because a filter that silently excludes rows on the subscriber is a data bug that no error message will surface.

What happens when the primary fails

Here is the blunt version most tutorials skip: logical replication has no automatic failover. If the publisher dies, your subscriptions stop, full stop. Subscribers keep serving stale reads, happily, with no error that your application will notice.

Since PostgreSQL 17, there is a supported path for surviving planned and unplanned failover of the publisher: create the subscription with failover = true, and the primary synchronizes the logical slot to its physical standby. When the standby is promoted, the slot is already there and the subscriber reconnects to the new primary. The requirements are strict, per the logical replication failover documentation:

  • You need a physical standby of the publisher anyway.
  • The slot sync is asynchronous. You must verify, before promoting, that the slots on the standby report synced and not invalid. The docs provide verification queries for exactly this.
  • The standby must be ahead of the subscriber, or data written after the slot's confirmed position is lost from the replication stream.

Miss the verification step and you get a promoted primary whose logical slots are behind your subscriber's confirmed flush position. That gap is silently dropped data. Not corrupted, dropped: transactions committed on the old primary but never decoded will never reach the subscriber, and nothing raises an error.

For planned failovers, use synchronized_standby_slots and check failover readiness on the standby before switching. For unplanned ones, accept that you may need to re-sync subscribers if the standby was behind. And test this. A failover drill on a staging cluster takes an afternoon and is the only way to find out your slots were never syncing. We follow a similar recovery-testing protocol in our playbook on business internet and infrastructure failover.

What most guides get wrong

Three claims repeat across vendor blogs, and all three cost me production time before I stopped believing them.

First: "logical replication is simple streaming with a filter." No. It is a decoding pipeline with persistent state (the slot) that couples the publisher's WAL retention to the subscriber's health. The filter is the easy part. The slot is the product.

Second: "just monitor lag." Lag, meaning apply delay on the subscriber, is the metric everyone graphs, and it is nearly useless as an early warning. Slot WAL retention on the publisher fills your disk long before apply lag becomes dramatic, and a dead subscriber has zero lag and an ever-growing WAL pile. Watch wal_status and the LSN gap on the publisher, then apply errors on the subscriber via pg_stat_subscription_stats. If you run security audits on your infrastructure and data layer, the same discipline applies in our web security fundamentals: the real vulnerability is almost never the headline metric.

Third: "failover = true fixes HA." It fixes one narrow scenario, publisher failover with a physical standby present, and only if you verified slot sync before promoting. It does nothing for subscriber failure, network partitions, or the dropped-transaction gap. Guides that present it as a checkbox are selling comfort, not reliability.

Operator's checklist

Run this daily, automate what you can, page on the starred items:

  • [ ] * wal_status = reserved for every logical slot; anything else is an incident
  • [ ] * Disk headroom above the max_slot_wal_keep_size budget on the publisher
  • [ ] confirmed_flush_lsn gap below your agreed rebuild threshold
  • [ ] pg_stat_subscription_stats shows no apply_errors
  • [ ] inactive_since null, or slot retention policy (idle timeout) in place for exceptions
  • [ ] For failover-enabled subscriptions: synced = true on the standby and invalidation_reason null
  • [ ] Migration runbook confirms subscriber-first DDL for any deploy touching published tables

Conclusion

Logical replication earns its keep for reporting offload, version upgrades, selective sharing, and cross-region consolidation, but only if you operate the slot as a first-class citizen: alert on wal_status and retention, not lag; run additive, subscriber-first migrations; and treat failover slot sync as a verified procedure, not a parameter. The failure modes are quiet until they are expensive, which is exactly why this is the checklist you build before the 2 a.m. page, not after.

title: A Drift Detector That Cries Wolf Is Worse Than No Detector
description:
My drift detector quarantined a healthy agent. The agent hadn't gotten worse — the benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions, so growing the benchmark from 10 tasks to 20 made a 10/10 agent look like it "failed" half the suite. Corpus growth looked like decay.

I built the drift detector for HivePlane v0.2.0 to catch the failure mode I'd written about in v0.1.0 — "the dangerous agent usually drifted, not got edited." The harder problem turned out not to be detecting drift. It was not detecting drift that wasn't there. A detector that cries wolf trains operators to ignore the signal, and an ignored gate is no gate.

The detector that ate its own benchmark

Finding What the detector did Why it was wrong
#530 Compared failure counts across corpus versions Growing the benchmark auto-quarantined a healthy agent
F-13 Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED Auto-quarantine resets to UNCERTIFIED — the gate refused its own quarantine
#609 / S24 The probe runner only checked admission A probe could never flag behavioral decay — only a refused run could fail one

The scariest line in the release wasn't a missed drift. It was a healthy agent quarantined because the detector compared it to a benchmark that no longer existed.

The benchmark that looked like decay

530 was the one that changed how I think about drift baselines. The detector compared failure counts across corpus versions. If the benchmark grew from 10 tasks to 20 — because the learning loop added a reviewed case — a healthy agent that passed 10/10 now "failed" 10 of 20 by the old accounting. Corpus growth looked like decay.

The agent hadn't gotten worse. The benchmark had gotten bigger. The detector couldn't tell the difference, so it quarantined a perfectly good agent.

The fix: drift is measured against the agent's own baseline on comparable corpora. You compare the same tasks across re-evaluations, not different counts. A corpus version change establishes a new baseline, not a drift signal. Growing the benchmark is growth, not regression.

tip: If your drift metric is a count, a benchmark change will look like behavior change. Compare the agent to itself on the same tasks, or any corpus edit becomes a false quarantine.

The reinstatement that refused its own quarantine

F-13 was the symmetry that broke. Drift auto-quarantine resets the certification status to UNCERTIFIED — not QUARANTINED. Reinstatement required status == QUARANTINED. So the gate that created the quarantine refused to lift it. A workload could be auto-quarantined and then never reinstated, because the precondition described a state the detector never set.

The fix was removing the stale precondition. An active quarantine record is reinstatable — the workload is re-certified and admission is re-checked. The status field is not the source of truth; the quarantine record is. The gate keyed off the wrong one.

The field test caught this in scenario S5, where reinstatement after S4's auto-quarantine failed in sequence. Two scenarios, one bug, and the lesson: the source of truth for "is this quarantined" is the quarantine record, not the certification status enum.

The probe that couldn't smell decay

609 / S24 was the most subtle. The synthetic probe runner ignored Spec.expected and only checked admission. So a probe could only fail if the run was refused — it could never flag that the agent ran and produced the wrong answer. The probe was a liveness check pretending to be a readiness check.

A probe's job is to catch decay before the drift threshold trips. If the probe only checks "did it run," it can't catch "did it run correctly." The fix: the runner starts the run, waits for terminal, and compares the output to expected. A mismatch fails the probe with a probe.decay warning. Now a probe can smell decay the drift detector hasn't measured yet.

What I learned

False-positive controls are the product, not a nicety: a single exceeding run is a warning, and quarantine requires N consecutive failures or a strong signal — a stable agent is never quarantined on noise. Measure drift against comparable baselines: the same tasks, the same corpus version; a corpus bump is a new baseline, not a regression. The quarantine record is the source of truth, not the status enum — reinstatement keys off the record, or it refuses the very quarantines it should lift. And a probe must assert the expected output, not just that the run was admitted — liveness is not readiness.

The v0.2.0 field test demonstrates the full loop — drift due/assess/probe, auto-quarantine, reinstatement after a fresh certification — as scenarios S4, S5, S8, and S24. The synthetic probe flags decay before the drift threshold in S24. Full evidence in the field-test report; the certification and learning-loop designs are in the certification v2 design and the learning loop design.

References

  • HivePlane — pip install hiveplane==0.2.0
  • Field test report (36/36)
  • Certification v2 design · Learning loop design
  • Operator runbook — drift & quarantine

When was the last time your detector quarantined something that was fine? If your operators have learned to reinstate without reading, your detector isn't a control — it's a checkbox.

title: Distributed Cron Jobs
description:
Regular cron runs on one server. What happens when you have 10 servers? Each runs the job 10 times. That's a problem.

The Problem 

Single server cron: ✅ Job runs once at 2am
10-server fleet:    ❌ Job runs 10 times at 2am — duplicate emails, double charges!

Solutions

1. Dedicated Scheduler Node

  • One designated machine runs all cron jobs
  • ✅ Simple
  • ❌ Single point of failure — if this node dies, no cron jobs run

2. Leader Election + Cron

  • Cluster elects a leader (using etcd/ZooKeeper)
  • Only the leader runs cron jobs
  • If leader dies → new leader elected → cron resumes
  • ✅ No SPOF | ❌ Leader election complexity

3. Distributed Lock Before Job Execution 

def run_job():
    lock = redis.set("cron:daily-email", "locked", nx=True, ex=300)  # 5min TTL
    if not lock:
        return  # another node is running it
    try:
        send_daily_emails()
    finally:
        redis.delete("cron:daily-email")
  • ✅ Simple, works with existing Redis
  • ❌ Lock expiry must be > job duration, or use heartbeat extension

4. Dedicated Scheduling Services

  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler — cron without servers
  • Temporal.io — workflow orchestration with scheduling
  • Airflow — DAG-based job scheduling
  • Sidekiq-Cron (Ruby), Bull (Node.js)

Exactly-Once Execution

For critical jobs (billing, emails):

  1. Use idempotency keys in the job itself
  2. Record execution in DB before running: INSERT INTO job_runs (job_id, run_date) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING → if 0 rows inserted, skip
  3. Use a distributed lock with heartbeat

Observability for Cron

  • Alert if a job DIDN'T run (missed heartbeat)
  • Track job duration — sudden increase = something is wrong
  • Log job result (success/failure, records processed)
  • Tool: Healthchecks.io — cron monitoring via ping

Measuring Website Conversion for Professional Services: A Technical Breakdown

As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, it is imperative to acknowledge that standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to effectively measure website conversion for professional services. This is primarily due to the unique nature of professional services, which require a nuanced approach to conversion measurement. Generic solutions neglect to account for the complex sales funnels, multiple touchpoints, and relationship-building aspects inherent to professional services.

Standard templates and forms are designed to cater to a broad range of industries, resulting in a one-size-fits-all approach that neglects the specific needs of professional services. They fail to provide the necessary depth and customization required to accurately measure conversion rates, leading to incomplete or misleading data. Furthermore, these generic solutions often focus on simplistic metrics, such as page views or click-through rates, which do not provide a comprehensive understanding of the conversion process.

To effectively measure website conversion for professional services, it is essential to adopt a tailored approach that takes into account the unique characteristics of the industry. The following engineering takeaways provide a foundation for developing a customized conversion measurement strategy:

  1. Implement Custom Event Tracking: Develop a system to track custom events that are specific to professional services, such as form submissions, phone calls, or email inquiries. This allows for a more accurate measurement of conversion rates and provides valuable insights into the user journey.
  2. Utilize Multi-Step Conversion Funnels: Design conversion funnels that account for the multiple touchpoints and stages involved in the professional services sales process. This may include tracking interactions such as initial consultations, proposal requests, and contract signings.
  3. Leverage Advanced Analytics Tools: Employ advanced analytics tools that can handle complex data sets and provide detailed insights into user behavior. This enables the identification of trends, patterns, and areas for improvement, ultimately informing data-driven decisions to optimize the conversion process.

title: Participant Lists in Live Calls — 4 Rules to Clean Empty Rooms
description:
Keep room membership as a server-owned lease, not as a side effect of an open socket. For a live-shopping video call, four invariants are enough to guide the design: one logical participant can own only one current session generation; stale disconnects cannot remove a newer generation; a room disappears only after its last lease expires; and every participant snapshot carries a revision. This produces accurate lists through reconnects without promising that a transient transport is perfectly reliable.

Short answer: expose a snapshot-plus-revision read path, issue a new generation on every successful reconnect, renew membership with bounded leases, and delay empty-room deletion until the final lease is unquestionably expired. Typing indicators may be lossy. Read receipts and membership transitions need identity, ordering, and idempotency.

That distinction matters in commerce. A missed "typing" event is cosmetic; an agent who vanishes from a buyer's call roster, or a receipt attributed to an earlier session, changes what people believe happened. Treating all three signals alike makes the most important path no safer and makes the least important path needlessly expensive.

How should Node.js list participants and clean empty rooms?

WebRTC defines peer connections and the media negotiation surface, but the application still owns signaling and participant presence. A connected peer connection is therefore evidence about media transport, not the canonical room roster. Browsers suspend, networks change, tabs duplicate, and reconnect attempts can overlap. The roster needs its own model. Use stable application identities for people and opaque identifiers for connection attempts. A useful membership record contains room_id, participant_id, generation, lease_deadline, and a small amount of display data. Keep authorization outside that display data: being listed in a room must never grant permission to join it. This model does add periodic writes and a sweeper, so it is not suitable for a disposable demo whose entire state may vanish with one process. That is a deliberate trade-off: production recovery is worth the machinery; a local prototype may reasonably skip it.

The generation is the sharp edge. Suppose generation 7 loses its network path, then generation 8 authenticates and joins. The delayed close callback for generation 7 may arrive afterward. If cleanup means "delete this participant," the valid generation 8 membership disappears. Cleanup must mean "delete this participant only if the stored generation is still 7."

One stale callback is enough.

The room also owns a monotonically increasing revision. Increment it for visible membership changes, not for every heartbeat. A list response can then return a coherent snapshot with revision 42, while a subscription continues from changes after 42. If the consumer sees a revision gap, it discards local assumptions and fetches another snapshot.

Name the failure boundaries before choosing storage

The delivery guarantee is bounded by the state transition, not by the fan-out mechanism. Once a join or leave is committed, notifications may be duplicated, delayed, or missed during a disconnect. Consumers must be able to recover from the durable snapshot. Exactly-once delivery across a database, a process, and a browser is not the invariant here; idempotent application and a repair path are.

State or signal Required behavior Recovery rule Retention
Participant membership Durable within its lease; ordered by room revision Fetch a snapshot after a gap Until explicit leave or lease expiry
Read receipt Idempotent and monotonic per message and reader Re-send the highest acknowledged position Product and compliance policy
Typing indicator Best effort and short lived Let it expire; do not replay it Seconds, in memory
Empty-room marker Conditional on no live membership Recheck after a grace interval Until cleanup completes

This table prevents a common overcorrection: persisting every keystroke-like signal because membership needs durability. A typing indicator should carry an expiry time and disappear without a compensating event. Replaying "agent is typing" after a reconnect is worse than dropping it.

Read receipts sit on the other side of the line. Model them as progress, such as the highest message sequence a participant has read, so retries are naturally idempotent. Do not model them as a growing bag of socket events. Compliance also enters here: receipt retention, access, and deletion should follow the message policy rather than the lifetime of an in-memory room.

The critical path is a compare-and-delete state machine

The following Python models the storage contract behind an HTTP framework and a realtime transport. It deliberately leaves database syntax out: the important operations are conditional writes that a transaction, compare-and-swap primitive, or server-side script can enforce atomically.

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from time import monotonic
from uuid import uuid4


@dataclass
class Member:
    participant_id: str
    generation: str
    lease_deadline: float


@dataclass
class Room:
    revision: int = 0
    members: dict[str, Member] = field(default_factory=dict)
    empty_since: float | None = None


class PresenceStore:
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds: float = 30.0, empty_grace: float = 15.0):
        self.rooms: dict[str, Room] = {}
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds
        self.empty_grace = empty_grace

    def join(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
        now = monotonic()
        room = self.rooms.setdefault(room_id, Room())
        generation = uuid4().hex
        room.members[participant_id] = Member(
            participant_id=participant_id,
            generation=generation,
            lease_deadline=now + self.lease_seconds,
        )
        room.empty_since = None
        room.revision += 1
        return generation, room.revision

    def renew(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        member.lease_deadline = monotonic() + self.lease_seconds
        return True

    def leave(self, room_id: str, participant_id: str, generation: str) -> bool:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id)
        member = room and room.members.get(participant_id)
        if member is None or member.generation != generation:
            return False
        del room.members[participant_id]
        room.revision += 1
        if not room.members:
            room.empty_since = monotonic()
        return True

    def snapshot(self, room_id: str) -> dict:
        room = self.rooms.get(room_id, Room())
        return {
            "revision": room.revision,
            "participants": sorted(room.members),
        }

    def sweep(self) -> list[str]:
        now = monotonic()
        deleted = []
        for room_id, room in list(self.rooms.items()):
            expired = [
                participant_id
                for participant_id, member in room.members.items()
                if member.lease_deadline <= now
            ]
            for participant_id in expired:
                del room.members[participant_id]
                room.revision += 1
            if not room.members and room.empty_since is None:
                room.empty_since = now
            if (
                not room.members
                and room.empty_since is not None
                and now - room.empty_since >= self.empty_grace
            ):
                del self.rooms[room_id]
                deleted.append(room_id)
        return deleted

The sample is single-process so the contract stays visible. In production, join, renew, leave, revision allocation, and the final empty check must use storage operations with equivalent atomicity. A process-local dictionary is correct only when one process owns every event for a room and restart loss is acceptable.

An Express application can expose the same contract through authenticated join, renew, leave, and snapshot handlers, while its socket layer publishes revisioned changes. The exact framework callback is secondary. Authenticate the participant before accepting participant_id; derive room access from server-side policy; and never trust a client-supplied generation until it has been matched to that participant's current stored record.

Fan-out follows commit. Publish a compact event containing the room, revision, operation, and participant identity after the state change succeeds. Duplicate events are harmless when clients ignore revisions they have already applied. A gap is actionable: fetch the list again. If publication can fail independently after commit, use an outbox record in the same transaction as the membership mutation, then let a worker retry publication.

How should reconnect races be tested?

Start with reordered operations, because happy-path integration tests rarely expose presence errors. Join generation A, join generation B for the same participant, then deliver A's close callback. B must remain. Next, expire A immediately before its renewal is processed; the renewal must either win atomically or receive a rejection that forces a fresh join. An ambiguous half-renewed state is unacceptable.

Test two participants leaving on different workers. Only the worker observing the atomic transition to zero may schedule cleanup, and the cleanup job must recheck emptiness before deletion. Then join a new participant during the grace interval. The room and its new revision must survive. There are more mundane cases too: duplicated leave messages, a heartbeat received after explicit leave, two browser tabs sharing one user identity, and a consumer reconnecting with an old revision. Put those permutations in a deterministic state-machine test. Reserve browser tests for signaling and UI behavior; they are slower and worse at exploring reorderings. Operationally, graph lease expirations separately from explicit leaves. A rising expiration ratio often points to transport trouble, suspended clients, or overloaded event loops. Track snapshot repairs caused by revision gaps, cleanup lag, current members per room, and rejected stale generations. Avoid participant identifiers in high-cardinality metric labels. Structured logs can carry a pseudonymous identifier under an access and retention policy. During a rolling restart, old processes may emit late disconnect callbacks after new processes have accepted reconnects, which is precisely why generation checks belong in shared state. A sweeper should be safe to run concurrently, and its work should be partitioned or claimed so a large room set does not create a synchronized scan spike.

Measure the boundary.

Rejected option: delete on the last socket close

Deleting a room as soon as the last locally known socket closes is attractive because it is short, cheap, and easy to explain. It is also the wrong default for horizontally scaled video-call presence. The closing process may not know about a connection accepted elsewhere, and a reconnect can race the deletion.

The option remains valid for an ephemeral, single-process prototype where rooms contain no durable state, all connections are owned by that process, and restart loss is explicitly acceptable. State those boundaries in the decision record. Once recordings, receipts, moderation state, or multiple workers enter the design, socket lifetime and room lifetime have separated.

The practical rule is compact: a disconnect is a hint; an expired, generation-matched lease is evidence. Make snapshots authoritative, make fan-out repairable, and make deletion conditional. Those choices keep participant lists believable during the exact moment a buyer or support agent is already dealing with a shaky call.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Why I built an open source alternative to Terra for wearable data
description:
Every wearable speaks its own dialect. Apple Health sends one JSON line per HealthKit sample, with heart rate in count/min and oxygen saturation as a fraction. Withings sends a daily activity object keyed by date and intraday series keyed by Unix epoch. Oura, WHOOP and Fitbit each have their own idea of what a day, a device and a duplicate are.

So every health app I worked on ended up writing the same layer: a parser per provider, a table per provider, a cron job per provider. It works until the second provider, the first re-sent upload, the first mapper bug that needs a backfill, or the first person who asks you to delete everything you hold about them.

The obvious answer is a hosted API

There is a whole category of products that solve this for you. Terra is the best known: one API, one widget for your users to connect their devices, and data pushed to your webhook or database. It advertises more than 500 integrations, Garmin included, and states SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA and GDPR compliance. If you need Garmin today, or a long tail of devices under one contract, and you don't want to run a server, it is a very reasonable choice.

It did not fit what I was building, for four reasons.

Price per connected user. Terra's public pricing starts at $399 a month billed annually ($499 monthly) with 100,000 credits, and each source a user connects costs 200 credits a month. By my arithmetic that covers about 500 connections. A product with 2,000 users who each connect one source would pay around $2,000 a month at the listed starting prices, before any volume discount. That is fair for a funded product. It is a lot for a free tier, a research study or a side project.

The data passes through someone else. With a hosted API, your users' health data lands in the vendor's cloud before it reaches you. Terra's end-user privacy policy says it is usually kept there for two days and at most six months. That is a short window, but for some projects any third party in the path is one too many.

Raw payloads. I wanted every payload kept verbatim, on my side, forever. Mappers have bugs. When I fix one, I want to re-process a user's whole history from the original files, not from a normalized copy that already lost the detail.

Standards. I wanted FHIR R4 that passes the official HL7 validator and Open mHealth data points, so the data can go to a clinical system or an analysis tool without another conversion.

What I built instead

Open Health Sync is an open source, self-hosted health data aggregator. It is one Go binary plus Postgres with TimescaleDB, and it does the boring parts once:

  • 13 sources: Apple Health and Health Connect (uploaded by a phone app, or imported from the Health app export), plus Withings, Oura, WHOOP, Fitbit, Polar, Strava, Suunto, Ultrahuman, intervals.icu, Dexcom and OMRON over OAuth, with provider webhooks triggering pulls of just what changed.
  • Raw first: every payload is stored verbatim on disk or S3 before anything else happens, and re-sent uploads are de-duplicated by content hash.
  • One model, one unit per quantity: UCUM units, LOINC codes, and "today" means the local calendar day of the record's time zone, not UTC.
  • One answer per question: when a ring and a watch both record the same night, reads return one merged view, with priorities per user and metric, and the raw rows stay available.
  • Many ways out: a REST API (OpenAPI 3.1), FHIR R4 Observations, Open mHealth, CSV and Parquet exports, signed webhooks, and a read-only MCP server so an AI agent can read one person's data with a token that cannot write.
  • Erasable: DELETE /v1/users/{id} removes the rows and the raw files.

It idles at about 22 MB of memory and runs on a Raspberry Pi 5.

Try it in a few minutes

You need Docker with Compose, plus curl, jq and openssl:

git clone https://github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync.git && cd open-health-sync
cp .env.example .env
sed -i.bak "s|^OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=.*|OHS_ENCRYPTION_KEY=$(openssl rand -base64 32)|" .env
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml up -d --wait
docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml run --rm ohs doctor

No wearable at hand? This loads 90 days of synthetic data from six overlapping sources and prints an API key with calls to try:

docker compose --env-file .env -f deploy/docker-compose.yml exec ohs /ohs seed --demo

It prints the demo user's id and an API key once. Export them, then read one merged day, or the same heart rate data as FHIR:

export OHS_URL=http://localhost:8080 OHS_API_KEY=ohs_sk_... USER_ID=...   # values printed above
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/daily"
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OHS_API_KEY" \
  "$OHS_URL/v1/users/$USER_ID/fhir/Observation?code=http://loinc.org%7C8867-4&limit=5"

Your own Apple Health history loads from the export the Health app writes on your iPhone (Health app, your picture, Export All Health Data), with the ohs binary from the releases page and a user token (the README shows how to create one):

OHS_TOKEN=$TOKEN ohs import apple-health export.zip --url $OHS_URL

It reads the zip as a stream, so memory stays flat whatever the size of the export, and running it twice uploads nothing twice.

What you give up

Self-hosting is not free of trade-offs, and I would rather say them up front:

  • You register your own developer app with Oura, WHOOP, Withings and the others. A hosted API does that part for you. Each connector guide lists the steps.
  • 13 sources, not 500. Garmin is not available.
  • No certification. There are building blocks for a compliant setup (consent per source and data category, an append-only audit log, hard deletes, a per-user archive), but compliance depends on how and where you run it.
  • AGPL-3.0. Using it unmodified, or calling it from closed source apps over HTTP, is fine. If you run a modified version as a service, you share your changes.
  • Early days. It is v0.1.0, and the API may change in any 0.x release.

It is not the only open source option

Open Wearables solves the same problem and came first. It has the larger community, a web dashboard, Garmin, and an MIT license, which matters if AGPL is a problem for you. I benchmarked both on the same machine with the same Apple Health data: Open Health Sync stored the records 2 to 3 times faster end to end and used about 22 MB of memory idle against about 494 MB, while Open Wearables used 3.4 times less disk. Those are numbers for one user, one machine and synthetic data, and the scripts are in the repository for anyone to run again.

I wrote two comparison pages that try to be fair, including when the other option is the better pick:

  • Open Health Sync and Terra
  • Open Health Sync and Open Wearables

Feedback welcome

The code is at github.com/soma-intelligence/open-health-sync. I would love to hear which source you need next, what you think of the data model, and what you would build if your users' health data were one SQL query away. Issues, discussions and pull requests are all open.
