title: Solid Glass Adds an AI UI Theme to shadcn/ui Projects
description:
Solid Glass is a public GitHub project that packages a glass-inspired design system for AI applications as a stylesheet intended to work with shadcn/ui. For developers building chat and agent interfaces, its practical proposition is narrow but useful: the stylesheet targets the data-slot attributes and classes that existing shadcn/ui components already carry, so adoption is presented as a theme integration rather than a component rewrite. Source: Solid Glass repository

A theme layer, not an AI framework

The project describes its visual treatment as sitting between flat design and “liquid glass”: surfaces retain outlines, borders, highlights and shadows, while avoiding the highly transparent treatment that can interfere with text legibility. Its stated design goals are tactility, precision, physicality and materiality; for interfaces with streaming responses, agent tasks and pending human decisions, it argues that neutral surfaces and reserved use of colour and motion help keep the UI calm and readable. Source: Solid Glass repository

The core distribution is one CSS file. The repository says it defines colours, three glass thicknesses, a state and motion, while also defining shadcn/ui’s variable names. It supports light and dark modes, although the project describes dark mode as the intended material treatment. Source: Solid Glass repository

Installation begins from a shadcn/ui project using React 19, Tailwind CSS 4 and Base UI components. Developers add the deeplethe/solid-glass/solid-glass stylesheet through the shadcn CLI, import it after Tailwind and shadcn styles, and remove the :root and .dark colour variables created by shadcn initialization because Solid Glass defines variables with the same names. Source: Solid Glass repository

Components for agent-facing screens

Beyond the theme, the project supplies installable components including status-glyph, panel, tag, dot-loader, turn-status, composer, tool-steps, diff-view, ask-card, context-ring, task-notice and reasoning. The README positions these around an agent workflow: showing activity, accepting a prompt, rendering tool steps and diffs, asking for user input, and displaying context usage. Source: Solid Glass repository

The repository also includes complete screen-level “Blocks,” including an agent-workspace, plus a Create page that exposes controls for thickness, tint, chart colour, type, radius, rim and blur and produces corresponding CSS variable changes. Source: Solid Glass repository

The compatibility trade-off

Analysis: Solid Glass’s most consequential choice is to treat shadcn/ui as the compatibility surface rather than create another self-contained component ecosystem. That should reduce initial adoption cost for teams already on the shadcn stack, because the theme is designed around existing slots and classes. It also leaves an unresolved maintenance question: the approach depends on those structural conventions remaining stable enough for a stylesheet to keep selecting the intended parts. The repository notes that some displayed shadcn/ui components differ slightly from stock versions, while saying the stylesheet does not depend on those differences. Source: Solid Glass repository

This is therefore best read as a focused UI layer, not evidence of a broader agent runtime or application framework. Its value will depend less on the glass treatment itself than on whether its component conventions fit a team’s existing shadcn/ui codebase and the information density of its AI workflows. The repository is licensed under MIT and includes contribution, code-of-conduct and security-policy materials. Source: Solid Glass repository

title: Go Scheduled Payment Data Cleanup — Compare 4 Cron Scheduler Latency and Cost Tests
description:
Short answer: choose a cron scheduler for nightly payment reconciliation by testing admission latency, duplicate delivery, missed-run recovery, and execution isolation; the cheapest trigger is a poor bargain if it can silently widen the cleanup backlog.

For a customer-support system, the job is deceptively plain: reconcile yesterday's payment-provider records, repair local status drift, and make corrected state available before agents begin answering billing tickets. The scheduling decision should follow the error budget for that outcome. If agents need corrected data by 06:00 UTC, a trigger at 05:59 with a one-minute runtime has no capacity margin. A trigger at 02:00, feeding bounded workers that can replay partitions, converts a brittle deadline into an observable batch SLO.

Don't optimize the clock first.

How should cost govern a cron scheduler comparison for scheduled data cleanup?

I would run four tests against the whole path, not just the timer: trigger admission latency, duplicate invocation, an intentionally unavailable worker, and a cleanup partition that exceeds its normal runtime. This is a capacity-planning exercise — arrival rate, service rate, backlog age, and deadline are the useful variables. A scheduler's dashboard can show a green invocation while the payment cursor remains twelve hours behind.

The bounded production scenario is one nightly reconciliation with 24 hourly partitions. Each partition reads a stable provider time range, compares external payment IDs with local records, and writes an idempotent result. That number is an example of partition shape, not a benchmark: use enough partitions to replay a narrow failure domain, but not so many that scheduling and database overhead dominate useful work. I'm not sure there is a universal best partition duration; provider rate limits, record skew, and the local write path settle it, and a load test with production-shaped distributions is what resolves the uncertainty.

A useful acceptance sheet is short:

Test Evidence to retain Failure decision
Admission latency Intended time and observed start time Does the remaining window preserve the batch SLO?
Duplicate trigger Two runs with the same logical date Do idempotency keys prevent repeated mutation?
Worker unavailable Trigger accepted while workers are stopped Is work durably recoverable without guessing?
Long partition One partition crosses the next tick Does overlap stay bounded by a lease or concurrency rule?

These tests separate a trigger from a job system. A trigger decides when work becomes eligible. A job system owns durable state, acknowledgements, retry policy, concurrency, and backlog. Combining those responsibilities can be convenient for a small workload, but treating them as the same thing makes incident diagnosis muddy: an absent trigger, a rejected enqueue, and a slow consumer create the same visible symptom — stale support data — while requiring different repairs.

Govern the payment data window before touching the clock

Consider a production incident as a tabletop rather than a claimed war story. The 02:00 trigger fires, the payment provider answers with HTTP 429 for several partitions, and the next run begins before the first has drained. If the job means “delete or update everything older than midnight,” the second run can race the first, retry already-applied writes, or move a shared cursor past records that were never reconciled. The invariant revealed by this scenario is more valuable than any scheduler feature list: each unit of cleanup needs a stable identity, a bounded input interval, and a result that can be applied more than once without changing the final state.

The obvious first model is cron -> cleanup(). It is also where SLOs disappear. The safer model is cron -> create logical run -> enqueue partitions -> workers -> reconcile run; its extra durable state costs storage and operational attention, but it gives on-call engineers a ledger of what should have happened, what did happen, and what remains eligible for retry. This doesn't create exactly-once execution. It makes at-least-once execution tolerable through idempotent effects. RabbitMQ's acknowledgement documentation is useful here because it distinguishes consumer acknowledgements from publisher confirms: the broker accepting a message and a worker completing its effect are separate events.

Here is the preventative boundary in Go. The scheduler calls Start, while the repository enforces uniqueness for the logical date and the queue carries partition identities. Implementations can use a database uniqueness constraint and a durable queue; the interface keeps vendor choice outside the reconciliation rule.

package reconcile

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

type Partition struct {
    RunDate string
    Start   time.Time
    End     time.Time
}

type RunRepository interface {
    CreateOnce(ctx context.Context, runDate string) (created bool, err error)
}

type Queue interface {
    Enqueue(ctx context.Context, key string, p Partition) error
}

type Starter struct {
    Runs  RunRepository
    Queue Queue
}

func (s Starter) Start(ctx context.Context, runDate string, dayStart time.Time) error {
    created, err := s.Runs.CreateOnce(ctx, runDate)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("create reconciliation run: %w", err)
    }
    if !created {
        return nil // A repeated trigger refers to the existing logical run.
    }

    var enqueueErrs []error
    for hour := 0; hour < 24; hour++ {
        start := dayStart.Add(time.Duration(hour) * time.Hour)
        p := Partition{RunDate: runDate, Start: start, End: start.Add(time.Hour)}
        key := fmt.Sprintf("payment-reconcile/%s/%02d", runDate, hour)
        if err := s.Queue.Enqueue(ctx, key, p); err != nil {
            enqueueErrs = append(enqueueErrs, fmt.Errorf("enqueue %s: %w", key, err))
        }
    }
    return errors.Join(enqueueErrs...)
}

One detail matters: after CreateOnce succeeds, failed partition enqueues must remain discoverable in the run ledger so a reconciler can enqueue the missing work. Returning an error is necessary for observability, but it isn't the recovery mechanism. A periodic sweeper can compare expected partition identities with accepted ones and fill gaps; because identities are stable, that repair is safe to repeat.

Slow down here.

Test each trigger boundary with the same harness

GitHub Actions scheduled workflows are attractive when cleanup already lives beside repository automation. Its documentation says scheduled workflows run from the latest commit on the default branch, can be delayed during high load, and may be dropped under sufficiently high load; the shortest interval is five minutes. Those properties can fit a non-urgent maintenance task, but they make the workflow history an inadequate system of record for a deadline-bound reconciliation unless the job also records durable run intent elsewhere. Repository access and workflow permissions also expand the blast radius beyond “wake a worker.”

Cloudflare Workers Cron Triggers invoke a Worker's scheduled handler on UTC time. Cloudflare documents that trigger changes can take several minutes, up to 15 minutes, to propagate. This model keeps the trigger close to lightweight edge code, while the execution limits and the need for durable reconciliation state still determine whether the work belongs in one invocation or should be handed to another worker path. It is a boundary choice, not a guarantee that a large batch finishes because the clock fired.

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler exposes one-time and recurring schedules, flexible time windows, retry policy, and dead-letter queue configuration. Those controls make delivery policy explicit, with the trade-off of cloud IAM, target configuration, and another provider-specific control plane. For teams already operating that environment, those dependencies may be normal; for a portable or self-hosted stack, they are lock-in and on-call surface that must earn their place.

BullMQ represents a different boundary. It is a Redis-backed Node.js queue with job scheduling and worker semantics, so choosing it means owning or buying the Redis layer and operating consumers rather than selecting a remote trigger alone. RabbitMQ can supply durable messaging and acknowledgement semantics, but cron eligibility remains a separate concern. These aren't rankings. They are different allocations of responsibility between source control automation, edge execution, a cloud scheduler, and an application-owned queue.

Option shape Best evidence from the four tests Operational cost to count
Repository-scheduled workflow Workflow start history plus external run ledger Repository permissions, variable start time, runner use
Edge cron handler Trigger event plus durable handoff record Execution limits, deployment propagation, state service
Cloud scheduler targeting a worker Delivery attempts, retry policy, dead-letter records IAM, target policy, provider control plane
Application queue with repeatable jobs Queue state, acknowledgements, backlog age Data-store operations, consumers, upgrades, paging

Price should be measured from the current official calculators against expected invocations, execution duration, storage, logs, egress, and on-call ownership; a trigger's sticker price alone excludes most of the system. Published rates and free allowances change, so hard-coding a winner into an architecture review ages badly. The latency side is equally contextual: nightly work rarely needs millisecond admission, but it does need enough recovery time before the support-data deadline.

A Go implementation for idempotent partition admission

The worker needs a lease or equivalent concurrency guard, an idempotency key at the mutation boundary, retry classification, and a checkpoint that advances only after the partition's effects are durable. A 429 response is retryable under the provider's policy; malformed input or an impossible state transition usually needs quarantine and review. Don't turn every error into an immediate retry. Correlated retries can consume the remaining batch window faster than ordinary processing.

For observability, retain logical run date, partition identity, attempt count, intended trigger time, accepted time, worker start time, completion time, and a low-cardinality outcome. From those fields, derive admission delay, queue delay, processing duration, oldest incomplete partition age, success ratio, and projected finish time. Alert on user impact or a threatened deadline rather than on one failed attempt; the retry can be healthy while the backlog trend is not. Logs help explain a partition, metrics show the fleet, and the run ledger answers the awkward audit question: which payment intervals were actually reconciled?

Capacity planning closes the loop. Let W be the available window in seconds, R the sustained records processed per second after rate limiting, and N the expected record count. Require N/R to sit comfortably below W, then test the margin with skew and retries. The exact headroom is an SLO policy decision, not a universal constant. If a provider permits only modest concurrency, earlier scheduling or incremental reconciliation can buy more safety than a larger worker fleet.

Deployment deserves the same skepticism. Pin the cleanup binary or image version, make schema changes backward compatible with in-flight workers, test duplicate and out-of-order partitions, and rehearse replay from the durable ledger. A scheduler configuration change should pass review and emit an auditable event. For a nightly job, a staging clock that runs every few minutes can validate orchestration, but test data must preserve the production invariants: stable external IDs, overlapping updates, pagination, and rate-limit responses.

No mystery metrics.

When should the deployment stay small?

Stick with a simple repository or host cron when the cleanup is disposable, quick, idempotent as a whole, easy to rerun, and has no hard completion deadline. A small cache purge whose next run safely catches up does not automatically justify a queue, run ledger, leases, and another pager. The catch is that “small” must be supported by observed duration and backlog, not by the current row count.

A managed scheduler is not suitable when provider-specific IAM and targets violate portability requirements, while a self-hosted queue is a poor fit when the team cannot own its data store, upgrades, and consumer capacity. An edge handler is the wrong execution home for work that exceeds its documented resource model, though it may still be a clean trigger. Repository automation should remain repository automation when production credentials or unpredictable start delay would breach the service boundary.

The decision rule is deliberately unbranded: define the reconciliation deadline, make run intent durable, test the four failure conditions, and choose the least operational machinery that still preserves the invariant under replay. Cost matters. So do the pages created by the architecture.

title: New setup page after domain checkout
description:
Buying a domain on Vercel now takes you to a setup page that tracks registration live, with direct paths to deploy a new project, connect an existing one, proxy or redirect a site you already run, or set up email.

Registration can take a few minutes. Each setup action unlocks as soon as the domain is ready. If registration fails, the page shows what went wrong and the status of your refund.

Deploy a new project or connect an existing one

Deploy something opens project creation with the domain preselected. Connect a Git repository, prompt with v0, or start from a template, and the domain is attached when the project deploys.

Connect an existing project attaches the domain to a project you pick from your team.

Proxy or redirect a site you already run

Enter an origin to proxy traffic to, and requests to the domain route through Vercel's CDN. Vercel will cache applicable requests at the edge, and Vercel Firewall's automated DDoS protections will automatically run. Enter a URL to redirect, and visitors are forwarded there. In both cases, Vercel creates a project to handle the routing and configures it for you.

Set up email with DNS presets

Choose your email provider and Vercel adds the DNS records it needs. Presets are available for Google Workspace, Outlook, iCloud, Proton Mail, Zoho, Mailgun, and ImprovMX. There's also a preset for using the domain as your Bluesky handle.

If you'd rather configure records yourself, Manage DNS records opens the domain's DNS records page. Search for a domain at vercel.com/domains to get started.

title: How to Charge for Your Vibe-Coded App: One-Time vs Subscription (and How to Set It Up)
description:
You built an app with Claude Code, Cursor or Codex. People are using it, a few have even said they'd pay for it. So now you're stuck on two questions: how should I charge, and how do I actually set that up without breaking anything?

I'm Deepak, a solo developer in Hyderabad, and I've wired payments into a lot of apps built with AI agents. This guide walks through the choice between charging once and charging every month, which payment company to pick, and the exact steps to get money flowing. No code required to follow along.

If you want the bigger picture on what goes wrong after someone pays, read my first post: How to add payments to an app you built with AI. This one is about the decision that comes before that.

The three ways to charge

Almost every small app uses one of these, or a mix:

  • One-time payment. The customer pays once and keeps access. Think of a template, a tool, a lifetime deal, or a downloadable pack.
  • Subscription. The customer pays every month or every year, and access stops if they stop paying.
  • Credits (pay as you go). The customer buys a bundle of uses, like 100 image generations, and buys more when they run out.

There's no "correct" answer. The right one depends on one simple question.

The one question that decides it

Does your app cost you money every time someone uses it?

If yes, you probably want a subscription or credits. If no, a one-time payment is often simpler and easier to sell.

Here's why. Many vibe-coded apps call an AI model, send emails, store files or run on a server that charges by use. Those costs keep coming as long as the customer keeps using the app. If you charge once, a heavy user can end up costing you more than they paid. A monthly price, or credits that run out, keeps what you earn in line with what you spend.

If your app is mostly a fixed thing, like a calculator, a template, a desktop tool or a set of files, your costs don't grow much with each user. Charging once is honest and easy for buyers to say yes to.

One-time payment: when it fits

Good for: tools that don't cost you much to run, templates and starter kits, downloadable products, and "lifetime access" launch offers.

Why people like it: buyers don't have to worry about another monthly bill. It's easier to explain, and there's nothing to cancel.

The catch: you get paid once. To keep earning, you need a steady flow of new buyers, or paid upgrades later. And be careful with "lifetime" deals on apps that call AI models, because those costs don't stop.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product in your payment company's dashboard with a single price.
  2. A "Buy" button that sends people to the payment company's checkout page.
  3. Your app listening for the payment message (developers call this a webhook: an automatic note from the payment company saying "this person paid") and marking that person as a buyer.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this person a buyer?" before letting them in.

That's it. No renewals, no cancellations, just refunds to handle.

Subscription: when it fits

Good for: apps people use regularly, apps with ongoing costs (AI, hosting, data), and apps you keep improving.

Why makers like it: income that repeats every month, which makes it easier to plan and to keep paying for servers.

The catch: more moving parts. People cancel, cards expire, payments fail, and some customers switch between plans. Your app has to react correctly to every one of those, not just the first payment. And buyers think harder before signing up for something that bills them forever.

What you need to set up:

  1. A product with a monthly price, and optionally a yearly price (often offered at a discount).
  2. A "Subscribe" button that goes to checkout.
  3. Your app listening for payment messages, not just "paid" but also "renewed", "cancelled", "payment failed" and "refunded", and updating the person's access each time.
  4. Paid pages that check "is this subscription active right now?"
  5. A "Manage billing" page where customers can change their card or cancel by themselves. Both Polar and Stripe offer a ready-made one, so you don't build it from scratch.

Step 3 is where most AI-written setups go wrong. The agent handles the first payment and forgets the rest, so cancelled users keep access forever. My first post has a checklist to catch that.

Credits: the middle ground

If your costs depend heavily on how much someone uses the app, credits can be fairer than either option. Customers buy a pack, each use takes some away, and they top up when they run low. Light users pay little, heavy users pay more, and you never lose money on one person.

The trade-off: your app has to keep an accurate balance for every user and never let it go below zero, even if someone clicks twice quickly. It's very doable, but test it carefully.

Not sure? Start simple

If you can't decide, here's a reasonable default:

  • Low running costs: start with a one-time price. You can add a subscription tier later.
  • Real running costs (like AI calls): start with one monthly plan. Just one. Add a yearly option or a second tier when people ask for it.

Whatever you pick, you can change it. Your first price is a guess, and that's fine. Real customers will tell you more than any pricing article.

Polar vs Stripe for indie devs

Once you know how you'll charge, you need a payment company. For most solo makers the choice is Polar or Stripe. Both handle one-time payments and subscriptions well.

Polar is a merchant of record. In plain words, Polar is the seller on paper: it collects and pays sales tax and VAT in the countries your customers buy from, then pays you. If you're selling worldwide on your own, that saves a lot of paperwork. The trade-off is a higher fee per sale than Stripe's basic rate, so check their current pricing page.

Stripe handles the payment, but you're the seller, so tax is your job. Stripe has a tax add-on that works out the right amount to charge, but registering and filing is still on you. In return you get more control and a huge set of features.

My rule of thumb: solo, selling digital products or subscriptions to many countries, and don't want to think about tax? Start with Polar. Already have a Stripe account or a business set up to handle tax? Use Stripe. Either way, first check that the one you pick can pay out to your country. And if tax worries you, a short chat with an accountant is money well spent.

How to set it up, step by step

This works whether your app is in Next.js (the most common setup for vibe-coded web apps) or something else. You'll ask your AI agent to do most of it, but you stay in charge of checking it.

  1. Create an account with Polar or Stripe and stay in test mode (a practice mode where no real money moves).
  2. Create your product and price in the dashboard: one-time, monthly, or both.
  3. Ask your agent to add checkout. Be specific: "Add a Subscribe button that sends logged-in users to Polar checkout for my Pro monthly product."
  4. Ask it to handle payment messages, and list them all: paid, renewed, cancelled, payment failed, refunded. Ask it to verify each message is genuine using the secret from the dashboard.
  5. Ask it to lock paid pages so they check access in your database, not just whether someone saw the thank-you page.
  6. Add the billing page so customers can cancel or update their card themselves.
  7. Test everything with a test card: buy, log out and in, cancel, refund, and try the billing page as a free user.
  8. Switch to live mode, copy over the live keys, make one real purchase yourself, then refund it.

Step 7 is the one people skip, and it's the one that saves you from angry emails.

The one-prompt way: ShipToPaid

I got tired of writing those prompts by hand and fixing the same mistakes, so I turned the tested steps into written instructions, called skills, that Claude Code, Cursor and Codex can follow. That's ShipToPaid.

Instead of steps 3 to 6 above, you type /add-paywall in your agent, say whether you want one-time or subscription, and it follows a checklist that already covers the traps: checking that payment messages are real, handling cancellations and failed payments, and locking paid pages properly. A launch audit then walks you through the testing.

Want to try it first? The free lite pack on GitHub includes Polar checkout, Polar payment messages and a short launch check. The full pack adds Stripe, subscriptions that control access, a customer billing page, credits, license keys and a working Next.js starter app. Every skill is a plain file you can read and change.

You don't need either to use this guide. Pick how you'll charge, pick a payment company, test the whole flow in test mode, and go get your first paying customer.

This post first appeared on the ShipToPaid blog.

title: Introducing Agent Plugins
description:
Today, Agent Plugins 1.0.0 is publicly available. Agent Plugins is an open, vendor-neutral standard for plugins that extend AI agents.

Agent Skills provide reusable instructions and resources for AI agents. MCP servers connect agents to tools and services. Both can be reused across clients, but clients often package and discover them differently.

Agent Plugins gives compatible clients a common format: a directory with a plugin.json manifest and fixed locations for its components. The format is intentionally small and easy to implement, and it leaves installation, distribution, policy, user experience, and client-specific capabilities to each client.

One package for the portable parts

Extension authors often adapt the same component to several client formats. Even though the underlying Skill or MCP server is identical, clients often expect different top-level metadata, discovery paths, or MCP configuration.

Agent Plugins gives those shared components one predictable, structured home:

A minimal JSON manifest (plugin.json) identifies the specification version and names the plugin:

Those two fields are the minimum requirement for the manifest, and the rest of the contract is represented in the file structure of the directory itself. A reusable component should not need to be repackaged for every client, so the format specifies only what a client needs to discover and load what is inside.

Every compatible client checks for plugin.json at the plugin root. Clients that support Skills discover them under skills/. Clients that support MCP servers read their configuration from mcp.json. A client can support either component type or both. After the client validates the manifest, components are validated independently, so one invalid component does not disable unrelated ones.

For plugin authors, that means fewer client-specific conventions for the same component. For client implementers, the specification defines a small, deterministic contract for discovery, validation, and loading.

Small on purpose

Agent Plugins defines the portable contract for a plugin and leaves the behavior of the client up to each client.

Version 1 focuses that contract on two component types: Agent Skills and MCP servers. Both already have specifications and meaningful adoption of their own, and Agent Plugins does not attempt to redefine them. Agent Plugins provides a shared definition of how clients find the components together in a distributable plugin.

Other components, such as commands, hooks, and agents, remain with clients. The Technical Steering Committee may consider additional component types in future versions as semantics converge and a demonstrated portability need emerges.

Keeping the boundary small makes the format easier to implement and gives the ecosystem room to converge before adding more portable surface area.

Clients retain flexibility

Clients need freedom to innovate while a shared format evolves, so Agent Plugins includes a namespaced extension mechanism for client-specific data and files.

Extensions remain outside the portable contract. Each client defines its own namespace, and other clients ignore it. This prevents client-specific behavior from leaking into the common format or blocking adoption of the shared components. A client-specific capability can remain client-specific until there is reason and consensus to standardize it.

An open, multi-vendor project

Vercel initiated the proposal, which representatives from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Anysphere, GitHub, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel refined collaboratively into Agent Plugins 1.0.0.

The initial Technical Steering Committee includes Core Maintainers from AWS, Cursor, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Vercel.

The project is openly licensed, and its maintainers, contribution process, and technical decisions are public. No single company's product roadmap sets the format's direction.

Build with Agent Plugins 1.0.0

The specification, its JSON Schemas, and guides for plugin authors and client implementers are available at agent-plugins.org. Governance and the contribution process live in the Agent Plugins specification repository on GitHub.

If you author agent extensions, you can use the specification to package Skills and MCP servers behind one portable manifest. If you build an agent client, the specification's conformance checklist defines the minimum requirements for discovering and loading Agent Plugins.

At launch, Agent Plugins are supported across:

  • ChatGPT and Codex

  • Cursor

  • GitHub Copilot

  • Kiro

  • VS Code

Plugin authors can package components once, and their plugin will automatically carry between supporting clients.

Agent Plugins is a contract between the authors who build extensions for agents and the clients that load them. That contract is now defined and open for both sides to shape.

title: pg_utl_smtp v2.0 released
description:
Antananarivo, Madagascar - October 06, 2026

PostgreSQL UTL_SMTP compatibility extension

pg_utl_smtp is a PostgreSQL extension to create, manage and use Oracle-style UTL_SMTP package. The use and behavior is just like with the UTL_SMTP Oracle package. This work is released from the HexaRocket project.

This extension allows email notifications to be sent from triggers or stored procedures. By integrating the extension directly into the database, you can trigger data-driven actions without waiting for application intervention. Examples include security alerts or notifications when certain minimum thresholds are reached.

pg_utl_smtp v2.0.0 has been released, this new major version adds an asynchronous mode with setting pg_utl_smtp.asynchronous enabled. The Oracle version doesn't support asynchronous mode but this feature can be useful if you want to port the MSSQL sp_send_dbmail() procedure using pg_utl_smtp.

Other changes in this release:

  • Raise an error when the SMTP server returns an error to HELO/EHLO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, end of DATA or QUIT.
  • Fix duplicate EHLO sent at connection
  • Implement SSL/TLS connections (secure_connection_before_smtp).
  • QUIT releases the connection, a second QUIT raises an error.
  • When the connection can not be established the WARNING gives the reason.
  • Add regression tests by GitHub Actions.

To upgrade an installed version 2.0.0 execute:

  ALTER EXTENSION pg_utl_smtp UPDATE;

This extension uses plperl stored procedures based on the Net::SMTP Perl module to provide the procedures of the UTL_SMTP package.

Links & Credits

pg_utl_smtp is an open project under the PostgreSQL license created by Gilles Darold at HexaCluster Corp. as part of the HexaRocket migration solution. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp/issues

About pg_utl_smtp

The pg_utl_smtp extension is an original work of HexaCluster Corp., HexaCluster is specialized in migration to PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL support. If you need more information please contact us

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/pg_utl_smtp#readme

title: React: mide la UX de un inbox de prueba
description:
Cuando un formulario depende de un correo de verificación, solemos medir si el mensaje llegó. Eso es importante, pero no alcanza. La persona también necesita saber si el inbox está cargando, si ya se revisó, si el código expiró o si debe intentar otra vez. Un inbox de prueba puede recibir el mensaje correcto y aun así ofrecer una experiencia confusa.

En proyectos de frontend me funciona tratar esa pantalla como una parte del producto, no como una ventana tecnica que solo sirve para QA. Si la interfaz tiene estados explícitos, foco estable y una lectura clara en móvil, es mas sencillo detectar los problemas del flujo completo. Este enfoque sirve tanto para un correo desechable usado durante una demo como para una bandeja aislada de pruebas automatizadas.

La UX del inbox también se puede medir

Antes de escribir componentes, separo tres preguntas:

  1. ¿La persona sabe qué está esperando?
  2. ¿Puede distinguir un mensaje nuevo de uno viejo?
  3. ¿Tiene una acción segura cuando el correo no aparece?

Un layout con una animación bonita no responde por sí solo a ninguna de ellas. En cambio, un encabezado que dice “Buscando el correo de verificación”, una marca de tiempo y un botón “Comprobar de nuevo” crean un modelo mental bastante mas útil.

También conviene conectar la interfaz con el flujo que la rodea. Por ejemplo, una lista de direcciones de prueba puede seguir las mismas reglas de aislamiento que unas seed lists para onboarding. Cuando el inbox es parte de una prueba de registro, esa relación evita que el equipo culpe al frontend por un mensaje enviado a otra dirección.

Un modelo de estados pequeño en React

No usaría un booleano llamado loading para representar toda la pantalla. Como mínimo, el inbox necesita distinguir entre cargar, vacío, listo, error y expirado. Un tipo pequeño hace visibles esas decisiones:

type InboxState =
  | { kind: "loading" }
  | { kind: "empty"; checkedAt: number }
  | { kind: "ready"; subject: string; receivedAt: number }
  | { kind: "expired" }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

function InboxStatus({ state }: { state: InboxState }) {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "loading":
      return <p role="status">Buscando el correo...</p>;
    case "empty":
      return <p role="status">Todavía no hay mensajes. Puedes comprobar de nuevo.</p>;
    case "ready":
      return <p role="status">Nuevo mensaje recibido: {state.subject}</p>;
    case "expired":
      return <p role="alert">Esta dirección ya no está disponible. Crea otra para continuar.</p>;
    case "error":
      return <p role="alert">No pudimos revisar el inbox: {state.message}</p>;
  }
}

La ventaja no es solo de tipado. El componente obliga a producto y QA a decidir qué se muestra en cada momento. Un mensaje vacío no debería parecer un fallo de red, y una dirección expirada no debería ofrecer un botón que seguirá haciendo polling para siempre. Si el sistema usa un servicio tipo tempail o tempail mail en una prueba manual, esa diferencia de estado ayuda a no confundir una bandeja vacía con una dirección que ya caducó.

Para mantener el foco, el cambio de estado debería actualizar una región de texto, no desmontar todo el formulario. El botón de volver a comprobar puede conservar su posición y su nombre. Eso hace el flujo mas predecible con teclado y tambien simplifica los tests de interacción.

CSS para que esperar no se sienta lento

El rendimiento percibido nace de detalles pequeños. Reservo un espacio para el mensaje y para la lista, incluso cuando todavía no hay datos. Así el contenido recibido no empuja el botón hacia abajo cuando llega.

.inbox-panel {
  min-height: 12rem;
  contain: layout paint;
}

.inbox-status {
  min-block-size: 3rem;
  display: grid;
  align-items: center;
}

.inbox-message {
  content-visibility: auto;
  contain-intrinsic-size: 0 5rem;
}

No aplicaría content-visibility a un control que debe estar disponible de inmediato, pero puede ser practico en una lista larga de mensajes. Para una bandeja pequeña, lo mas importante es evitar saltos de layout y no mostrar un spinner que ocupa toda la pantalla por una consulta de pocos cientos de milisegundos.

Accesibilidad: anunciar lo necesario

role="status" es útil para cambios informativos como “mensaje recibido”. Reservaría role="alert" para errores que necesitan atención inmediata. Si todo se anuncia como alerta, la experiencia se vuelve ruidosa, sobre todo cuando el polling ocurre cada pocos segundos.

El texto visual no debe depender solo del color. Un estado expirado puede usar un icono, pero también necesita una frase y una acción. El foco visible del botón debe tener contraste suficiente y no desaparecer al usar un reset de estilos. En móvil, además, el área táctil y el orden de lectura importan mas que una tarjeta compacta.

Para los mensajes de incidentes o fallos intermitentes, puede ser útil enlazar la interfaz con runbooks cortos para incidentes de email. El usuario final no necesita ver el runbook, claro, pero el equipo que mantiene la pantalla sí necesita una ruta de diagnóstico coherente.

Qué medir en una prueba real

No hace falta instrumentar veinte eventos. Empezaría con cuatro:

  • tiempo desde “enviado” hasta “recibido”;
  • cantidad de comprobaciones antes de encontrar el mensaje;
  • porcentaje de sesiones que terminan en expiración o error;
  • activaciones de “comprobar de nuevo” después de que el mensaje ya llegó.

El último dato es curioso: si se activa mucho, quizá el mensaje recibido no destaca, la actualización no se anuncia o el usuario no confía en el estado mostrado. Una métrica de backend puede decir que todo está bien mientras la interfaz comunica lo contrario.

Checklist antes de publicar

  • Cada estado tiene texto visible y una acción razonable.
  • El inbox conserva la posición del botón al recibir datos.
  • El foco no salta durante el polling.
  • Los cambios informativos usan una región status y no una alerta global.
  • La lista funciona sin depender del color.
  • Hay una forma de distinguir mensaje nuevo, viejo y expirado.
  • Los errores dejan una siguiente acción clara.

Q&A

¿Necesito un inbox complejo para una prueba de signup?

No. Un panel con estado, asunto, hora de recepción y una acción de reintento suele ser suficiente. La complejidad debe aparecer solo cuando una necesidad concreta la justifique.

¿Conviene consultar cada segundo?

Generalmente no. Un intervalo moderado con un límite de tiempo y una acción manual suele ser mas amable con el navegador y con el servicio de correo. Cuando el mensaje llegue, detén el polling y registra el resultado.

¿Qué pasa si el correo de prueba expira?

Muéstralo como un estado propio, explica la consecuencia y permite crear una nueva dirección. Ocultar la expiración detrás de un “sin mensajes” deja a la persona adivinando por que la prueba no avanza.

title: October 15, 2026
description:
Apigee Edge for Private Cloud

Announcement

Released Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Designated Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.00 a long-term support (LTS) release: 18 months of full support ending April 2028, then 18 months of maintenance ending October 2029. After October 2029, 4.54.00.00 receives no software updates, security mitigations, or technical support.

Installing a later 4.54 minor release or patch does not change those dates. To extend the support lifecycle, upgrade to the next LTS release.

For the support lifecycle phases, release cadences, and version numbering, see Apigee Edge for Private Cloud release and lifecycle policy.

Announcement

This release replaces Java 8 with Java 17 and Java 21, removes the Classic UI and the apigee-sso component, and updates the bundled Cassandra, Postgres, OpenLDAP, ZooKeeper, Qpid Broker-J, Nginx, and Consul versions. These changes are not backward-compatible.

For the 4.54.00 versions and the 4.53.01 versions they replace, see Supported software and supported versions.

Before upgrading, read Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00, then Update Apigee Edge 4.53.00 or 4.53.01 to 4.54.00 or New installation overview. For known issues, see Known issues with Edge for Private Cloud.

Announcement

Replaced the Classic UI (edge-ui) with the New Edge UI (edge-management-ui).

The New Edge UI is the only management UI in 4.54.00 and is installed by default. Deployments running the Classic UI must transition to it before upgrading. Custom Classic UI properties do not carry over automatically. The default port also changes from 9000 to 3001, configurable with conf_uebe_port, so firewall rules and load balancer target ports that point at 9000 fail until they are updated.

For the migration steps and the supported feature list, see Migrate to the New Edge UI and What features are supported?.

Breaking

In deployments with Apigee SSO enabled, an integrated OIDC identity broker in apigee-openldap replaces the standalone apigee-sso component and Apache Tomcat 9.0.x. Before upgrading, take a complete and validated LDAP backup; existing apigee-sso configurations do not migrate automatically. Deployments not using Apigee SSO require no action.

For migration prerequisites, validation checks, and rollback constraints, see Option 2: Upgrade UI (with Apigee SSO).

Breaking

4.54.00 runs Java in mixed mode: Java 17 for Cassandra and ZooKeeper, Java 21 for the Management Server, Message Processor, Router, and Qpid Broker-J. Both Oracle JDK and OpenJDK are supported at those versions.

Oracle JDK 8 and OpenJDK 8 are no longer supported.

API proxies with custom JavaCallout policies or custom resource JARs can break on Java 21. For details, see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Upgraded Nginx on the Edge Router to 1.30.0.

If you are upgrading from Nginx 1.20.x, see Nginx 1.30 changes in Apigee Edge 4.54.00 for the full list of changes.

Change

Changed the TLS defaults on Message Processors to the Java 21 cryptographic baseline.

Message Processors run on Java 21, which enables TLS 1.3 by default (JEP 332) and prefers it for outbound backend connections, falling back to TLS 1.2. No configuration change is required if your target servers and load balancers negotiate TLS 1.3, or negotiate TLS 1.2 with forward-secret (ECDHE) cipher suites.

Java 21 also disables the non-forward-secret static RSA key-exchange suites (TLS_RSA_*). If you have overridden conf_http_HTTPTransport.ssl.cipher.suites.whitelist or conf_message-processor-communication_local.http.ssl.ciphers with static RSA suites only, backend calls fail with no cipher suites in common and the Router cannot complete a TLS handshake with the Message Processor. Replace the TLS_RSA_* entries with modern cipher suites and restart the Message Processor.

For the remediation path, see Legacy backend requirements and remediation.

Feature

Added Basic authentication to the New Edge UI, which lets you sign in without configuring an identity provider.

The New Edge UI supports Basic authentication without additional configuration. You can also configure Apigee SSO, or an external identity provider such as SAML or OIDC. This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Feature

Added automated pre-flight validation checks to apigee-setup and apigee-service, which surface environment configuration problems before a component is installed.

This feature is generally available in 4.54.00.

Security

Fixed multiple security vulnerabilities in Apigee Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

These fixes ship as part of the component upgrades in this release; see Changes in Edge for Private Cloud 4.54.00.

Change

Changed the default garbage collector on Message Processors to the Garbage-First garbage collector.

Message Processors set useG1GC=true and useStringDeduplication=true by default in 4.54.00. In 4.53.01 neither was set by default. To configure garbage collection, see Configure the garbage collector for Message Processors.

Apigee Edge for Public Cloud

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we began releasing Single Sign-On (SSO) updates for Apigee Edge for Public Cloud.

Fixed

Bug ID Component Description
560310696 SSO Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee Integrated Portal

Announcement

On October 15, 2026, we released a new version of the Apigee integrated portal.

Fixed

Bug ID Description
560310696 Fixed an issue where the Portal SSO endpoint inadvertently accepted deprecated TLS 1.1 connections. The endpoint now strictly enforces TLS 1.2+.

Apigee X

Fixed

Bug ID Description
466116259 Updated the startup script for the managed instance group (MIG) that routes external traffic to Apigee. net.ipv4.ip_forward is now written to /etc/sysctl.d/, so an instance no longer stops forwarding traffic when a reboot or an OS update resets it. The script does not change unrelated iptables NAT rules. Instances pick up the change the next time they are restarted or recreated.

BigQuery

Feature

You can copy tables across regions. This feature is now generally available (GA).

Feature

You can now use column aliases in GoogleSQL. This feature lets you define an alias for an expression in the SELECT clause of a SQL query and immediately reference that alias within the same SELECT list or in the WHERE clause of the same query block.

Column aliases also streamline the migration of workloads from other data warehouses such as Snowflake and Teradata, by supporting their syntax.

This feature is generally available, and is opt-in only. To use column aliases, you must first enable the feature.

Feature

You can export a conversational analytics agent's answer, including text, visualizations, tables, and citations, to a PDF or CSV file. This feature is generally available (GA).

Cloud Vision

Deprecated

Face detection model update

The emotion label response in the Cloud Vision API is deprecated. Going forward, the Cloud Vision API face detection (FACE_DETECTION feature) will return UNKNOWN for all emotion-related labels.

Compute Engine

Feature

Preview: You can create regional disks, including Hyperdisk Balanced High Availability volumes, by cloning a zonal boot disk.

For more information, see Duplicate a disk with clones.

Change

If you try to create an on-demand reservation or increase the number of reserved Compute Engine instances in a reservation when the zone has reached its reservation capacity limit for your requested machine family, then the request fails with a RESERVATION_CAPACITY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error. For more information, see Reservation capacity limit exceeded.

Feature

Generally available: The storage-optimized Z4M machine series is generally available for Compute Engine. Powered by fifth generation Intel Emerald Rapids Xeon Scalable processors and Titanium offload processors, Z4M instances are purpose-built for workloads that require larger storage capacity, such as:

  • Parallel file systems to support AI/ML workloads
  • I/O intensive workloads such as SQL, NoSQL, and vector databases
  • AI/ML training and inference workloads such as checkpointing and distributed Key-Value (KV) cache

The Z4M machine series delivers up to 1,536 GB of memory and 168,000 GiB of local Titanium SSD capacity. Z4M also supports up to 400 Gbps of network bandwidth using two physical NICs. Z4M instances use Titanium and Cloud RDMA to help enable higher levels of networking performance, isolation, and security.

For more information, see Storage-optimized machine family.

Dataflow

Feature

Dataflow Auto VM Selection now supports 4th generation Compute Engine machine series. When Auto VM Selection is enabled, the service prioritizes these newer generation VMs for improved performance. If 4th generation VMs are unavailable at startup, the service automatically falls back to widely available 2nd generation machine families to ensure that your jobs can start without unnecessary delays.

For more information, see Auto VM Selection.

Gemini Enterprise

Feature

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic models are available in the Gemini Enterprise app

Administrators can make Anthropic models—Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5—available to users in the Gemini Enterprise app. After an administrator turns on a model in the Enable third-party models section of the Feature Management tab, users can select the model in the model selector. Claude models are available in the global location and the us and eu multi-regions, and are charged on a pay-as-you-go basis.

This feature is generally available. For more information, see Enable third-party models.

Looker

Feature

The Looker 26.18 features have begun to be enabled for Looker (Google Cloud core) instances.

NetApp Volumes

Announcement

Google Cloud NetApp Volumes now supports the Flex Unified service level, including custom performance, in the following region:

  • europe-west8 (Milan)

For more information about available regions, see Supported regions.

Security Command Center

Feature

To increase the precision of attack path analysis and provide attack exposure scores that help you prioritize confirmed internet exposures, Risk Engine attack path simulations support the EXTERNALLY_EXPOSED_VM_INSTANCE External Exposure finding category (Preview). This finding category identifies Compute Engine or Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) resources with a direct public IP address that allows host OS access.

For more information, see Detect exposed resources, Risk Engine feature support, and Overview of attack exposure scores and attack paths.

Video Intelligence API

Deprecated

We are deprecating the emotion label response in the API. Going forward, the API will return UNKNOWN for all emotion related labels.

title: These are ALL you NEED to get started with Python PANDAS
description:
Pandas is a Python library used for data manipulation, analysis, and cleaning. It provides fast and flexible data structures designed to work with tabular data (similar to an Excel spreadsheet or a SQL table)

Dataframes and Series

  • DataFrame: A 2-dimensional labeled data structure with rows and columns (a complete table)
  • Series: A 1-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data type (like a single column in a spreadsheet).

Before getting started with pandas we need to install it first.

pip install pandas

import pandas as pd

# 1. Create a simple DataFrame
data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35],
    'City': ['New York', 'London', 'Paris']
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

# 2. Load data from an external file
# df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

# 3. View the first 5 rows
print(df.head())

Reading files in pandas

CSV Files (.csv): Use pd.read_csv() to import comma-separated values.

df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

Excel Spreadsheets (.xlsx, .xls): Use pd.read_excel() to load spreadsheets. You can specify a sheet using the sheet_name parameter.

df = pd.read_excel('budget.xlsx', sheet_name='Q1_Report')

JSON Data (.json): Use pd.read_json() to convert JSON strings or files into tabular format.

df = pd.read_json('users.json')

Parquet Files (.parquet): Use pd.read_parquet() for highly optimized, columnar storage files common in big data workflows.

df = pd.read_parquet('large_dataset.parquet')

SQL Database Tables: Use pd.read_sql() to pull data directly into Pandas via a database connection (e.g., utilizing an engine from the SQLAlchemy project)

import sqlalchemy
engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine('sqlite:///my_database.db')
df = pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM employees', con=engine)

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

  • Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) using Pandas is the foundational step in any data science workflow. It allows you to understand the structure, distributions, relationships, and anomalies within a dataset before moving to modeling

.head()

  • first n rows of a DataFrame or Series. It is primarily used to quickly inspect and verify the structure, column names, and data types of a dataset after loading it.
  • Inside the brackets you can put the number of rows you want to inspect. 
df.head()
df.head(10)

.tail

  • The df.tail() method in pandas returns the last n rows of a DataFrame or Series. 
df.tail()

.shape

  • df.shape is an attribute that returns a tuple representing the dimensions of a DataFrame or Series. It provides a quick way to see how many rows and columns your dataset contains. 
df1.shape

Output:

(5632, 27)

Structural & Descriptive Summaries

  • Before analyzing trends, verify how data types are registered and look at basic statistical summaries. 
# Check data types, memory usage, and non-null counts
df.info()

Output:

# Summary statistics for numerical columns (mean, min, max, quartiles)
df.describe()

Output

# Summary statistics for ALL columns (including categorical frequencies)
df.describe(include="all")

Output

Exploring Single Variables

  • Examine individual variables to understand their distribution, frequency, and pull out any categorical unique counts 
# For Categorical Data: Count frequencies of unique values
df["category_column"].value_counts()
df["category_column"].unique()  # List unique entries
df["category_column"].nunique()  # Total number of unique entries

# For Numerical Data: Quick pandas native plotting
df["numeric_column"].hist(bins=20)  # Check skewness and distribution
df["numeric_column"].plot(kind="box")  # Identify outliers

Data Cleaning

  • Before cleaning is done, a quick EDA must be done to know the areas to clean and what to clean. Below is a sample code to have a sneek- peek of what to actually clean. 
# Find duplicate rows and drop them
print(df.duplicated().sum())
df.drop_duplicates(inplace=True)

# Find missing values
print(df.isnull().sum())

Deal with missing values

  • Missing values in a dataset can either be dropped or imputed depending on the size of the data, importance and number of missing values.
  • Here are some of the ways to deal with missing values: 
df.dropna(subset=["critical_column"], inplace=True)  # Drop missing rows

df["numeric_column"] = df["numeric_column"].fillna(
    df["numeric_column"].median()
)  # Impute with median

Dealing with DataTypes

  • Values may be recorded in a datatype which may not be fit for them. In anycase this occurs, they can be changed to the correct datatypes.

  • Using pd.to_numeric() Best for converting text or mixed-type columns into numbers. Use errors='coerce' to turn unconvertible entries (like random text or symbols) into NaN.

df['price'] = pd.to_numeric(df['price'], errors='coerce')
  • Using pd.to_datetime() Converts date and time strings into proper datetime64 objects 
df['sale_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['sale_date'], errors='coerce')
  • Dealing with mixed date formats e.g dd/mm/yyyy, mm/dd/yyyy, yyyy/mm/dd 
df1['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(
    df1['order_date'],
    format='mixed',
    errors='coerce'
)

df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].str.strip().str.capitalize()
  • replace(), used when you want to change items inside a column to ensure consistency in values recorded and reliability. 
df1['payment_method'] = df1['payment_method'].replace({
    'Mpesa' : 'M-pesa',
    'Visa': 'Card'
})
  • If the column has mixed characters and values for example here in unit_price, you can also use replace function to standardize the column and maybe change the datatype if need be. 
df1['unit_price_kes'] = df1['unit_price_kes'].str.strip().str.replace(r'[^0-9]','', regex = True).astype(float)

Creating new columns

  • You can also be required to create a new column maybe from from a condition as below or from a calculation. In such a scenario, here's how to deal with it. 
df1['phone_validity'] = np.where(df1['customer_phone'].astype(str).str.len() == 10, 'valid', 'invalid')

# Calculate total cost (multiplication)
df['total_cost'] = df['price'] * df['quantity']
  • The code above will create a new column called total_cost.

Deleting columns

  • You can delete columns from a DataFrame using .drop() 
# deleting a single column
df = df.drop(columns=['B'])

#  deleting multiple columns
df = df.drop(columns=['C', 'D'])

Aggregation in pandas

  • Aggregations in Pandas reduce a collection of numerical or categorical values into a single summary value (such as a sum, mean, or count). You can perform these operations on an entire Pandas DataFrame, specific columns, or groups of data using the groupby() 
# Clean, flat DataFrame output with custom column names
clean_summary = df.groupby('Department').agg(
    total_salary=('Salary', 'sum'),
    average_bonus=('Bonus', 'mean'),
    employee_count=('Employee', 'count')
).reset_index()

Concatenation and Merging in Pandas

Concatenation (pd.concat)

  • Use pd.concat() when your datasets have the same structure and you want to glue them together along an axis. • axis=0 (Default): Stacks DataFrames vertically (appends rows). • axis=1: Stacks DataFrames horizontally (appends columns) aligned by their index. 
import pandas as pd

df1 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df2 = pd.DataFrame({'A': [5, 6], 'B': [7, 8]})

# Stack vertically (Row-wise)
vertical_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True)

# Stack horizontally (Column-wise)
horizontal_stack = pd.concat([df1, df2], axis=1)

Merging (pd.merge)

  • Use pd.merge() when you have different datasets that share a common identifier column (like an ID or SKU) and you want to align them side-by-side. 
left = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 3], 'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie']})
right = pd.DataFrame({'User_ID': [1, 2, 4], 'Salary': [50000, 60000, 70000]})

# Merge on a matching column
merged_df = pd.merge(left, right, on='User_ID', how='inner')

Saving the final dataframe

  • You can save a Pandas DataFrame to different file formats in Python using specific df.to_*() export methods 
import pandas as pd

# Assume 'df' is your existing DataFrame
# 1. Save as CSV (excluding the default index)
df.to_csv("data.csv", index=False)

# 2. Save as Excel
df.to_excel("data.xlsx", index=False)

# 3. Save as JSON
df.to_json("data.json", orient="records")

# 4. Save as Parquet (requires pyarrow or fastparquet)
df.to_parquet("data.parquet")

# 5. Save as Pickle
df.to_pickle("data.pkl")

Conclusion

Python pandas is the foundational, industry-standard tool for modern data manipulation, cleaning, and analysis. Built around its core DataFrame and Series structures, it transforms raw, messy data into structured, tabular insights by providing powerful, intuitive functions for merging datasets, handling missing values, and performing complex aggregations like groupby. While it integrates seamlessly with the broader Python ecosystem—including NumPy, Matplotlib, and scikit-learn—pandas does suffer from high memory usage and reduced performance when processing massive, multi-gigabyte datasets. Despite these scaling limitations, it remains an indispensable cornerstone of data science workflows, unmatched for exploratory data analysis and rapid prototyping.

title: The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB
description:
The Domain Was Just the Beginning: Building GraphGuard AI with FalkorDB

One suspicious domain. A web of relationships. A different way to investigate.

By Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026 | Track 1 — Agents That Act on Connected Data

Every Threat Leaves a Trail. Can You Connect It?

Imagine an analyst investigating a suspicious domain.

At first, there is only a name on a screen.

But that name might point to an IP address. It might be associated with a digital certificate. It might appear in a threat-intelligence report. Each connection offers another clue, and every clue raises a new question.

Is this connection meaningful? Where did the information come from? What should the analyst investigate next?

The challenge is not simply collecting more security data. It is discovering how the pieces connect without confusing a clue with proof.

That question became the starting point for GraphGuard AI.

We are Team SynapGraph, and for Graph Hacks 2026, we set out to explore how graph databases and AI-assisted investigation workflows could make cybersecurity evidence easier to follow, understand, and investigate.

Our chosen track was Track 1: Agents That Act on Connected Data.

Our central idea was simple:

Don't just show the indicator. Show the relationships that give it context.

Meet GraphGuard AI: An Investigation That Follows the Connections

GraphGuard AI is a graph-powered cybersecurity investigation prototype designed to explore relationships between domains, IP addresses, certificates, and reports.

Instead of treating every indicator as an isolated record, the application uses a connected graph to retrieve related information and present it through an investigation workflow.

The technology stack brings together three key components:

  • FalkorDB — the relationship engine. Stores and queries the connected cybersecurity entities that underpin the investigation.
  • FastAPI — the investigation interface. Connects the backend workflow to API endpoints.
  • Streamlit — the analyst's workspace. Provides a dashboard for submitting indicators and reviewing results.

Docker supports the local development and demonstration environment.

Together, these components form a practical experiment in making connected security evidence easier to explore.

Why We Chose a Graph Instead of Another List

Traditional lists are useful when you need to know what you have.

Graphs become especially useful when you need to understand how things are connected.

Consider a simplified investigation:




Suspicious Domain
demo.example



RESOLVES_TO



IP Address
192.0.2.10 · documentation-only example IP



MENTIONED_IN



Intelligence Report
REPORT-001 · synthetic demonstration data

Illustrative graph path based on the project's synthetic demonstration data, not a real threat finding.

In FalkorDB, these connections can be represented as relationships between nodes and retrieved using graph queries.

GraphGuard AI's model includes paths such as:

  • Domain → RESOLVES_TO → IPAddress
  • Domain → PRESENTED_CERTIFICATE → Certificate
  • IPAddress → MENTIONED_IN → Report

This structure lets an investigation move beyond a single indicator and inspect the related entities that the graph contains.

The difference is important: the graph does not automatically establish guilt. It gives the analyst more context to evaluate.

Under the Hood: Turning Connections into Context

The investigation begins when a user submits a domain through the dashboard.

The backend receives the request and queries FalkorDB for matching graph entities and their relationships. The returned information can include associated IP addresses, certificate records, and intelligence-report references when those records exist in the graph.

The application then presents the available findings to the user.

The process follows a clear path:

Indicator → Graph Query → Connected Evidence → Analyst Review

FalkorDB is central to this workflow because the investigation depends on retrieving connected entities, not merely storing unrelated records.

The project also explores the wider possibility of passive intelligence enrichment, including DNS, registration information, certificate transparency, and public threat-intelligence sources. Any live enrichment must be distinguished from existing graph records so that users can tell where each observation originated.

The Most Important Feature Is What We Don't Claim

In cybersecurity, an incorrect conclusion can be more dangerous than an incomplete result.

Two domains sharing an IP address does not automatically make them malicious. A certificate connection does not prove an attack. A mention in a report must be interpreted in context.

That is why GraphGuard AI is designed around an evidence-first principle:

A connection is a lead. Evidence supports a hypothesis. Verification builds confidence.

The prototype's synthetic dataset demonstrates the investigation workflow; it is not proof of real-world detection accuracy. Likewise, any confidence value shown by the application should not be mistaken for a statistically validated probability of maliciousness.

Our aim is to help users follow the evidence, understand the relationships, and decide what deserves further investigation—not to replace human judgment with an unexplained verdict.

Building Under Hackathon Pressure

Graph Hacks 2026 gave us an opportunity to turn a concept into a working prototype within a short development window.

As Team SynapGraph, we focused on connecting the database, backend API, and dashboard into one locally runnable application.

The process involved more than writing code. We needed to think about the graph data model, how relationships should be queried, how findings should be presented, and how someone else could run the project.

We used AI-assisted development tools to accelerate parts of the workflow while keeping the project's actual implementation and limitations in view.

One lesson stood out: a project becomes much easier to explain when the architecture follows a clear idea. For GraphGuard AI, that idea is the relationship between an indicator and the evidence surrounding it.

What Comes Next: From Connected Data to Better Investigations

GraphGuard AI is a starting point, not a finished security platform.

Future work could explore:

  • More passive intelligence providers and clearly attributed observations.
  • Stronger provenance, freshness, and source-quality indicators.
  • Additional graph traversal and relationship analysis.
  • More comprehensive tests using carefully labelled datasets.
  • Better ways to explain why a particular connection is relevant.
  • Evaluation against known examples to measure where the approach succeeds and fails.

The long-term goal is not simply to produce a larger graph. It is to make the graph more useful to the person investigating it.

See the Project in Action

Explore the source code:

https://github.com/sudhir734/GraphGuard-Ai

Watch the demo:

https://youtu.be/gMyqtCTPSv8

GraphGuard AI is a hackathon prototype intended for demonstration and experimentation. Its findings should be independently verified before use in operational security decisions.

One Final Thought

A suspicious domain is a starting point, not a conclusion.

The real investigation begins when we ask what connects to it, what those connections actually mean, and which pieces of evidence deserve our attention.

With GraphGuard AI, we are exploring a simple but powerful idea: cybersecurity is not only about finding signals. It is about understanding the relationships between them.

Follow the connections. Question the evidence. Investigate with context.

Team SynapGraph | Graph Hacks 2026
