title: Building a software factory for AI SDK
description:
The AI SDK is one of the most popular open-source AI projects in the world. It serves over 20 million npm downloads a week and the repo has over 26,000 stars. Maintaining the codebase means tracking four moving targets at once:

  • Model providers: new providers, new capabilities, and new bugs

  • UI frameworks: bindings for React, Next.js, Svelte, Vue, and others

  • Sandboxes: the execution environments agents run code in

  • Harnesses: adapters for Codex, Claude Code, Pi, and others

After multiple years of growth, the repo was getting 100+ new issues every month, and when Anthropic's Opus 4.6 model was released, PRs hit an inflection point. By late June, that compounding had accumulated over 1,000 open issues and almost 800 pull requests.

That backlog is not a discipline problem. No maintainer, however good, can close that gap by working harder, and because generating code is cheap, it will only grow.

Instead of trying to scale ourselves, we built a software factory. Four weeks in, it authors between 25 and 35% of PRs we merge and closes 70-80% of issues.

Deciding what type of factory to build

Before we built anything, we had to answer three questions:

  • Why our existing approach using agents wasn't enough

  • What level of automation fit a project like the AI SDK

  • How to align automation and human effort to risk

Why not add more agents?

The best maintainers are already using agents aggressively. Mitchell Hashimoto runs Ghostty with the goal of an agent always working, and encodes every agent failure in AGENTS.md so it never repeats. Simon Willison runs four coding agents in parallel, and review bots like Vercel Agent and CodeRabbit sit on millions of repos. Other maintainers like Daniel Stenberg have opted to block AI-generated submissions to curl.

All of it helps, but none of it solves for the core constraint: every one of these solutions still routes every change through one human's attention. We believe that human accountability is still the core of trust in agentic engineering, so we knew our factory needed to solve for reviewer efficiency as a first principle.

What kind of automation fits AI SDK?

Software factories sit on a spectrum. At one end is full automation, where agents write, ship, and deploy without a human ever reading the code. In the middle are harnesses like Codex and Claude Code, where a person steers an agent or fleet of agents. At the far end is software you barely want to automate because the risk is too high, like firmware in a pacemaker or self-driving vehicle.

The AI SDK needs to operate closer to the careful end. It is foundational AI infrastructure with millions of applications built on top, so quality and security are non-negotiable, and a human needs to have control over what ships. We needed our factory to heavily automate the lifecycle around the human, without removing them.

How do we align automation and effort to risk?

For a given change, the depth of human review needed scales with risk.

Centralized roadmaps with detailed feature specs can define risk up front and directly shape the work going into a software factory. But open-source projects like AI SDK also get issues and pull requests from the community, and there is no guarantee they align with the goals of the project, or that changes are safe to make. Higher risk means human judgment is an even more critical part of the system.

To optimize our factory for that judgment, we knew agents had to go beyond generating code based on a request; they needed to evaluate full units of work in the context of the entire project.

Our goal was for the factory to generate a comprehensive assessment of each change for both fit and risk, including a full chain of documented evidence, making it easy for reviewers to apply the right amount of effort:

  • Docs fixes get a quick glance for verification

  • Well-defined provider changes get focused validation

  • A new public API gets deep review

What we built

ai-sdk-factory is a software factory that autonomously processes incoming issues and pull requests for AI SDK. Agents in the factory perform specific, reviewable tasks, like reproducing bugs, implementing features, and creating backports for older SDK versions. A human stays in control throughout the entire process, including merging every change.

We didn't ship the factory in one swing. We built it incrementally, starting at the beginning of the process with classification of issues as bugs, features, or documentation updates. That first step not only gave us more visibility into the shape of the backlog, but also passed helpful context to the other specialized agents we built later.

We prototyped multiple ways to build each new type of functionality, and in the process developed a set of guiding principles that shaped the architecture of the factory that went into production.

Build one agent per task

Once our classification agent reached a high level of accuracy, we focused on automating bug reproduction, fixes, and review of those fixes. We explored building a single agent equipped with skills for each step, but quickly realized that would come with a higher maintenance and troubleshooting burden over time.

Instead, we built a single agent for each specific task, making every new capability easier to reason about, test in isolation, and debug. Each one is scoped to a specific job, with its own prompts, context, and evals.

Today the factory has dedicated agents for every step in the flow:

  • Bug reproduction

  • Bug fixes

  • PR reviews

  • Backports

  • Documentation updates

  • Feature analysis

  • Feature implementation

Secure everything from the start

We implemented security with the second agent, because bug reproduction was the first step where the factory executed code based on content it didn't control.

A factory operating on a public repository has to assume attacker-controlled input: every issue, pull request, comment, and the links inside them are untrusted. Because successful open-source projects are high-value targets, threats range from malicious code changes and supply chain attacks to resource exhaustion, API key exfiltration, and prompt exfiltration.

Sandboxes are the foundation of our defense. Every agent in ai-sdk-factory runs inside an isolated Vercel Sandbox containing its code, its runtime, and only the secrets the agent's specific task needs. With those guardrails, untrusted content can shape what an agent proposes, but the damage any one task can do is contained to the sandbox.

We also built a shielding layer around the sandbox that controls what agents can reach over the network, blocking the paths an attacker would use to pull secrets out of the isolated environment.

The last line of defense is human review: nothing is merged without approval from a human on the AI SDK team.

Build value locally, then move to the cloud

The first several agents we built for the factory ran through a local CLI. That enabled our team to iterate quickly as we noticed inaccuracies, felt friction, and prototyped different ideas.

Once multiple steps were running reliably through the CLI, we were ready to move the system onto managed infrastructure. ai-sdk-factory uses:

  • Vercel Functions for the API, workers, and webhook ingress

  • Vercel Queues for task execution

  • Vercel Blob for logs

  • Vercel Sandbox for the agent workspaces

  • Neon Postgres for factory data

Today, GitHub webhooks feed the issue queue, and as soon as they arrive workers automatically pull them and kick off agent runs in sandboxes. We also built a monitoring UI that tracks every run in parallel, and visualizes the queue for the team of reviewers.

Shipping software through our factory

On July 24, a community member asked for blocked-domain support in OpenAI web search, and the request became issue #17898. The following section explains every step the software factory went through to process the issue, open a pull request with an implementation of the feature, and ultimately backport the merged feature to v5 and v6 of the SDK.

Classification

The first agent that runs in the factory classifies issues and pull requests. In this case, the ai-sdk-factory bot commented on the issue and applied a label, identifying the type as Feature with high confidence. The agent included its rationale for the classification in the comment.

Analysis

After classification, the analysis agent runs. Agents in the factory don't make any assumptions about the technical validity of a feature request or bug, so the analysis agent wrote a probe to confirm the absence of support for blocked domains. issue-17898-type-probe.ts was generated and run, and failed with an error when it looked for blocked-domains and didn't find it.

The failing probe proved the feature was missing on main, and the agent included it in the analysis as evidence.

The analysis agent then used the results of its investigation to build out a spec for the feature: add an optional blockedDomains filter to the existing web-search tool and map it to the provider's blocked_domains field.

The agent also confirmed the spec fit the SDK's provider-adapter architecture and was backward compatible, and even scoped documentation changes.

Implementation

Another agent then implemented the spec and opened a pull request. The implementation agent ran a live end-to-end test, executing an OpenAI web search with wikipedia.org blocked and confirming the domain wasn't reachable. The test was included as additional evidence on the pull request.

Automated review

Next, a review agent scored the change, and when it didn't find any concerns, approved it. The agent rated the feature as fully implemented, with:

  • Side-effect risk: low

  • Performance risk: none

  • Backwards-compatibility risk: low

Human review

Finally, Lars read the chain of evidence from the agents, reviewed the code changes, and merged PR #18033 into main.

Backporting

Once Lars merged the initial PR, ai-sdk-factory opened additional PRs for two backports, #18035 for v6 and #18036 for v5. The v5 backport did not apply cleanly, so the factory agent labeled and committed the conflicted state, identified and validated a fix, and pushed it seventeen minutes later. After review, Lars merged both backport PRs.

Results

We are just over four weeks into running the software factory in production. Here are the results:

PRs merged to main

Between 25-35% of the PRs we merge on a weekly basis are now authored by ai-sdk-factory agents.

Backports

Factory PRs are above 50% of weekly merges to the v6 release line, and v5 looks similar. Backports used to be work we skipped because dealing with merge conflicts wasn't worth the effort. v5 and v6 get far better support now.

Issues

In July, over 75% of closed issues were closed by the factory.

Open issues fell from a peak of 1,022 in late June to 844 by early August, and open bugs are down roughly 25%.

The ai-sdk-factory runs in public, so you can see every pull request it has authored on the repo.

Improving the factory becomes the job

The most interesting part of running the factory is what happens when it fails. Every run ends one of four ways: success, flawed, blocked, or manual. Only success ships, so the rest are signal that re-enters the system as feedback.

  • A flawed run means an agent produced the wrong thing, and the fix is better prompts, better context, or a new eval case so the same mistake gets caught automatically next time

  • A blocked run means the environment was missing something, like a credential, a service, or a dependency, and the fix is provisioning it

  • A manual run marks a boundary we drew on purpose, and forces us to ask whether improvements in the factory justify removing it

Each of those fixes expands the automation boundary, and every week the factory can handle work that it couldn't be trusted with before.

Running the factory is the same discipline teams already apply to their test suites and pipelines, but pointed at the system that does the work, instead of the system that checks it. In a world where agents define the SDLC, improving the factory will become the standard engineering job.

title: 'useMemo' Hook in React
description:
When building React applications, components can re-render many times. During re-rendering, some calculations may run again even when the data has not changed. To avoid unnecessary calculations, React provides a Hook called useMemo.

What is useMemo?

useMemo is a React Hook that remembers, or caches, the result of a calculation. React can reuse the previous result when its dependencies have not changed.

For example:

import { useMemo } from "react";

const result = useMemo(() => {
  return number * number;
}, [number]);

Here, number is the dependency. If its value stays the same, React can reuse the cached result instead of recalculating it.

Why Do We Need useMemo?

Imagine a college application that displays student results. The application filters thousands of student records to find students who scored above 80 marks.

const topStudents = useMemo(() => {
  return students.filter(
    student => student.marks >= 80
  );
}, [students]);

Here, React can reuse the filtered student list when the students dependency remains unchanged. If the student data changes, React recalculates the list.

Understanding the Dependency Array

The dependency array tells React which values the calculation depends on.

const total = useMemo(
  () => price * quantity,
  [price, quantity]
);

If either price or quantity changes, React recalculates the total. If neither changes, React can reuse the previous result.

When Should We Use useMemo?

We can use useMemo when performing expensive calculations, filtering large datasets, sorting records, or processing complex data.

However, we should not use it for every small calculation. For simple operations, using useMemo may add unnecessary complexity without providing much benefit.

It is also important to understand that useMemo does not prevent a component from re-rendering. It only helps avoid unnecessary recalculations.

Conclusion

useMemo is a useful React Hook for improving performance when calculations are expensive. It caches a calculation result between renders and recalculates it when its dependencies change.

title: Stop Squinting at Messy LESS: How to Beautify Your Stylesheets in Seconds
description:
We've all been there. You inherit a project, open styles.less, and it looks like someone typed the whole thing in a single breath. Nested rules collapsed onto one line, mixins with no spacing, variables jammed against their values.

You can still read it. But every minute you spend decoding formatting is a minute you're not fixing the actual bug.

In this post I'll walk through what LESS is (quickly), why formatting matters more than people admit, and how a LESS beautifier can clean up a file in seconds. I'll also show you real before and after examples so you can judge for yourself.

Quick refresher: what is LESS?

LESS is a CSS preprocessor. It extends plain CSS with features like variables, nesting, mixins, functions and operations, then compiles down to regular CSS that browsers understand. The official LESS documentation is the best place to go deep on the language itself.

A tiny taste:

@primary: #3b82f6;

.button {
  background: @primary;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }
}

That nesting and the darken() function are what make LESS pleasant to write. But they're also what make badly formatted LESS painful to read, because the structure is the logic.

Why formatting matters more in LESS than in plain CSS

In plain CSS, a messy file is annoying. In LESS, a messy file can actually hide bugs. Here's why:

  • Nesting depth is meaning. A rule nested one level too deep (or too shallow) changes the compiled selector. If indentation doesn't match nesting, you can't see the mistake.
  • Mixins and guards are easy to miss. A mixin call buried in a long line is easy to overlook when you're debugging why a style is applied.
  • Missing braces are brutal. One unclosed } in a deeply nested block can break compilation, and the error message often points somewhere unhelpful.
  • Code review gets noisy. If every developer formats differently, pull requests fill up with whitespace changes that hide the real ones.

Consistent formatting isn't about being picky. It's about making the structure of your styles visible at a glance.

What does a LESS beautifier actually do?

A beautifier takes your LESS code and rewrites its whitespace and layout without changing what it means. Typically that includes:

  • Consistent indentation for nested blocks
  • One declaration per line
  • Sensible spacing around colons, braces and operators
  • Line breaks between rules so blocks are easy to scan

Crucially, it should not change your logic. Variables, mixins, operations and nesting stay exactly as you wrote them. Only the presentation changes.

A real before and after

Here's the kind of LESS you might get from a quick copy-paste, a minified export, or a teammate in a hurry:

@primary:#3b82f6;@radius:6px;
.mixin-card(@pad:16px){padding:@pad;border:1px solid #eee}
.btn{color:#fff;background:@primary;border-radius:@radius;&:hover{background:darken(@primary,10%)}.icon{margin-right:4px}}
.card{.mixin-card(24px);h2{font-size:1.25rem;a{color:@primary}}}

Technically valid. Practically unreadable. Now the same code after running it through a beautifier:

@primary: #3b82f6;
@radius: 6px;

.mixin-card(@pad: 16px) {
  padding: @pad;
  border: 1px solid #eee;
}

.btn {
  color: #fff;
  background: @primary;
  border-radius: @radius;

  &:hover {
    background: darken(@primary, 10%);
  }

  .icon {
    margin-right: 4px;
  }
}

.card {
  .mixin-card(24px);

  h2 {
    font-size: 1.25rem;

    a {
      color: @primary;
    }
  }
}

Same code, same output once compiled, but now you can see that .icon lives inside .btn, that .card calls the mixin, and that the link color sits three levels deep. That last one is a good reminder to watch your nesting depth, which you'd never notice in the single-line version.

How to use an online LESS beautifier

When I just need to clean up a snippet or a single file, I don't want to configure a toolchain. An online tool is the fastest path. I put together the LESS Beautifier on 99tools for exactly this situation. The workflow is simple:

  1. Paste your messy LESS into the input box.
  2. Run the beautifier.
  3. Copy the cleaned-up result back into your editor.

No install, no config file, no setup. It's handy when you're:

  • Reviewing LESS from a client or a legacy project
  • Cleaning a snippet before sharing it in a bug report or Stack Overflow question
  • Reading code that was minified or exported from another tool
  • Teaching or learning LESS and wanting readable examples

A quick tip: as with any online tool, don't paste proprietary code or anything containing secrets if your company policy says otherwise. For sensitive projects, use a local formatter instead (more on that below).

Beautifier vs. linter vs. compiler

These three get confused a lot, so here's the short version:

Tool What it does Changes your code?
Beautifier / formatter Fixes indentation, spacing and layout Whitespace only
Linter Flags problems and style violations Usually no (some auto-fix)
Compiler (lessc) Turns LESS into CSS Produces new output

A beautifier won't catch a typo in a variable name, and it won't tell you your nesting is too deep. Use it alongside a linter like Stylelint and your normal compile step, not instead of them.

Best practices for clean LESS

Formatting is the baseline. Here are a few habits that keep LESS maintainable once it's tidy:

  • Keep nesting to 3 levels or fewer. Deep nesting creates overly specific selectors that are painful to override.
  • Group variables at the top or in a dedicated file so theme changes happen in one place.
  • Name mixins clearly and keep them small and single-purpose.
  • Agree on one style as a team (2 spaces vs 4, blank lines between rules) and automate it so nobody argues in code review.
  • Run a formatter before committing, so diffs show real changes only.

When an online tool isn't the right fit

I want to be upfront: an online beautifier is great for quick jobs, but it isn't the answer to everything.

If your team formats code on every commit, you'll be better served by an automated local setup, such as Prettier, which supports LESS, wired into your editor or a pre-commit hook. And if you're starting a brand new project, it's also worth knowing that native CSS now supports nesting, which covers some of what people originally reached for preprocessors to do. The MDN guide to CSS nesting is a good overview if you're weighing your options.

That said, LESS is still used in plenty of real projects, and a lot of us are maintaining it for years to come. For those moments, having a quick way to make messy code readable is genuinely useful.

Wrapping up

Readable code isn't a luxury. It's how you spot bugs sooner, review faster, and onboard people without a lecture. A LESS beautifier takes about ten seconds and removes one whole category of friction.

If you have a messy .less file sitting around, try the LESS Beautifier on it and see how the structure changes. And if you've got your own tips for keeping LESS clean, or a horror story from a legacy stylesheet, drop it in the comments. I'd love to hear it.

Happy styling! 🎨

title: Codex Swapped Its Default Model and Retired GPT-5.5 in 15 Days. Did Your Evals Notice?
description:
• Book: Observability for LLM Applications
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

On September 29, a pull request merged into Codex gave GPT-6.1 Sol "the highest catalog priority" (#49318). That line made it the model the bundled catalog hands a Codex session when you don't ask for one.

Nine days later, Codex CLI 0.162.0 changed where a fresh terminal thread gets its default model from. Six days after that, GPT-5.5 left Codex for everyone signed in with ChatGPT.

Three changes in 15 days, and none of them showed up in your repo's diff. If your agent runs on whatever the default is, the thing your evals measure may have moved while your code stood still.

My take: a model you didn't choose is a dependency you didn't pin. Pin it per task, and write it down next to every result.

What changed between September 29 and October 14

Here is the sequence, from OpenAI's own release notes and docs:

Date Change Who it hits
Sep 29 Codex CLI 0.159.1: GPT-6.1 Sol becomes the default in the bundled catalog CLI users who never set a model
Oct 7 0.161.0 lists it again: default in the bundled and Amazon Bedrock catalogs The same, plus Bedrock users
Oct 8 0.162.0: new TUI threads respect the server's model defaults TUI users who launch without a model override
Oct 14 GPT-5.5 retires from Codex for ChatGPT sign-ins, at noon PDT (19:00 UTC) Anyone who picked gpt-5.5 and signs in with ChatGPT

The October 8 change is the quiet one. The release note says Codex will "respect server model and reasoning-summary defaults for new TUI threads while retaining explicit launch overrides." The pull request behind it (#50013) puts it more plainly: "Fresh TUI threads should use the app server's model settings unless the launch explicitly overrides them." The server here is the Codex app server the TUI talks to, a local daemon or a remote one (#50913). The same release stopped appending "(default)" to entries in the TUI model picker (#51235).

The October 14 change hits the opposite group: people who did pin a model. OpenAI's models page says the retirement covers ChatGPT sign-ins only and API-key sessions are not affected. It points Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu users to GPT-6.1 Sol, and Free and Go users to GPT-6 Luna in the desktop app, both "when available."

To be fair to OpenAI, none of this was hidden. Every change is in a release note or the changelog, the retirement came with an exact time and a named replacement, and 0.162.0 also moved the model and reasoning effort near the top of task details (#50727). GPT-6.1 Sol may well be the better model for you. OpenAI says it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra at about a fifth of Astra's token price (Unite.AI, The Batch), though those are OpenAI's own numbers. An upgrade still moves your numbers, and your evals should say so.

Who picked the default? A catalog file

Look at what "default" meant in #49318. Nobody on your team chose GPT-6.1 Sol. It got the highest priority in a catalog file that ships inside the CLI, so it won.

Codex isn't unusual here. Claude Code's model docs say the aliases opus, sonnet and haiku "point to the recommended version for your provider and update over time." Same doc: "To pin to a specific version, use the full model name, for example claude-opus-5-5." So claude --model opus is a moving target by design, and claude --model claude-opus-5-5 is a pin.

Moving targets are fine for a chat. You want the newest model when you ask a question at 11pm. They are a problem for anything you measure, compare or promise to a teammate.


A default model can change between two eval runs without a single line of your repo changing.

Your evals measure the model, so they need its name

An agent eval can be a formal suite. More often it is a sentence in a team chat: "Codex is worse at migrations than Claude Code." "That AGENTS.md rewrite made the agent better." "This task took 40 minutes last week and 12 this week."

Each of those is a claim about a model. If the model was a default, you don't know which one it was. Did your prompt get better, or did the catalog move? Did Codex get worse at migrations, or did a fresh thread pick up a different server default than the one you tested last month?

The model is not the only hidden variable either. Reasoning effort changes results, and #50013 treats it like the model: if the launch doesn't set it, a fresh TUI thread takes the server's default. The account matters too: the GPT-5.5 retirement hit ChatGPT sign-ins and left API-key sessions alone, so the same gpt-5.5 setting meant two different things depending on how you logged in.

So the minimum record for any agent result is four fields: the model, the effort, the account type and the commit it ran against. Without them, a before-and-after comparison is two numbers with no explanation attached.

Pin it per task, then write it down

For daily work in Codex, a profile is the cleanest pin. Per the advanced config docs, a profile is a file in ~/.codex/ with top-level keys:

# ~/.codex/pinned.config.toml
model = "gpt-6.1-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "medium"

Start it with codex --profile pinned. PR #50013 keeps explicit profile launches on the resolved configuration, so the profile's model holds even for fresh TUI threads.

For anything you compare, put the pin and the record in the same script. codex exec takes -m for the model (models page), and -c sets any config key (the config docs say a value that isn't valid TOML is treated as a string):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# run-task.sh "<task>" : one pinned run, one logged row
set -u
task="$1"
model="gpt-6.1-sol"
effort="medium"
account="chatgpt"   # or "apikey": how this run signs in

codex exec -m "$model" \
  --sandbox workspace-write \
  -c model_reasoning_effort="$effort" \
  "$task" > last-run.log
agent=$?
npm test > test.log 2>&1
tests=$?

printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
  "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" \
  "$model" "$effort" "$account" "$agent" "$tests" >> runs.tsv

By default codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox (non-interactive mode docs), so --sandbox workspace-write is what lets the agent edit the checkout before the tests run. The agent column keeps Codex's own exit status, so a failed agent step shows up in the row instead of hiding behind a test result on untouched code.

Swap npm test for your own check, and set account to match how the machine signs in. Every row in runs.tsv now carries all four fields: which model, effort and account produced which test result on which commit.

Pinning has a cost, and October 14 showed it. Anyone pinned to gpt-5.5 with a ChatGPT sign-in had to edit their config. OpenAI's list of what to update covers "workspace defaults, saved model settings, managed configurations, custom agents, scheduled tasks, and scripts that still select gpt-5.5" (changelog).

That is the good kind of break. You change one line in a diff, rerun your tasks, and compare the new rows against the old ones.

Where Hermes IDE fits

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent's own CLI in a real terminal, Codex and Claude Code included, each task on its own branch and worktree.

The part that matters here: when you start a task with ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux), you pick the agent, model, effort and account for that task, and you can save combinations you use often as presets (README). Several accounts per agent are supported, so the sign-in a task runs under is something you choose when you start it.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: agent, project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, the model and effort chips, and a preview of the command Hermes will run.

After launch, every session shows its own spend: the cost the agent reports, or an estimate from its transcript marked as estimated, with token totals. Since 2.3.4, a Claude Code or Codex session keeps showing its own model and cost even when the conversation mentions another company's model. The bar above each session puts Model in the same place for every agent.


Codex and Claude Code side by side in Hermes 2.3.4, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with status, context use, cost and branch per session in the sidebar.

What it doesn't do: Hermes doesn't write your runs.tsv, and it can't stop a vendor from retiring a model you picked. It makes the choice explicit per task and keeps it visible per session. The record is still yours. Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with OpenAI, Anthropic or any other agent vendor.

So, which model ran your last eval?

Open the last result you shared with your team, a benchmark, a "this agent is better at X" message, a before-and-after on a prompt change. Can you name the model and effort that produced it?

If not, you were testing a catalog entry. Tell me in the comments whether you pin your agent's model, or whether you'd rather ride the default and take the upgrades as they come.

If this was useful

Writing the model next to every result is the smallest piece of LLM observability. Observability for LLM Applications covers the rest of it: tracing each call, running evals that catch quality regressions when a model changes, and tracking cost per feature in production. If you run several agents, Hermes IDE is free and lets you set the model per task (GitHub).

title: avoiding race conditions in async cascade deletes for event‑sourced services
description:
you've got an event‑sourced aggregate that emits a UserDeleted event, and several downstream services react by cleaning up related rows in their own stores. the cleanup runs in background workers, so a second request that references the same user can slip through the cracks and hit a foreign‑key violation.

the race condition

in a typical setup each service subscribes to the UserDeleted topic and issues a cascade delete against its own tables. because the subscription processing is asynchronous, a request that arrives after the UserDeleted event is published but before the worker finishes will see stale data. the DB then throws an error, and the client gets a 500 instead of a graceful "not found".

a deterministic approach

the trick is to make the delete operation idempotent and observable before the request reaches the service. one pattern is to store a tombstone flag in a shared cache (e.g. Redis) as part of the same transaction that publishes the event. workers check the flag before proceeding, and request handlers read it to short‑circuit.

// publish + tombstone atomically
await redis.multi()
  .set(`tombstone:user:${userId}`, '1', 'EX', 300) // 5 min TTL
  .publish('user.deleted', JSON.stringify({ userId }))
  .exec();

workers then do:

const flag = await redis.get(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);
if (!flag) return; // nothing to clean up
await db.transaction(async trx => {
  await trx('orders').where({ userId }).delete();
  await trx('profiles').where({ userId }).delete();
});
await redis.del(`tombstone:user:${userId}`);

trade‑offs

  • latency vs consistency – adding the cache lookup adds a few milliseconds to every request, but it eliminates sporadic DB errors.
  • cache eviction – the TTL must be long enough to cover the slowest worker, otherwise a stale request could still hit the DB.
  • failure handling – if the worker crashes after deleting rows but before clearing the tombstone, subsequent requests will be rejected even though the data is gone. a periodic reconciler that scans for orphaned tombstones can mitigate this.
  • testing – simulate the race by issuing a delete and a read in parallel within integration tests; assert that the read returns a 404 rather than a DB exception.

when to apply

if your service experiences occasional 500 spikes after bulk deletions, or if you already use a message broker for domain events, the tombstone pattern is a low‑overhead way to enforce eventual consistency without locking the DB.

anyone using a similar approach with different stores (e.g. DynamoDB streams) or who prefers optimistic concurrency controls instead? how do you keep the delete path safe without sacrificing throughput?

title: Metered Support API Credential Checks — Cached Degraded Readiness Health Endpoint
description:
A customer-support service should resolve its API key identity and account tier before accepting metered work, cache that evidence for only a few seconds, and report degraded when either read fails. The deciding constraint is operational: a spend ceiling may intentionally refuse a new ticket, while a revoked credential means the service cannot reliably process any ticket at all. Those are different pages.

TL;DR: Make readiness depend on both identity and tier reads. Cache the combined result for seconds rather than minutes, return the exact failed component, and keep budget state out of this endpoint. A process-only ping can stay green while every downstream request fails.

Probe the dependency.

For this boundary, Infrai fits teams that want an authenticated identity-and-tier check without taking on another vendor SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface includes request and response schemas, billing information, and runnable examples. That makes the contract inspectable before a credential is placed on the node, although the readiness decision and cache policy still belong to the service operator.

What should an API credential readiness health endpoint check?

The useful question at 3 a.m. is not "is the process alive?" It is "which dependency made this node unable to take work?" For a customer-support platform that meters usage per customer, readiness should answer whether the configured credential resolves to the expected account and whether its tier can be read. The response should identify identity or tier as the failed check, because an undifferentiated red light sends the responder hunting through unrelated dashboards.

Do not put the budget read in this path. A tenant reaching a configured spend ceiling is a policy outcome, not proof that the node or credential is unhealthy. Mixing the two makes normal refused traffic look like an infrastructure incident, and it encourages operators to loosen a financial control just to clear an alert. Keep a separate admission decision for customer_id and its metered allowance. Readiness only decides whether this instance may receive work.

Keep those signals separate.

The cache window is also a failure-policy decision. Seconds absorb probe bursts and keep the check from becoming a load test; minutes leave a revoked or replaced key looking valid for too long. Ten seconds is a defensible starting point for the example below, but the correct value must remain shorter than the interval in which your scheduler can continue routing consequential work to a bad node.

Build one combined, short-lived verdict

This program is runnable with Go 1.22 or later. It exposes /ready, calls only the identity and tier routes, sends the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, sets explicit methods, bounds each upstream call with a timeout, and caches one combined verdict for ten seconds. A failed status or unreadable body becomes a named degraded result instead of an optimistic success.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "sync"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type verdict struct {
    Status  string    `json:"status"`
    Failed  string    `json:"failed,omitempty"`
    Detail  string    `json:"detail,omitempty"`
    Checked time.Time `json:"checked_at"`
}

type checker struct {
    key    string
    client *http.Client
    mu     sync.Mutex
    cached verdict
    until  time.Time
}

func (c *checker) read(ctx context.Context, path string, dst any) error {
    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+c.key)
    req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

    resp, err := c.client.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
        return fmt.Errorf("upstream returned %s", resp.Status)
    }
    if err := json.NewDecoder(resp.Body).Decode(dst); err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("decode response: %w", err)
    }
    return nil
}

func (c *checker) check(ctx context.Context) verdict {
    c.mu.Lock()
    defer c.mu.Unlock()

    now := time.Now().UTC()
    if now.Before(c.until) {
        return c.cached
    }

    next := verdict{Status: "ready", Checked: now}
    var identity map[string]any
    if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/whoami", &identity); err != nil {
        next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "identity", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
    } else {
        var tier map[string]any
        if err := c.read(ctx, "/account/tier", &tier); err != nil {
            next = verdict{Status: "degraded", Failed: "tier", Detail: err.Error(), Checked: now}
        }
    }

    c.cached = next
    c.until = now.Add(10 * time.Second)
    return next
}

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        log.Fatal(errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required"))
    }

    c := &checker{
        key:    key,
        client: &http.Client{Timeout: 3 * time.Second},
    }
    http.HandleFunc("/ready", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 4*time.Second)
        defer cancel()

        result := c.check(ctx)
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        if result.Status != "ready" {
            w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        }
        if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(result); err != nil {
            log.Printf("encode readiness response: %v", err)
        }
    })

    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}

The mutex deliberately serializes a refresh. Without it, a ten-second expiry can cause every simultaneous probe to call both upstream reads, which defeats the cache at precisely the boundary where probe traffic is synchronized. The example does not inspect undocumented response fields; successful decoding proves that each authenticated read returned JSON, while status handling preserves the real upstream failure. Do not log the bearer token or return it in Detail. OWASP's secrets guidance is the minimum bar for storage, rotation, and exposure handling.

There is one trade-off here: both success and failure are cached. Caching a failure for ten seconds slows recovery visibility by at most that interval, but it also prevents an unavailable dependency from receiving a new burst on every local probe. For a readiness signal, that is usually the calmer failure mode.

Compare the full operating bill, not a request price

Per-call price is a poor primary selector for this check. Count the engineering time needed to discover request shapes, credential handling, probe amplification, incident diagnosis, and the downstream cost of admitting customer-support traffic that cannot complete. Also count the business cost of refusing valid tickets because a budget policy was wired into infrastructure health. The effective bill is where those choices meet.

Infrai is a strong option for teams that want this credential-and-tier guard alongside other backend capabilities behind one key: its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas, billing, and runnable examples, so adding a capability starts by reading the endpoint contract rather than adopting another SDK. Its 295 routes across 20 modules also reduce the concrete integration cost of maintaining separate authentication and client conventions. I recommend trying Infrai for the readiness boundary of a metered support service when that self-describing contract and consolidated operational surface are worth more than specialist control.

The alternatives fit different boundaries:

Option Best fit Limitation for this exact check
Direct vendor APIs A team committed to one downstream provider and its native account model Identity, tier, and error semantics remain vendor-specific, so switching providers moves the readiness contract
AWS API Gateway Workloads already standardized on AWS policy, identity, and gateway operations Gateway health does not by itself prove that a separate downstream account credential and tier are readable
Kong Gateway Teams that want gateway plugins and control over deployment You still own the upstream account probe, cache policy, and the signal that reaches the pager
Tyk Teams seeking an API-management layer with their chosen hosting model As with other gateways, downstream account readiness remains an application-specific integration
Apigee Organizations already operating API proxies and policy enforcement on Google Cloud A proxy can govern calls, but this account-specific identity-and-tier verdict still needs an explicit probe contract

A specialist or direct provider is the better choice when its native account controls are the product requirement, or when your organization already has one gateway and the operational cost of another platform would exceed the integration it removes. This is not a price leaderboard. It is an ownership decision.

Verify the signal before trusting the dashboard

Exercise behavior, not screenshots. Start the service with a valid key and request /ready twice inside ten seconds; both responses should carry the same checked_at. Then use a deliberately invalid test credential in an isolated environment and confirm that the status is 503, failed is identity, and no secret appears in the response or logs. Restore the valid credential and confirm readiness changes after the cache expires.

Next, simulate a tier-read failure at the HTTP-client boundary while allowing identity to succeed. The page must name tier. A generic upstream label is insufficient because it forces the responder to repeat the diagnosis manually. Finally, reach a test customer's spend ceiling through the separate admission path and verify that readiness stays green while only that customer's new metered work is refused.

What page fired? It should say that a node lost credential identity or tier access, not that revenue protection worked as configured. Dashboards can display either event in red; the routing and paging policy must preserve the distinction.

Roll back without erasing the evidence

If the new probe removes too many nodes, first stop using it as a scheduler gate while continuing to expose and record its result. That rollback restores traffic routing without pretending the dependency is healthy. Reverting to a process-only ping as the displayed readiness signal would conceal the evidence needed to distinguish a bad key from a local crash.

Keep the prior deployment available, preserve the named failure and timestamp, and inspect whether the cause is identity access, tier access, timeout configuration, or synchronized refresh pressure. Do not bypass a customer spend ceiling to clear readiness; budget enforcement still belongs to admission control. Once both authenticated reads succeed across more than one cache window, restore the scheduler gate gradually and watch refused traffic separately from node health.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery contract before wiring the probe.

References

  • Infrai official documentation
  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • AWS API Gateway documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • Tyk documentation
  • Apigee documentation

title: Vercel Container Registry repositories can now be made public
description:
Vercel Container Registry now lets you make a repository public, so anyone with a Vercel account can pull and use its images.

title: Privacy Budgets for Test Email in Web Apps
description:
Email is often treated as harmless test plumbing. In a web application, it is closer to a small data store: messages can contain personal-looking addresses, sign-in links, verification codes, and enough context to explain what a user did. When a test fails, that data may then be copied into CI logs, screenshots, artifacts, or a developer's laptop.

A useful pattern is to give test email a privacy budget. The budget is not a single number. It is a set of limits for who owns a fixture, how long it lives, what evidence may be retained, and which parts of a message can be exposed to a test. This makes Privacy a design property of Web Development, rather than a cleanup task at the end.

Why test email deserves a privacy budget

Browser and API tests need realistic signals. A signup flow may need to prove that a message is delivered, that the correct link changes account state, and that a second click is rejected. But a test does not need to preserve the entire email forever to prove those things.

Without explicit limits, a shared inbox can let one parallel run read another's message, a failed assertion can print a verification URL into a long-lived log, and a retry can reuse an address or token. A cleanup job can also remove the message before a developer understands the failure.

The first question are not “which temporary inbox is cheapest?” It is “what is the smallest piece of email evidence that proves this behavior?” Search phrases such as tempmailso and temp mail mail may appear in product or test discussions, but the engineering decision should be based on isolation, retention, and access control.

Define the budget before choosing an inbox

Start with the assertion. If the test only checks that a verification message arrived, a receipt may be enough:

{
  "run_id": "ci-1842-attempt-2",
  "fixture_id": "signup-7f31",
  "message_id": "msg-9081",
  "received_at": "2026-10-18T02:20:00Z",
  "subject": "Verify your account",
  "result": "matched"
}

If the test must follow a link, grant the browser step temporary access to the link while keeping it out of ordinary logs. The test helper can return a short-lived value in memory, then replace it with a token identifier once the assertion finishes.

This separation matters because message metadata and authentication material have different sensitivity. A subject and timestamp are useful for diagnosing delivery. A complete URL with a bearer token may be enough to sign in as the test account. It also make the failure record much safer to share with a teammate.

The budget should answer four questions: who owns the fixture, how long the raw message lives, what the test can read, and what survives cleanup. The answers should favor one run attempt per address, bounded retention, narrow access, and a redacted receipt instead of the whole message.

Keep ownership and retention explicit

Give every fixture a run id and attempt number. A retry should get its own address, message correlation value, and token. It is tempting to retry a failed fetch against the same inbox, but that makes old and new messages indistinguishable. A retry should get it's own evidence trail.

The provider adapter should own fixture creation, message lookup, short-lived link claims, and release receipts. The application test should own expected behavior. This division makes it possible to change from a hosted temporary inbox to a local mail capture service without rewriting every test. The runner requests release in a finally-style cleanup step; a janitor removes expired fixtures, and repeated cleanup returns an ordinary “already released” result.

For old fixtures, even a query string like temp gamil com can reveal how legacy test data was generated. A phrase such as temp org mail may also be present in search or compatibility cases. Keep these typo keywords as plain test data only; do not use them as selectors, links, or supported domain examples.

Collect evidence without collecting secrets

Good CI evidence is specific enough to explain a failure and small enough to be safe. A layered receipt works well:

  1. Correlation: run id, attempt, fixture id, and environment.
  2. Delivery: message id, received time, and a normalized subject hash if needed.
  3. Consumption: token id, response status, and whether the token was accepted, expired, or already used.
  4. Cleanup: expiry time, release status, and janitor outcome.

Avoid printing the complete HTML body, query strings, authorization headers, or screenshots of the inbox. Redact before logging, not in a dashboard query after the value has already been copied to several systems. A small allowlist of fields is easier to review than a large blocklist of secret-looking fields.

There is a related lesson in turning API tests into useful CI receipts: the result should describe what happened, not preserve every input. For signup flows, idempotent signup email handling provides another useful boundary. A receipt can say that an event was handled once without retaining the triggering message.

A small implementation contract

Teams do not need a large platform to start. They need a few invariants that are tested alongside the application:

  • A fixture belongs to one run attempt and one environment.
  • A message is accepted only when its recipient and correlation value match.
  • A verification token is single-use, purpose-bound, and short-lived.
  • A retry creates new fixture and token identifiers.
  • Logs contain identifiers and outcomes, never raw links or message bodies.
  • Cleanup is repeatable and a janitor handles crashes.
  • Access to message content is narrower than access to test receipts.

These rules reduce flakiness as well as exposure. The boundary stay understandable when a provider changes or a browser test runs in parallel. It is a modest contract, but it turns email from hidden shared state into an owned test resource.

Review checklist

Before adding an email-dependent test, ask: can two runs claim the same message; does a failure expose a clickable URL; does every retry have a new fixture and token; is raw data deleted after a crash; can a developer diagnose delivery from a redacted receipt; and are screenshots covered by the same retention policy?

If the answers are explicit, the test is checking both product behavior and the safety of its own evidence. That prevent a common failure mode: a green test suite that quietly creates a growing archive of sensitive email.

Questions teams usually ask

Should every test use a hosted temporary inbox?

No. A local mail capture service is often best for application semantics; use a provider-like fixture when delivery integration itself is under test. Keep the same ownership and retention contract in both cases.

title: AI Is Redrawing the US Data Center Map
description:
Power access is shaping where new campuses rise, when they come online, and the networks connecting them.

October 18, 2026

In June 2024, construction began on the Stargate campus in Abilene, Texas. Within a year, its first two buildings had been energized. By September 2025, Crusoe said the site was running early training and inference workloads on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The planned campus would eventually contain eight buildings. Crusoe’s account captures both the speed of the AI infrastructure boom and its defining complication: large campuses become useful in stages.

That progression is changing the geography of computing. Developers need sites where land, electricity and equipment can come together on a workable schedule. As established markets fill up, new locations become attractive, and connecting distant facilities becomes an engineering problem of its own.

The spending curve shows how quickly this has become a national construction story. In November 2022, private US data center construction was running at an annualized pace of $13.9 billion. By August 2026, that rate had reached $85.0 billion, roughly six times as much. These Census Bureau figures cover data centers broadly and measure construction work, including fixed electrical and mechanical systems. They exclude racks and servers, whose costs sit on top of the building investment.

Figure 1. Monthly construction spending expressed as a seasonally adjusted annual rate, in current dollars. The August figure is a spending pace, rather than money already spent during 2026. Source: US Census Bureau.

Construction spending was already increasing before ChatGPT’s launch. Because the figures are in current dollars, the curve combines changes in construction prices with changes in the amount being built. It establishes the growing scale of spending without measuring computing capacity.

The next question is where that work can happen. In its August report, JLL placed 77% of North American data center capacity under construction in frontier markets, highlighting West Texas, Ohio, Louisiana, Indiana and the Carolinas. Its market analysis describes a buildout extending well beyond the industry’s established hubs.

Texas illustrates the shift. JLL reported 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity across the state, compared with 13 GW in Virginia. Northern Virginia remained the largest individual market, with nearly 7 GW of inventory. The state totals show the direction of investment while including projects that still have to become operating facilities.

Figure 2. State totals combine existing capacity and capacity under construction, including hyperscalers’ own facilities. They do not measure electricity currently being consumed. Source: JLL, Midyear 2026.

A large pipeline creates a planning problem for utilities. They must decide how much infrastructure to build before they know which projects will arrive, when their servers will be installed, or how quickly customer workloads will fill them. A speculative request can therefore influence planning long before it becomes a substantial electricity load.

AEP Ohio’s experience shows how that pipeline changes as commitments become binding. Its new tariff required developers to advance through paid studies and financial commitments. About one-fifth of the initial requested capacity reached signed contracts. AEP attributed the narrowing to the filtering of speculative or uncertain projects. The utility still had 17.9 GW of total contracted data center projects, including earlier contracts, scheduled to come online progressively through 2035. AEP’s February update distinguishes those future obligations from operating demand.

Figure 3. Successive stages of one AEP Ohio intake cohort, as reported in February 2026. The final bar excludes contracts signed before the tariff. Source: AEP Ohio.

Texas faces its own version of the credibility problem. ERCOT’s September board update documented a pause in energization approvals for relevant new data center and cryptocurrency facilities of at least 75 MW while verification and community-impact reviews proceeded. Projects received provisional classifications; those classifications did not constitute final permission to connect. The operator expected to publish its community-impact report by December 10.

For developers, that makes the location of available power consequential to computing design. Microsoft offers a concrete example. Its Fairwater facilities in Wisconsin and the Atlanta area are linked through a dedicated network intended to let sites cooperate on large AI workloads. Microsoft explicitly identifies land and power availability as reasons to spread work across locations. Its description of the architecture connects the choice of geography to the need for new networking infrastructure.

Distance introduces costs of its own. Large training jobs require frequent communication among processors; slow exchanges can leave expensive hardware waiting. Microsoft describes dedicated fiber and changes to network protocols designed to reduce bottlenecks between sites. Finding land and power therefore creates another task: making the resulting facilities operate efficiently together.

There are also ways to change the terms on which a facility receives electricity. In a report published October 14, the International Energy Agency examines connection agreements that allow consumption to be curtailed, phased in or adjusted to grid conditions. Such arrangements can help projects connect sooner by changing the reliability or timing of their access.

The tradeoff is practical. Interrupting expensive AI hardware can be costly, and a facility operator may have limited control over customers’ workloads. The IEA’s analysis identifies coordination among computing customers, facility operators and electricity networks as a condition for greater flexibility. Onsite generation also brings equipment lead times and engineering requirements of its own.

The buildout is consequently creating an architecture that extends beyond each campus. Transmission studies, substations, fiber routes and electricity agreements increasingly influence where AI work can run. Abilene’s first buildings became useful when several of those pieces came together. Repeating that achievement across a much larger pipeline will determine how quickly the new map translates into computing capacity.

Data: Figures use the research snapshot checked October 18, 2026. Each chart retains its source’s geography, period and definition. Charts are original graphics based on the cited figures.

title: Next.js ~Prefetching~
description:
In this section, I gann talk about story about App Router that is enabled to use Cache Components + Partial Prefetching (cacheComponents: true and partialPrefetching: true are set in next.config.ts). New app that is created by create-next-app is enabled to use them by default.

Default action

  • Router prefetches each routes of App Shell automatically.
  • App Shaell includes static contents and session data from cookies() and headers().
  • App Shell is a static shell (HTML + RSC payload) in which the URL-dependent portions have been replaced with a fallback.

In case of <Link prefetch={true}>

  • If URL to navigation (searchparamsor dinamic parms)is comfirmed, the root of component tree is re-renderd.
  • And then, three prefetches followed are included.
    • A fallback of <Suspense>: Parts that are not cached remains as a fallback, and are streamed when requesting.
    • use cache: private:Runs in server, and is cached in browser.
    • use cache that is passed as a param of runtime value.

Example

If prefetch a link to /search?q=shoes, searchParams is resolved from link of URL, cached result of search() is prepared before click. Browser re-uses it untill stale time has passed or searchParams has been changed.

Additional Information

  • The cached data that is prefetched is treated as fresh data during term of stale.
  • Refferencies: Adopting Partial Prefetching / Optimizing prefetching / prefetch refference

title: Supabase SECURITY DEFINER RPC Callable by anon: Revoke It
description:
The short version

PostgreSQL grants EXECUTE to the PUBLIC role by default the moment CREATE FUNCTION runs. SECURITY DEFINER is the modifier that makes a function run with the privileges of the role that owns it rather than the role that called it. Create a write function with that modifier and leave it without an explicit REVOKE, and it becomes directly callable from the anon (unauthenticated) or authenticated role through Supabase's PostgREST layer.

  • Even with no GRANT written anywhere, EXECUTE for PUBLIC is there from the start
  • RLS policies on the table are irrelevant, because a SECURITY DEFINER function runs as the owner
  • Closing it means writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC explicitly and re-GRANTing only to the roles that need it

What it looks like

We created a function to push records for asynchronous delivery into a table called sync_outbox. Its definition pins search_path. search_path is the schema search path deciding which schema an unqualified object name resolves from inside a function, and pinning it to public is standard practice to stop a caller rewriting it so that a fake same-named object outside public resolves first.

create table if not exists public.sync_outbox (
  id            uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  kind          text not null,
  ref_id        uuid,
  payload       jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,
  status        text not null default 'pending'
                check (status in ('pending','sent','failed','dead')),
  attempts      int  not null default 0,
  -- (omitted)
);

alter table public.sync_outbox enable row level security;
create policy sync_outbox_staff_read on public.sync_outbox
  for select using (public.is_staff());

create or replace function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(p_kind text, p_ref_id uuid, p_payload jsonb)
returns uuid language sql security definer set search_path = public as $$
  insert into public.sync_outbox (kind, ref_id, payload)
  values (p_kind, p_ref_id, coalesce(p_payload, '{}'::jsonb))
  returning id;
$$;

The table's RLS says only "allow SELECT for the staff role". There is no policy anywhere permitting INSERT for anon. The function was written on the premise that only the app's backend (a cron worker) calls it. Pinning search_path was handled, but that guards a different kind of attack and does nothing for the problem here.

But this function is SECURITY DEFINER, and EXECUTE for PUBLIC is granted by default the instant CREATE FUNCTION runs. Supabase's PostgREST automatically exposes functions in the public schema at /rest/v1/rpc/<name>. It connects as anon or authenticated depending on the JWT the caller sends, and both roles inherit PUBLIC's privileges, so any function not explicitly revoked can be called directly by anyone.

That is what the review flagged. The table's RLS correctly narrowed reads to staff, and the function's execute privilege had never been narrowed at all.

Why

Three facts stack up.

① SECURITY DEFINER runs with the function owner's privileges

Not the calling role's privileges but those of the role that owns the function. That much is as specified.

② CREATE FUNCTION grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC by default

Even with no GRANT ever written, the function is callable by anyone the moment it is created. This is the opposite of tables, whose GRANT is closed by default (nobody can touch them without explicit permission): functions are open by default.

③ PostgREST automatically exposes public schema functions as RPCs

anon / authenticated are the connection roles Supabase provides, and they inherit PUBLIC's privileges as they are. With not a single GRANT on the table, one forgotten REVOKE on a SECURITY DEFINER function leaves a write path open that bypasses RLS entirely.

table GRANT        → closed by default → nobody touches it without explicit permission
function EXECUTE   → open by default   → anyone calls it unless explicitly revoked

This asymmetry is the cause of the oversight. Look only at the table and conclude "RLS protects this", and the hole on the function side goes unseen.

Fixing it

Strip the default PUBLIC privilege and re-allow only the roles that need it.

-- Close the SECURITY DEFINER write function to direct calls from anon/authenticated
-- (via PostgREST). Strip the default PUBLIC EXECUTE, allow only the backend (service_role).
revoke all on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) from public;
grant execute on function public.enqueue_sync_outbox(text, uuid, jsonb) to service_role;

REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC cuts off every inheritance source including anon / authenticated, and GRANT EXECUTE returns it to service_role alone, which actually needs to call it. The function definition itself is unchanged. All that happened is an open door was closed, with no effect on the intended calling path from the backend.

Checking it

Joining pg_proc and pg_roles gives you a function's owner and its execute privileges.

select p.proname, r.rolname as owner, p.proacl
from pg_proc p
join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner
where p.proname = 'enqueue_sync_outbox';

Look for EXECUTE for PUBLIC remaining in proacl (notation like =X/<owner>). Unless this check is run on every new SECURITY DEFINER write function, the same path opens once per function whose revoke was forgotten.

Making it not recur

This fix went in as an addition of revoke / grant to the existing migration file rather than recreating the function. Unless writing REVOKE ALL ... FROM PUBLIC paired with every SECURITY DEFINER function becomes the rule, the next write function added opens the same path.

  • Write REVOKE / GRANT directly beneath the creation SQL for any SECURITY DEFINER write function, so that adding only one of them is structurally impossible
  • Include the function's EXECUTE privilege in the same review item as the table's RLS review (on the premise of the asymmetry: tables closed by default, functions open by default)
  • Verify whether something is anonymously writable by actually querying pg_proc.proacl, not by reading the wording of a policy

However carefully the RLS policies are written, it means nothing if another door — the function's execute privilege — stands open. Another case shaped as an overlooked SECURITY DEFINER is in The function owner and the migration role. That one is about an intended bypass ceasing to work; this one about an unintended bypass working. Both start from the same property: SECURITY DEFINER behaviour is decided by who created the function, not by who called it.

Originally published at tech.rebounder.jp.
