title: How to Get Google Trends Data in Python Without 429 Errors (a pytrends Alternative for 2026)
description:
If you've ever written pytrends.build_payload(...) and seen TooManyRequestsError: The request failed: Google returned a response with code 429, you're not alone. pytrends was archived, Google's official Trends API is still invite-only alpha, and Trends now rate-limits automated traffic aggressively. This tutorial shows a dependable way to pull interest over time, interest by region and related queries for hundreds of keywords from Python, and explains why the usual fixes stop working.

Why pytrends gets 429s

The Google Trends front end calls a handful of internal endpoints:

  1. /trends/api/explore returns a list of "widgets", each with a short-lived token.
  2. /trends/api/widgetdata/multiline returns the timeline.
  3. /trends/api/widgetdata/comparedgeo returns regions.
  4. /trends/api/widgetdata/relatedsearches returns related queries and topics.

Every response starts with an anti-JSON-hijacking prefix ()]}'), and every call needs a valid NID cookie. When you send many requests from one IP, Google returns 429 or redirects you to /sorry/. The common advice of time.sleep(60) plus retries=3 works for ten keywords. It doesn't work for a thousand, and it doesn't work from cloud IPs at all, because those are often blocked from the very first request.

What actually works is:

  • a fresh session (cookie plus new tokens) after each block,
  • rotating egress IPs,
  • per-widget retries, so one failed section doesn't throw away the whole query,
  • honest status reporting, so you know which rows are complete.

You can build that yourself, or use a hosted Actor that already does it.

Option A: a hosted API (about 5 minutes)

Reliable Google Trends API on Apify handles the warmup, proxy rotation, retries and residential fallback. It charges $0.002 per successful query, and failed queries are free. In our 34-query gate runs on Apify, it returned 34 of 34 results in every proxy mode we tested.

Install the client:

pip install apify-client pandas

Run a comparison:

import os
import pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/reliable-google-trends").call(run_input={
    "searchTerms": [
        "chatgpt, claude, gemini",     # one query comparing 3 terms
        "air fryer",                   # a second query
    ],
    "geo": "US",
    "timeframe": "today 12-m",
    "interestOverTime": True,
    "interestByRegion": True,
    "relatedQueries": True,
})

rows = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
for r in rows:
    print(r["keywords"], r["status"], r["errors"])

Turn the timeline into a DataFrame 

def timeline_df(row):
    recs = [{"date": p["time"], **p["values"]} for p in row["interest_over_time"]]
    return pd.DataFrame(recs).set_index("date")

df = timeline_df(rows[0])
print(df.tail())
df.plot(title="ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini, US, 12 months")

Rising queries (breakouts) 

for kw, rq in rows[1]["related_queries"].items():
    for q in rq["rising"][:10]:
        print(kw, "->", q["query"], q["formatted_value"])

Bulk keyword lists

Each searchTerms entry is its own query, so you can pass 500 entries in one run. To set different options for each query, use customQueries:

run_input = {"customQueries": [
    {"keywords": "bitcoin, ethereum", "geo": "GB", "timeframe": "today 5-y", "property": "news"},
    {"keywords": "lofi music", "property": "youtube"},
]}

Every run also writes a RUN_SUMMARY record to the key-value store with the success rate and block counts:

summary = client.key_value_store(run["defaultKeyValueStoreId"]).get_record("RUN_SUMMARY")["value"]
print(summary)

Option B: roll your own (what you need to handle)

If you'd rather run it yourself, here's the minimum:

import httpx, json, time, random

def warm(client):
    # A headers-only request is enough to obtain an NID cookie
    with client.stream("GET", "https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?geo=US") as r:
        pass

def explore(client, kw, geo="US", tf="today 12-m"):
    req = {"comparisonItem": [{"keyword": kw, "geo": geo, "time": tf}],
           "category": 0, "property": ""}
    r = client.get("https://trends.google.com/trends/api/explore",
                   params={"hl": "en-US", "tz": 0, "req": json.dumps(req)})
    if r.status_code == 429:
        raise RuntimeError("blocked")
    return json.loads(r.text[r.text.index("{"):])["widgets"]

From here you still need to: call each widget endpoint with its token; rotate the session and the IP whenever you get a 429 or /sorry/; back off with jitter; and treat related topics as optional (Google often withholds them from sessions it labels USER_TYPE_SCRAPER). In practice the proxy bill and the maintenance cost far more than the code.

Gotchas that apply either way

  • Values are relative (0–100), not search volume. Only compare keywords that were in the same query.
  • More than 5 keywords? Use a shared anchor term in every batch (for example "weather") and rescale each batch against it.
  • Timeframe strings follow the Trends URL format: now 7-d, today 3-m, today 5-y, all, 2024-01-01 2024-06-30.
  • Last data point is often is_partial: true. Drop it before you fit a forecast.

Schedule it

In the Apify console, open the Actor, save your input as a Task, and add a Schedule (for example, daily at 06:00). Then use a webhook or the n8n/Make/Zapier Apify app to push new rows into Google Sheets or your warehouse.

Wrap-up

pytrends taught a generation of analysts to love Trends data, but the 429 wall is real. If you need a few queries a week, a careful DIY script with backoff can be enough. If you need hundreds of keywords on a schedule, without babysitting proxies, try Reliable Google Trends API. It's pay-per-result, and failed queries are free.

title: Delivery Failure Feature Flags: React Next.js Polling Client Authority Boundaries
description:
A React or Next.js feature flags polling client for a customer-support notification service has an awkward constraint: it should reveal delivery-status UI changes quickly, but a stale browser must never decide whether a paid message is sent. That constraint changes the design.

TL;DR: fetch the current flags when the app loads, poll at a modest interval, and use the result only for low-stakes presentation such as hidden navigation, beta badges, and optional panels. Keep billing, authorization, and emergency delivery stops on the server. Polling works here. It isn't an instant kill switch.

Should a frontend feature flag client use polling?

The useful question isn't whether polling is sophisticated. It is whether the maximum stale interval is acceptable for the decision behind the flag.

For an agent-facing badge that labels a new delivery-failure view, 30 seconds may be fine. For a switch that prevents another paid notification from leaving the system, even one stale browser decision is the wrong architecture. The server must enforce that rule at send time. The browser can mirror it, but it cannot own it.

This split also keeps cost attribution credible. A UI flag may reveal an experimental failure dashboard. The event that incurs cost should still be tagged and recorded by the server that performs the send, rather than inferred from whichever flag snapshot happened to be in a tab. Those are different records with different jobs.

There is no realtime push in this setup, so the client loads all current flags once and refreshes them on an interval. There is also no flag evaluation history or change audit trail. If product or compliance needs to answer who changed a rollout, when it changed, or which evaluation produced a send, record those decisions in a separate system.

The smallest implementation I would ship

Do not put a service key in browser JavaScript. The small implementation has two pieces: a server-only loader and a client hook. The loader calls one upstream route, checks every status, and backs off on 429, honoring Retry-After when the server provides it.

The response schema should be validated against the discovery schema during integration. I leave the payload as unknown below because guessing undocumented fields would create a prettier example and a worse client.

const API_ORIGIN = process.env.INFRAI_BASE_URL;
if (!API_ORIGIN) throw new Error("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required");
const FLAGS_URL = new URL("/v1/flags/get_all", API_ORIGIN);

function retryDelay(response: Response, attempt: number): number {
  const retryAfter = response.headers.get("retry-after");
  if (retryAfter && /^\d+$/.test(retryAfter)) {
    return Number(retryAfter) * 1_000;
  }
  return Math.min(1_000 * 2 ** attempt, 30_000);
}

const wait = (milliseconds: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, milliseconds));

export async function loadFlags(): Promise<unknown> {
  const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(FLAGS_URL, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
      cache: "no-store",
    });

    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      await wait(retryDelay(response, attempt));
      continue;
    }
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Flag fetch failed (${response.status}): ${await response.text()}`);
    }
    return response.json() as Promise<unknown>;
  }

  throw new Error("Flag fetch exhausted retries");
}

Expose that loader through an authenticated, same-origin application handler such as /api/flags. That handler should validate the upstream payload and return only the non-sensitive keys the UI is allowed to know. The hook below then owns bootstrap, refresh, cleanup, and the unglamorous failure case.

import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

type UiFlags = Readonly<Record<string, boolean>>;

export function useUiFlags(intervalMs = 30_000) {
  const [flags, setFlags] = useState<UiFlags>({});
  const [error, setError] = useState<Error | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();

    async function refresh() {
      try {
        const response = await fetch("/api/flags", {
          method: "GET",
          signal: controller.signal,
          cache: "no-store",
        });
        if (!response.ok) {
          throw new Error(`Local flag fetch failed (${response.status})`);
        }
        setFlags((await response.json()) as UiFlags);
        setError(null);
      } catch (value) {
        if (!controller.signal.aborted) {
          setError(value instanceof Error ? value : new Error("Flag fetch failed"));
        }
      }
    }

    void refresh();
    const timer = window.setInterval(() => void refresh(), intervalMs);
    return () => {
      controller.abort();
      window.clearInterval(timer);
    };
  }, [intervalMs]);

  return { flags, error };
}

The deliberate behavior is easy to miss: a refresh error preserves the last known flags. For cosmetic UI, that avoids a panel blinking away during a transient network failure. A fresh page starts from {}, so optional features default off until bootstrap completes. Benchmark time-to-first-flag, request volume per active tab, and staleness under background-tab timer throttling before changing the 30-second interval.

Short code. Real boundaries.

Where the vendor choice changes the design

The products aren't interchangeable because their client delivery models and governance surfaces differ. Compare the mechanism you need, not the number of dashboard screenshots.

Option Practical fit Boundary to account for
LaunchDarkly Teams that want mature client SDK behavior and documented streaming or polling controls More platform surface and SDK integration than this tiny read-only client needs
ConfigCat Frontends that benefit from documented auto-poll, lazy-load, or manual-poll modes Still requires a deliberate choice about client-visible flags and stale values
Unleash Teams that want an open-source feature-management stack and a frontend API model Operating or integrating that stack is a larger decision than adding one endpoint
A broad backend API Small teams that want flags beside other backend capabilities under one contract Client delivery is polling; flag audit history, evaluation statistics, and parent-child dependencies are absent

Infrai's concrete advantage is breadth behind one credential: 295 routes across 20 modules use one key, so a team that already needs several backend capabilities can add flags without collecting another authentication scheme.

Infrai's second advantage is a single REST API that can be called directly over HTTP from any language or runtime; no SDK is required. For this notification service, the server loader stays a small fetch call instead of bringing another client library into the build. The public discovery surface is self-describing and requires no key, exposing request and response schemas, billing details, and runnable examples. Every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. That cuts the mechanical work between inspecting the flag contract and making the first call.

The trade-off is sharp. Teams that require streaming client updates, flag dependencies, evaluation analytics, or a built-in audit trail should use a dedicated flag platform.

LaunchDarkly is the strongest fit of these four when controlled rollout telemetry and an established client SDK ecosystem dominate the decision. ConfigCat is appealing when explicit polling modes are the main requirement. Unleash makes sense when deployment control and open-source operation outweigh setup work. A free tier may help a prototype, but it doesn't fix the wrong delivery model.

What I would change at scale

First, collapse browser traffic. Ten thousand active tabs polling every 30 seconds can create roughly 333 requests per second before cache effects, even though the underlying flag set may barely move. Put a short-lived shared cache behind the application endpoint, add random jitter to client intervals, and revalidate once per cache window.

Measure it. Don't tune by vibe.

Second, separate three concepts that often get mashed into one boolean: UI exposure, server authorization, and cost-bearing execution. The first may tolerate a cached flag. The second must use trusted server state. The third needs an immutable event carrying the notification type, provider or route choice, tenant, flag snapshot identifier, and resulting cost metadata available to the sending service. This article doesn't prescribe that event schema because the flag API doesn't define one.

At higher stakes, the polling design stops being the right tool. Emergency shutdowns need a server-enforced control path. Compliance-sensitive rollouts need an audit system. Silent scheduled-job failures need a heartbeat monitor such as Healthchecks; a flag poller cannot tell you that a task never ran.

The same restraint applies to adjacent observability work. Log records may carry trace_id and span_id, but that doesn't create a distributed trace query or span tree. Error capture doesn't imply source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. Sentry is the more direct candidate for error grouping and application exception workflows. Datadog fits a team seeking a wider hosted observability suite, while Grafana fits teams building around dashboards and an observability stack. Better Stack is another dedicated option for logs and uptime. These products don't replace feature flags; they cover limitations that a polling flag client cannot solve.

Decision rule

Use this polling client when the flag changes presentation, a bounded stale window is acceptable, and the server remains authoritative for sensitive actions. Choose a dedicated platform when streaming updates, evaluation statistics, dependencies, or change history are part of the requirement. For delivery failures, keep the dashboard toggle in the browser and the decision to send, suppress, or bill on the server.

That line is boring. It is also testable.

Sources

  • LaunchDarkly, “Streaming”: https://launchdarkly.com/docs/sdk/features/streaming
  • ConfigCat, “Advanced usage”: https://configcat.com/docs/sdk-reference/js/overview/#polling-modes
  • Unleash, “Frontend API”: https://docs.getunleash.io/reference/front-end-api
  • OpenFeature, “Web SDK”: https://openfeature.dev/docs/reference/technologies/client/web/
  • Healthchecks documentation: https://healthchecks.io/docs/
  • Sentry, “Event grouping”: https://docs.sentry.io/concepts/data-management/event-grouping/
  • MDN, “Using the Fetch API”: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API/Using_Fetch

title: Go 1.27 Finds Leaked Goroutines With the Garbage Collector. Here's What It Misses
description:
• Book: The Complete Guide to Go Programming
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

When researchers pointed a prototype detector at one of Uber's production Go services, it found hundreds of previously hidden partial deadlocks: goroutines parked on a channel or a lock that nothing would ever release. Each one kept its stack and everything that stack pointed to. None of them raised an error.

That detector now lives in the Go runtime. Go 1.26 shipped it as an experimental profile behind GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile. Go 1.27, released on 19 August 2026, made the goroutineleak profile generally available and deleted the experiment flag. You read it from runtime/pprof or from the /debug/pprof/goroutineleak endpoint.

The interesting part is how it decides that a goroutine is leaked. There are no timers and no "blocked for more than ten minutes" heuristics. The runtime asks the garbage collector a reachability question. Once you see the question, you can predict which leaks it will report and which ones it will never notice.

What "leaked" means to the runtime

The release notes define it precisely: a leaked goroutine is one "blocked on some concurrency primitive (channels, sync.Mutex, sync.Cond, etc) that cannot possibly become unblocked."

Think about what it takes to wake a goroutine stuck on ch <- v. Some other goroutine has to run <-ch. To do that, it needs a reference to ch. If no goroutine that could ever run again holds a pointer to that channel, the send can never complete. And "who holds a pointer to what" is exactly what the garbage collector computes on every cycle.

The Go blog post on leak profiles states the rule inductively. A goroutine is live if it is not blocked, or if at least one primitive blocking it is referenced by another live goroutine. Everything else is leaked.

The primitives covered are channel sends and receives (nil channels included), blocking select (empty select {} included), sync.Mutex, sync.RWMutex, sync.WaitGroup and sync.Cond, per the same post. A goroutine blocked on file or network IO, a raw system call, or a hand-rolled primitive that is not built on those is never reported.

How the mark phase answers "can anything wake this up?"

In a normal GC cycle, every goroutine's stack is a root. A leak-detection cycle changes that. The design document by Georgian-Vlad Saioc and Milind Chabbi lays out the loop:

  1. Treat only runnable goroutines as goroutine roots.
  2. Mark everything reachable from the roots.
  3. Check each unmarked, blocked goroutine. If the primitive it waits on was marked, some live goroutine can reach it, so this goroutine is "eventually runnable." Add it as a root.
  4. Resume marking from step 2. Stop when no new goroutine gets promoted.
  5. Every blocked goroutine that never became a root is leaked. Mark from those too, so the heap ends up marked the same way a regular cycle would mark it, then sweep as usual.

That final step matters for what you expect in production. The profile reports leaks; it does not reclaim them. The blog says the last round lets the GC "mark all the memory it would have marked during a regular run."

There is one wiring problem the loop has to solve. A blocked goroutine is attached to its channel through a sudog, the runtime's record for "a g in a wait list." In runtime2.go, the sudog's channel field is a maybeTraceableChan and its data field is a maybeTraceablePtr. Sudogs are reachable from the global goroutine list and the semaphore table, according to the design doc. If the GC traced those fields normally, every channel with a waiter would be marked through the waiter itself, and nothing would ever look leaked.

So the pointer is stored twice: once as a uintptr (vu, the "source of truth") and once as an unsafe.Pointer (vp, "for liveness only"). When a leak-detection cycle starts, the runtime makes the vp half of every sudog untraceable, so the GC cannot follow the pointer while the address stays recorded. When the cycle ends, it makes them traceable again. The waiter still knows which channel it is parked on, and that knowledge no longer counts as a reason to keep the channel alive.

The blocked goroutine's own stack gets the same treatment by construction. It is not a root until it gets promoted, so the ch variable sitting in its closure does not mark the channel either. A goroutine that survives the whole loop ends up in a new status, _Gleaked, which runtime2.go documents as "a leaked goroutine caught by the GC."

A leak it catches

Here is the classic timeout leak. The worker sends on an unbuffered channel, the caller gives up first, and the send blocks forever.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "os"
    "runtime/pprof"
    "time"
)

func fetch(ctx context.Context) error {
    ch := make(chan error) // unbuffered: the bug
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        ch <- nil // nobody receives after a timeout
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-ch:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

func main() {
    for range 3 {
        ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(
            context.Background(), 10*time.Millisecond)
        _ = fetch(ctx)
        cancel()
    }
    time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond) // senders block

    p := pprof.Lookup("goroutineleak")
    if p == nil {
        fmt.Println("needs Go 1.27, or 1.26 with " +
            "GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile")
        return
    }
    p.WriteTo(os.Stdout, 1)
}

On Go 1.27, go run . is enough. On Go 1.26, build with GOEXPERIMENT=goroutineleakprofile go run .. Writing the profile triggers a leak-detecting GC cycle and waits for it, as the design doc describes, and debug=1 gives you the text format with function names and line numbers.

Walk through it with the loop above. After each fetch returns, main's frame no longer holds ch. The only remaining references live in the sender's closure and in its sudog. The sender is blocked, so its stack is not a root. The sudog's channel pointer is hidden for the cycle. Nothing marks the channel, so none of the three senders gets promoted, and all three should land in the profile with stacks pointing at the ch <- nil line. I haven't run this exact snippet, so treat that as what the mechanism predicts, not pasted output.

The fix is the one the Go blog gives for its own timeout example: give the channel a buffer of size 1. Then make(chan error, 1) lets the late sender drop its value and exit.

A leak it cannot see

Now move the channel to package level.

var results = make(chan error) // package-level

func fetchGlobal(ctx context.Context) error {
    go func() {
        time.Sleep(50 * time.Millisecond)
        results <- nil // same leak as before
    }()
    select {
    case err := <-results:
        return err
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }
}

The leak is the same: every timed-out call can strand a sender. Sharing the channel also adds a second bug, because a later call can now receive an earlier call's stale result. The profile stays quiet.

Package-level variables are always roots. In step 2 the GC marks results straight from the global, the blocked senders look "eventually runnable" in step 3, and they never reach the leaked set. The Go 1.26 release notes spell this out: "the runtime may fail to identify leaks caused by blocking on concurrency primitives reachable through global variables or the local variables of runnable goroutines."

The second half of that sentence catches more real code than the first. A long-lived worker goroutine that keeps a map of per-request channels in a local variable, and never reads some of them, keeps every one of those channels marked. So does a struct of channels hanging off a server object that a running goroutine still references. The design doc puts it plainly: the detector's "effectiveness is reduced the more heap resources are over-exposed in memory."

That gives you a design rule the detector rewards. Create channels as close to their use as you can, scope them to one request or one call, and do not park them in registries that outlive the work. The narrower the reachability, the more the GC can prove.

Running it in production and in tests

If a service already imports net/http/pprof, Go 1.27 adds the endpoint with no code change. The blog's workflow, with the address left as a placeholder:

# ADDR: wherever net/http/pprof listens in your service
curl "$ADDR/debug/pprof/goroutineleak" > leak.prof
go tool pprof leak.prof

Inside pprof, list fetch (or whatever function spawned the goroutine) shows the blocked line in context.

On cost, the Go 1.26 notes say the feature is designed "to not incur any additional run-time overhead unless it is actively in-use." When you do request it, there is a worst case. The blog describes a leak-free "daisy chain" where runnable G0 references the primitive blocking G1, G1 references the one blocking G2, and so on. Each link only proves live after the previous one, which serializes marking and gives O(n²) steps for one GC cycle, with n the number of goroutines. The blog's answer is to profile periodically, every 4 hours in its example, since a leak that can be observed once stays observable.

The design doc calls the approach "theoretically sound, i.e., there are no false positives," and the blog describes it as "precise" with "little-to-no false positives," so treat a goroutine in the report as a strong signal that it is stuck. The detector also only sees leaks that have already happened. The blog recommends pairing it with goleak in test suites, which flags goroutines still running when a test ends, and with testing/synctest, whose fake clock lets a timeout path run deterministically.

When the profile comes back empty and memory still climbs, check your package-level channels first.

If this was useful

The leak profile makes sense once you know what the runtime does underneath your code: how goroutines park on channels and what the garbage collector treats as a root. The Complete Guide to Go Programming covers the runtime and its concurrency primitives with that picture in mind, including the channel and context patterns that keep a goroutine from getting stranded in the first place.

title: Agent Mail: Tencent Just Gave AI Agents Their Own Mailbox
description:
Agent Mail: Tencent Gives AI Agents Their Own Mailbox (@agent.qq.com), Open Source & Free in Beta | Lieke AI

  • @agent.qq.comDedicated agent mailbox Apache-2.0Open source 50/dayBeta send quota 6+ platformsMajor agents supported

In one line: why AI agents need their own mailbox

Two old paths for letting agents handle email — grant access to your personal inbox (privacy risk) or run your own SMTP (ops cost). Tencent QQ Mail's answer: give the agent a digital identity independent from humans: an isolated xxx@agent.qq.com address that can never touch your personal QQ/WeChat mail.
Internal beta opened June 23, 2026. Source code is Apache-2.0 on GitHub (Tencent/AgentlyMail); official site: agent.qq.com.

3-step setup, tested in ~5 minutes

Let the agent install it: ask your agent to read https://agent.qq.com/doc/cli-setup.md and follow the steps to install & configure Agent Mail CLI.

  • It runs automatically:npm install -g @tencent-qqmail/agently-clinpx skills add Tencent/AgentlyMail -g -yagently-cli auth loginOpen the printed authorization link in a browser.

  • Scan to authorize: after OAuth, run agently-cli +me — it returns xxx@agent.qq.com when configured.

Works with WorkBuddy, Claude Code, Cursor, Kimi Work, Doubao, Codex, Hermes and other mainstream agents. Read, send, search, attachments and live watch — all via one CLI.

Security: three layers built for agent workloads

Layer What it does
Physical isolation Agent gets a fresh data space; even a compromised agent cannot reach personal mail
Two-stage confirmation Send/reply/forward/delete requires the agent to generate a summary + confirmation token, then the user approves
Prompt-injection defense Malicious instructions inside inbound mail are treated as plain text, never as system commands

Six practical use cases (hands-on)

  • Invoice auto-expense: agent extracts amount/tax ID and files reimbursement reports

  • Newsletter digest: forward newsletters, get a daily AI summary

  • Order reconciliation: agent pulls order numbers into your sheets

  • A2A business email: procurement agent ↔ supplier agent, fully auditable

  • Verification-code relay: use Agent Mail for signups, agent auto-fills codes

  • AI job applications: dedicated address for resumes and interview scheduling

Competitive landscape: the agent-mail race

Agently Mail (Tencent) AgentMail (YC) Mail4Agent
Integration WeChat scan + CLI API + SDK API-first
Pricing Free in beta 3 mailboxes free, $20-200/mo paid Not public
Security Two-stage confirm + injection defense (unique) DIY DIY
China access No VPN needed VPN needed Fair
Ecosystem CLI + Skill path Python/TS SDK, MCP Server, Webhook Multi-framework

Bottom line: Agently Mail is the lowest-friction option for CN developers; AgentMail suits large overseas API/SDK deployments.

Beta limitations (stated honestly): 50 sends/day, 1GB per address — not production-ready until quotas open up; official Skill has Windows HTML-email layout issues (community fixes exist); A2A cross-domain protocol not yet documented; mailbox prefix can be changed only once.

Before your agent can run 24/7, you need reliable cloud compute

Agently Mail is just the first piece of agent infrastructure. The real backbone is elastic cloud servers that keep agents online around the clock. Lieke AI helps you get official promotional pricing.

Check Alibaba Cloud ECS deals →

FAQ

Does authorization leak my QQ password? No. It uses the standard OAuth device-code flow; the CLI never stores your QQ password.
Install fails or is slow? Make sure npm can reach the public registry; if the auth link won't open, check access to agent.qq.com.
How does this differ from AgentMail / Mail4Agent? Same category, different positioning: Agently Mail focuses on China accessibility + CLI/Skill + unique security; AgentMail targets overseas API/SDK scale.
Production-ready? Beta quotas are tight (50/day, 1GB). Start with daily reports and newsletter digests; wait for quota release for production scale.

title: RingBreaker: An AI Agent That Breaks UPI Mule Rings on FalkorDB
description:
RingBreaker is an AI agent that investigates UPI mule rings inside a FalkorDB graph, freezes the ring only after a human approves, and then proves with one more graph query that no money path is left.

  • Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com
  • Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker
  • Built for: Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (FalkorDB), Track 01: Agents That Act on Connected Data. Solo, built Oct 15 to 18, 2026.
  • The loop in one line: investigate → verdict → human approval → freeze → verify ("13 open routes, then 0").

The problem

A scam victim pays a "KYC update" fee over UPI. Within hours the money has hopped through four accounts and is gone.

  • Each hop looks harmless. A Rs 8,000 transfer between two accounts is normal on its own.
  • The pattern lives in the connections. Brand-new accounts, minimal KYC, shared phones and devices, money fanning in and out within minutes.
  • Tables hide it. Following money four hops deep in SQL means four self-joins, and the query has to know the shape in advance.
  • Most fraud demos stop at "flagged". Nobody acts on the alert, and nobody checks that the action worked.

In simple words

Think of a bucket brigade passing stolen water down a line of people. You could question each person on their own, and each one would only say "I passed a bucket."

  • RingBreaker looks at the whole line at once: who passed to whom, who stands on the same spot (a shared phone or device), and where the water ends up.
  • It then asks a person: "Remove these five from the line?"
  • After they say yes, it checks again that no bucket can still reach the end. That last check is the point of the project.

The stack

  • FalkorDB: the only datastore. Accounts, transactions, devices, alerts, verdicts and the audit trail all live in one graph. Docker locally, FalkorDB Cloud in production.
  • Node.js + Express: the API, the agent loop and the tools, using the official falkordb client.
  • Groq (groq-sdk) with function calling: openai/gpt-oss-120b as the main model, qwen/qwen3.8-27b as a fallback when the daily quota runs out.
  • React + Vite + react-force-graph-2d: the three-pane dashboard and the live graph canvas.
  • Server-Sent Events: each tool call streams to the browser as it happens.
  • Render: one Docker image serves the API and the built UI on a single URL.

The agent reaches FalkorDB only through read-only tools; the single write path runs from the API after a person approves.

How it actually works, step by step

  1. You click an alert, for example a victim complaint: "paid ~25,000 for a fake KYC update; money moved on within hours."
  2. The API starts the agent and streams every step over SSE. The agent picks graph tools (get_alert, money_trail, fan_stats, shared_identity, expand_ring and others). Each one runs a parameterized Cypher query.
  3. The canvas lights up the exact nodes and edges each query touched. A "Show Cypher" toggle reveals the query behind every step.
  4. The agent submits a structured JSON verdict: ring_confirmed, suspicious or benign, ring members with roles (victim, layer, collector, cashout), evidence citing graph facts, and recommended freezes.
  5. The server validates the verdict and saves it as a Case node in the graph.
  6. You review the evidence, untick anything you disagree with, type your name and press Approve freeze.
  7. The server freezes the approved accounts, writes an audit edge for each, re-runs the verify query and shows the result, for example 13 open routes → 0. The alert then moves to Closed.

The agent proposes; a person decides; the graph proves it.

The dashboard: alert queue with live status on the left, the graph canvas in the middle, the agent trace on the right, and the four-stage tracker in the header.

Mid-investigation on ALT002 (Ring B, the device farm). Every account, device and phone the agent touched is on the canvas, with its latest step glowing. The trace shows each tool call, its arguments and timing, and the switch to the fallback model when the daily quota ran out.

The graph and the agent's tools

One FalkorDB graph, ring, with 7,847 nodes and 25,962 edges, all synthetic and generated from a seeded random generator so every demo is reproducible.

  • Nodes: Account (1,911), VPA, Device, Phone, Alert (7), plus Case nodes written at run time.
  • Edges: SENT (20,007, one per transaction, with amount and ts), USES_DEVICE, LINKED_PHONE, HAS_VPA, ABOUT, and the audit edges INCLUDES {role} and ACTION {type, ts, approved_by}.
  • Transactions are edges, not nodes. A trail of N transfers is an N-hop path, so -[:SENT*1..4]-> answers "where did the money go?" in one query.
  • Planted scenarios:
    • Ring A, a layering chain: 4 victims → 3 first-layer mules → 2 second-layer mules → 1 collector → 1 cash-out, with amounts split into chunks minutes apart.
    • Ring B, a device farm: 6 accounts on 2 devices and 1 phone, each collecting small payments from many senders, then sweeping to one account.
    • Ring C, a decoy: 3 accounts on a shared device but with no money link. The right answer is "suspicious, monitor", not a freeze.
    • Benign look-alikes: a busy merchant with high fan-in, and a family sharing one phone. Neither may be flagged.
  • Tools the model can call (read-only):
Tool What it asks the graph
money_trail Follow money forward or backward up to N hops, with all(r IN relationships(p) WHERE r.ts >= $since) on every edge
shared_identity Who else uses this device or phone: `(a)-[:USES_DEVICE\
{% raw %}fan_stats In/out degree, totals and pass-through ratio
expand_ring Grow a candidate ring along money and identity links at once (UNION ALL)
account_profile Age, KYC level, and how many accounts share each device or phone
get_alert The alert and its target account
run_readonly_cypher A guarded free-form fallback for anything else
  • Every tool starts from an indexed lookup (Account.id, Device.id, Phone.number, VPA.handle, Alert.id, Case.id). Queries take 5 to 30 ms locally and 230 to 470 ms from Render to FalkorDB Cloud.
  • Every tool call emits a trace event: tool, arguments, the exact Cypher, a one-line summary, and the node and edge IDs it touched. The canvas highlights from those IDs.

Act, then prove it

Flagging is half the job. RingBreaker acts on the verdict and then checks its own work.

  • The model cannot freeze anything. Action tools (create_case, freeze_account, verify_cutoff, close_case, generate_report) are never offered to the LLM. Only the approval API calls them.
  • The approval gate is one Cypher statement. It freezes an account only if the case proposed it and it is still active, and writes the audit edge in the same query: 
MATCH (c:Case {id: $case_id}), (a:Account {id: $account_id})
WHERE $account_id IN c.proposed_freezes AND a.status = 'active'
SET a.status = 'frozen'
CREATE (c)-[:ACTION {type: 'freeze', ts: $now, approved_by: $approved_by, reason: $reason}]->(a)
  • Verify counts open money routes into the ring's end account that avoid every frozen account: 
MATCH p = (src:Account)-[:SENT]->(m:Account)-[:SENT*0..5]->(t:Account)
WHERE m.id IN $ring AND t.id IN $terminals AND NOT src.id IN $ring
  AND none(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.status = 'frozen')
RETURN count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id]) AS routes
  • It counts distinct routes, not raw paths. Each transaction is its own edge, so split payments multiply paths: Ring A has 1,488 raw paths but 13 distinct routes. After the freeze: 0.
  • A leak check stops the proof from fooling itself. It counts ring money that already reached an active account the case never named. The cut-off counts as verified only when routes and leaks are both 0.
  • Alerts close themselves from graph state. Each alert shows Open, Awaiting approval, Closed, Needs review, Monitoring or Dismissed, derived from its latest case.
  • A report is generated from graph data only: accounts and roles, the agent's evidence, every approved action with approver and time, and the live verify result.

Safety: an agent that writes Cypher on untrusted data

The agent reads text it cannot trust and writes queries, so safety lives in code, not in the prompt.

  • Reads physically cannot write. Every read tool runs as GRAPH.RO_QUERY, so FalkorDB itself refuses any write. A test bypasses our own guard and confirms the database still blocks it.
  • Free-form Cypher passes a guard (guard.js): it rejects CREATE, MERGE, DELETE, SET, REMOVE, DROP, CALL, LOAD, FOREACH and multiple statements, enforces a LIMIT of at most 100, and runs with a server-side timeout.
  • Every query is parameterized. Values arrive as $parameters, never spliced into query text, including the seed script.
  • Verdicts are grounded. The validator rejects ring members no tool returned, freezes on victims or non-members, and any freeze on a verdict weaker than ring_confirmed. An invalid verdict gets one retry.
  • Graph text is data. Holder names, UPI handles and alert text are marked untrusted in the system prompt. Even a successful prompt injection could not freeze anything: the model has no action tools.
  • Hard limits per run: 10 model steps, a 10-minute timeout, a 120K-token cap, and one investigation at a time.
  • Public demo hygiene: investigations and approvals need a demo passcode, resetting the graph needs an admin secret, both compared in constant time. No secrets in the repo.

Built to run on a free tier

The whole project runs on Groq's free tier: about 8K tokens per minute and 200K tokens per day, per model. The agent loop is designed around that.

  • Compact tool results. Tools return summaries and distinct transactions, not hundreds of near-duplicate paths.
  • Context trimming. Once the prompt passes about 5.5K tokens, older tool results shrink to their one-line summaries.
  • Model fallback mid-run. When the main model's daily quota runs out, the loop switches to the fallback model and continues from the same step. The trace shows the switch.
  • Self-adjusting requests. If a model rejects a request as too large (Qwen allows 7K input and 1K output tokens per minute), the loop trims the context or lowers the output cap and redoes the step.
  • Malformed tool calls are retried with a hint to send shorter arguments, so a truncated verdict does not fail the same way twice.
  • The report is a template, not LLM prose. It costs zero tokens and can only contain facts that are in the graph.
  • Cost of one investigation: roughly 18K to 35K tokens and 1 to 5 minutes, almost all of it waiting on rate limits. The graph queries are a rounding error.

What fought back

  • The proof could fool itself. In the final test the agent stopped at the collector and missed the cash-out account, which still held Rs 65,202. Verify still said "11 routes → 0". The route count only looks at paths through the case's own members, so freezing everything proposed always gives 0. The fix: a leak check that asks whether ring money already sits in an active account the case never named. That run now reads "Routes cut, but money leaked" instead of a false pass.
  • One transaction, one edge, hundreds of paths. Split payments multiply paths fast: 1,488 raw paths for 13 real routes. Counting distinct sequences of account IDs (count(DISTINCT [n IN nodes(p) | n.id])) made the number something a reviewer can read.
  • Some things cannot be Cypher parameters. Edge direction, variable-length bounds and labels cannot be $params. money_trail pre-builds one query per (direction, hops) pair from constants, so user input never becomes query text.
  • Epoch milliseconds vs date strings. The agent compared ts to '2026-10-07' in free-form Cypher and got empty results. The tool description now says times are epoch ms.
  • Free-tier walls. A daily quota that runs out mid-investigation, a fallback model with 1K output tokens per minute, and verdicts cut off mid-word (tool_use_failed). Each became a handled case in the loop, with a test that replays the real error.
  • Prompting is not free. Telling the agent to also trace forward from the collector raised Ring A recall from 0.57 to 0.71. A stricter "run both trails" rule made it loop until the step cap, so it was dropped. Every prompt change was measured, not assumed.

What it does now

npm run eval runs the agent on all 7 alerts and scores it against a ground-truth file. 7 of 7 verdicts correct, 0 unsafe freezes: no victim, merchant or family account was ever recommended for freezing.

Alert Scenario Expected Got Freeze precision / recall
ALT001 Ring A complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 0.71
ALT002 Ring B complaint ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT003 Ring B fan-in ring_confirmed ring_confirmed 1.00 / 1.00
ALT004 Ring C decoy suspicious suspicious, no freeze
ALT005 Merchant benign benign
ALT006 Family benign benign
ALT007 Noise benign benign
  • Live run on the deployed site: Ring A's complaint named all 8 accounts (the victim plus all 7 mules, including the cash-out); after approval, verify went from 13 open routes to 0 with no leak, and the alert closed.
  • 53 automated tests: the Cypher guard, the read-only backstop, the approval gate, verify and the leak check, the passcode, verdict validation, and every free-tier failure mode, replayed with a fake LLM client so they cost no tokens.
  • The dashboard: an alert queue with live status, the graph canvas with role-colored rings and a step-by-step HUD, the agent trace with each step's Cypher, the verdict card with a confidence meter and run stats, and a before/after proof card.

The live demo after approval: Ring A frozen (red) with roles on the canvas, each proposed freeze and its reason, and the proof card: 13 open routes before the freeze, 0 after, no leak.

Who this is for

Fraud and risk teams at banks, payment apps and UPI providers who already get alerts but spend hours tracing each one by hand. It is also a pattern for anyone building agents that act on data: let the model read and recommend, keep writes behind a human and a single audited query, and end every action with a query that proves it worked.

What I learned

  • Graphs make the question short. "Where did this money go, four hops out, after Tuesday?" is one Cypher pattern, not four joins.
  • Put safety in the database, not the prompt. GRAPH.RO_QUERY is a stronger guarantee than any instruction to "only read".
  • Verify the verifier. A proof that only checks the agent's own case can pass while money sits in an account the agent missed.
  • Give the model less, not more. Compact tool results, one-line summaries and a short required checklist beat long instructions on a small token budget.
  • Measure every prompt change. A rule that sounded better made the agent worse; only the eval showed it.

What's next

  • Upstream leak detection: flag a missed mule that feeds money into the ring, not only one that receives from it.
  • Streaming ingestion: real-time transaction feeds into FalkorDB, so investigations start the moment a pattern appears.
  • Real integrations: bank and UPI freeze APIs behind the same approval gate.

Try it

Needs Node.js 22.9+, Docker and a free Groq API key.

git clone https://github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker && cd ringbreaker
cp .env.example .env               # add GROQ_API_KEY
docker compose up -d               # FalkorDB on :6379, Browser on http://localhost:3000
(cd server && npm install) && (cd web && npm install)
npm run generate && npm run seed   # seeded synthetic graph into FalkorDB
(cd server && npm start)           # API on http://localhost:8080
(cd web && npm run dev)            # UI on http://localhost:5173

Open the UI, click ALT001, approve the freeze, and watch the open routes drop to 0.

Disclosures: all data is synthetic; no real people, accounts or UPI handles. Built with help from an AI coding assistant; I reviewed the code and can explain every part of the architecture and its safety model.

Built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents by FalkorDB, Track 01. Live demo: ringbreaker-5o88.onrender.com · Code: github.com/Jeevesh2605/ringbreaker

title: Introducing @zervonex/baileys - A Tailored Fork of the Baileys WhatsApp Web API
description:
As developers working heavily with automation, we often rely on the incredible WhiskeySockets/Baileys library to interact directly with the WhatsApp Web API.

However, maintaining long-term stability, implementing niche patches, and ensuring rapid upstream syncs for specific organizational workloads can sometimes require custom overrides.

To solve this for our production pipelines, we have officially published and open-sourced our custom-tailored ecosystem variant: @zervonex/baileys.

🚀 Why Use @zervonex/baileys

The @zervonex/baileys package is a dedicated, scoped fork built to ensure predictability, seamless integration, and stable session management in Node.js environments. By utilizing a scoped npm package under @zervonex, we ensure that updates are controlled, thoroughly tested, and safe from unexpected upstream breaking changes.

Key Highlights:

  • Fully Scoped & Managed: Eliminates package naming collisions and guarantees clean dependency trees.
  • Production Ready: Built out of a necessity for reliable, automated multi-device connectivity.
  • Seamless Transition: Maintains structural compatibility with the core Baileys API so you don't have to rewrite your codebase.

🛠️ Quick Start & Installation

You can integrate our fork into your Node.js or TypeScript application instantly using your preferred package manager.

# Using npm
npm install @zervonex/baileys

# Using yarn
yarn add @zervonex/baileys

# Using pnpm
pnpm add @zervonex/baileys

Basic Initialization Example 

async function connectToWhatsApp() {
    // Dynamically importing the modules using await import
    const { default: makeWASocket, useMultiFileAuthState } = await import("@zervonex/baileys");

    const { state, saveCreds } = await useMultiFileAuthState('auth_info_zervonex');

    const sock = makeWASocket({
        auth: state,
        printQRInTerminal: true
    });

    sock.ev.on('creds.update', saveCreds);

    sock.ev.on('connection.update', (update) => {
        const { connection, lastDisconnect } = update;
        if(connection === 'close') {
            console.log('Connection closed, reconnecting...');
            connectToWhatsApp();
        } else if(connection === 'open') {
            console.log('Opened connection successfully via @zervonex/baileys!');
        }
    });
}

connectToWhatsApp();

📦 View on Registry

Take a look at the live release, version history, and dependencies directly over on the npm registry:
👉 View @zervonex/baileys on npm

We are actively looking forward to refining this fork. Feel free to leave a comment below if you have any feature suggestions or compatibility questions!

title: Node.js Error Alerting by Polling Metrics APIs (with 429 Retry Backoff)
description:
For a nightly Node.js pipeline, use a small cron worker to poll error search or metrics, retry HTTP 429 responses with bounded exponential backoff, and suppress duplicate notifications inside an incident window. Choose a specialist alerting stack instead when you need managed threshold evaluation, notification routing, or traces.

TL;DR: polling is a sound alerting shape only if three invariants hold: the same failed run cannot page twice, rate limiting delays an evaluation rather than dropping it, and a separate heartbeat detects the run that never emitted an error. Infrai fits the query side of this design because it exposes observability through a plain REST API, so the worker needs no vendor SDK. Infrai uses a single API key across 295 routes in 20 modules, reducing credential sprawl if this pipeline later calls another backend capability. It does not provide native alert delivery or threshold routing; the worker owns that control loop.

This distinction matters during incident reconstruction. “The job failed” is an alert. “Which tenant, import stage, attempt, and pipeline run failed together?” is a logging question. Preserve those fields as structured data and make pipeline_run_id the deduplication anchor. Otherwise the first page becomes an invitation to search loose strings at 03:00.

How should a Node.js cron worker poll an error or metrics API?

There are two viable architectures.

The first is a polling control loop: the Node.js job writes structured errors and metrics, then a separate cron worker queries them. That worker classifies the result, acquires a dedupe key such as nightly-import:2026-10-09:failed, and calls the team's notification system. Infrai is a deliberate option for the query service in this shape. Its API is genuinely self-describing, and its public discovery surface requires no key; each documented capability includes request and response schemas plus runnable examples. That is useful here because the filters for logs search and metrics query are not fully declared in discovery parameters: start with a simple query, inspect the documented schema and returned envelope, and promote a filter to production only after that probe succeeds.

The invariants are operational, not cosmetic:

  • Evaluation has a stable time window with a small overlap, so a delayed event is not lost at the boundary.
  • Dedupe state outlives all retries and is keyed by the pipeline run, not by the poll attempt.
  • A 429 advances the retry schedule; it never becomes “no failures found.”
  • Alert delivery is recorded separately from query success.
  • A heartbeat deadline covers silent non-execution.

The second architecture sends metrics to Prometheus, evaluates rules there, and routes alerts through Grafana Alerting or another alert manager; Sentry can own application error grouping and richer error investigation, while Healthchecks watches the cron deadline. This has more components, but notification policy, grouping, and escalation live in systems designed for them. Its invariant is different: instrumentation labels must remain bounded, and alert state must survive individual application processes. Prometheus explicitly warns against high-cardinality labels. A tenant ID or run ID belongs in logs, not in a metric label that grows without limit.

My decision rule: use the polling architecture when the team already has a notification destination and needs a narrow failure detector over searchable structured events. Use the specialist architecture when paging policy itself is production infrastructure.

Build the poller as a control loop

Do not place the poll inside the nightly job. A process cannot report that it was never scheduled, and a crash can interrupt its own last notification. Run the poller independently, a few minutes after the expected completion time, with its own timeout and durable dedupe storage.

I would try Infrai for the error-search or metrics-query leg when a team wants one plain HTTP integration across backend capabilities and does not want another client library lifecycle in the cron worker. It uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which lets this worker reuse the same credential and interface conventions if the pipeline later needs another backend capability. The supporting advantage is discovery: every documented capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages, so the worker can validate the capability schema before rollout instead of pinning an SDK merely to issue a query. The limitation is firm. It does not own threshold rules, phone, SMS, webhook routing, uptime checks, distributed trace trees, source-map decoding, crash symbolication, or session replay. If managed paging policy or specialist error investigation is the requirement, Infrai is not a fit; use Grafana Alerting or Sentry for that responsibility.

The following Go program is intentionally limited to transport behavior. It calls the verified error search route and lets a separate classifier consume the successful JSON body. That separation prevents an undeclared filter shape or response assumption from getting buried in retry code.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "math/rand"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queryURL := "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/errors/search"
    if apiKey == "" {
        log.Fatal("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()

    body, err := queryWithBackoff(ctx, http.DefaultClient, queryURL, apiKey, 5)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(string(body))
}

func queryWithBackoff(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, queryURL, apiKey string, maxAttempts int) ([]byte, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, queryURL, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query transport: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<20))
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read response: %w", readErr)
        }

        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return body, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("query status %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if attempt == maxAttempts-1 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("rate limited after %d attempts: %s", maxAttempts, body)
        }

        delay := retryDelay(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt)
        timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
        select {
        case <-ctx.Done():
            timer.Stop()
            return nil, ctx.Err()
        case <-timer.C:
        }
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("unreachable retry state")
}

func retryDelay(retryAfter string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    base := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    return base + time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(base/2)+1))
}

Five attempts produce base delays of 1, 2, 4, and 8 seconds before the final request, with jitter unless the server supplies Retry-After. Those numbers are an example policy, not a service guarantee. Bound the entire operation with a deadline, as the sample does. A retry loop without a wall-clock budget can make a late alert indistinguishable from a missing one.

Keep dedupe outside this process. A unique row in Postgres or an atomic insert in the team's existing durable store is enough: key it by rule, pipeline run, and alert state; record the delivery result; expire it only after the incident window. In-memory maps reset during deploys. Bad choice.

Compare the ownership boundaries

Tool choice follows the failure you need to explain. These products overlap, but they do not erase one another's boundaries.

Option Strong fit in this pipeline Boundary to accept
REST query service Error or metrics queries from a small cron worker; public discovery helps verify schemas The team implements evaluation, dedupe, delivery, and heartbeat monitoring
Prometheus Numeric time-series collection and rule evaluation High-cardinality run or tenant identifiers should stay out of labels; logs remain necessary for reconstruction
Grafana Alerting Central alert rules, grouping, and contact-point workflows over supported data sources Adds an alerting control plane that must be configured and operated
Sentry Application error grouping and investigation It is a specialist error workflow, not proof that a scheduled job ran at all
Healthchecks Dead-man-switch monitoring for a cron job that missed its expected ping It detects absence; structured logs still explain the failed stage and affected data

Sentry is the better choice when developers need specialist error investigation beyond a query result. Prometheus plus Grafana Alerting is the better choice when metric rules, pending durations, and managed routing are central requirements. Healthchecks belongs beside either architecture for missed runs. For JVM services that feed the same B2B pipeline, a Logback appender is another ingestion boundary, not an alert manager; keep that distinction visible when a mixed-language estate shares an incident process.

There is also a privacy and retention boundary to assess before standardizing. The REST option described here does not expose per-user log deletion, bulk export, or subscription interfaces, and retention or cold-storage configuration is not exposed. A system with strict deletion or archival workflows needs another log store or an upstream data-minimization design. Logs can carry trace_id and span_id for correlation, but that is not a distributed trace query or span tree.

Verify, page, and roll back

Ship the detector in shadow mode first. For three scheduled executions, store its decision without sending a notification. Seed one known failed run, one successful run, and one run that emits nothing. The failed run should yield one incident key even when the polling window overlaps; the successful run should stay quiet; the absent run should be caught by the heartbeat system rather than the log query.

Then force the transport cases. Return a 429 with Retry-After in a staging proxy and confirm the next request waits. Return a non-429 4xx and confirm the response body reaches the operator rather than being treated as an empty result. Stop the worker mid-retry and restart it. Durable dedupe should prevent a second delivery.

Page on evidence, not on parser accidents.

The rollback is uncomplicated: disable notification delivery while leaving decision records enabled, then revert the rule version or query shape. Do not delete dedupe rows during rollback; doing so can replay the same incident when the old rule returns. If a production query begins returning an unexpected shape, fail the evaluation visibly and keep the previous known-good rule active. “Zero matching failures” is a business result. “Could not evaluate” is an operational failure, and those states must never share a code path.

Finally, put four links in the runbook: the query discovery page used to validate the request, the poller's last-success record, the dedupe record, and the heartbeat status. An incident commander should be able to answer, in order, whether the job ran, whether it failed, whether the detector evaluated, and whether a notification was delivered.

If this ownership boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's public discovery documentation and validate the chosen query schema before enabling delivery.

References

  • Prometheus instrumentation practices
  • Grafana Alerting documentation
  • Sentry Alerts documentation
  • Healthchecks documentation
  • Logback appenders manual
  • Infrai discovery: errors.capture
  • Infrai documentation

title: EIA's January "forecast" of this year's solar additions was the developers' plan, 2020-2024
description:
Every January EIA publishes two numbers for how much utility-scale solar will be added that year. Today in Energy reports what developers plan, from the EIA-860M inventory. The Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), the same month, says what EIA forecasts. Last week I compared the two for 2025 and called it one year, not a track record. So I pulled the archived STEO PDFs for 2020-2025, wrote four predictions down before reading the 2020-2022 editions, and scored both numbers against what EIA's own Form EIA-860 finally recorded.

For solar in 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 the two numbers were the same number. The STEO's own capacity table implies same-year solar additions of 13.5, 15.4, 21.4 and 36.4 GW. The developers' plans were 13.5, 15.4, 21.5 and 36.4 GW. Wind agreed within 0.3 GW in 2020-2023. The STEO carried the EIA-860M schedule into its forecast rather than discounting it.

What the scoring shows:

  • Neither was better. Over 12 solar and wind cases, 2020-2025, the STEO was closer to the final in 5, the plan in 6, with one tie. Mean solar error: STEO 6.0 GW, plan 5.7 GW.
  • Both overshot solar almost every year. The plan was above the final in all six years, the STEO in five. In 2022 both were about 10 GW too high (21 GW expected, 11.1 GW built).
  • EIA departed from the schedule three times. 2024 wind: STEO 7.0 GW against 8.2 planned, 5.2 built, so the discount helped. 2025 solar: 25.7 against 32.5, 29.5 built, so it over-corrected and 2025 is the only year the STEO was under the final. 2023 solar: the STEO was above the plan (31.7 against 29.1; 18.9 built).
  • All four pre-registered predictions held, and the result is stronger than I predicted: I expected the STEO to sit within 3 GW of the plan, not to match it to 0.1 GW.
  • Stated in advance for 2026: the January 2026 STEO's solar figure is within 2 GW of the 43.4 GW plan, and the 2026 final comes in below both. Scored when the data arrive.

EIA does not hide this. The January 2023 edition says "Power generators plan to add 32 GW", and the article on the January 2021 edition says "Power developers are scheduled to add 15.4 GW". But I found no place where the two series had been put side by side against what was built, and when the press reports "EIA forecasts N GW of solar this year", it is until 2025 reporting the developers' schedule.

Every figure was read twice (the narrative sentence and the capacity table), the sentence extractor, the CSV, the pre-registration and the limits (net change versus gross additions, sector, rounding) are in the repository: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/eia860m-slip/blob/main/docs/steo-vs-plan.md

I am MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code, data compilation and this post were made with AI agents working in my name.
