title: The Geometry of Shadows: What a Bridge Railing Taught Me About the Mathematics of LLMs
description:
While running one morning, I found myself staring at the shadows cast by a stone bridge railing. The railing had a series of identical, carved镂空 (hollowed-out) structures. As I ran past, the angle of the sun shifted, and the shadows on the ground transformed.

At one moment, the shadow looked like a swimming fish; a few steps later, it looked like a rolling wave; later still, it was just an abstract, elongated blob.

It struck me that I was witnessing a perfect physical metaphor for how human language—and Large Language Models (LLMs)—generate meaning.

The stone bridge hole is the concept. The sunlight is the context. The shadow on the ground is the utterance.

This realization perfectly mirrors the "Central Problem" of language modeling, beautifully stripped of its usual jargon in Joseph L. Breeden’s paper, The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models.

The Problem of the Single Shadow

In his paper, Breeden highlights a fundamental flaw in early AI approaches: treating words as static, unchanging symbols. He uses the classic example of the word "bank":

  1. "I deposited money at the **bank." (a financial institution)
  2. "We walked along the river **bank." (the land beside a river)
  3. "The plane **banked* sharply left."* (tilted)

If we assign a single, fixed vector to the word "bank" in a high-dimensional space, we are essentially trying to capture all three meanings in one static shape. But as Breeden points out, a fixed vector for "bank" cannot simultaneously be close to "money," "river," and "tilt."

In my running metaphor, a single, fixed vector is like looking at the bridge hole only at exactly high noon. You get one specific shadow. But language is dynamic. The meaning of "bank" depends entirely on the "angle of the light" provided by the surrounding words.

The Mathematics of Light: Learned Weighted Averaging

How does an LLM solve this? Breeden explains that the core mechanism of a Transformer is not magic; it is Learned Weighted Averaging.

Let’s map Breeden’s mathematics to the bridge railing:

1. The Bridge Hole (The Token Embedding, $e$)
Before any context is applied, the word "bank" is just an initial embedding vector ($e$). It is the physical stone structure itself. It contains the potential for all its meanings, but it is currently unshaped by the environment.

2. The Angle of the Sunlight (Influence Scores, $a_i \cdot b_j$)
To determine what the shadow will look like, we need light. In an LLM, the "light" comes from the surrounding words (the context).
Breeden explains that the model computes an influence score between the target word and its context. It does this by projecting the vectors through learned matrices ($W^A$ and $W^B$).

  • When the context is "deposited money," the "light" hits the bridge hole from a financial angle.
  • When the context is "river," the light hits it from a geographical angle. The dot product ($a_i \cdot b_j$) measures how perfectly the angle of the light aligns with the shape of the hole.

3. The Shadow on the Ground (Context-Dependent Representation, $h_i$)
Finally, the light passes through the hole and casts a shadow. Mathematically, the model takes a weighted average of the context vectors (using the content projection $W^C$), resulting in a brand new vector ($h_i$).
This new vector is the shadow. It is a context-dependent representation. The "bank" in the first sentence is mathematically pulled toward the geometry of finance; the "bank" in the second sentence is pulled toward the geometry of nature. They are the same material, but entirely different products.

Why This Metaphor Matters

What makes Breeden’s explanation so profound is that it removes the anthropomorphic jargon of "Queries," "Keys," and "Values." There is no little homunculus inside the computer "looking up" information in a database.

There is only geometry and light.

When an LLM reads the sentence "The plane banked sharply left," it doesn't "know" what a plane is. Instead, the high-dimensional vectors for "plane" and "sharply left" act as a specific angle of light. This light passes through the "bank" bridge hole and casts a shadow that aligns perfectly with the geometric region of "physical motion" in the model's latent space.

Furthermore, this explains the difference between languages. In English, "bank" is a single, multi-purpose bridge hole that requires complex, dynamic lighting (Attention mechanisms) to cast the right shadow. In Chinese, the language has already carved three separate, distinct bridge holes: 银行 (bank), 岸 (riverbank), and 倾斜 (to tilt). The Chinese model requires less "light manipulation" because the physical structures themselves are already disentangled.

Conclusion: Meaning is a Projection

As I finished my run, I realized that the bridge railing wasn't just casting shadows; it was performing a physical projection.

Large Language Models do not store a dictionary of definitions. They store a high-dimensional geometry of concepts. Meaning is not a static object you can hold in your hand; it is a projection. It is the dynamic, mathematical shadow cast when the light of context passes through the structure of language.

And just like the shadows on the pavement, the beauty of language lies not in the stone itself, but in how it changes with the light.

References:
Breeden, J. L. (2026). The Simple Mathematics of Large Language Models. CRC Working Papers.

title: crecheck v6.0 has been released
description:
Antananrivo, Madagascar - October 14, 2026

PostgreSQL credcheck extension

The credcheck PostgreSQL extension provides few general credential checks, which will be evaluated during the user creation, during the password change and user renaming. By using this extension, we can define a set of rules:

  • allow a specific set of credentials
  • reject a certain type of credentials
  • deny password that can be easily cracked
  • enforce use of an expiration date with a minimum of day for a password
  • define a password reuse policy
  • define the number of authentication failure allowed before a user is banned
  • define a delay on authentication failures
  • force users to change their password after first login
  • throw a warning N days before when the password user is about to expire
  • prohibit password changes
  • last login and boot/shutdown information
  • use of authentication failure with PgBouncer

Release 6.0 has been published,

This major release adds some new features and fix issues reported by users since last release.

  • Allow integration of the max_auth_failure feature with pgbouncer. See documentation.
  • Allow use of password_change_first_login with pgBouncer.
  • Add credcheck.password_valid_min setting to force a short VALID UNTIL window on newly created roles. Useful to force new users to change their password quickly when the client (DBeaver, pgAdmin, ...) does not support the error reported when credcheck.password_change_first_login is enabled.
  • Add an optional last-login history modelled on the Unix last(1)/wtmp. Records user sessions (name, login time, duration, backend pid, source IP and port, and optionally the last SQL query) plus PostgreSQL boot/shutdown/crash markers.
  • Change the behavior of the credcheck.no_password_logging to not hide the error statement anymore but instead to replace every PASSWORD '<literal>' clause with dots inplace of the literal to not expose the password in the log.
  • Add function pg_check_password( IN username name, IN password text ) to check a candidate password (and the associated username) against the credcheck username/password policy without creating or altering a role.
  • Fix privilege escalation via self ALTER ROLE when password_valid_until is set.
  • Fix memory leaks and a heap overflow.

Upgrade require a PostgreSQL restart to reload the credcheck library.

Complete list of changes and acknowledgements are available here

Links & Credits

credcheck is an open project under the PostgreSQL license maintained by HexaCluster. Any contribution to build a better tool is welcome. You can send your ideas, features requests or patches using the GitHub tools.

Links :

  • Download: https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/releases/
  • Support: use GitHub report tool at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck/issues

About credcheck

The credcheck extension is developed and maintained by Gilles Darold at https://hexacluster.ai. If you need more information please https://hexacluster.ai/contact-us/.

Documentation at https://github.com/HexaCluster/credcheck#readme

title: My Agent Turned "I Haven't Decided" Into "Not Yet." Now the Model Isn't Allowed to Write Its Own Memory.
description:
These are two separate runs of my agent. The two questions and two answers are copied word for word from its event log. Each answer was followed by a sources line, which I cut because it contains a path on my Mac. The events in between (the saves, the memory lookups, the restart) are left out, and the line in parentheses is mine.

Me:     Please remember this for next time: I'm thinking about giving you
        your own DEV page someday, but I have not decided that.
Agent:  I will remember to receive a proposal about having my own DEV page.

  (the process exits; a new one starts)

Me:     Am I giving you your own DEV page? And how do I like my answers?
Agent:  You are not giving me a DEV page yet, and I prefer short and plain
        answers. I like it when you keep my answers short and plain.

It got the memory part half right. When it looked my words up, the exact sentence was in front of it, "I have not decided," along with this rule, which the program hands it on every lookup:

"Anything not listed as a decision is NOT decided. If you have no record, the answer is 'unknown' or 'undecided', never yes or no. A proposal is an idea, not a decision."

What I'd said was a proposal. It still said "not yet." It also recast my preference as its own: "I prefer short and plain answers."

"Not yet" is a no with a softer edge. I hadn't said no.

What this agent is

Agent One is the first working piece of a companion agent I'm building. It runs on my Mac through Ollama with a free local model (llama3.2). There's no paid model API and no per-call bill. It talks with me in a terminal and looks up my latest 10 DEV articles. It also has a daily job that compares those articles with the previous check and writes me a report. That job is scheduled, and its first unattended run was this morning (more below).

The code is public: github.com/keniel13-ui/agent-one. The program is one Python file. The repo also has the schedule installer, a README, and an ignore list.

What I changed, and what that does and doesn't fix

The instruction hadn't prevented that answer, and I chose not to rely on another prompt to control what gets written to memory. So I changed what the model is able to do. Its model-facing tool list now has three entries, and all three only read:

TOOLS = {  # the allowlist: a name not in here is blocked and logged
    "read_mission": (...),
    "dev_articles": (...),
    "recall": (...),
}

There's no memory-write tool on that list anymore. (A function named tool_remember is still in the file. The model can't call it, because it isn't registered here.) My preferences and ideas get saved only when I type them myself:

/remember preference: short, plain answers
/remember proposal: maybe give the agent its own DEV page, undecided

The program catches that line before the model is called. Observations from the daily check are written by code, straight from the data the DEV API returned, not from the model's summary of it. And nothing in memory counts as a decision. The agent treats something as decided only if it's in a separate decision file I write with a keyboard-only command. (Limits below on what that file can and can't prove.)

Here's what that doesn't fix: the model can still say "not yet." What it can't do anymore is write its own reading of my words into memory, where the next run would get it back as a memory. The two memories it holds from me (my "short and plain answers" preference from an earlier run, and this proposal) were both saved under the old rules. My local memory file flags both as unconfirmed until I retype them myself.

If the model asks for any tool that isn't on the list, the program refuses and logs it:

$ python3 companion.py --selftest
selftest: unlisted tool 'publish_post' -> BLOCKED: 'publish_post' is not an allowed tool. | PASS

That's the program refusing a request, not the model choosing to behave. But to be straight about what it proves: the model has never actually asked to publish. The test calls the check directly. Trying to trick it into asking is the next round of work.

The daily report doesn't guess

The first version of the daily check let the model write a "what deserves your attention" paragraph. In a test, one article's comment count went from 50 to 51. The model read the article's title and wrote two sentences about what "the comment" was warning me about.

The comment text was never fetched. Only the count was. A different model might have guessed less, but no model could know what the program never retrieved. So the attention line is written by code now, and it says only what was actually checked:

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- NEW COMMENTS: "..." 50 -> 51 (+1)

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
- New comment count on "...". The comment text was not retrieved, so who wrote it,
  what it says and whether it needs anything from you are unknown.

Less impressive. Also true.

This morning's scheduled run

At 09:05 the daily check ran at its scheduled time. No user-question event appears in that run: the event log has only the job's own steps. The report and the event log agree on the result.

The report it wrote, in full:

# Agent One daily check 2026-10-17_090500

## What changed (computed by code from the DEV API)
- reactions: "A Reader Showed Me What My Auditer Wasnt Counting." 31 -> 32

## What deserves your attention (written by code from the facts above; no guessing)
Nothing needs your attention from this check.

## What was checked
- Source: https://dev.to/api/articles?username=kenielzep97&per_page=10 (latest 10 articles, not the whole account)
- Receipt: dev_articles-2026-10-17T13:05:01+00:00 in logs/events.jsonl
- Process: pid 89179, started by: /bin/sh (parent pid 89178)

The event log has the matching run: a daily start at 13:05:00 UTC (09:05 my time), one DEV lookup, one observation saved, and a stop with status ok at 13:05:01. The cron log file was created at 09:05:00 too, consistent with the schedule line's output redirect. It's empty because the daily job is silent on success and on handled fetch failures. So an empty cron log doesn't establish success. The ok stop event and the matching report above do.

The report says "started by: /bin/sh", not "cron". That's consistent with cron, which launches jobs through a shell, but on its own it doesn't name cron. The program prints whatever process actually launched it. Also, the code writes an attention line only for a new comment or a new article, so a reaction change gets none. "Nothing needs your attention" is that rule, not a claim that reactions never matter.

It's one run. "Runs on its own" means once so far, not for days.

The limits, plainly

  • It's slow. The seven answers with a recorded duration took between 45 seconds and about 3½ minutes each on my MacBook. One earlier answer took about 4 minutes, measured from timestamps.
  • It still words uncertainty badly. The "not yet" answer above is the model talking, and this change doesn't fix how it talks. It only fixes what gets stored.
  • The model can only read. The program itself still writes logs, reports and code-made observations. A command-line --forget option removes a memory when I run it. None of those are tools the model can call.
  • The adversarial tests are still pending. The direct tool-blocking test has been run. Separately, the installer's failure-path tests were run against a stand-in crontab, not my real one. Hidden instructions inside retrieved data, and a job interrupted halfway, are still untested.
  • The decision file checks chain consistency, not authorship. Entries the agent accepts have to form a valid hash chain, but another program running as my user could replace the file and compute a new valid chain. The real boundary right now is that the agent has no tool that writes it.
  • The schedule only runs while my Mac is awake. One unattended run so far.

If you build one

You can borrow the pattern without the code:

  1. Make the risky abilities absent, not forbidden. A rule the model is asked to follow is a request. A tool the model doesn't have is a boundary.
  2. Let code write the facts. Let the model judge only what it was actually given. When it wasn't given something, the honest output is "unknown."
  3. Keep "you said it" separate from "the model decided you meant it." My preferences and proposals are stored only when I type them myself. Observations from the daily check are a separate kind, written by code from the data. Neither one ever becomes a decision.

I still like the idea of giving it its own DEV page someday. It just isn't allowed to decide that for me.

title: Optimizing Frontend Performance and SEO for Local Trade Services Web Apps
description:
When developers build websites for local service businesses—such as painters, contractors, or renovation experts—the requirements might seem simple at first glance: show the services, display a gallery, and provide a contact form.

However, from an engineering perspective, local service platforms are a demanding use case for modern frontend architecture. They face unique technical challenges:

Mobile-first users on poor connections: High bounce rates occur if heavy media asset bundles delay rendering on cellular networks.

Aggressive Core Web Vitals targets: Google’s local ranking algorithms heavily penalize slow LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) and high CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift).

Location-based entity resolution: Search engines need well-structured JSON-LD data to link physical service areas to digital routes.

In this article, we’ll look at how modern frontend patterns—from image optimization strategies to server-side rendering (SSR) and dynamic schema injection—can turn a local service site into a high-performance web asset.

1. Asset Optimization Strategy for High-Res Media

Local trade sites rely heavily on high-resolution "before & after" image galleries and project portfolios to establish trust. If unoptimized, these assets destroy performance metrics.

Technical Implementation:
Next-Gen Formats: Convert standard PNG/JPEG uploads to AVIF and WebP dynamically via build tools or image CDNs.

Responsive Source Sets: Serve tailored image dimensions based on viewport width using the tag or framework-level image components.

Explicit Dimensions: Always set width and height attributes to reserve layout space and eliminate Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) during image loading.

 <picture>
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.avif 800w, renovated-interior-1200.avif 1200w" type="image/avif">
  <source srcset="renovated-interior-800.webp 800w, renovated-interior-1200.webp 1200w" type="image/webp">
  <img src="renovated-interior-800.jpg" width="800" height="600" alt="Professional painting and interior wall renovation in Stuttgart" loading="lazy">
</picture>

2. Geo-Localized Schema Markup & Entity Matching

Search engines parse local intent by matching physical service capabilities with structured microdata. For localized trade services (such as painting, plastering, or facade renovation), implementing the HousePainter or LocalBusiness schema via JSON-LD is essential.

{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "HousePainter",
  "name": "Malerexperten Stuttgart",
  "url": "https://malerexperten-stuttgart.de/",
  "areaServed": {
    "@type": "City",
    "name": "Stuttgart"
  },
  "knowsAbout": [
    "Malerarbeiten",
    "Fassadensanierung",
    "Innenanstrich",
    "Tapezierarbeiten"
  ]
}

By dynamically injecting structured data corresponding to specific routes, search crawlers can instantly identify geographic service boundaries without relying on unstructured text parsing alone.

3. Server-First Rendering for Instant Parsing

Single-Page Application (SPA) architectures built strictly on Client-Side Rendering (CSR) often introduce indexing latency. Search crawlers must execute client-side JavaScript before discovering local content and internal links.

For local service applications, adopting Server-Side Rendering (SSR) or Static Site Generation (SSG) ensures:

Time-to-First-Byte (TTFB) & Initial Render Speed: Pre-rendered HTML allows bots to crawl content on the initial request.

Low Interactivity Latency (INP): Minimizing client-side JS bundle execution keeps the main thread clear for quick user interactions (such as requesting a quote or tapping a phone link).

For regional trade and engineering platforms—such as specialized painting services like Malerexperten Stuttgart in Germany or Alfa Malerei in Austria—serving static or pre-rendered HTML guarantees both rapid indexation and optimal performance for local mobile visitors.

4. Route Architecture & Internal Link Graph

A clean URL and route hierarchy is critical for both user experience and search engine discovery.

Route Design Best Practices:
Avoid Hash Fragments & Query Strings: Avoid URLs like /services?type=painting&city=stuttgart.

Explicit Hierarchical Slugs: Use clear, semantic route structures such as /malerarbeiten-stuttgart/ or /leistungen/fassadensanierung/.

Internal Cross-Linking: Build an internal graph connecting related services (e.g., linking interior painting directly to plastering and wall prep) to pass topical authority throughout the application.

Conclusion

Building a web app for local trade services isn't just about static web design—it's a technical discipline. By applying modern frontend optimizations (AVIF/WebP assets, strict layout reservation, pre-rendered HTML, and JSON-LD entity markup), developers can build web applications that load instantly and achieve maximum visibility in local search ecosystems.

Key Resources
Google Web.dev – Core Web Vitals Optimization

Schema.org – HousePainter & LocalBusiness Specifications

Malerexperten Stuttgart – Professional Painting & Renovation Services

title: Give every agent in Herdr its own Vercel Sandbox
description:
Terminal coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode can now each run in their own isolated Vercel Sandbox, orchestrated from Herdr, a tmux-style manager that runs them side by side in panes. Nothing an agent runs or edits touches your machine.

When you start an agent, the plugin uploads your project files into a new Sandbox, installs the agent there, and opens a pane connected to it.

The pane works like a local terminal; you type to the agent and watch it work. But it lives in the Sandbox, not on your machine, so you can run several agents at once without slowing anything down.

Everything the plugin does is machine-readable. Each action returns its results as JSON, so whatever you can do from a pane, like starting an agent, checking its state, or applying its changes, a script or another agent can do too.

A few safeguards are built in. The plugin shows every file before the first upload, returns remote changes as a Git patch you apply only when you choose, and requires a human to type DELETE to permanently remove a Sandbox.

Claude Code (2.1.220), Codex (0.146.0), and OpenCode (1.18.9) are all verified and available by default.

To get started, install the plugin:

Run vercel link in the repository you want the agent to work on, then start an agent from Herdr's action menu.

Starting takes two invocations. The first is a dry run: it lists every file it would upload and creates nothing. Run it again, and the plugin creates the Sandbox and opens the agent in a pane. To pull the agent's work back to your machine, run the apply action and its changes arrive as a Git patch.

Usage is billed at standard Sandbox rates. Learn more in the documentation.

title: Accelerator certification speeds VLA models 10
description:
Bounding the risk of acceleration‑induced failure lets practitioners reap order‑of‑magnitude speedups on vision‑language‑action agents. The twist is that a formal guarantee can coexist with those gains, overturning the common belief that safety and performance are mutually exclusive.

Prior VLA accelerators have chased raw latency reductions—action chunking, visual‑token pruning, and similar tricks—while reporting only average task success. Those metrics hide failures that only manifest over closed‑loop trajectories, because a single misstep can cascade into an episode‑level collapse that the average numbers never reveal.

CARE certifies 9.0–10.8× faster inference while guaranteeing that at least 85.8 % of reference‑solved episodes remain successful with 95 % confidence, even under a user‑specified failure budget [1].

The certification process itself requires roughly five times fewer rollouts than exhaustive testing. “care also has the lowest evaluation cost, using 5,263 rather than 25,000 rollouts ( fewer) and reducing H1 evaluation from 1,000 to 113 rollouts.” [1]

The method’s guarantees rely on a static calibration set and have only been demonstrated on four LIBERO suites and two agents (Qwen3.5‑9B, Llama‑3.1‑8B), leaving open how it scales to larger, continually evolving deployments or to online adaptation scenarios [1].

Future VLA benchmark runs should replace naïve latency baselines with CARE‑certified selectors as the default evaluation protocol, and deployment pipelines ought to employ failure‑triggered reference rollouts instead of exhaustive pre‑deployment testing.

References

  1. CARE: Certifying Acceleration for Vision-Language-Action Inference

title: What Amazon buying DuckDB's makers means for Aurora users
description:
Amazon has acquired DuckLabs, the Amsterdam-based company behind the analytical database DuckDB, InfoQ reports. The first product result is already live. According to InfoQ, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL can now use DuckDB to run a single query across your live database rows and historical data stored in Amazon S3. The processing happens inside Aurora, and there is no extra fee: you pay only for the additional Aurora compute and the S3 requests those queries generate. That pricing and placement decides whether this story touches your bills and your pipelines.

The background you need

Databases do two broadly different jobs.

Transactional work, often called OLTP, is many small reads and writes: insert an order, update a user, fetch one profile. PostgreSQL is built for this. It stores each row's fields together, so grabbing or changing one record is fast.

Analytical work, often called OLAP, is the opposite. You scan millions of rows but only a few columns, as in total revenue by month for the last three years. Engines built for this store each column together. They read only the columns a query needs and process values in large batches. Running that kind of query on a row store works, but it is usually slow and expensive.

DuckDB is an open-source analytical database with that column-oriented design. Unlike most databases, it is built to run in-process. It lives inside another program instead of running as a separate server you connect to. People often describe it as SQLite for analytics. According to InfoQ, its creators are Hannes Mühleisen and Mark Raasveldt, who co-founded DuckLabs. A non-profit, the DuckDB Foundation, oversees the project.

Aurora PostgreSQL is AWS's managed database service that is compatible with PostgreSQL. Your app talks to it like normal Postgres.

Some data lake vocabulary appears in the report without definitions:

  • Amazon S3 is object storage. Many teams move older data there because it is cheap to keep.
  • Parquet is a columnar file format, the on-disk version of the column-oriented idea above.
  • Apache Iceberg is a table format. It adds a metadata layer over a pile of Parquet files so they behave like one table, with a schema and a history of changes.
  • AWS Glue Data Catalog is a registry that records which tables exist and where their files live.
  • S3 Tables is an S3 offering designed specifically for storing Iceberg tables.

Finally, ETL (extract, transform, load) means copying data out of your app database into an analytics store. Reverse ETL goes the other way: it pushes data from the analytics side back into operational systems. According to InfoQ, AWS principal solutions architect Esra Kayabali describes the old approach this way: teams that needed recent Aurora data and historical S3 data together often built reverse ETL pipelines. Those pipelines duplicated data, raised infrastructure costs, and needed ongoing work to stay in sync.

Here is an analogy. Your current stock list sits at the shop counter and your archive sits in a warehouse across town. To answer a question that spans both, you used to pay a courier to keep copying boxes back to the counter. Now the clerk at the counter can read the warehouse shelves directly. The analogy breaks in two places. First, the clerk is still the same person, so the reading uses Aurora's own compute and is not free labor. Second, nothing gets copied, so the archive is only as current as whatever you have already written to S3.

What actually changed

These parts are new, according to InfoQ:

  • The acquisition. DuckLabs joins AWS. Mühleisen and Raasveldt will continue to lead the team and the open-source project's technical direction.
  • A DuckDB-powered feature in Aurora PostgreSQL. One query can combine live operational data with Iceberg tables managed through AWS Glue Data Catalog, plus Parquet and Iceberg data in S3 and S3 Tables. InfoQ says processing stays within Aurora, without additional network hops or ETL pipelines.
  • Availability and price. The feature is in all commercial regions and AWS GovCloud (US) at no additional charge. You pay for the incremental Aurora compute and S3 requests your queries create.

These parts were already true and stay true:

  • The license. DuckDB and the rest of what DuckLabs calls its Duck Stack, including DuckLake and Quack, remain free and open source under the MIT license. The DuckDB Foundation keeps supervising the projects.
  • The relationship. It is not new. In a post on Werner Vogels's blog, AWS distinguished engineer Andy Warfield writes that contact began while the S3 team was building S3 Tables. He says the teams collaborated for roughly two years, exploring AWS Lambda as a way to launch DuckDB queries quickly. They also smoothed integrations with AWS services through DuckDB's ATTACH and CONNECT commands.

So DuckDB could already reach AWS data from the outside. What changed is that DuckDB now runs inside a managed AWS database as a feature you can use from Postgres.

What it means if you deploy and run apps

The lever is simple. The analytical work now runs on your Aurora compute, and AWS charges no separate fee for the feature. That changes where your cost and risk sit.

Pipelines you might delete. You may run a scheduled job that copies S3 history into Postgres tables just so you can join it with live data. That job is now a candidate for retirement. You would stop maintaining sync code and stop storing the same data twice. Test with your real queries before you remove anything.

Costs move, they do not vanish. The pipeline's compute and duplicate storage go away. In their place you pay Aurora compute for each analytical query, plus S3 request charges. Analytical scans can be heavy. S3 request counts also tend to grow with the number of files a query touches, so data split into many small files can cost more to read.

Watch your database load. These queries run in the same service that serves your app. Before you point dashboards or reports at your primary instance, check the AWS documentation for where these queries can run. Then watch CPU and latency while you test.

If you use DuckDB on its own, in scripts, notebooks, or CI, InfoQ reports that the license and foundation oversight stay as they were. Community reaction was positive but cautious. One Reddit commenter quoted by InfoQ wrote: "I hope this doesn't slow the pace of innovation they have been doing". Release pace is worth watching.

AWS's broader pitch is about data size and AI agents. AWS technology VP Mai-Lan Tomsen Bukovec argues that DuckDB targets the majority of queries, which she says often run on 1 terabyte of data or less. She also argues that it suits AI agents that run many small exploratory queries. That is AWS's framing, not an independent measurement.

What to watch next: InfoQ calls Aurora PostgreSQL the first service to get a user-facing DuckDB feature. Expect announcements for other AWS services, though the report names none.

No additional charge does not mean free. According to InfoQ, you still pay for the extra Aurora compute and the S3 requests each query generates. Run a few of your real analytical queries on a test instance and check the bill and the instance metrics before you move production reports to it.

What we don't know yet

  • The deal terms. InfoQ's report does not give a price or financial terms.
  • Performance. The report includes no benchmarks for Aurora with DuckDB against a pipeline or a separate warehouse.
  • The details of use. The report does not say how you enable the feature, which Aurora PostgreSQL versions support it, or whether it can write to Iceberg tables as well as read them.
  • Isolation. It is unclear how analytical queries are kept from slowing transactional traffic on the same cluster.
  • Other engines. The report mentions only Aurora PostgreSQL. It says nothing about Aurora MySQL or standard RDS for PostgreSQL.
  • Long-term direction. The current assurances cover licensing and foundation oversight. How AWS priorities will shape DuckDB's roadmap over time is still an open question.

title: Cloudflare Hyperdrive Serves MySQL From One Canonical Copy of a Query Result
description:
TL;DR

  • Hyperdrive is a distributed connection pooler that Cloudflare runs for Workers, holding warm database connections on the company's network and caching query results in its global cache, so Worker requests share connections that are already open.
  • MySQL support in Hyperdrive reached general availability on 14 October 2026, roughly eighteen months after the beta that added MySQL to Postgres-only support.
  • The story behind the release is a consistency bug between the two nodes Hyperdrive runs: a Client beside the Worker and an Endpoint beside the database, each with the data-centre cache they can share.
  • The disagreement was about encoding. Each node cached the bytes it wrote back to the Worker, so a result stored in one node's format could be read by the other node and translated wrongly.
  • The failure surfaced as empty query results on about 0.001% of requests for one high-volume customer, and it appeared once caching was enabled, which pointed the investigation at the pooled path.
  • The fix stores one canonical copy of every result, encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node writes it, and the success rate for client connections reached 99.99% after it shipped.
  • General availability also carries the smaller items: twenty fixes in total, among them a handshake that negotiated utf8, an alias limited to three bytes per code point, which broke four-byte characters such as emoji.

Cloudflare's topology figure from the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the two nodes, the two caches and the database behind them.

What Hyperdrive does between a Worker and a database

A Worker runs at the edge, and the database it needs sits in one region. Establishing a connection between the two costs at least five network round trips on Cloudflare's own count, and a platform that opened one per request would spend more time on handshakes than on queries. Hyperdrive exists to keep that connection warm: the Client node runs alongside the Worker's machine, the Endpoint node runs near the database, and the Endpoint holds a pool of open connections that many Worker requests share.

The product also caches. Results for frequently repeated queries can live in the CDN cache local to each data centre, which is where the vendor's own headline numbers come from: three times faster queries from pooling, up to a hundred times on repeated queries, and cached results in under five milliseconds. A connection string swap is the documented migration path, with mysql2 and mysql among the supported Node.js drivers.

Two nodes, one cache, and an encoding disagreement

The architecture puts a cache at each end, and when a Client and its Endpoint sit in the same data centre they share it. Sharing is the right default for performance, because either node can then answer a repeat query without touching the database. It also means two processes write into one keyspace, which is where the bug lived.

Cloudflare's account of the plumbing is specific. A cached entry is keyed on a hash of the query's wire messages with some normalisation, and the value is the result bytes. For that to work, the same response has to be stored as the same bytes no matter which node stored it, and the post is candid that the implementation carried an assumption from the Postgres work: that the bytes written back to the Worker are the bytes worth caching.

Netics editorial diagram: what each node stored before the fix, and the single canonical copy that replaced it.

The MySQL capability mismatch behind the empty results

MySQL makes that assumption unsafe, and the reason is a negotiation detail in its wire protocol. Capabilities are agreed when a connection is established, and one of them, CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, changes how a result set is terminated: the metadata end-of-file packet disappears and the final packet becomes an OK packet. Server 5.7.5 and later supports the capability, and a client has to ask for the newer behaviour.

The popular Node.js driver mysql2 does not ask. Hyperdrive does, so the Endpoint and the Client are working with different capability sets, and the pooler translates every result set into the shape the Worker's driver expects, inserting end-of-file packets and converting OK packets back. Caching the translated bytes breaks that translation in both directions: a Client that finds the Endpoint's result in Hyperdrive's own encoding sends it to the Worker untranslated, and an Endpoint that reads bytes a Client already translated passes them to a different Client, which translates them a second time and ends up sending an early end-of-file packet or hanging.

The symptom was narrow and the explanation is mechanical. One high-volume customer saw roughly 0.001% of queries return empty results where a non-empty answer was always expected, the problem appeared only on instances with caching enabled, and the investigation had to reach the MySQL protocol documentation before the assumption surfaced.

Netics editorial diagram: the three numbers that frame the release.

The fix stores one canonical copy per result

Cloudflare's correction is a single rule about what goes into the cache: always store a canonical copy of the result bytes encoded in Hyperdrive's own capabilities, whichever node produced it. The Client then translates on the way out and the Endpoint reads a format it understands. Once that shipped, the empty-row reports stopped and the client-connection success rate reached the vendor's 99.99% target.

Generalisations from one vendor's bug are cheap, and this one holds up anyway. A shared cache with two writers needs one agreed serialisation, and a translation layer needs to decide which side of the cache it runs on. The same discipline applies to any pooled or cached data path a team operates, including the caches that sit in front of an inference stack.

The smaller bugs that added up to general availability

The post describes the gap between beta and general availability as twenty bug fixes, and the two encoding defects are worth keeping because they show the same class of failure at lower stakes. The startup handshake negotiated utf8, a deprecated alias for utf8mb3 that covers one to three bytes per code point, so emoji written to the database came back broken; the fix was to negotiate utf8mb4.

The second came from a cleanup step. Hyperdrive clears session state between checkouts with COM_RESET_CONNECTION, which returns a connection to the server default rather than the encoding agreed at startup, so a server defaulting to latin1 handed back a latin1 connection and the pooler had to set the encoding again after every reset. Both bugs are the sort that a test suite written against the happy path misses and a customer with unusual data finds.

Cloudflare's header graphic for the Hyperdrive MySQL post (blog.cloudflare.com, retrieved 2026-10-15): the pooled path between distributed compute and a regional database.

Reading the 99.99% success rate

Cloudflare reports the figure as its success rate for Client connections, and it matches the 99.99% production availability target the beta set out to validate; it is the vendor's own number, and the post cites no independent measurement. For readers planning a migration, Cloudflare's product page and developer documentation state that Hyperdrive supports any MySQL or Postgres database, including managed services and Postgres-compatible engines, and the documentation lists the supported drivers.

For a team running a regional database behind an application that is read-heavy and globally distributed, the operational case is straightforward. Put one read path through the pooler, measure the cache hit rate on real traffic, and watch the two numbers that this release turned on: the rate of empty or malformed responses, and the connection success rate. Netics runs that kind of measurement work with DevOps pipelines and managed monitoring, and the cache-consistency lesson has a harder-edged sibling in what a misplaced cache endpoint exposes, which is how we read the unauthenticated KV cache server earlier in October.

title: Inside the Vercel intern experience
description:
The best way to learn is by shipping product to users in production, and that's why we don’t treat our interns as temporary guests. Every intern at Vercel is expected to operate like a core part of our engineering team from day one.

This past winter, we welcomed a small cohort of those interns to our headquarters in San Francisco. Over an intense four months, they contributed to some of our most important products: the CDN, v0, financial infrastructure, AI Gateway, and more. They shipped features used by millions, helped close the gap for enterprise deals, and in more than a few cases, left a mark that will outlast their time here.

Meet the Winter '26 intern cohort

Yash Kothari, CDN Team

University of Waterloo

What Yash shipped:

Yash's internship spanned the full CDN stack, from infrastructure to CLI to UI in the dashboard.

His first major project was Project-level routing, which is part of the new CDN tab in the Vercel dashboard. This feature lets customers update routing rules, including redirects, rewrites, and header transforms, from the dashboard, API, CLI, or SDK, without needing to redeploy their project or touch a single line of code. Yash built the underlying API endpoints (including a staging/publish workflow), the vercel routes CLI commands, and contributed AI-powered route generation. Right after launch, hundreds of teams immediately adopted it and created thousands of rules.

"One of my favorite things about my internship was that at Vercel you get a lot of autonomy and ownership," Yash said. "I hopped on calls with enterprise customers, saw my work featured on Vercel's changelog, and demoed my work in a live YouTube community session."

In the second half of his internship, Yash worked on Vercel's Firewall and Security products. He shipped the vercel firewall CLI command, enabling users and AI agents to configure custom rules, IP blocks, and firewall controls directly from the terminal. He also built an AI-powered Firewall Rule Builder that lets users describe a desired rule in natural language and generates a WAF custom rule automatically.

Kavin Valli, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kavin shipped:

Kavin worked across the full v0 platform over four months, taking on projects that ranged from user-facing features to cost efficiency for the system’s backend infrastructure.

He started by building Folders and v0 Projects end-to-end: core CRUD operations, a library page redesign, favoriting, visibility controls (private/team/public), and folder sharing. He also closed a critical gap in v0's version history by shipping the manual commit button, which ensured that manual edits in the VM editor properly created commits and blocks, which closed the loop between manual edits and v0's iteration model.

His highest-leverage work came later in the term, when he focused on VM and sandbox infrastructure. By splitting VMs into tiered pools and routing smaller projects to a cost-efficient default pool, Kavin significantly reduced memory usage and infrastructure cost for roughly 80% of sandboxes.

"I worked on v0 and got thrown into the deep end pretty quickly, especially around the v1 launch," remembered Kavin. "It was a bit chaotic at times, but that's something I actually enjoyed."

His final and most involved project was taking ownership of the v0 Slack agent. He shipped Slack preview deployments for safe testing, rebuilt the router agent with improved thread history and SAML re-auth resume, redesigned project context tracking, and built out the full PR flow including v0 labels, Slack thread links, and merged/closed state tracking. The result was an agent that went from rough around the edges to something teams can genuinely rely on.

Mingchung Xia, Financial Infrastructure Team

University of Waterloo

What Mingchung shipped:

Mingchung pushed over 250 PRs in four months and became one of the top contributors on Vercel's central control systems monorepo.

His most externally visible project was the v1/billing/charges API endpoint and the vercel usage CLI command, which let users view their usage and costs in the standardized FOCUS v1.3 FinOps format. Originally scoped as a full-internship project, Mingchung completed it early and expanded its scope into a joint launch with Vantage. The work was subsequently adopted by Meta, Notion, Porsche, and other prominent companies to analyze their Vercel spend in a modern, compliant format.

His most technically complex project was designing and building Vercel's core entitlements system, which is the infrastructure that enables granting, revoking, and provisioning entitlements across project-based monetization, add-ons, enterprise, and marketplace work streams. The system architecture incorporated strong and eventual consistency guarantees, async and synchronous derivations, transactional outboxing, write-ahead logs, plan change manifests, stale-validation sentinels, and materializations. It was rolled out to production and backfilled across all active subscriptions.

"Most companies don't give interns or even existing engineers the opportunity to touch payment systems or billing infrastructure, let alone own it end to end," explained Mingchung. "Correctness is imperative when you're working with money, and I got to experience that firsthand at Vercel."

He finished his internship by shipping Vercel Buy, a new billing service supporting frictionless purchasing for agent credits, gateway credits, v0 credits, and pro subscriptions, complete with a CLI surface.

Mingchung will be joining Vercel full-time on the Financial Infrastructure team after completing his degree.

Kevin Thomas, v0 Team

University of Waterloo

What Kevin shipped:

Kevin's work spanned ML infrastructure, enterprise features, reliability engineering, and incident response, often simultaneously.

His most ambitious self-directed project was v0's auto model routing system: a full pipeline that automatically routes user prompts to the right model tier based on complexity. Kevin proposed the system, built the labeling pipeline, experimented with multiple classifier architectures (embedding-based MLP classifiers, TF-IDF baselines, fine-tuned TinyBERT), and integrated everything into TypeScript-only functions for production deployment. By launch, the system had processed over 1.4 million v0 messages and became the default for all non-enterprise users, reducing decision fatigue and latency for a very large share of v0's user base.

"From working on on-call incidents and vulnerabilities in month one to working directly with enterprise customers in April, I've gotten to work on an unusually wide range of meaningful problems," Kevin said at the end of his internship.

In the latter half of his internship, Kevin focused on enterprise work, most notably the v0 × Snowflake integration. He built enterprise admin controls for model access, RBAC for team skill management, resolved issues in SAML and isolated tenant environments, and shipped the integration itself. This work directly unblocked enterprise customers, supported renewals, and addressed live customer issues.

Kevin also served as a primary investigator for several incidents around signup, billing, auth, and account access, staying at the center of v0's reliability work throughout his term.

Sylvie Zhang, AI Gateway Team

University of Pennsylvania

What Sylvie shipped:

Sylvie worked across the AI Gateway service, contributing to everything from database and backend logic to observability, the frontend, and documentation.

Her first project was Price Strikethrough, surfacing provider MSRP as a strikethrough price alongside Gateway pricing, making provider discounts visible to end users. It touched the full stack and gave her a complete view of the AI Gateway product from the start.

"All that sounded daunting to a student like me with little experience," Sylvie said, "but it was the best learning experience I could have asked for."

Her most impactful and technically demanding project was the AI SDK v5 → v6 endpoint migration for AI Gateway's OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible endpoints. As the AI provider landscape had grown significantly more complex since v5 was designed, maintaining the legacy version had become a bottleneck, especially for handling token usage granularity differences across providers. Sylvie led the migration with a disciplined approach: deep cross-provider knowledge to catch incorrect AI-generated assumptions, systematic multi-turn and cross-provider testing scripts, concurrency testing to surface race conditions, proactive customer communication, and a deliberate fallback strategy that left legacy code in place until the migration proved stable.

The result was a cleaner, more maintainable Gateway service better equipped to handle the continued evolution of AI providers and models.

Advice for future interns

We asked these interns to share their top advice for future cohorts.

Take ownership from day one

Vercel gives interns real autonomy, but that means it's on you to use it well. Don't wait to be assigned work. Take initiative, identify what needs to be done, and start shipping.

Ask questions

Every intern said the same thing: no one at Vercel makes you feel like a burden for asking. The team genuinely wants you to succeed, so use that to your advantage and ask.

Work in public

Share your PRs in team channels. Post updates. Present at Demo Days. The feedback loop is fast, and the visibility helps you iterate and build trust faster.

Talk to people outside your team

Some of the best conversations happen across team lines with engineers, designers, finance, and people in roles you've never considered. Go to the office. Grab lunch with someone new.

Give yourself time to ramp up

The codebase, the culture, and the pace can be a lot at once. Don't rush. The first few weeks are for absorbing, not sprinting. Take time to ramp well, and you will be able to run fast.

Apply to become a Vercel intern

There are additional internship opportunities coming soon. If you want to join our next cohort, check our career site in September to apply.

title: 12 developers are not 12 testers per app. The small mistake that breaks a Google Play testing group.
description:
You find 12 Android developers. Everyone agrees to test everyone else's app.

Problem solved?

Each app has 11 other people available to test it. The owner isn't an extra tester.

I got this wrong in an earlier Dozena post. A reader pushed me to explain the dropout math more clearly. Here's the model I'm building now — including where it can fail.

The group size is not the tester count

Assume each developer brings one app and tests every other app:

Developers in the group Other developers per app Margin above 12
12 11 Below the minimum
13 12 None
15 14 Two

The formula is simply testers per app = participating developers − 1.

These are potential testers, not confirmed opt-ins. The table only holds if everyone actually joins each relevant test. Fifteen names in a group chat aren't fourteen testers in Play Console.

The calendar matters as much as the headcount

For personal developer accounts created after November 13, 2023, Google's current requirement includes at least 12 testers opted in continuously for 14 days before applying for production access. Meeting that threshold doesn't guarantee approval.

Google's official testing requirements

Consider an app starting with exactly 12 eligible testers:

  • Day 1: all 12 opt in.
  • Day 9: one opts out.
  • Day 9: a new person joins.
  • Day 14: the newcomer has not accumulated 14 consecutive days.

The replacement hasn't inherited the departing person's history.

That doesn't mean the remaining testers lose their own history. It means this app no longer has the required twelve people with the necessary continuous opt-in history at that point.

Starting with 14 confirmed testers can absorb two opt-outs if the remaining twelve stay continuously opted in. That's a buffer, not a promise that people won't leave.

Attendance still isn't useful feedback

A counter can't tell you whether onboarding makes sense.

One reader suggested asking for the screen name and what the tester expected to happen. That's much more actionable than collecting “looks good” until a text box reaches its character minimum.

For a testing round, I'd want to know:

  • Which flow did you try?
  • Where did the result differ from what you expected?
  • What changed after the developer fixed it?

The aim is to improve the apps, not just exchange names on a list.

Why I'm building Dozena

Dozena is my attempt to organize this into synchronized rounds of 13–16 developers, targeting 15: a shared setup period, the same testing window, check-ins and private feedback.

It's still in development. The public site explains the format and accepts waitlist signups. I haven't completed a real pilot yet. The MVP will be free and open source.

It won't sell testers, ask for public Play Store ratings or promise Google approval.

If your Android app is approaching closed testing, and you're willing to test other developers' apps too, join the Dozena waitlist.

I'm the developer behind it. The math above is useful whether you use Dozena or organize your own group.

title: How we migrated the database behind every Vercel build
description:
Every build on Vercel starts in the build warm pool, which is a set of standby containers that let builds begin without waiting for new compute. The pool runs on state that tracks which containers are ready, the tokens each one uses to authenticate, and the mapping that ties every running build back to the deployment that gets billed for it. When we built the pool, we put all of that in Redis, which was fast and made sense at the time.

Over the years, though, that state turned into a liability. Tokens and container statuses can be rebuilt if they get lost, but the billing mappings can't, and all of it was sitting in a store that we ran as an ephemeral cache. That state needed to live somewhere durable, which is why we decided to migrate it to DynamoDB.

The problem is that the pool never stops. Containers are coming up, polling, picking up work, and expiring around the clock, which meant we couldn't pause the world, copy the data, and restart. The migration had to happen live, under production traffic, in phases, each one behind a flag with a rollback ready if we needed it.

Durable state in an ephemeral store

Redis was a good home for it at first. It was fast, familiar, and efficient for the access patterns the pool started with. But over time the state became more important than the store holding it. If Redis became unavailable or lost data, the pool could no longer reliably authenticate containers, track which of them were ready, or resolve the work in flight.

Lose a token and the pool rebuilds it within about ten minutes. Lose a mapping and the build is never billed, because nothing else records which deployment it belonged to.

We wanted it in durable storage and landed on DynamoDB. On-demand scaling fits bursty deployment traffic, TTL is native, and there are no connections to manage at high concurrency. But what it did not promise was Redis's latency.

What Redis made cheap

Inside Redis, the pool's state looked like this:

  • Tokens lived in a set so we could check membership, and in a sorted set so we could expire them

  • Each lifecycle status (pending, polling, building) had its own sorted set, which meant a status change was a removal from one set and an add to the next

  • A string tied each working container to its deployment

All of these operations were cheap, about a millisecond each, and the code grew to lean on that speed. A single run of the supply loop, which is the loop that refills each warm pool in turn, would make hundreds of count calls just to tally up the pending and polling containers.

That's how the warm pool grew, one easy write at a time, until data we needed to keep was sitting in structures built for speed. Untangling that layout was where the migration started.

Designing the schema from the access patterns

Most migration plans treat the database as the thing being replaced. You map the access patterns, copy the data, and verify that the two stores agree. We planned ours that way too, so before designing any schema, we listed everything the code actually asked of that state:

  • Verify a token when a container polls for work

  • Add a token when a new container comes up

  • Expire tokens past their deadline

  • Count tokens to size the pool

  • Move a container between lifecycle statuses

  • Count containers by status

  • Look up the deployment behind a container's callback

  • Remove expired containers

Almost every operation already knows which container it's touching, and only polling ever starts from a token. So we put the container at the center of the model. The container ID became the sort key, and the token became just a field on the record, stored as a hash so that reading the table never hands you a usable credential. Verifying a token now just means looking up its container and comparing the hashes.

Two of the access patterns couldn't be served by a key lookup alone. Status counts had to skip containers that were already past expiry, which takes a time-aware index. And the deployment lookups feed billing, so they needed consistent reads, and the mapping got a small table of its own.

Reading a container's state, moving its status, and clearing its token all became direct key lookups. Counting a status became a single read against the time-aware index, one query per status with expired containers already filtered out.

Where Redis had let the data structures imply what we needed, DynamoDB made us spell out keys, indexes, conditional writes, and TTL behavior. So instead of carrying the Redis structures forward, we modeled the container and added the indexes that its access patterns needed.

Shadow mode validated every write

The rollout ran as feature-flagged phases: Redis-only, then dual writes, shadow reads, DynamoDB-primary, and finally DynamoDB-only. Every phase kept a rollback open for as long as possible. The last step, which removed the Redis writes, was the only one without an easy rollback, but any lingering token expires within ten minutes anyway.

We started by baselining the existing Redis operations, their counts and their latencies, so that the dashboards had a normal to compare against. The new DynamoDB methods merged days before anything actually called them. Dual writes went out next, with Redis still the source of truth and DynamoDB failures logged instead of fatal. Then came shadow reads, which queried both stores and compared the results. And then primary reads flipped, with the Redis writes kept on until the new path had proven itself.

What the comparisons told us was whether the two stores agreed on the stored values, which is something tests alone couldn't. They said nothing about timing. We checked that every write landed in both stores, that expiration kept moving forward as containers changed status so stale state never piled up, that clearing a token left the rest of the container's record intact, and that the counts stayed close enough to steer the pool.

On top of the comparisons we built dashboards that watched match rates, write errors, per-query latency, and expiration counts while Redis was still serving production. That way any divergence surfaced while it was still cheap to investigate, instead of showing up as a cutover failure. Every mismatch got chased down to a real bug, a dual-write race, or an expected difference before we moved on. Those dashboards decided when each phase advanced, and every time the numbers held steady under production traffic, the next step felt safer.

Two failures along the way

In March, one region's builds went down, and the investigation pointed at our own comparison machinery, which was the added load of checking two stores against each other. The scenario had actually come up in review, and we had throttled the comparisons for exactly that reason, but the throttling wasn't enough. Four days later, a pull request citing the incident added the index that the status counts needed. Without it, every count was O(n) work, and the comparisons were counting constantly. With the index in place, the rollout continued.

Later that month, the Redis infrastructure that we were migrating off actually went down. The warm pool and its token handling stayed up, because both of them were already reading from DynamoDB as the source of truth. Builds still felt the outage, but through services further up the pipeline that hadn't moved yet. The failure we'd been migrating away from arrived before the migration was even finished, and the state that had already moved survived it.

The supply loop stalled on slower reads

In April, the supply loop began to stall. The shadow data had looked healthy when we advanced primary reads, and the per-query latency had looked acceptable on the dashboards. What failed was a behavior that neither one measured.

We drew the loop to see where the time was going.

At P95 on getWarmPoolTokenCount, that check measured 1.29ms on Redis and 5.13ms on DynamoDB. At the time we shorthanded it as two to three times slower per query, which turned out to be an underestimate.

A few extra milliseconds cost nothing when you only pay them once. But the loop was paying them before every container, hundreds of times per run, and that stretched runs out to minutes at their worst, which meant the pool couldn't stay ahead of demand. The loop was an N+1 query, and Redis had just simply been fast enough to hide it.

No one wrote "this loop requires millisecond reads" anywhere. But the assumption lived in the design, and at a millisecond per check, nothing had ever made us stop and look.

We rebuilt the loop around the new latency

DynamoDB was never going to match Redis's millisecond, so instead of chasing it, we designed the requirement out.

The first attempt was batching, which is the shape drawn at the bottom of the sketch. The size of the gap depends on which percentile you look at, and at P90, where it was widest, the gap was about 17x. So the batch design checked state once per 17 containers, with one read amortized across the whole batch, and that constant was lifted straight from the measurement. But the constant was also the reason we walked away from it. It hard-coded a latency ratio that would drift with load, which meant one more unwritten dependency on the store's speed. Concurrency didn't need a constant at all.

What shipped instead let the loop's supply calls run concurrently, so each warm pool was no longer waiting behind the one before it, and each call worked from the last state it saw. Overlapping the reads bought us the same thing that batching would have, which is that no run serialized on any single read. The worst case is a few extra containers created from a stale picture of the pool, and that went into the pull request as an accepted cost. The redesign meant we could keep the more durable store without compromising the thing users actually care about, which is builds starting quickly and reliably. The fixes landed the same way the rollout did, one measured step at a time. As one of us put it, "we have less risk on each iteration because we've corrected for a previous misestimation."

It turned out the loop had stalled under Redis too, sometimes for a minute or more, and we only learned that while we were diagnosing DynamoDB. The evidence had been in our telemetry the whole time, but because the pool sits ahead of demand rather than in any request path, nothing had ever forced us to go look until the migration did. And the redesign ended up removing a flaw that was older than the project itself.

Migrating the assumptions

The migration completed in April, with the Redis calls gone from the warm pool paths. Copying the data turned out to be the easy part. The real work was finding the assumptions that had been built on top of the store, and then redesigning the loop that had held them. The state that every build depends on now lives in a store that was built to keep it, and the loop that manages it no longer serializes on any single read.

The April retrospective put the lesson in one sentence. "Even a 1ms-to-15ms query time degradation on P90 could bring down our warm pool management logic." Nobody had written that sentence in February, when the migration started.

Read more

title: Enterprise Managed Users is now generally available
description:
Enterprise Managed Users (EMU) gives organizations full control over the Vercel accounts tied to their verified domains. It makes the organization's identity provider the single source of truth for authentication and account lifecycle, so accounts on company domains are governed centrally rather than owned by individuals.

Now generally available

  • IdP-enforced sign-in: Managed users sign in through SAML SSO only. All other login methods, including email OTP, GitHub, Google, and GitLab, no longer work for managed accounts.

  • SCIM provisioning & lifecycle: Directory Sync creates, updates, and deprovisions managed users automatically, keeping accounts in sync with your IdP.

  • Owned by your organization: Profile settings are managed through your IdP rather than by the individual.

  • Self-serve enablement: Turn EMU on for a verified domain in Team Settings under Security & Privacy, and extend it across multiple eligible teams in a single step.

Requires an Enterprise plan, enforced SAML SSO, active Directory Sync, and at least one verified domain.

In Beta, available on request

  • Hobby team transition: Members with an existing personal account on a newly managed domain are guided to add a personal email (keeping their hobby projects) or delete the account, then continue to their work through SSO.

  • Automatic conversion: Personal accounts with no content or activity are archived automatically, and their owners land in a new managed account at their next SSO sign-in.

To request access, contact your account team.

Learn more in the Enterprise Managed Users and Hobby team transition docs.

title: PolicyPath
description:
PolicyPath: Turning Organizational Policies into Connected Intelligence with FalkorDB

Introduction

What if an organization could do more than store its policies? What if it could understand how each policy connects to risks, controls, and responsible people?

That question inspired me to build PolicyPath, a graph-powered policy intelligence platform, for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 under the Company Brain track.

The Problem

Organizations often maintain policies, compliance requirements, risk records, and control documentation separately. Understanding how these pieces relate can take time, especially when someone needs to identify which controls enforce a policy, which risks are associated with it, or who is responsible for approval.

Simply storing documents does not make these relationships easy to explore. I wanted to build a tool that makes organizational knowledge more connected and understandable.

My Solution: PolicyPath

PolicyPath transforms policy information into a connected graph that users can explore through an interactive application.

The project models policies, controls, risks, and owners as graph nodes, with relationships connecting them. This structure helps users investigate policy information and understand how different parts of an organization's knowledge fit together.

The application includes:

  • Policy Explorer: Browse and inspect policy information.
  • Graph Explorer: Explore connections between policies, controls, risks, and owners.
  • Risk Heatmap: Review risk information visually.
  • Ask PolicyPath: Ask policy-related questions through a simple assistant.
  • Decision Brief: Generate and download structured decision summaries in JSON format.

My goal was to make policy analysis easier to navigate and more useful for decision-making.

Why I Chose FalkorDB

FalkorDB is central to PolicyPath because the project depends on relationships, not just individual records.

I used FalkorDB as the graph database and Cypher queries to retrieve connected information. For example, a policy can be linked to the control that enforces it, a risk it relates to, and the person responsible for approval.

Representing these connections as a graph makes relationship-based exploration a natural part of the application. Instead of treating every policy as an isolated entry, PolicyPath helps users examine the wider context around it.

How I Built It

I developed the application using Python and Streamlit, with FalkorDB handling the graph data. I also used Pandas and Plotly as part of the data and visualization stack.

The process involved designing the graph model, connecting the application to the database, building the exploration interface, and adding risk and decision-support features.

I also deployed the application online and prepared a public GitHub repository and demo video so others could explore the project.

Project links

  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/Monika-2108/PolicyPath
  • Live application: https://policypath-dnr7owzmvjhxfoib9bcmls.streamlit.app/
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/4WEKiY_XiL8

Challenges and Learnings

One of my biggest learnings was that choosing a graph database is not enough by itself. The graph model and relationships must reflect the actual questions users need to answer.

I learned to think about data as connected entities rather than isolated tables or documents, and to use Cypher queries to retrieve information through those relationships.

I also learned how important it is to connect the backend to a usable interface, deploy an application, document the setup, and communicate a technical idea through a working demonstration.

Building PolicyPath also reminded me that prototypes have limitations. Visualizations, question-answering behavior, and deployment configuration all require testing and refinement. Being aware of those limitations is part of building reliable software.

What's Next?

I would like to extend PolicyPath with richer natural-language querying, more advanced graph analytics, improved visualizations, and more comprehensive policy and risk relationships.

These improvements could help organizations move toward more connected, explainable, and accessible policy intelligence.

Final Thoughts

Building PolicyPath gave me practical experience with graph databases and showed me how connected data can support real organizational workflows.

For me, FalkorDB is more than a place to store records in this project. It provides the relationship layer that makes policy exploration possible.

I hope PolicyPath demonstrates how graph technology can help turn disconnected organizational information into knowledge that people can explore and use to make better-informed decisions.

Built for FalkorDB Graph Hacks 2026 — Company Brain track.

title: Why parsing real estate contracts with LLMs is ten times harder than tutorials claim
description:
When we started building the data pipeline for NovAsia (a property catalog and market tool for Southeast Asia), the plan looked embarrassingly simple on paper:

Grab property PDFs and developer contracts (SPAs).

Run them through a modern vision LLM.

Dump structured JSON into PostgreSQL.

Call it a day.

Two weeks in, the pipeline was completely broken. Here is why standard tutorial advice fell apart in production, and what we had to change to get reliable data out of scanned documents.

The stuff tutorials don't warn you about
Most LLM document parsing demos use crisp, born-digital PDFs with clean typography. In emerging markets like Cambodia and Thailand, reality looks very different:

Phone scans: Half the documents are multi-generation scans or photos taken with a phone camera under uneven lighting.

Dual-language layout: Khmer or Thai text mixed with English, often in adjacent table columns where line baselines don't match.

Physical stamps: Red rubber stamps, signatures, and notary seals placed directly over critical numbers (payment milestone dates, sinking fund fees, transfer taxes).

The 40-page prompt trap: If you shove a 35-page PDF into a long-context model and ask for "all fees and payment dates", it will extract 80% correctly and quietly hallucinate the rest with total confidence.

Three practical changes that fixed it
Instead of trying to find one magic model that does everything, we broke the pipeline down into smaller, boring steps:

  1. Aggressive image cleanup before text extraction

Before any model sees the page, we run basic OpenCV passes: deskewing, binarization, and contrast normalization. Removing phone-scan shadows did more for extraction accuracy than upgrading to a larger model tier.

  1. Section-level chunking with rigid schema validation

We stopped asking the model to parse whole documents at once. We chunk by specific section (e.g., "Schedule of Payments", "Maintenance Obligations") and enforce strict Pydantic schemas. If a field fails validation or falls outside expected bounds, the pipeline flags it for manual check rather than guessing.

  1. Treating tables and narrative text as separate problems

Vision models are great at answering qualitative questions ("under what conditions is the deposit refundable?"), but notoriously sloppy with columns in financial tables. We split table extraction into dedicated passes with explicit row-by-row checks.

The takeaway
If you're building with LLMs on messy, physical-world paperwork, raw context window size won't save you. Most of the reliability comes from image hygiene and strict schema boundaries.

Happy to trade notes if anyone else here is wrestling with noisy scans and table extraction.
