title: How to Choose Colors for a Website: A Practical Guide
description:
Choosing colors for a website can be harder than it looks. A color palette needs to feel consistent, keep text readable, and support the purpose of the design.

Here is a simple process you can use for your next project.

  1. Start with a Primary Color

Choose one color that represents the overall mood of your website.

For example:

Blue can feel dependable and professional.

Green can suggest growth or nature.

Orange can create a sense of energy.

Purple can give a design a creative feel.

These are common associations, not fixed rules. The right choice depends on your audience and context.

  1. Build a Small Color Palette

You do not need dozens of colors. Start with a few practical roles:

Primary: The main brand or interface color.

Secondary: A supporting color for variety.

Background: A color that keeps the layout comfortable to read.

Text: A color with strong contrast against the background.

Accent: A color for important actions or selected elements.

A limited palette is usually easier to apply consistently across buttons, cards, headings, and backgrounds.

  1. Check Contrast and Readability

A color combination may look attractive but still make text difficult to read.

Check the contrast between text and its background, especially for small text and buttons. WCAG guidance generally recommends a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.

Do not rely on color alone to communicate information. Use labels, icons, or other visual cues when necessary.

  1. Test Colors Together

View your colors in context rather than judging each swatch separately. Try them on a sample button, a heading, and a card.

You can use a color palette tool to explore combinations, compare shades, and refine your choices before applying them to a full design.

For a quick starting point, explore Clicktoolset and its color tools.

  1. Keep the Palette Consistent

Once you settle on a palette, reuse the same colors for the same purposes. For example, keep primary buttons consistent and reserve accent colors for elements that deserve attention.

Documenting your colors as HEX values also makes it easier to reuse them in CSS:

:root {
  --color-primary: #2563EB;
  --color-secondary: #14B8A6;
  --color-background: #F8FAFC;
  --color-text: #1E293B;
  --color-accent: #F59E0B;
}

These values are only an example. Test your actual combinations for contrast and suitability before using them in a project.

Final Thoughts

A useful website palette does not have to be complicated. Start with a primary color, add a few supporting roles, check readability, and test the result in a real layout.

A small, consistent palette is often easier to maintain than a collection of unrelated colors.

title: DeepSeek overtakes Google on volume, cost per token falls 13.6%
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — August 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs. That traffic gives us a view of what AI usage actually looks like in today's enterprise, and we publish it here monthly. See the Production Index reports from May, June, and July.

August 2026 Summary

The August index reports on AI Gateway data collected through July 2026.

  • The average price paid per token fell 13.6% in July, after rising almost 20% in May and holding steady in June. Token consumption grew so quickly that even with 37% growth in spend, cost per token saw a double-digit drop.

  • DeepSeek became the second-largest lab by token volume, now running more than twice Google's volume.

  • Anthropic collected 65% of gateway spending on 30% of token volume, at 4.4 times the average price of every other lab's tokens.

  • Both media leaderboards changed hands. Google's Nano Banana took the lead in image volume from OpenAI's GPT Image, and ByteDance's Seedance led video in both volume and dollars.

Kimi K3 launched into agent work

Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16. Like Z.ai's GLM 5.2 released in June, it is built for long-horizon agent work, so its usage was heavy from the start at about twelve times the tokens per request of its predecessor, K2.5.

It scaled quickly. K3's daily volume tripled between launch week and the final week of July, and by month end its requests were as heavy as Claude Opus 4.8's. On the last full day of July it ranked eighth on the gateway by token volume.

The demand was new rather than diverted. K3 processed nearly two-thirds of all Kimi tokens within two weeks and 82% by the final week, while the rest of the family's volume fell only slightly.

Open weight's share of gateway spend more than doubled in July to 8.6%. More than 90% of that growth is Moonshot and Z.ai. Moonshot's share of total gateway spend quadrupled, to 2.3%. Cheap open-weight models have been taking volume for months without taking revenue. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are the first to capture significant volume at more than eleven times DeepSeek's rate per token.

DeepSeek is now second by volume

In June, this report said DeepSeek had entered the fight for token volume. Last month, we said an open-weight lab would soon be second by volume. In July, DeepSeek surpassed Google to take that place.

Google ran nearly 40% of the gateway’s token volume in April, and DeepSeek less than 1%. By July, DeepSeek ran a quarter, more than twice Google’s 11%. DeepSeek V4 Flash, its cheapest model, ran more tokens alone than all of Google.

The reversal is concentrated in consumer-facing work. Google's share of personal-assistant tokens fell by more than half in a month while DeepSeek's more than tripled, and most of the token share Google gave up went to DeepSeek. DeepSeek's V4 Flash ran more tokens than any other model on the gateway in July, nearly a fifth of the total and 70% more than the next model.

Open-weight models previously owned the cheap end of the market. Their share of gateway token volume nearly tripled between April and June, from 11% to 29%, while share of spend stayed under four cents of every gateway dollar.

In July, volume continued its growth trend, increasing to 36%. Spend broke its trend, more than doubling to nearly nine cents of every dollar, the highest in the index's history.

The four largest frontier labs' combined share of token spend, which had not fallen below 93% in seven months, fell to 89%. Google accounted for most of the decline. Almost none of the spend it lost went to DeepSeek, whose share barely moved even as its volume grew. Z.ai and Moonshot's latest models account for the entire open-weight spend increase.

Buyers sort models by what the task requires, then choose inside that tier according to price. DeepSeek and Opus were never competing. GLM 5.2 and Kimi K3, both released in the last two months, are the first open-weight models running a meaningful share of the workloads historically owned by closed-weight labs.

Average price per token fell 13.6%

Companies bought more inference in July and ran more of it on cheap models. Volume grew 59%, spend grew 37%, and the average price paid per token fell 13.6%.

Holding June's mix of models constant, the average price would have held essentially flat instead of declining. OpenAI is one example: the average cost of an OpenAI token fell to 58% of its June level, because 85% of the volume it added went to GPT-5-Nano, the cheapest model in the GPT-5 family.

The entire decline in average price came from what companies chose to route. Among the thousands of teams that ran more than 10 million tokens in both months, three in four changed at least a tenth of their model mix. Three in five changed at least a quarter.

The median team's cost per token fell 2.9%, but only one team in six stayed within five percent of where it started.

A quarter pared cost by more than 30%, typically teams that entered the month paying well above the gateway average per token. Another quarter paid at least 20% more, typically teams that had been paying below the average. Concurrently, the expensive end shifted down and the cheap end migrated up.

81% of July’s tokens ran on models that were not on the gateway six months ago. Open-weight models crossed a third of all volume, at about a seventh of frontier rates. Google fell from 24.0% of gateway token volume to 10.7%. Anthropic slipped two points to 29.8%, and OpenAI’s share rose to 12.8%.

Gateway spend is up 74% since May and volume has doubled, with July's token growth running at nearly double June's pace. Spend on inference continues to increase even as each dollar buys more tokens than it did in the previous month.

Anthropic's premium widened as prices fell

Anthropic has held more than 60% of gateway spend in every month we have measured, through a period in which open weight tripled its share of volume. In July, it collected 65.1% of all spend on 30% of total volume.

The average price per Anthropic token ran 4.4 times the average across every other lab, up from 3.4 in June. Part of that rise was Claude Fable 5, which returned on July 1 after a three-week export-control suspension and quickly grew to 13.2% of all gateway spend, second only to Opus 4.8. In coding agents, the gateway's largest use case by tokens, Anthropic collected more than 80% of spend.

Anthropic has no model at the bottom of the market. Haiku 4.5, its least expensive, runs just over two-thirds of the gateway average price per token. OpenAI's GPT-5-Nano runs a sixth; DeepSeek's V4 Flash a sixteenth.

Customers cutting costs on OpenAI or Google can stay in the catalog. Cutting costs on Anthropic means leaving Anthropic, and in July it still took a majority of all spending. Anthropic’s premium is the gap between what the cheap tier can do and what its customers need done.

Switching models on the AI Gateway is a one-line change, so nothing locks a customer in. When Fable 5 came back, daily volume returned to the pre-ban level almost exactly, but nine in ten of the teams running it in July had not used it before. The work returned; the customers were different.

The rest of the market's tokens averaged less than a quarter of Anthropic's price, and Anthropic still took two of every three dollars spent on the gateway. Price competition is happening, but it's happening in the part of the market with the least money in it.

Google took images, ByteDance took video

In June, OpenAI's GPT Image generated most of the gateway's images. In July, Google's Nano Banana led, at 45% of images to GPT Image's 42%, with spend split almost evenly between them. Nearly all of Nano Banana's gain came from one model, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite Image. Google took the image lead in the same month it fell to fourth by token volume.

ByteDance's Seedance led video on both counts, in videos generated and dollars spent. xAI's Grok Imagine, June's volume leader, fell to second. Chinese labs collected about seven of every ten dollars spent on video.

Also in July’s data

  • Within coding, the gateway's largest workload by tokens, DeepSeek ran nearly a third of the volume and Anthropic collected more than four of every five dollars.

  • Back-office agents remain the most expensive work per token, with a share of spending roughly two and a half times their share of volume.

About this report

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through July 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Volume counts all tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • Spend values every request at the lab's published list price.

  • Price per token is calculated as total spend divided by total volume.

  • Open-weight volume and spend shares count the four open-weight labs serving their own models at scale (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot, and Z.ai).

  • Image and video figures count media generated, not requests or tokens.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as methodology is updated.

title: I ran 50 orders at 1 unit of stock. Here’s what stopped the oversell.
description:
Last week I built a small grocery-style order system to learn how event-driven services handle the classic problem: two customers click “buy” on the last item at the same time.

A caveat first. I built this in about 24 hours using AI coding agents (Cursor), and I directed the design. I’m writing this after going back through the code to understand why it works, which is a different thing from writing every line myself. If you’re after a hand-coded reference, this isn’t one. If you want to see how these patterns fit together and how I tested them, read on.

What it is

Three Spring Boot services (order, inventory, payment), each with its own PostgreSQL database, talking only through Kafka. There’s no central coordinator. Each service reacts to events and publishes its own, which is called a choreographed saga. A Next.js storefront sits on top, and an optional ELK stack lets me trace any order by its ID.

Happy path: an order goes PENDING, then RESERVED, then CONFIRMED. If stock runs out or the payment is declined, the order goes to CANCELLED and any reserved stock is released through a compensation event.

The problem

Writing to your database and publishing to Kafka are two separate operations. If the service crashes between them, you either have an order nobody hears about or an event for an order that doesn’t exist.

The three things that handle it

Transactional outbox. The order service writes the order and the event into the same database transaction. A separate step then publishes the event to Kafka. Either both are saved or neither is.
Idempotent consumers. Kafka can deliver a message more than once. Each consumer records the events it has processed (a processed_events table), so a duplicate does nothing the second time.
Atomic stock updates plus per-order keys. Stock is decremented in a single atomic update, so two orders can’t both read “1 left.” Events for one order use that order’s ID as the Kafka key, which keeps them in order.

The test

I wrote a k6 script that resets one item to a stock of 1, then fires 50 concurrent orders at it, one per virtual user. Afterward it checks that available stock never went below zero and that confirmed orders didn’t exceed the starting stock.

On my MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 16 GB), all 50 requests were accepted. After the saga settled, exactly one order was confirmed and stock sat at 0. The whole run, including setup and waiting for outcomes, took about 6.8 seconds. The other orders are designed to end up CANCELLED. [check your database and put the real count here]

What this does and doesn’t prove

It’s a correctness test, not a performance benchmark. It shows the system doesn’t oversell under a burst of 50 on a laptop. It says nothing about throughput at scale, and I haven’t run a long soak test. Payments are simulated too: a token of ok succeeds and fail declines.

What surprised me

[one or two honest sentences: something you learned or got wrong when you traced the code, e.g. what you expected the outbox to do versus what it actually does]

Try it

Everything runs with docker compose up --build. The repo has the architecture notes, the acceptance scenarios, and the benchmark results:

ArnavPoswal15 / orderflow-platform

Event-driven order platform: Spring Boot microservices + Kafka choreographed saga, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, Redis, PostgreSQL, Next.js storefront, ELK, k6 load test

Orderflow Platform

Event-driven order platform for grocery-style orders: order, inventory, and payment services each own a database and coordinate through Kafka using a choreographed saga (no central orchestrator).

Status: Phases 1–7 complete (saga, storefront, ops, ELK observability, k6 proof load test, GitHub Actions CI, demo docs).

title: S3 Lifecycle Rules, Step by Step: Move Old Data to Cheaper Storage Without Surprise Fees
description:
Most S3 buckets start the same way. Someone creates a bucket, an app writes files into it, and nobody looks at it again. Months later the bucket holds years of logs, old exports and copies of files nobody remembers. Every byte sits in the default storage class, S3 Standard, and every byte is billed at that rate.

S3 Lifecycle rules fix this. A lifecycle rule tells Amazon S3 to move objects to a cheaper storage class after a number of days, or to delete them when they are no longer needed. You write the rule once, and S3 applies it every day.

The catch is that cheaper classes come with conditions. Some charge for a minimum number of days. Some charge to read data back. Some charge per object moved. A careless rule can cost more than it saves. This guide from CloudSkill Consulting LLC walks through S3 lifecycle rules one step at a time, so you can lower storage cost without surprise fees.

Step 1: Learn the storage classes in plain words

A storage class is a price plan for an object. Each object in S3 has one. The data is the same; what changes is the price to store it, the price to read it, and how fast you can get it back.

Here are the classes this guide uses, in order from "used often" to "almost never used":

  • S3 Standard (STANDARD): the default. No minimum storage time and no retrieval fee. Best for data you read often.
  • S3 Standard-IA (STANDARD_IA): "IA" means infrequent access. Cheaper to store, but there is a fee each time you read data, a 30-day minimum storage charge, and a 128 KB minimum billable size (see the S3 pricing and storage-class pages linked in Sources).
  • S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (GLACIER_IR): for data read about once a quarter, still with millisecond access. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (GLACIER): archive storage. You must restore an object before you can read it, and that takes minutes to hours. It has a 90-day minimum.
  • S3 Glacier Deep Archive (DEEP_ARCHIVE): the lowest-cost archive, with restores measured in hours. It has a 180-day minimum.

There is also S3 Intelligent-Tiering (INTELLIGENT_TIERING). It watches how each object is used and moves it between tiers for you, for a small monitoring fee per object. It has no retrieval fees. It is a good choice when you honestly don't know how often data is read.


Figure 1: Each step down is cheaper to store, but has a longer minimum stay and slower or paid reads.

Step 2: Find out what is in the bucket before you write a rule

Never write a lifecycle rule from memory. Look at the data first. Two questions matter:

  1. How big are the objects? Small objects behave differently. By default, S3 Lifecycle does not transition objects smaller than 128 KB to any storage class. AWS explains why: you pay a transition request for each object, so for small objects the request cost can outweigh the savings.
  2. How often is each prefix read? A prefix is the start of an object key, like logs/ or exports/2025/. Logs written once and almost never read are good candidates. Product images that a website loads all day are not.

AWS gives you tools for this. S3 Storage Class Analysis watches access patterns on a bucket or prefix and helps you decide when to move data from Standard to Standard-IA. S3 Storage Lens shows storage use across buckets. Turn one of them on and give it time before you choose your day counts.

A good habit: write down each prefix, who owns it, how often it is read, and how long it must be kept. "How long it must be kept" is a business question, not a technical one. Ask the data owner.

Step 3: Understand the three rules that cause surprise fees

These three rules are where most lifecycle mistakes come from.

Rule A: minimum storage duration. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum, Glacier Instant Retrieval and Glacier Flexible Retrieval have 90 days, and Deep Archive has 180 days (minimum storage charges, per the S3 pricing and storage-class pages). If you delete, overwrite or move an object out before that time, you are charged for the rest of the minimum. A rule that moves logs to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and then deletes them 30 days later still pays for 90 days.

Rule B: small objects. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval bill each object as at least 128 KB. Objects archived to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive also carry about 40 KB of extra metadata each: 8 KB billed at the Standard rate and 32 KB at the archive rate. Millions of tiny files can cost more after archiving than before.

Rule C: reads cost money and time. IA and Glacier classes charge per GB retrieved. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive objects are not readable until you restore them, and while restored you pay for both the archive copy and a temporary Standard copy.


Figure 2: Check every lifecycle rule against these three conditions before you turn it on.

Step 4: Write a first rule that is hard to get wrong

Start with one prefix that is clearly "write once, read rarely", such as application logs. Here is a full lifecycle configuration in the JSON format the AWS CLI expects. It has three rules.

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "logs-tier-then-expire",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
        { "Days": 120, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 400 }
    },
    {
      "ID": "old-versions-cleanup",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": {
        "NoncurrentDays": 30,
        "NewerNoncurrentVersions": 3
      }
    },
    {
      "ID": "abort-stuck-uploads",
      "Filter": {},
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

Here is what each part does, in plain words:

  • logs-tier-then-expire applies only to keys starting with logs/. After 30 days the objects move to Standard-IA. After 120 days they move to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. After 400 days they expire. The gaps are chosen on purpose: 90 days in Standard-IA is more than its 30-day minimum, and 280 days in Glacier Flexible Retrieval is more than its 90-day minimum. No early-deletion charge applies. Since July 2026 you can move objects to Standard-IA from day 0. We wait 30 days because new logs are read most often in their first weeks.
  • old-versions-cleanup matters only if versioning is on. When you overwrite or delete an object in a versioned bucket, the old copy stays as a noncurrent version, and you keep paying for it. This rule permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent, but always keeps the 3 newest ones. Be sure that matches your recovery needs, because deleted versions can't be brought back.
  • abort-stuck-uploads cleans up multipart uploads that started but never finished. Their parts are stored and billed, yet they don't appear as normal objects. AWS notes that expiration rules don't remove incomplete multipart uploads; you need this separate action.

An empty Filter ({}) means "every object in the bucket".

S3 rounds lifecycle timing to the next midnight UTC. An object created at 10:30 AM UTC with a 3-day rule becomes eligible at midnight UTC four days later. Transitions to Glacier also run in the background, so the physical move can lag behind the date. You are still billed at the destination rate from the date the rule is met.


Figure 3 (example rule): One object's life under the logs/ rule, with each stay longer than that class's minimum.

Step 5: Apply it safely with the AWS CLI

First, save any rules that already exist. This step matters. The AWS CLI documentation says put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration replaces the whole existing configuration. Any rule you leave out of your file is gone.

# 1. Back up the current configuration (an error here usually means none exists yet)
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data > lifecycle-backup.json

# 2. Check your new file is valid JSON
jq . lifecycle.json

# 3. Apply the new configuration
aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket example-app-data \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

# 4. Read it back and compare
aws s3api get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration --bucket example-app-data

If an older rule existed, merge it into lifecycle.json before step 3. A bucket has one lifecycle configuration with up to 1,000 rules.

To see stuck uploads before and after, list them:

aws s3api list-multipart-uploads --bucket example-app-data

Step 6: Check the result, then widen slowly

Lifecycle rules don't act the moment you save them. Give it a few days, then check:

  1. Billing: in AWS Cost Explorer, group S3 cost by usage type. Storage cost for the moved classes should rise while Standard storage falls.
  2. Request and retrieval costs: watch for a jump in transition requests (many small objects) or in retrieval fees (data that is read more than you thought).
  3. Complaints: if someone needs an archived object, they will find it isn't instantly readable. That tells you the day count was too short for that prefix.

When the first prefix looks right, add the next one as a new rule. One prefix at a time keeps every change easy to undo: set its Status to Disabled and apply again.


Figure 4: Grow your lifecycle configuration one prefix at a time.

A short checklist

  • Know each prefix's size, read pattern and required retention.
  • Leave small objects in Standard or Intelligent-Tiering.
  • Make every stay longer than the class's minimum duration.
  • Add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to every bucket.
  • On versioned buckets, decide how many old versions to keep, then expire the rest.
  • Back up the current configuration before every put.

At CloudSkill Consulting LLC, we test lifecycle rules like this on a small prefix before applying them to a whole bucket. Storage tiers are often the first place a cloud bill can shrink. We do this kind of FinOps check for teams on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. If a rule here behaves differently in your account, write to info@cloudskillconsulting.com.

Sources (official documentation, checked Oct 17, 2026)

  • Amazon S3 storage classes and comparison table (minimum storage duration charges): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html
  • Transitioning objects using S3 Lifecycle (128 KB default, minimum durations, archive overhead, billing timing): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html
  • Lifecycle configuration elements (filters, noncurrent versions, multipart uploads, midnight UTC timing, 1,000 rules): https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/intro-lifecycle-rules.html
  • AWS CLI put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/get-bucket-lifecycle-configuration.html
  • AWS CLI list-multipart-uploads: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/s3api/list-multipart-uploads.html
  • Amazon S3 pricing (minimum storage duration charges): https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/
  • AWS What's New, Jul 16, 2026: S3 removes the 30-day minimum before lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/07/s3-removes-30-day-transitions-standard-ia-one-zone-ia/

title: UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18: uuidv7() vs UUIDv4 vs bigint Primary Keys, Benchmarked
description:
I loaded 10 million rows into PostgreSQL 18 tables keyed by bigint, UUIDv4 and UUIDv7 and compared load time, WAL, index size and insert throughput. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

UUIDv7 is a UUID that starts with a 48-bit Unix timestamp in milliseconds, so new IDs sort in creation order. PostgreSQL 18 generates it natively with uuidv7(). As a primary key it keeps the B-tree index compact like a bigint sequence does, while staying globally unique like a random UUIDv4.

I loaded 10 million rows into three otherwise identical PostgreSQL 18.6 tables, keyed by bigint, uuidv4() and uuidv7(). UUIDv7 matched bigint on load time (37.3 s each), while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL. I also found one trap: filtering with uuidv7(interval ...) directly in a WHERE clause skips the index.

TL;DR: should I use UUIDv7 primary keys in Postgres?

Yes, if you want UUID primary keys and the IDs do not need to hide when a row was created. On PostgreSQL 18, use id uuid primary key default uuidv7(). On PostgreSQL 17 or older, generate UUIDv7 in your app. Keep UUIDv4 for tokens and IDs whose creation time must stay private, and keep bigint if you never need IDs outside one database.

bigint identity UUIDv4 UUIDv7
Size 8 bytes 16 bytes 16 bytes
Generated by One sequence in the database Anyone, anywhere Anyone, anywhere
Sort order Insert order Random Creation time (ms)
Reveals Row count, insert order Nothing Creation timestamp
10M-row load (my test) 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
PK index after load 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Postgres built-in Always gen_random_uuid() / uuidv4() uuidv7() since 18

What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version defined in RFC 9562, published in May 2024. The first 48 bits hold the Unix timestamp in milliseconds, then 4 version bits, then random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, sorting UUIDv7 values as bytes sorts them by creation time, which B-tree indexes handle well.

The RFC describes it as featuring "a time-ordered value field derived from the widely implemented and well-known Unix Epoch timestamp source," and says "implementations SHOULD utilize UUIDv7 instead of UUIDv1 and UUIDv6 if possible."

A UUIDv7 from my test database, read left to right:

01a14a80-6c02-7160-b932-6c5ecd65f3c7
└──────┬─────┘ │
  timestamp    version 7   (rest: sub-millisecond precision + random)

Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added uuidv7(), an alias uuidv4() for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp(), which reads the timestamp back out. The PostgreSQL 18 docs say the timestamp uses "millisecond precision + sub-millisecond timestamp + random." PostgreSQL 17 and older have no uuidv7().

```sql title="PostgreSQL 18.6"
SELECT uuidv7(), uuidv4();
-- 01a14a74-450a-7a7e-a2f5-713a6b1da251 | 8c13f904-b813-4570-92de-5622dbb59443

SELECT uuid_extract_version(uuidv7()), uuid_extract_timestamp(uuidv7());
-- 7 | 2026-10-17 20:21:36.266+05

SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'); -- a UUIDv7 with a timestamp shifted one hour back




On PostgreSQL 17 the same call fails with `ERROR: function uuidv7() does not exist`. There, generate UUIDv7 in your application (Prisma's `uuid(7)` or the npm `uuid` package's `v7()`), or upgrade.

The [PostgreSQL 18 release announcement](https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-18-released-3142/) calls it "the database-friendly uuidv7() function that provides better indexing and read performance for UUIDs." Here is what that looked like in my test.

## Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4?

For inserts, yes. Loading 10 million rows took 37.3 s with UUIDv7 and 84.2 s with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 4.6 GB of WAL against 2.1 GB. With 8 clients each inserting one row per transaction, UUIDv4 managed about 15% fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 was within 2% of a `bigint` sequence on every insert test.

![UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 B-tree inserts: random UUIDv4 keys land on any leaf page and split pages across the index, while time-ordered UUIDv7 keys append to the rightmost leaf like a bigint sequence](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251441/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-btree.jpg)

### Benchmark setup

- PostgreSQL 18.6 with default settings (`shared_buffers` 128 MB), on an 8 vCPU Xeon with 15 GB RAM.
- Three tables: `id` (the key under test), `created_at timestamptz default now()` and a 64-character `payload`.
- Bulk load: one `INSERT ... SELECT` of 10,000,000 rows per table after a `CHECKPOINT`. WAL is measured with `pg_current_wal_lsn()` and index density with [pgstattuple](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/pgstattuple.html)'s `pgstatindex()`.
- Concurrent inserts: `pgbench`, 8 clients, 60 seconds of single-row `INSERT`s into the preloaded tables, 2 rounds. The table shows the average of the two rounds.



```sql title="The three tables"
CREATE TABLE t_bigint (id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY, created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv4 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv4(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE t_uuidv7 (id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),                created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), payload text NOT NULL);

Results

Metric bigint UUIDv4 UUIDv7
10M-row bulk load 37.3 s 84.2 s 37.3 s
WAL written by the load 1,964 MB 4,598 MB 2,098 MB
Table (heap) size 1,116 MB 1,202 MB 1,202 MB
Primary key index size 214 MB 385 MB 301 MB
Index leaf density 90.0% 70.3% 90.0%
Index leaf fragmentation 0.0% 49.8% 0.0%
Single-row inserts, 8 clients 49,528/s 41,331/s 48,690/s

UUIDv7's index is 41% larger than bigint's, because each key is 16 bytes instead of 8, but it is packed just as tightly (90% leaf density). UUIDv4's index is 28% larger again than UUIDv7's, because random inserts split pages all over the tree and leave them about 70% full.

Why are random UUIDv4 primary keys slow?

Each new UUIDv4 lands at a random position in the B-tree, so inserts touch pages spread across the whole index. Once the index is larger than memory, every insert can mean reading a cold page, dirtying it, and logging a full-page image to WAL after each checkpoint. UUIDv7 keys always go to the rightmost leaf, the same hot page a sequence uses.

That explains each number in the table. The 2.2x WAL comes from full-page writes for thousands of different leaf pages. The 70% leaf density comes from 50/50 page splits in the middle of the tree. In my test the UUIDv4 index (385 MB) was three times shared_buffers (128 MB), so the gap in single-row inserts (15%) was smaller than in bulk loading (2.3x). It will grow as the table and index outgrow memory.

How do I use UUIDv7 as a primary key in PostgreSQL 18?

Declare the column as uuid with DEFAULT uuidv7(). Keep the native uuid type, not text: it stores 16 bytes instead of 36 characters plus overhead. Existing UUIDv4 rows can stay. Both versions share one uuid column, and new UUIDv7 keys simply sort after the old random ones.

```sql title="New table"
CREATE TABLE orders (
id uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7(),
total_cents integer NOT NULL,
created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);






```sql title="Existing table: new rows get UUIDv7"
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN id SET DEFAULT uuidv7();

Changing the default does not rewrite old rows or rebuild the index. It only changes how future keys are generated, so the right edge of the index starts behaving like a sequence from then on.

How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma and Drizzle?

In Prisma, use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) to let PostgreSQL 18 generate it. In Drizzle, use uuid().primaryKey().default(sql\uuidv7()). I tested all three on PostgreSQL 18.6. Every ID came out as version 7, and 1,000 sequential creates sorted exactly in creation order.

```prisma title="prisma/schema.prisma (Prisma 7.10.1)"
// UUIDv7 generated by Prisma Client in Node.js
model Order {
id String @id @default(uuid(7)) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}

// UUIDv7 generated by PostgreSQL 18
model Invoice {
id String @id @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) @db.Uuid
total Int
createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}




The two Prisma options are not equivalent. `prisma migrate dev` created `"id" UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT uuidv7()` for `Invoice` but no default at all for `Order`. So a raw SQL insert into `Order` failed with `null value in column "id" ... violates not-null constraint` (code 23502), while the same insert into `Invoice` worked. If anything other than Prisma Client writes to the table (SQL scripts, another service, a queue worker), use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`. The [Prisma schema reference](https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/reference/prisma-schema-reference) documents both.



```ts title="schema.ts (Drizzle 0.45.4)"
import { sql } from "drizzle-orm";
import { integer, pgTable, timestamp, uuid } from "drizzle-orm/pg-core";

export const invoices = pgTable("invoices", {
  id: uuid().primaryKey().default(sql`uuidv7()`),
  total: integer().notNull(),
  createdAt: timestamp({ withTimezone: true }).notNull().defaultNow(),
});

drizzle-kit generate turned that into "id" uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT uuidv7() NOT NULL. Drizzle's .defaultRandom() still means gen_random_uuid(), which is UUIDv4. For which ORM to pick in the first place, see my Drizzle vs Prisma benchmark.

Can I query by time using a UUIDv7 key?

Yes, because UUIDv7 order is time order: ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 returns the newest rows from the primary key alone. For a time range, compare against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap it in a subquery. Used directly, the volatile function forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test.

```sql title="Rows from the last 30 seconds"
-- Slow: uuidv7() is VOLATILE, so it cannot be an index condition
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds');
-- Parallel Seq Scan, Rows Removed by Filter: 5,280,621 per worker, 3,430 ms

-- Fast: a scalar subquery is evaluated once (InitPlan) and used as the index bound
SELECT count(*) FROM t_uuidv7 WHERE id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-30 seconds'));
-- Parallel Index Only Scan using t_uuidv7_pkey, Index Cond: (id >= (InitPlan 1).col1), ~42 ms




Both queries returned the correct count. The fix only changes the plan. The boundary is approximate within a millisecond, because the bound has random bits after the timestamp, so keep a real `created_at` column for exact cut-offs and reports. `ORDER BY id DESC` on a UUIDv4 table also runs fast, but its "latest" rows are random ones.

## Is UUIDv7 safe to expose in URLs?

Only if creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the timestamp from a UUIDv7: `uuid_extract_timestamp()` returned `2026-10-17 20:32:57.748+05` for a row whose `created_at` was 10 ms earlier. RFC 9562 says "if UUIDs are required for use with any security operation within an application context in any shape or form, then UUIDv4 SHOULD be utilized."

Practical rules:

- **Fine as UUIDv7:** orders, posts, messages, events, internal IDs, anything you would happily sort by date.
- **Use UUIDv4 or a random token:** password reset tokens, invite links, API keys, session IDs, and records where signup time is private (for example, user IDs in a service where account age matters).
- **Never rely on any UUID for authorization.** Unguessable is not the same as access control.

## UUIDv7 vs bigint vs ULID: which should I use?

Use `bigint` identity when IDs are created only by one database and never leave it: smallest index, fastest joins. Use UUIDv7 when clients, services or offline devices create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. ULID gives similar time-ordered properties, but it needs a text column or a conversion, while UUIDv7 fits the native 16-byte `uuid` type.

![Decision chart: bigint identity for single-database internal IDs, UUIDv7 for distributed or client-generated IDs, UUIDv4 for secrets and tokens, ULID only when you need its text format](https://res.cloudinary.com/wasicloudinary/image/upload/v1792251442/fabwaseem/blog/uuidv7-postgres/diagram-decision.jpg)

| Need | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| Internal IDs, one database, maximum speed | `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` |
| IDs generated in the app, mobile or other services | UUIDv7 |
| Merging rows from several databases or regions | UUIDv7 |
| IDs that must not reveal creation time | UUIDv4 |
| Secrets: tokens, reset links, API keys | Random token (UUIDv4 or longer) |
| Existing ULID system | Keep ULID, or store it as `uuid` (both are 128 bits) |

Before relying on `uuidv7()`, run `SELECT version();` on every environment, including CI and local Docker containers, since a server still on 17 will reject it. If you self-host Postgres next to your app as in my [Coolify self-hosting guide](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/self-host-nextjs-with-coolify), the major version is set by the database image you choose.

## Common UUIDv7 mistakes

- **Storing UUIDs as `text` or `varchar(36)`.** Use the `uuid` type: 16 bytes, faster comparisons.
- **Calling `uuidv7(interval ...)` directly in `WHERE`.** Wrap it in `(SELECT ...)` or compute the bound in the app, or the index is skipped.
- **Using Prisma `uuid(7)` when other writers exist.** It sets no database default. Use `dbgenerated("uuidv7()")`.
- **Expecting `uuidv7()` on PostgreSQL 17.** It does not exist there. Generate in the app or upgrade to 18.
- **Exposing UUIDv7 where timing is private.** Its first 48 bits are the creation time.
- **Dropping `created_at`.** The UUID timestamp is approximate and set by whoever generated the ID. Keep a real column for reporting.

## Key takeaways

- UUIDv7 starts with a 48-bit millisecond Unix timestamp, so IDs sort by creation time; PostgreSQL 18 generates it with uuidv7().
- In my 10M-row test, UUIDv7 loaded as fast as bigint (37.3 s) while UUIDv4 took 84.2 s and wrote 2.2x more WAL.
- UUIDv4's primary key index ended 28% larger than UUIDv7's, with 70% leaf density and 50% fragmentation.
- With 8 concurrent clients, UUIDv4 inserted about 15% fewer rows per second than UUIDv7.
- Wrap uuidv7(interval ...) in a scalar subquery for time-range filters; called directly, it forced a full table scan.
- Prisma's uuid(7) generates IDs in the client with no database default; dbgenerated("uuidv7()") puts the default in Postgres.
- UUIDv7 reveals creation time, so keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for secrets and private timestamps.

## FAQ

### What is UUIDv7?

UUIDv7 is the time-ordered UUID version from RFC 9562, published in May 2024. Its first 48 bits are a Unix timestamp in milliseconds, followed by version bits and random or counter bits. Because the timestamp comes first, UUIDv7 values sort by creation time, which keeps B-tree indexes compact when they are used as primary keys.

### Does PostgreSQL support UUIDv7?

Yes, since PostgreSQL 18, released on September 25, 2025. It added the uuidv7() function, an optional interval argument that shifts the timestamp, uuidv4() as an alias for gen_random_uuid(), and uuid_extract_timestamp() to read the time back. PostgreSQL 17 and older return an error that uuidv7() does not exist.

### Is UUIDv7 faster than UUIDv4 in Postgres?

For inserts, yes. In my PostgreSQL 18.6 test, a 10-million-row load took 37.3 seconds with UUIDv7 and 84.2 seconds with UUIDv4, and UUIDv4 wrote 2.2 times more WAL. With 8 clients inserting single rows, UUIDv4 managed about 15 percent fewer inserts per second. UUIDv7 stayed within 2 percent of bigint.

### Should I use UUIDv7 or bigint as a primary key?

Use bigint identity when one database creates every ID and the IDs never leave your system, because its index is smallest and joins are fastest. Use UUIDv7 when the app, mobile clients or other services create IDs, or when you merge data across databases. In my test UUIDv7's index was 41 percent larger than bigint's.

### How do I use UUIDv7 with Prisma?

Use @default(uuid(7)) to generate the ID in Prisma Client, or @default(dbgenerated("uuidv7()")) on PostgreSQL 18 to generate it in the database. Add @db.Uuid for the native type. The uuid(7) option sets no database default, so raw SQL inserts fail with a not-null error; dbgenerated works for every writer.

### How do I use UUIDv7 on PostgreSQL 17?

PostgreSQL 17 has no uuidv7() function, so generate UUIDv7 in your application and store it in a uuid column. Prisma's uuid(7) default and the npm uuid package's v7() both produce RFC 9562 version 7 values. When you upgrade to PostgreSQL 18, switch the column default to uuidv7() without rewriting old rows.

### Is it safe to expose UUIDv7 in URLs?

Only when creation time is not sensitive. Anyone can decode the first 48 bits, and uuid_extract_timestamp() returns the time in PostgreSQL. RFC 9562 says UUIDv4 should be used if UUIDs are involved in any security operation. Keep UUIDv4 or random tokens for reset links, invites, API keys and private user records.

### Can I query a time range using UUIDv7 ids?

Yes. Compare the key against uuidv7(interval '-1 hour'), but wrap the call in a scalar subquery such as id >= (SELECT uuidv7(interval '-1 hour')). Because uuidv7() is volatile, calling it directly in WHERE forced a full parallel scan of 15.8 million rows in my test, about 3.4 seconds instead of about 42 milliseconds.


---

*Originally published on [fabwaseem.com](https://www.fabwaseem.com/blog/uuidv7-postgres).*

title: Sign JWTs from your Functions without managing private keys
description:
Vercel KMS lets you sign JWTs and arbitrary messages from your Vercel Functions using managed asymmetric signing keys, so private keys never live in your code or environment variables. Your function authenticates with its Vercel OIDC token, and the private key stays inside Vercel's key management service while verifiers use only the public key.

With Vercel KMS you can:

  • Create and rotate issuers and signing keys (RSA and ECDSA) from the CLI and dashboard.

  • Sign JWTs with custom claims and a configurable TTL, or sign raw bytes, using the @vercel/kms package.

  • Grant a project signing access per environment, including production, preview, development, and custom environments.

  • Constrain the claims a project can request per grant, and validate token claims against a JSON Schema.

  • Verify signed tokens anywhere. Each issuer publishes a public OpenID Connect Discovery document at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/.well-known/openid-configuration and a JWK set at https://kms.vercel.com/<issuerId>/jwks.json, so any standard OIDC or JOSE library can validate tokens without Vercel-specific code.

Sign a token inside a function:

Verify a token anywhere with a standard JOSE library, using the issuer's public JWKS:

Set up an issuer and grant a project access from the CLI:

As a best practice, create a separate issuer per project and environment. Isolating issuers keeps each token audience distinct, scopes signing access to exactly one project and environment, and lets you rotate or revoke keys for one without affecting the others.

To get started, read the docs or open Key Management in your team's dashboard.

title: What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure
description:
What I Learned Building the Cloud Resume Challenge on Azure

I'm working toward a cloud and systems administration career, and I wanted a project that proved I can do more than pass certification exams. So I took on the Cloud Resume Challenge (Azure): build a resume website, add a live visitor counter, and do it the way a real team would, with infrastructure as code, automated pipelines, and good security habits.

Live site: https://stresumelvoc8r.z1.web.core.windows.net/
Code: frontend · backend

Below is what I built, what broke along the way, and how each lesson connects to the jobs I'm applying for.

What I built

  • Frontend: an HTML/CSS resume hosted as a static website on Azure Storage.
  • Visitor counter: a small JavaScript file calls an API every time the page loads.
  • API: a Python Azure Function on the Flex Consumption plan (serverless, scales to zero).
  • Database: Cosmos DB (NoSQL, serverless) stores one record: the visitor count.
  • Infrastructure as code: everything in Azure is defined in Terraform.
  • CI/CD: GitHub Actions pipelines test, plan, and deploy every change, and production changes wait for my approval.

The rule I set for myself: no passwords, keys, or secrets stored anywhere. Not in the code, not in GitHub, not in the database connection.

Lesson 1: Infrastructure as code beats clicking around the portal

I've built plenty of things by clicking through the Azure portal. Terraform changed how I think about it. My entire environment (storage, database, function, monitoring, permissions) lives in text files I can read, review, and rebuild.

The concept that clicked for me was Terraform state. Terraform keeps a record of what it has built. I stored that state remotely in an Azure Storage account with versioning and soft delete turned on, so a mistake can be rolled back.

On the job: any team managing more than a handful of resources needs repeatable builds. Being able to say "I can define and rebuild an environment from code" is the difference between an admin who maintains things and one who can scale them.

Lesson 2: Pipelines without stored secrets (OIDC)

The old way to let GitHub deploy to Azure is to create a service principal, copy its secret, and paste it into GitHub. That secret can leak, and it expires at the worst possible time.

Instead I used OIDC (workload identity federation). GitHub proves to Azure who it is with a short-lived token, and Azure trusts that token only if it comes from my repo, in a pull request or the production environment. No secret exists to steal.

What broke: my first deploy failed with AADSTS700213: No matching federated identity record. The error showed that GitHub's token now includes the numeric IDs of my account and repo, not just their names. That stops someone from deleting a repo and recreating one with the same name to hijack the trust. My Azure configuration only trusted the old name-only format. Once I added credentials matching the new format, it worked.

On the job: reading an authentication error carefully and comparing "what was sent" with "what was expected" is everyday identity troubleshooting, the same skill I use for Entra ID sign-in issues.

Lesson 3: Least privilege, for real

It's easy to give a pipeline Owner and move on. I didn't. The pipeline's identity is:

  • Contributor on one resource group, not the whole subscription.
  • Allowed to grant permissions only from a short approved list of data roles, enforced with an Azure ABAC condition. Without that limit, an identity that can assign roles could make itself Owner.

On the job: "who has access to what, and why" comes up in every audit and security review. I can now explain role scope, privilege escalation risk, and how to prevent it, not just in theory.

Lesson 4: Managed identities mean no database keys

The Function App connects to Cosmos DB with a managed identity: Azure gives the app its own identity, and I granted it a database role. Cosmos DB has key-based access disabled entirely, so even if someone found my code, there's no key in it to use.

On the job: removing stored credentials from apps is one of the most effective security improvements an admin can make, and managed identities are how you do it in Azure.

Lesson 5: MFA isn't just for the portal anymore

Partway through, every Azure CLI command started failing with AADSTS50076, an MFA requirement, and it never actually prompted me for MFA. The cause: on Windows, the CLI was quietly reusing a cached sign-in through the Windows account broker, and that cached sign-in had no MFA. Clearing the cached tokens and signing in with az login --use-device-code forced a proper MFA sign-in.

On the job: Microsoft now requires MFA for Azure management from the CLI and other tools, not just the portal. When scripts or users suddenly fail to authenticate, knowing about cached tokens and broker sign-ins saves hours.

Lesson 6: The small stuff breaks things

Some of my most useful lessons were the least glamorous:

  • Line endings: Windows saves files with different line endings than Linux. A bash script saved the Windows way fails with confusing errors. A .gitattributes file fixed it for good.
  • Git Bash path conversion: Git Bash on Windows quietly rewrites anything starting with /, which broke Azure resource IDs until I turned that behavior off.
  • Ignored files don't reach the pipeline: my Terraform variables file worked on my PC but not in GitHub Actions, because my .gitignore (correctly) excluded it. I passed the value as a GitHub variable instead.

On the job: most real outages aren't exotic. They're a setting, a path, or an assumption about which machine a file lives on. Patience and methodical checking matter more than knowing everything.

Lesson 7: Pull requests and approval gates

Every change goes through the same path:

  1. Open a pull request, and the pipeline runs a Terraform plan that shows exactly what would change.
  2. Merge, and the deploy pauses for my approval.
  3. Approve, and it deploys.

I also learned to wait for green checks before merging. I merged a failing change once, and the deploy failed in exactly the way the check had warned me it would.

On the job: this is change management. Reviewing a change before it runs, and having an approval step for production, is the same idea as a change advisory process, just automated.

Lesson 8: Writing code I can test

The counter logic is small, but I wrote it carefully:

  • It uses a Cosmos DB atomic increment, so two visitors arriving at the same moment can't overwrite each other's count.
  • The logic is separate from the web layer, so I could write pytest tests that use fake (mocked) database objects. The tests run on every pull request without touching Azure.
  • Errors return a generic message to the browser, and the details go to Application Insights for me to investigate.

On the job: even as an admin, I write scripts that other people depend on. Testing them before they run in production, and logging errors somewhere useful, is a habit that prevents incidents.

How this applies to the jobs I'm applying for

What I did in this project Where it shows up at work
Defined infrastructure in Terraform Building and rebuilding environments consistently; documenting what exists
OIDC and managed identities Removing stored passwords and keys; securing automation accounts
Scoped roles and ABAC conditions Access reviews, audits, least-privilege design in Entra ID and Azure
Troubleshot MFA and token errors Sign-in and Conditional Access issues for users and service accounts
Pull requests and approval gates Change management and peer review
CI/CD pipelines Automating repetitive admin tasks safely
Monitoring with Application Insights Finding the cause of failures quickly
Serverless and pay-per-use services Keeping cloud costs low and predictable

What's next

  • Custom domain with HTTPS through Cloudflare.
  • An end-to-end test that checks the live site and API after every deploy.
  • A containerized app on Kubernetes, to build on what I learned here.

If you're working through the Cloud Resume Challenge yourself, my advice is: read the error message twice before searching it. Almost every problem I hit was explained right there in the error, once I slowed down enough to compare what was sent with what was expected.

Thanks for reading! Feel free to connect with me on LinkedIn.

title: Trust Is a Feature: Verification Lessons From Building the Calendrz Mobile Backend
description:
Trust was everywhere in my LinkedIn feed last week. LinkedIn is testing a feature that lets verified members confirm their connections’ work and school history, with enough confirmations earning a profile badge. Its engineering team also explained how it detects low-quality AI content. And in Europe, the AI Act’s transparency rules had their first real effect: OpenAI said it will add invisible watermarks to text generated in the EU.

Each of those is a different problem, but the theme is the same. “Trust me” isn’t good enough any more. Platforms are being asked to prove things: that a person really worked where they say, that a piece of text really came from where it claims, that an account is really who it says it is.

I’ve spent the last couple of weeks on a less glamorous version of the same problem: preparing the Calendrz backend for native iOS and Android apps. Most of that work wasn’t about features. It was about making sure that the thing calling our API really is who it claims to be, and that the trust stops when it should.

Why mobile apps make trust harder

A web app has an easy setup: a session cookie, on a domain you control, in a browser that enforces a lot of rules for you. A mobile app is a public client. It runs on a device you don’t control, it can’t keep a secret (anything shipped in an app binary can be extracted), and it stays signed in for weeks. If a token leaks, you need to know, and you need to be able to shut it down.

Calendrz holds access to people’s work and personal calendars. That’s sensitive data: who you meet, when, and often why. So the bar here isn’t “good enough for a to-do app”.

What we built: verification at every hop

Here’s a quick tour of the trust-related pieces that landed in the Calendrz backend over the past couple of weeks.

1. Proof of who’s calling: PKCE public clients

The iOS and Android apps are registered as first-party OAuth clients with no secret, because a secret in an app isn’t really secret. They sign in with PKCE instead, which proves that the app finishing the login is the same app that started it. A malicious app that intercepts the redirect can’t do anything with the code it grabbed.

2. Proof that the link is really ours: Universal Links and App Links

When a login finishes, the browser has to hand control back to the app. Custom URL schemes can be claimed by any app, so we serve the Apple and Android “well-known” verification files from our own domain. That’s how the operating system knows a link to calendrz.com really belongs to the Calendrz app. If an environment isn’t configured, the files return a 404, so a misconfigured server can never claim links it shouldn’t.

3. Detecting stolen tokens: refresh-token reuse detection

This is the one I’m proudest of. The mobile apps get short-lived access tokens (60 minutes) and a refresh token that rotates: every time it’s used, it’s replaced. The catch is that a plain rotation setup only knows about the current token. If an attacker copied an older one, the server just sees an unknown token and rejects it, but never notices that something is wrong.

So we now keep a record (a SHA-256 hash, never the token itself) of every refresh token that has been rotated out. If one of those shows up again, that’s the signature of a stolen token chain, as described in the OAuth security best-practice RFC (RFC 9700). Calendrz then revokes the whole authorization, so both the attacker and the legitimate app have to sign in again, while the user’s other sessions are left alone. Refreshes for a given authorization are serialized at the database level, so two refreshes racing each other can’t be mistaken for an attack, and can’t undo a revocation.

4. Trust that ends when it should: revoke on account deletion

When you close your Calendrz account, or unlink one of your connected calendar accounts, every OAuth authorization tied to that identity is now removed. That covers the mobile apps and any AI assistants you’ve connected over MCP. Their refresh tokens die with the account. The revocation runs only after the deletion has committed, so a failure can’t leave you half-deleted.

5. Failing honestly instead of failing quietly

A smaller one, but it’s the same idea. When the new mobile event endpoints can’t load your calendar from Google or Microsoft, they now return an explicit “service unavailable” error instead of an empty list. An empty calendar is a claim (“you’re free all day”), and an app or agent would act on it. If we can’t verify the answer, we say so.

Trust is a feature, even if nobody sees it

LinkedIn’s colleague vouching will show up as a badge on a profile. Most of the work I’ve described won’t show up anywhere. Nobody opens an app and thinks “great refresh-token rotation”. But it follows the same principle: don’t take identity on faith; verify it, and be able to revoke it.

There’s also a lot of AI in this story. Much of this backend work was planned, written and code-reviewed with AI agents, and several of the review rounds caught real issues: a race between two concurrent refreshes, a revocation that could have been rolled back, a log line that leaked more than it should have. As more code gets written this way, having automated checks verify the work before it ships is the engineering version of the trust problem LinkedIn and the EU are trying to solve for content.

The Calendrz mobile apps are still in progress, but most of the trust layer underneath them is already in place. That felt like the right order: build the part people need to rely on before the part they’ll see.

Calendrz keeps your work and personal calendars in sync, privately and securely. Find out more at calendrz.com.

title: TIL: What the User Count Option Really Affects in GBase Database
description:
During a typical installation of GBase Database (GBase 8s), the installer asks you to select an expected user count:

1 - 1–100
2 - 101–500
3 - 501–1000
4 - 1000+

It's tempting to accept the default 1–100 and move on. For a quick test, that may be perfectly reasonable. But this option is worth understanding before you initialize an instance for a larger workload.

What Does the User Count Option Affect?

The expected user count helps the installer choose initial instance configuration parameters appropriate for the anticipated workload.

Depending on the installation script and configuration template, these settings may include resource limits related to concurrent connections and other instance resources.

In other words, you're giving the installer a rough indication of how many users the database is expected to serve. It is a sizing input, not a guarantee that the instance will support exactly that number of concurrent connections.

Important: The selected range should not be treated as a direct connection limit. Actual connection capacity depends on the resulting configuration, available system resources, workload, and other relevant limits.

Which User Count Should You Choose?

A simple rule of thumb can help:

  • Feature validation: The default 1–100 range is generally a reasonable starting point.
  • Development and functional testing: Choose a range that reflects the expected test environment.
  • Concurrency testing: Select a range based on the planned workload, then verify the resulting connection and resource settings.
  • Larger deployments: Review the generated configuration and size the instance according to actual workload requirements rather than relying on the installer choice alone.

For example, if you're only validating SQL syntax or checking whether an application can connect, a small user-count range may be sufficient.

If you're preparing a concurrency test with hundreds of simulated users, accepting the default without checking the resulting configuration could leave the instance poorly suited to the test.

Don't Stop at the Installation Wizard

After the typical installation finishes, inspect the generated instance configuration to understand which values were selected.

Check the relevant resource and connection parameters, and confirm that they match your testing or deployment requirements. The exact parameters to review depend on the configuration produced by your GBase Database installation.

For production environments, also consider memory, CPU, storage performance, connection behavior, and workload characteristics. The user-count selection is only one part of database sizing.

Final Takeaway

The user-count option in the GBase Database (GBase 8s) typical installer is more than a cosmetic question. It helps guide the initial instance configuration based on the expected scale of use.

For quick feature validation, the default may be enough. For concurrency testing or larger deployments, choose the range deliberately and verify the resulting settings.

A useful installation habit: don't just ask what value the wizard wants. Ask what configuration that choice will produce.

Have you ever discovered that an installation default affected your database testing or deployment? Share your experience in the comments.

title: AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity
description:
AsyncHttpClient CVE-2026-107282: when a replayed request carries the wrong identity

The failure class, not just the identifier

CVE-2026-107282 is one entry in a batch of fixes published for AsyncHttpClient (AHC), the Java library that a large share of JVM services use to make outbound HTTP calls. The batch matters more than any single item because every entry in it has the same shape: the client decides who it is, or who it is talking to, from state that was computed for a different request. The result is a library that is diligent about authentication and still sends credentials to the wrong place.
The headline issue, affecting versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1, concerns cross-host request replay. When AHC re-issues a request against a different host, it updates the current request object but leaves the target request and the associated proxy context pointing at the original host. Path, Host header, Authorization credentials, or a cleartext body computed for host A can therefore be transmitted to host B.

Why that is a credential disclosure rather than a cosmetic bug

Consider a service that talks to an internal API and, after a redirect or a retry against a different endpoint, replays a request. The Authorization header was minted for the first host. The second host may be a third-party service, a different tenant's endpoint, or an attacker-controlled redirect target. Because the client decided the request was a replay, from its point of view nothing unusual happened; from the receiving end, a valid bearer token for an unrelated system just arrived in plaintext or in a header the receiver can read.
The same reasoning applies to the body. A replayed POST whose payload was assembled for the original destination can carry internal identifiers, query fragments or credentials to a host that was never meant to see them. In a microservice mesh where dozens of internal services trust bearer tokens issued by a shared issuer, a single misplaced header is enough to move laterally.
The practical lesson is about the object model, not about HTTP. Replay is inherently a copy operation, and every field of the copy has to be re-derived for the new destination. When one field is treated as immutable context, the copy is incomplete, and the incompleteness is invisible to any test that only checks whether the retry succeeded.

The rest of the batch

CVE-2026-107281 is arguably the more interesting sibling. The HTTP/1.1 connection pool key excludes the authenticated principal when connection-oriented NTLM or Negotiate authentication is in use, in versions before 3.0.13 and 2.16.1. A pooled connection that was established under one identity can therefore be handed to a different identity. Connection reuse is the entire point of a pool, and NTLM authenticates the connection rather than each request, so the substitution is not visible at the request layer. Any multi-tenant service that authenticates to a downstream system with NTLM through a shared client instance is exposed, and the failure is silent on both ends.
CVE-2026-107283, rated Low, is a cryptographic hygiene defect: Realm.Builder generates the HTTP Digest client nonce with ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographically secure source, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. A predictable nonce weakens the replay protection that Digest was designed to provide, which makes an unrelated credential-exposure bug worse rather than better.
CVE-2026-107284, also Low, concerns WebSocketHandler.upgrade: a handshake whose Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or invalid is aborted, but the handler continues into pipeline installation. Failing to stop on a failed validation is exactly the pattern that turns a validation routine into a formality.
CVE-2026-107285, Medium at 5.9, involves proxy authentication on WebSocket requests tunnelled through CONNECT, where NettyRequestFactory.newNettyRequest and requestUri decide whether to attach proxy credentials, in versions before 3.0.12 and 2.16.1. The details differ from the cross-host replay case, the reasoning does not: a decision about credentials is made from context that does not describe the request actually being sent.
A related defect in a different Java client shows how common the shape is. CVE-2026-107314 describes pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC driver, in versions 42.7.11 through 42.7.13: when the requireAuth connection property excludes every authentication method the driver knows, for example by listing them all with negation, the driver enforces nothing and accepts any method the server offers. A configuration intended to restrict authentication produces no restriction at all. The score is 5.9 and the consequence is a downgrade to whatever the server proposes.

What to do

Upgrade. The AHC fixes are in 3.0.13 and 2.16.1 for the replay and pool-key issues, and in 3.0.12 and 2.16.1 for the proxy and WebSocket items, so the practical target is the newest build in the line you maintain. Because the library is a transitive dependency in most projects, the version that matters is the one resolved into the final artifact, not the one you typed.
Inventories should be resolved dependency trees, not dependency files. Ask the build for the effective version of org.asynchttpclient:async-http-client in every deployable, and rerun the query after a framework upgrade, because spring and cloud libraries routinely pin the version for you.
If NTLM or Negotiate authentication to a downstream system is in play, treat CVE-2026-107281 as the priority. It is the item that can cross an identity boundary inside your own infrastructure without any external redirect, and it will not appear in a request log that only records that a 200 was returned.
Review your own use of copies. Where your code builds a request for one destination and then reuses it for another, verify that the URI, Host header, credentials and body are all recomputed. The library fix closes the library's path; application-level copies have the same failure mode.
Rotate where exposure was possible. Any deployment that ran an affected version between the release of the fix and the upgrade may have delivered a credential to a host that should never have received it, and rotating is cheaper than reasoning about whether it did.

title: Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence
description:
Boutique Law Firm Website Design: A Customized Approach to Digital Excellence

In the realm of legal services, boutique law firms distinguish themselves through specialized expertise and personalized client relationships. However, when it comes to their online presence, many firms rely on standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms, which can dilute their unique value proposition and fail to resonate with their target audience. These generic solutions often lack the sophistication and tailored approach that boutique law firms require to effectively communicate their brand identity and services.

The failure of standard templates and generic forms can be attributed to their inability to capture the nuances and complexities of a boutique law firm's practice areas, attorney profiles, and client success stories. Such websites typically lack a deep understanding of the firm's history, mission, and values, resulting in a digital presence that feels impersonal and unengaging. Furthermore, generic templates often prioritize aesthetics over functionality, leading to poor user experience, low engagement, and ultimately, a lack of conversions.

From an engineering perspective, there are several key takeaways for designing a boutique law firm website that truly reflects the firm's unique character and drives meaningful results:

  1. Customized Information Architecture: A well-structured website with clear navigation and categorized content helps visitors quickly find the information they need, whether it's learning about the firm's practice areas, reading attorney bios, or accessing resources and news.
  2. Personalized User Experience: Implementing personalized elements, such as dynamic content recommendations based on user behavior or location-specific practice area highlights, can significantly enhance the user experience and encourage deeper engagement with the website.
  3. Integrated Conversion Optimization: By incorporating conversion rate optimization (CRO) strategies, such as prominent calls-to-action, streamlined contact forms, and strategically placed trust badges, boutique law firms can increase the likelihood of visitors taking desired actions, whether it's scheduling a consultation, signing up for a newsletter, or simply getting in touch.

title: I Built Kiver: A Discovery Marketplace for Telegram Bots and Mini Apps
description:
Building a Telegram bot is one thing. Getting people to discover it is another.

That problem is what led me to build Kiver.

"https://www.getkiver.com" (https://www.getkiver.com)

The problem I wanted to solve

Telegram has an ecosystem of bots and Mini Apps for almost everything: AI assistants, productivity tools, finance, education, gaming, automation and more.

Developers spend time building these products, improving their features and trying to attract users. But once a bot is ready, discovery becomes a challenge of its own.

A Telegram link is useful, but it doesn't always give a product the broader visibility it needs. Potential users may not know the bot exists, and developers need more ways to put their work in front of relevant audiences.

I wanted to build something that could help bridge that gap.

What is Kiver?

Kiver is a discovery marketplace for Telegram bots and Mini Apps.

The idea is straightforward: help users find useful Telegram tools and give makers a public place to showcase what they've built.

On Kiver, users can:

  • Browse Telegram tools across different categories.
  • Search for bots by name, username or use case.
  • Explore individual product pages.
  • Upvote tools they find useful.
  • Open listed bots directly in Telegram.

For developers and makers, Kiver provides a way to turn a Telegram link into a dedicated, shareable product listing.

Giving Telegram tools a public home

One part of Kiver I'm particularly interested in is discoverability beyond Telegram itself.

A maker can submit a public Telegram link, review the listing details, select a category and publish a product page.

That page gives the tool a dedicated URL that can be shared in communities, included in documentation or discovered through search engines.

The goal is to create another discovery channel for Telegram products instead of relying entirely on someone already knowing a bot's username or receiving its link from another person.

Of course, a public page doesn't guarantee search rankings or new users. The challenge is building a useful directory that people actually want to visit.

I'm still growing it

Kiver is an early-stage project, and I'm starting to see traffic coming to the website.

It's not massive traffic, and I'm not going to pretend it is. But seeing people visit a product you're building is useful feedback. It gives me a reason to keep improving the experience, expanding the directory and thinking more carefully about how users discover and evaluate tools.

The next challenge is turning visits into something more meaningful: people finding useful products, makers getting discovered, and visitors returning because the directory helps them.

That's the kind of growth I want to build toward.

What I'd like to improve

There are several areas I'm interested in developing further:

  • Better discovery: Helping users find relevant tools without having to know their names beforehand.
  • More useful listings: Making it easier to understand what a bot does before opening it.
  • More makers: Bringing more developers into the directory so users have a wider selection of tools.
  • A stronger community: Making product feedback and voting more useful for both users and builders.

The important part is making the directory valuable to both sides. More listings are useful, but only if people can find tools that genuinely solve their problems.

Try Kiver

If you've built a Telegram bot or Mini App, you can explore the directory and submit your own project.

Website: https://www.getkiver.com

Browse the directory, see how listings work, or launch your own Telegram tool on the platform.

I'm building Kiver in public and would appreciate feedback from developers, indie hackers and anyone working in the Telegram ecosystem.

If you build Telegram tools, what is the biggest challenge you've faced when trying to get your first users?

I'd be interested to hear what has worked for you.
