title: Building a liquid glass card with CSS
description:
A glass card can look great over a gradient and become unreadable the moment you put real content behind it. The blur is only one part of the effect. Tint, edge highlights and the backdrop matter just as much.

I built GradientDeck, formerly Gradienty.codes. Its liquid glass tool lets you adjust those pieces visually. Here’s a smaller, standalone CSS version you can use without the generator.

Start with something behind the glass

A flat background gives the filter very little to work with. This example uses two radial gradients so you can actually see the material.

<div class="scene">
  <article class="glass">
    <div class="glass-content">
      <h2>Make room for the good stuff.</h2>
      <p>A small glass card, built with plain CSS.</p>
    </div>
  </article>
</div>

.scene {
  min-height: 28rem;
  display: grid;
  place-items: center;
  padding: 2rem;
  background:
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 20% 25%, #0d9488, transparent 60%),
    radial-gradient(ellipse at 80% 75%, #7c3aed, transparent 60%),
    #0f172a;
}

.glass {
  position: relative;
  width: min(100%, 24rem);
  box-sizing: border-box;
  padding: 2rem;
  border: 1px solid rgb(255 255 255 / 24%);
  border-radius: 1.75rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
  box-shadow:
    0 20px 70px rgb(0 0 0 / 24%),
    inset 0 1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 35%),
    inset 0 -1px 0 rgb(255 255 255 / 8%);
}

@supports ((backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) or
           (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1px))) {
  .glass {
    background: rgb(15 23 42 / 48%);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
    backdrop-filter: blur(18px) saturate(150%);
  }
}

.glass-content {
  position: relative;
  z-index: 1;
}

.glass h2 { margin: 0 0 0.75rem; }
.glass p { margin: 0; line-height: 1.6; }

The card starts with a solid background. Browsers that support backdrop filtering get the translucent version through @supports.

Add a highlight without washing out the text

The thin border defines the silhouette. The inset shadows catch the upper and lower edges. A separate highlight layer adds a little sheen:

.glass::before {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: 0;
  border-radius: inherit;
  pointer-events: none;
  background: linear-gradient(
    135deg,
    rgb(255 255 255 / 14%),
    transparent 45%
  );
}

Keep the highlight subtle. A bright white overlay across the entire card quickly makes the surface look cloudy.

Tune it in this order

  1. Backdrop: put the card over the actual page or image you plan to use.
  2. Tint: increase the background alpha until the text is comfortable to read.
  3. Blur: soften distracting detail without losing all the color behind it.
  4. Highlights: add enough light to define the edges.

A blur value alone won’t guarantee readable text. Check the card over both the brightest and busiest parts of the background, especially if content scrolls underneath it.

When nothing seems to blur

First, check that the card’s background is translucent and that there is something behind it.

Then inspect its ancestors. A parent with opacity below 1, a filter, a mask or its own backdrop filter can limit which pixels the child samples. Nested glass panels are a common place to encounter this. MDN explains the behavior in its backdrop-filter reference.

Use an alpha background color to make the surface translucent. Setting opacity on the whole card also fades its text and children.

Give people a solid option

Where the browser exposes the reduced-transparency preference, you can honor it with an opaque surface:

@media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce) {
  .glass {
    background: #172033;
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: none;
    backdrop-filter: none;
  }

  .glass::before { display: none; }
}

This also removes the decorative highlight. It doesn’t replace checking contrast in the default design.

For performance, start with one filtered surface. Avoid animating the blur radius, and be cautious about adding several overlapping blur layers to every card in a scrolling list. Check the result on the devices your readers actually use.

Try the settings visually

GradientDeck’s liquid glass generator has 20 presets, editable material controls and CSS and Tailwind CSS v4 exports. It’s free and doesn’t require an account. You can also preview the glass over an image from your device.

The example above recreates a glass-like appearance with CSS; it doesn’t implement optical refraction. Start simple, put it over your real UI, and let readability decide how transparent it should be.

title: ChaosProxy: Bulletproof Your Microservices with Automated Fault Injection and Network Chaos Testing
description:
Modern distributed architectures are inherently fragile. Microservices, multi-region database clusters, third-party payment gateways, and external SaaS dependencies fail continuously, unpredictably, and silently.

Most engineering teams rely on unit tests, integration tests, and staging environments to validate reliability. Yet, traditional testing paradigms suffer from a fatal assumption: the network is reliable. The first of the eight fallacies of distributed computing continues to trigger multimillion-dollar outages across the tech sector.

When a downstream payment processor suddenly introduces a 4,500ms tail latency spike, does your service timeout gracefully, or does it saturate connection pools, trigger cascading thread starvation, and bring down your entire ingress tier?

Enter ChaosProxy—the lightweight, programmable, high-performance fault-injection reverse/forward proxy engineered to simulate real-world network turbulence before it hits your production revenue.

The Chaos Engineering Imperative: Why Unit Tests Lie

In modern cloud computing, standard synthetic tests run under pristine local network conditions. In production, your microservices face:

  • Jitter and bufferbloat across cross-zone cloud boundaries.
  • Intermittent HTTP 502/503/504 errors during rolling deployments.
  • Malformed payloads and truncated responses caused by abrupt connection resets.
  • TCP half-open connections that bypass simplistic health-check implementations.

Without real-world validation, your resilience mechanisms—circuit breakers (e.g., Resilience4j, Envoy retries), dead-letter queues, and fallbacks—are merely untested theoretical constructs.

ChaosProxy bridges the gap between static testing and chaotic production realities.

What is ChaosProxy?

ChaosProxy is an ultra-low-latency, zero-dependency proxy built for engineers and platform teams who need deterministic failure testing. Positioned inline between your service and upstream/downstream dependencies, ChaosProxy dynamically manipulates network traffic based on declarative rules or dynamic API calls.

+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
|  Your Service    | ------> |    ChaosProxy    | ------> |  Target Dependency   |
| (API/Worker/K8s) |         | (Fault Injection)|         | (DB/Gateway/REST/gRPC|
+------------------+         +------------------+         +----------------------+
                                      ^
                                      | Dynamic Rules via REST / CLI
                             +------------------+
                             | Chaos Controller |
                             +------------------+

Whether deployed as a local Docker container in continuous integration pipelines, a Kubernetes sidecar, or an edge interceptor, ChaosProxy allows developers to inject chaos deterministically with microsecond accuracy.

Core Capabilities of ChaosProxy

1. Deterministic Latency Injection & Tail-Jitter

Simulate real-world network delays using granular mathematical models:

  • Fixed Latency: Force exact delays (e.g., 350ms) to verify timeout configurations.
  • Normal & Pareto Distributions: Simulate tail latency (p95, p99, p99.9) to detect thread exhaustion and queuing vulnerabilities.
  • Jitter: Add variance buffers to uncover synchronization and race condition bugs.

2. Protocol-Level Fault Simulation (HTTP, gRPC, TCP)

  • Status Code Forcing: Intercept outgoing calls and return arbitrary status codes (500 Internal Server Error, 429 Too Many Requests, 503 Service Unavailable).
  • Connection Resets & Drops: Sever the TCP stream mid-transmission (RST packets) to verify how clients handle dropped sockets.
  • Truncated Responses: Deliver partial HTTP response bodies to test parser resiliency and deserialization error handling.

3. Bandwidth Throttling & Packet Manipulation

  • Emulate constrained cellular or satellite environments (e.g., 2G/3G/4G bandwidth caps).
  • Corrupt arbitrary byte sequences across network payloads to validate cryptographic checks and defensive schema validation.

4. Headless Dynamic Control via REST API

Manage chaos on the fly without restarting pods or containers. Integrate directly into CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) to fail PRs that violate recovery SLAs.

Technical Deep Dive: Implementing ChaosProxy

Quickstart Deployment via Docker

Run ChaosProxy alongside your local service stack with zero overhead:

version: '3.8'

services:
  web-api:
    image: my-company/web-api:latest
    environment:
      - PAYMENT_GATEWAY_URL=http://chaos-proxy:8080
    depends_on:
      - chaos-proxy

  chaos-proxy:
    image: ghcr.io/chaosproxy/engine:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:8080" # Proxy Port
      - "9090:9090" # Control API Port
    environment:
      - TARGET_UPSTREAM=https://api.stripe.com
      - PROXY_PORT=8080
      - CONTROL_PORT=9090

Injecting Faults Dynamically via API

Once running, programmatically trigger network anomalies using a simple REST request:

Example: Injecting a 2.5-second p99 Latency Spike with 30% Probability 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "latency",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "delay_ms": 2500,
      "jitter_ms": 500,
      "probability": 0.30
    }
  }'

Example: Simulating Upstream Gateway Collapse (HTTP 503) 

curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "fault": "http_error",
    "target_path": "/v1/charges",
    "params": {
      "status_code": 503,
      "body": "{\"error\": \"Service Temporarily Unavailable\"}",
      "probability": 1.0
    }
  }'

Automated CI/CD Integration (GitHub Actions)

Add continuous resilience testing directly to your pull requests:

- name: Run Chaos Proxy Resilience Suite
  run: |
    # 1. Start test environment
    docker compose up -d

    # 2. Inject 5000ms latency on downstream dependencies
    curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/v1/faults \
      -d '{"fault": "latency", "params": {"delay_ms": 5000, "probability": 1.0}}'

    # 3. Execute End-to-End Test (Must gracefully fallback within 500ms)
    npm run test:resilience

Architectural Comparison: Why ChaosProxy?

Feature Standard Mocks Linux tc / netem Chaos Mesh / Gremlin ChaosProxy
Layer Application OS / Kernel Kubernetes Cluster Application / L7 Proxy
Privileges Unprivileged Root Required Root / Cluster Admin Unprivileged / App Level
Granularity Static endpoints Network interface Pod/Container level HTTP Route / Payload / Header
CI/CD Fit Easy (but blind) Complex Too Heavy Instant / Native
Dynamic API No No Complex CRDs Simple JSON REST API

Unlike low-level kernel tools like iptables or tc netem, ChaosProxy requires zero elevated root permissions, making it completely secure for shared enterprise CI/CD runners and restricted cloud deployments. Unlike heavyweight cluster tools, ChaosProxy starts in under 15 milliseconds with less than 20MB of memory overhead.

The Economic ROI of Chaos Engineering

Downtime is not an abstract engineering metric—it is a direct financial loss.

  • The average cost of enterprise downtime ranges between $5,600 to $9,000 per minute (Gartner).
  • 70% of enterprise microservice failures are caused by unhandled cascade effects rather than root-cause logic bugs.

By identifying fragile downstream calls, misconfigured timeouts, and missing fallbacks during development, ChaosProxy:

  1. Reduces MTTR (Mean Time to Resolution) by 60% through deterministic bug reproduction.
  2. Eliminates cascading outages before code reaches production environments.
  3. Validates SLAs with concrete empirical data before signing upstream vendor agreements.

Supercharge Your Resilience Engineering Today

Do not wait for a midnight PagerDuty incident to discover that your circuit breakers don't trip properly. Build systems that embrace entropy, absorb downstream failures, and guarantee 99.99% availability under adverse network conditions.

title: How to Design Daily Report Email Queues in Go — 2026 Practical Limits
description:
Short answer: keep each daily report email queue message small by storing the rendered report elsewhere and publishing only report and send references; use one message per recipient or small batch, and treat delayed delivery as a short postponement rather than the daily scheduler.

For a gaming platform, reservation expiry and the email that reports it are different reliability problems. Expire a stale reservation after its fixed hold window through an idempotent worker, then let the daily report summarize durable reservation results. Don't make a large midnight message carry every expired reservation, every recipient, and the rendered email. That couples the latency-sensitive expiry path to a cost-sensitive reporting batch, and one oversized payload can stop the entire run before useful work begins.

My operational recommendation is to set an application limit well below the platform's 256KB body cap, measure the encoded bytes before publish, and fan out by recipient or small batch. Teams that already use several backend capabilities should try Infrai for the queue leg when reducing credential and SDK sprawl matters: one key and one bill cover the broader backend surface, while the queue is called through plain HTTP without installing another vendor SDK. The supporting benefit is practical — its public discovery surface exposes the current request schema and runnable Go examples, shortening the path from an empty client to a validated request.

How should daily report email queues handle batch size and message limits?

Start with capacity planning, not a vendor default. The hard message-body limit is 256KB, but 256KB is a ceiling, not a sensible target. A report job should contain identifiers such as a report reference, recipient reference, and a stable send key. The rendered HTML, reservation rows, and attachments belong in a database or object storage. This keeps retries cheap, makes duplicate deliveries harmless when the consumer records the stable key, and lets the worker fetch the latest authorized data instead of trusting a stale blob copied into the queue hours earlier.

Small messages also make the failure domain legible. Suppose a daily gaming report covers many players whose holds expired during the prior day. One giant payload turns a single bad address or serialization mistake into a batch-wide retry. One job per user gives the cleanest isolation and fastest retry decisions; a small batch reduces publish and consume operations when cost dominates and the recipients have similar processing characteristics. I'm not sure which batch width is right for your workload until the team measures rendered-reference size, send latency, retry rate, and peak worker concurrency. Pick an initial width from those constraints, then revise it against an SLO such as “99% of eligible daily reports handed to the mail provider within 20 minutes,” rather than copying an arbitrary round number.

Keep slack.

The same separation protects deletion workflows. Queue retention tops out at 30 days and acknowledgment deletes the message, so the queue cannot be the audit record for who received what. Store the durable report state under the retention and erasure policy appropriate to the user, and keep the queue as an operational work list. A reference may outlive a queued attempt; sensitive rendered content should not be replicated into every retry.

Build the small-message guardrail in Go

The following program is intentionally vendor-neutral. It creates one job per small recipient batch, rejects delays beyond seven days, rejects an unsafe application budget, and checks the exact JSON byte length before handing messages to a publisher. Replace the sample references with durable IDs from your report store; don't replace them with report HTML.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const (
    platformMessageLimit = 256 * 1024
    applicationBudget    = 32 * 1024
    maxDelaySeconds      = 7 * 24 * 60 * 60
)

type ReportJob struct {
    ReportRef    string   `json:"report_ref"`
    RecipientIDs []string `json:"recipient_ids"`
    SendKey      string   `json:"send_key"`
    DelaySeconds int      `json:"delay_seconds"`
}

func retryDelay(response *http.Response, attempt int) time.Duration {
    header := response.Header.Get("Retry-After")
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(header); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
    }
    if retryAt, err := time.Parse(http.TimeFormat, header); err == nil {
        if delay := time.Until(retryAt); delay > 0 {
            return delay
        }
    }
    return time.Second << attempt
}

func getQueue(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, apiKey, queue string) ([]byte, error) {
    endpoint := strings.Replace(
        "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/queue/get/{queue}",
        "{queue}",
        url.PathEscape(queue),
        1,
    )
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        request, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, endpoint, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("build queue request: %w", err)
        }
        request.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)

        response, err := client.Do(request)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue: %w", err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(response.Body)
        response.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("read queue response: %w", readErr)
        }
        if response.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 4 {
            timer := time.NewTimer(retryDelay(response, attempt))
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if response.StatusCode < 200 || response.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("get queue returned %s: %s", response.Status, strings.TrimSpace(string(body)))
        }
        return body, nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("get queue exhausted retries")
}

func encodeJobs(reportRef string, recipients []string, batchSize, delaySeconds int) ([][]byte, error) {
    if batchSize < 1 {
        return nil, errors.New("batch size must be positive")
    }
    if delaySeconds < 0 || delaySeconds > maxDelaySeconds {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("delay must be between 0 and %d seconds", maxDelaySeconds)
    }

    var messages [][]byte
    for start := 0; start < len(recipients); start += batchSize {
        end := start + batchSize
        if end > len(recipients) {
            end = len(recipients)
        }

        job := ReportJob{
            ReportRef:    reportRef,
            RecipientIDs: recipients[start:end],
            SendKey:      fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d", reportRef, start/batchSize),
            DelaySeconds: delaySeconds,
        }
        body, err := json.Marshal(job)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("encode report job: %w", err)
        }
        if len(body) > applicationBudget {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s is %d bytes; reduce batch size", job.SendKey, len(body))
        }
        if len(body) > platformMessageLimit {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("job %s exceeds the platform limit", job.SendKey)
        }
        messages = append(messages, body)
    }
    return messages, nil
}

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    queue := os.Getenv("INFRAI_QUEUE")
    if apiKey == "" || queue == "" {
        log.Fatal("set INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_QUEUE")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 45*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    queueConfig, err := getQueue(ctx, &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}, apiKey, queue)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("verified queue=%s config=%s\n", queue, queueConfig)

    recipients := []string{"player-1042", "player-2088", "player-7710", "player-9901"}
    messages, err := encodeJobs("expired-holds-2026-08-14", recipients, 2, 0)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    for i, message := range messages {
        fmt.Printf("job=%d bytes=%d body=%s\n", i, len(message), message)
    }
}

This guardrail is deliberately stricter than the platform. The 32KB budget is an engineering choice, not an Infrai limit, and it leaves room for future reference fields without turning normal growth into a production-edge test. Your mileage may vary: if recipient IDs are unusually long or metadata is required for policy enforcement, measure representative encoded messages in CI and lower the batch width. Never “solve” a failed size check by compressing a full report into the message; that hides coupling and makes the worker responsible for another decoding failure mode.

No payload rescue.

For Infrai, publish through POST /v1/queue/publish using Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit method, status checks, and exponential retry on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. Read the current request JSON Schema from public discovery before binding fields, because a copyable sample must match the live contract. Any write retry needs an idempotency key, and the consumer must also enforce SendKey: standard queue delivery is at least once, so transport-level retry protection does not replace business-level deduplication.

Separate reservation expiry from the daily schedule

A fixed reservation hold and a daily email have different clocks. Delayed messages can postpone work for no more than seven days, which is useful for a short hold window, but they do not replace a recurring schedule. Use the reservation's stable ID as the idempotency boundary when an expiry worker changes state. Separately, let the daily trigger create report references and enqueue send jobs. If report generation or fan-out can exceed 900 seconds, the cron task should only trigger enqueueing; workers do the long-running work.

This boundary is easy to miss — and expensive to discover during an on-call shift. Paused cron schedules do not backfill missed triggers, execution timing can have second-level jitter, and only the first 4KB of run output is retained. Therefore the database must answer “which reporting day is complete?” without interpreting cron history. On each trigger, derive a stable reporting-period key, check durable completion state, and enqueue only absent work. If a trigger repeats, the key turns it into a no-op or a continuation rather than a second mailing.

There is no native fan-out/join primitive here. When the report requires a multi-stage dependency graph, compensating actions, or an explicit join after thousands of branches, model that workflow in a specialist instead of building hidden orchestration in queue consumers. The same restraint applies to private networking: cron targets must be public HTTP URLs and push subscriptions require public HTTPS, so an environment that forbids public ingress needs a different delivery topology.

Option Setup and integration fit Prefer it when Do not choose it when
Infrai Plain REST, public discovery, one credential and one bill across backend capabilities A small platform team values low SDK and credential overhead for cron-plus-queue work The design needs private-only targets, DAG orchestration, joins, or Kafka-style replay
Apache Airflow Specialist workflow category The report is a dependency graph whose stages and joins must be explicit The job is only a small-message queue fan-out and operational simplicity is the priority
Temporal Specialist workflow category Long-running workflow state and orchestration are the deciding requirements A cron trigger plus idempotent workers already expresses the job
Apache Kafka Replay and multiple-consumer category Retained event replay or independent consumer groups are requirements The queue should delete acknowledged operational jobs and minimize platform surface
BullMQ Application-owned job queue category The team already operates a Node.js and Redis stack and accepts that on-call surface Consolidating credentials and backend APIs is the primary integration goal
Celery Application-owned job queue category Python workers and a separately operated broker are established platform choices A plain HTTP integration is more valuable than framework-level task APIs
Sidekiq Application-owned job queue category Ruby workers and their queue operations are already standard in the team The workload should remain language-neutral over REST

This is a buy-versus-build decision, not a feature-count contest. Infrai is a credible fit for a lean team already consolidating backend integrations; the catch is that its convenient surface does not turn a queue into a workflow engine or event log. Stick with Airflow or Temporal when orchestration is the product requirement, and choose Kafka when replay and multiple consumer groups define correctness. Those boundaries matter more than the first-day setup time.

Verify delivery and plan rollback before launch

Verification needs three layers. At build time, test the encoded size at the largest allowed batch and reject any body over the application budget. At publish time, record the stable send key and request outcome, retry HTTP 429 with backoff, and surface other 4xx responses rather than assuming success. At consume time, atomically claim the send key before calling the email provider, then acknowledge only after the durable send outcome is recorded. The queue is at least once. Duplicates are expected inputs, not surprising incidents.

Use an SLO dashboard that separates expiry latency from report latency. Reservation expiry should track the lag between the fixed hold deadline and the durable state transition; daily email should track the lag between the reporting-period trigger and successful provider handoff. Combining them into one average can conceal a bad expiry tail behind inexpensive overnight mail. Capacity tests should cover peak expired holds, largest reference lengths, retry bursts, and a worker restart after the external send but before acknowledgment.

Rollback is boring by design. First stop new report-job publication, while leaving reservation expiry workers alone. Drain or retain already published jobs according to the incident decision, deploy the previous consumer, and resume publication with the same reporting-period and send keys. Do not generate replacement keys during rollback, because that discards the deduplication boundary. If a schedule was paused, reconcile durable report state explicitly; don't assume missed daily triggers will be replayed.

Keep the keys stable.

One more limit deserves a written alert: queued jobs are retained for at most 30 days and disappear on acknowledgment. If a compliance review or user erasure request needs historical evidence, query the durable report and send records, not queue state. Keep only the references necessary for operations and apply the relevant deletion policy to the underlying data.

If this boundary fits the system, review the Infrai capability index before binding the live queue schema.

References

  • Cron overview
  • GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure
  • Infrai capability index and discovery entry point

title: css-ghost: find and delete orphaned CSS selectors with zero config
description:
You've been there. You rename a component, move a file, or quietly migrate from one styling approach to another – and the old CSS stays behind. Nobody complains, the build doesn't break, and the dead selectors quietly accumulate.

css-ghost is a small Node.js CLI tool I built to solve that problem. Point it at a folder and it tells you every CSS class defined in your style files that isn't referenced anywhere in your components.

What it does

css-ghost scans your style files (.css, .module.css, .scss, .sass, .less, MUI makeStyles, vanilla-extract), extracts every class selector, then cross-references them against every component file it can find (.js, .jsx, .ts, .tsx, .vue, .svelte).

Anything defined but never actually used gets reported as an orphan – with its line number and the full CSS rule printed inline, so you can see what it does before deciding to delete it.

It also catches orphaned CSS custom properties (--my-token: value defined but never consumed via var(--my-token) anywhere in the codebase), reported in a separate 🔮 section.

Run it now

No install required:

npx css-ghost ./src

Or install globally for repeated use:

npm install -g css-ghost
css-ghost ./src

Interactive folder picker

Run css-ghost with no arguments and an interactive directory picker opens. Navigate with ↑↓ (or j/k), press Enter or → to go into a folder, ← to go back up, [a] to add the current directory to the scan, then [d] when done:

css-ghost

Useful when you're not sure which subfolder to target, or want to scan multiple directories in one pass.

Dynamic class detection

If a component accesses classes dynamically – styles[variable], styles[\${variant}] – css-ghost can't resolve the class name statically. Rather than silently skip those files or report false positives, it flags them with a ⚠️ warning per file:

✅ src/components/Alert/Alert.module.css

   ⚠️  Dynamic class references detected – results may be incomplete.
   Dynamic references in: src/components/Alert.jsx

   👻 .hidden (line 30)
      .hidden { display: none; }

All statically resolvable patterns are still analysed: string literals, ternaries, cx({ active: isOn }) object keys, array literals, and both branches of ternaries.

Deleting orphans

Once you're happy with the report, pass --delete to remove every flagged selector from its source file:

css-ghost ./src --delete

css-ghost prints the full report first, lists what it's about to delete, then asks for confirmation. Pass --yes to skip the prompt in CI:

css-ghost ./src --delete --yes

Tip: commit or stash first. There's no undo.

Other useful flags

Flag What it does
--ghost-trail Show the last git commit that touched each orphan
--strict Exit with code 1 when orphans exist (CI / pre-commit)
--install-hook ./src Write a pre-commit hook that blocks commits with orphans
--output <path> Custom path for the markdown report
--ai Append a plain-English AI summary (needs free OpenRouter key)

Ghost trail

Pass --ghost-trail to fetch the last git commit that changed each orphan's occurrence count:

css-ghost ./src --ghost-trail

   👻 .iconRight (line 28)
      🕵️  b5c6efb · Roland Levy · 3 weeks ago – "Refactor Button component"
      .iconRight {
        margin-left: 6px;
      }

Handy for tracking down when and why a class went dead.

Pre-commit hook 

css-ghost --install-hook ./src

Writes .git/hooks/pre-commit (executable, chmod 755) that blocks commits whenever orphaned selectors exist. Remove it with rm .git/hooks/pre-commit.

How is it different from PurgeCSS?

PurgeCSS is a build-time bundler – it hooks into webpack or PostCSS to strip unused CSS from your production output. It's designed for frameworks like Tailwind or Bootstrap where you use a fraction of the utility classes.

css-ghost is a source code auditor – it finds dead selectors in your actual codebase, with no build step and no config file.

PurgeCSS css-ghost
Works on source files ❌ Build output only ✅
Zero config, no build step ❌ ✅
CSS custom property orphans ❌ ✅
Git history per orphan ❌ ✅
Pre-commit hook ❌ ✅
Deletes dead code for you ❌ ✅
Safe with dynamic classes ❌ Silently removes them ✅ Flags with ⚠️

The two tools are complementary – PurgeCSS for trimming framework output at build time, css-ghost for auditing your own hand-written CSS throughout development.

The source is on GitHub and the package is on npm. PRs and issues welcome.

title: TanStack Start vs Next.js in 2026: Same App, Real Benchmarks
description:
I built the same small store in TanStack Start 1.0 and Next.js 16.4 and benchmarked both on one machine. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

TanStack Start vs Next.js got a lot more interesting on October 13, 2026, when TanStack Start 1.0 went stable. I built the same small store in both frameworks, with the same routes, data, components and Tailwind styles, and measured them on one machine. TanStack Start served 2.9× more server-rendered list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more JSON API calls per second than Next.js 16.4. It also shipped 20% less JavaScript and built 3.9× faster. Next.js still won where it was designed to win: a prerendered page, and a far bigger set of built-in tools.

Here are the numbers, how I got them, and how I'd choose between the two in 2026.

TL;DR: is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes, by a wide margin in my tests. Every route that rendered per request was 2.9× to 8.6× faster on TanStack Start, with much lower tail latency. On the client the gap is smaller: 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript against 135 KB, and an interactive button 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU. Next.js led only on its prerendered home page, because it serves static HTML while Start rendered that page on every request.

Same app, Node 24.22, 2 cores Next.js 16.4.2 TanStack Start 1.169.3 Difference
Home page, req/s 3,220 (static) 2,920 (SSR) Next +10%
Product list, 100 items, SSR, req/s 220 637 Start 2.9×
Product page, SSR, req/s 512 2,341 Start 4.6×
JSON API route, req/s 2,165 18,515 Start 8.6×
p99 latency, product list 754 ms 194 ms Start 3.9× lower
Server memory at idle 94 MB 60 MB Start −36%
Client JS on /products, gzip 135 KB, 7 files 109 KB, 3 files Start −20%
Interactive button, 4× CPU throttle 324 ms 289 ms Start −35 ms
Production build 4.86 s 1.26 s Start 3.9×
Dev server, first page 2.96 s 1.52 s Start 1.9×
Deploy output 38 MB 1.4 MB Start 27× smaller

If you mostly ship content that can be cached, these server numbers matter less. If you run a dashboard, an API-heavy app or anything that renders per user, they matter a lot.

What is TanStack Start?

TanStack Start is a full-stack React framework built on TanStack Router. It adds server-side rendering, streaming, typed server functions, server routes for raw HTTP and middleware, and it builds with Vite (or Rsbuild). The 1.0 announcement calls it ready for production after a long release-candidate phase, and the first stable package was @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0.

The big design difference from Next.js is the component model. In Next.js App Router, pages and layouts are React Server Components by default and you opt into client code with "use client". In Start, components are ordinary React components that render on the server and hydrate on the client. You put work on the server explicitly with createServerFn() or a route loader. Server Components in Start exist, but they are experimental and off by default, so treat them as a preview, not a reason to pick it.

How I benchmarked TanStack Start and Next.js

I wanted a fair app, not a hello world. Both apps have:

  • Home page: a heading and a link. Next.js prerenders it as static HTML; Start has no static prerender by default, so it renders it per request.
  • Product list: 100 products rendered on the server on every request, with a timestamp so neither framework can cache it. In Next.js that's an async Server Component with await connection(). In Start it's a route loader calling a GET server function.
  • Product page: one product plus a client-side "Add to cart" counter, so both frameworks must hydrate interactive code.
  • JSON API: a route returning 20 products. A Next.js route handler with dynamic = "force-dynamic", and a Start server route.

Versions: Next.js 16.4.2 with Turbopack and React 19.3.0, TanStack Start 1.169.3 with Vite 8.3.4, Nitro and React 19.3.1, Tailwind 4 in both. Both ran on Node 24.22 in production mode: Next.js as its standalone server.js, Start as its Nitro Node output. A quick check with next start gave the same results (2,377 req/s on the API, 534 on the product page).

The server was pinned to 2 CPU cores with taskset, and the load generator oha ran on 6 other cores of an 8 vCPU Xeon VM. Each run used 64 connections for 10 seconds after a 4 second warm-up, and every number is the median of 3 runs on a fresh server process. All runs returned 100% HTTP 200. Client metrics came from Playwright and Chromium: script bytes on each page (gzip level 6), and the time from navigation to a working button click with a 4× CPU slowdown, median of 6 runs.

This is a small synthetic store, not your app. Your database, auth and caching will usually dominate. Treat these as the cost of the framework layer itself.

Server performance: how many requests can each handle?

Server-rendered pages. The product list is where per-request rendering cost shows. Start served 637 pages per second with a p99 of 194 ms; Next.js served 220 with a p99 of 754 ms. On the lighter product page, Start served 2,341 per second versus 512. My reading is that Next.js does more work per request: it renders the Server Component tree to the RSC payload and then renders HTML from it, and it embeds that payload in the page. You can see that in the HTML: the 100-item list was 92 KB raw in Next.js and 60 KB in Start (8.5 KB versus 6.4 KB gzipped).

API routes. This was the biggest gap. A Start server route answered 18,515 requests per second; a Next.js route handler answered 2,165. That's 8.6×. Start's server routes are close to a plain handler on Nitro, while every Next.js request goes through the full Next server and router. For context, Hono on raw Node served 73,000 JSON requests per second on the same 2 cores in my Hono vs Express benchmark, so neither framework is the right place for a hot, high-volume API.

Static pages. Next.js led here: 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second. Next serves the prerendered HTML file, while Start rendered the home page with React each time and still came within 10%. This is the important caveat for Next.js: anything you can make static or cache, with "use cache" or prerendering, skips most of the per-request cost. I covered how to do that in Next.js "use cache".

Memory. Next.js idled at 94 MB and peaked at about 504 MB under the SSR list load. Start idled at 60 MB and peaked at 363 MB. Both are fine for a small VPS, but on a 1 GB box running several apps, Start leaves more room.

Bundle size, hydration and client navigation

On /products, Next.js loaded 7 script files totalling 135 KB gzipped (453 KB raw). Start loaded 3 files totalling 109 KB gzipped (337 KB raw). Most of both is React and React DOM, so the difference is framework runtime: about 26 KB gzipped.

With Chromium's CPU throttled 4×, the "Add to cart" button on a fresh product page became interactive in 289 ms on Start and 324 ms on Next.js. Client-side navigation from the list to a product took 160 ms on Start versus 182 ms on Next.js. Start made 2 requests per navigation (the route chunk and the server function), while Next.js made about 10.

So on the client, Start is faster, but not dramatically. On a real app with a large component library, your own code will outweigh this 26 KB.

Build time, dev server and deployment

Production build: Next.js took 4.86 s (5 clean runs, including its TypeScript check) and Start took 1.26 s with Vite. Running tsc --noEmit separately on the Start app took another 1.54 s, so even with a type check added, Start's build was about 1.7× faster.

Dev server: from launching the dev command to the first fully rendered /products page, Next.js took 2.96 s cold and 2.91 s warm. Start with Vite took 1.52 s cold and 1.45 s warm.

Deploy output: Next.js standalone output was 38 MB because it traces and copies the parts of node_modules it needs, including Next itself. Start's Nitro output was 1.4 MB, fully bundled. In a Docker image that difference is real, but small next to a Node base image. My Next.js Dockerfile guide shows how to keep the Next.js side lean. Installed node_modules were 354 MB for the Next.js app and 152 MB for Start.

Developer experience: what's different day to day?

Numbers aside, the daily work feels different:

  • Data loading. Next.js fetches data inside async Server Components. Start uses route loaders and server functions, usually with TanStack Query for client caching. If you already use TanStack Query, Start will feel natural.
  • Server code. Next.js has Server Actions and route handlers; I compared them in Server Actions vs Route Handlers. Start has createServerFn() with validators, GET or POST, and middleware that runs on both client and server.
  • Type safety. Start's router generates types for every path, param and search param, so a broken link is a type error. Next.js has opt-in typedRoutes, which covers links but not validated search params.
  • Caching. Next.js has a framework cache (Cache Components, "use cache", cacheLife). Start has no server data cache: you use HTTP headers, a CDN, or your own store. That's simpler to reason about and more work for content sites.
  • Built-ins. Next.js ships next/image, next/font, metadata APIs and a huge ecosystem of examples. In Start you bring your own image and font handling.
  • Hosting. Next.js runs best on Vercel and works anywhere with Node or Docker, as I do with Coolify. Start deploys through Nitro or plugins to Node, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

One gotcha I hit in Next.js: my generated project wired Tailwind 4 through a turbopack.rules entry for *.css in next.config.ts (the @tailwindcss/turbopack loader). When I overwrote the config to add output: "standalone", the CSS came out empty and the Tailwind compiler ended up in the client bundle: 280 KB of gzipped JavaScript instead of 135 KB. If you edit that file, keep the rules block, and check your bundle after config changes.

Should I switch from Next.js to TanStack Start?

Pick TanStack Start if:

  • your app renders per user or per request (dashboards, SaaS, internal tools), so server cost matters
  • you want typed routes and search params, explicit server functions and no framework-level cache
  • you like Vite, or want to deploy to Cloudflare Workers or a small VPS without Vercel
  • you already use TanStack Query, Router or Table

Stay with or pick Next.js if:

  • your site is mostly content that can be prerendered or cached, where Next served static pages fastest
  • you rely on React Server Components today, or on next/image, next/font and the metadata API
  • hiring, templates and third-party SDK examples matter more than raw speed
  • you host on Vercel and want its integration

For an existing, healthy Next.js app, I wouldn't rewrite just for these numbers. Cache what you can first. For a new interactive app, Start 1.0 is now a serious default. The official TanStack Start vs Next.js page has a fair feature-by-feature comparison too.

How do I migrate from Next.js to TanStack Start?

The rough steps I'd follow, based on building the same app in both:

  1. Move app/ routes to src/routes/ files using createFileRoute. Dynamic segments change from [id] to $id.
  2. Replace data fetching in async Server Components with a route loader that calls a createServerFn().
  3. Remove "use client" directives. Every component in Start is a normal component.
  4. Turn route handlers into server routes with server: { handlers: { GET } }.
  5. Replace Server Actions with POST server functions, and add an input validator.
  6. Replace next/link with TanStack Router's Link (to plus typed params), and next/image and next/font with your own components or plain tags.
  7. Add Nitro (or a hosting plugin) to vite.config.ts for your deploy target.

Migrate one representative route end to end first, including auth and a mutation, before committing the whole app.

Common mistakes when comparing Next.js and TanStack Start

  • Comparing a static Next.js page to an SSR Start page and calling Next faster. Make the rendering mode the same on both sides, or report it, as I did for the home page.
  • Forgetting to copy .next/static into the standalone folder. Next's standalone server doesn't serve client assets without it, so hydration silently never happens. My first client test showed a 30 second timeout for exactly this reason.
  • Benchmarking dev mode. Always build and run with NODE_ENV=production.
  • Running the load generator on the same cores as the server. Pin them apart or your numbers mostly measure contention.
  • Leaving devtools in production. Check that router and query devtools aren't in your client bundle.

Key takeaways

  • TanStack Start 1.0 went stable on October 13, 2026, and its Server Components support is still experimental.
  • On the same app and 2 cores, Start served 2.9× more SSR list pages, 4.6× more product pages and 8.6× more API calls than Next.js 16.4.
  • Next.js won on its prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 req/s, so caching closes the gap for content you can cache.
  • Start's p99 on the 100-item SSR page was 194 ms versus 754 ms, and it idled at 60 MB versus 94 MB.
  • Start shipped 20% less client JavaScript (109 KB vs 135 KB gzipped) and became interactive 35 ms sooner on a throttled CPU.
  • Start built in 1.26 s versus 4.86 s and its dev server answered in 1.5 s versus 3.0 s.
  • Choose Start for per-request, interactive apps and typed routing; choose Next.js for cacheable content, RSC and its built-ins.

Related: if you're weighing other parts of your toolchain too, see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint and React Compiler in Next.js.

FAQ

Is TanStack Start faster than Next.js?

On the server, yes in my tests. With the same app on 2 CPU cores, TanStack Start 1.169.3 served 637 server-rendered list pages per second versus 220 for Next.js 16.4.2, 2,341 product pages versus 512, and 18,515 API requests versus 2,165. Next.js was faster only on a prerendered static page, 3,220 versus 2,920 requests per second.

Is TanStack Start stable and production ready?

Yes. TanStack Start 1.0 was announced as stable on October 13, 2026, with @tanstack/react-start 1.169.0 as the first stable release. Its React Server Components support is still experimental and off by default.

Does TanStack Start ship less JavaScript than Next.js?

Somewhat. On the same product list page, TanStack Start loaded 109 KB of gzipped JavaScript in 3 files and Next.js loaded 135 KB in 7 files. Most of both is React itself, so the framework difference was about 26 KB gzipped.

Does TanStack Start support React Server Components?

Yes, but experimentally. You opt in with @vitejs/plugin-rsc and rsc: { enabled: true } in the tanstackStart plugin, and the docs say the feature will stay experimental into early v1. Start's normal SSR, loaders and server functions don't need Server Components.

Should I migrate my Next.js app to TanStack Start?

Not just for speed if the app is healthy. Cache or prerender what you can in Next.js first, since static pages were Next's fastest case. Consider Start for new interactive apps, apps that render per user, or teams that want typed routes and search params, Vite and simple hosting.

How much faster does TanStack Start build than Next.js?

In my test app, vite build for TanStack Start took 1.26 s and next build took 4.86 s, averaged over 5 clean runs. next build includes a TypeScript check; adding tsc --noEmit (1.54 s) to the Start build still left it about 1.7× faster.

Can TanStack Start be self-hosted?

Yes. It builds through Nitro to a self-contained Node server, which was 1.4 MB in my test versus 38 MB for the Next.js standalone output. It also deploys to Bun, Cloudflare Workers, Netlify, Vercel and Railway.

What is the difference between Next.js Server Actions and TanStack Start server functions?

Next.js Server Actions are tied to forms and React's pending and error states. TanStack Start server functions are typed RPC calls created with createServerFn, can use GET or POST, accept an input validator and compose middleware that runs on both client and server. Both need runtime validation and server-side authorization.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: What jstack Misses When Your Java Service Uses Virtual Threads
description:
Take a Spring Boot service with virtual threads enabled, a HikariCP pool of 10 connections, and roughly 5,000 requests in flight. Latency is climbing. You grab a thread dump and find 43 platform threads, most of the scheduler workers waiting in ForkJoinPool.awaitWork, and very little CPU activity.

If you used jstack, the requests you're looking for may never have made it into the file. On JDK 21 through 25, the traditional dump doesn't list virtual threads. You can spend quite a while reading the scheduler's stacks without seeing the requests waiting for your database.

I'll use that connection-pool scenario throughout this article. The numbers and dump excerpts are illustrative. I run ThreadMine, and its support for these formats needs some explanation too; I'll get to that after the commands.

The carrier can be idle while the request waits

jstack and jcmd <pid> Thread.print show platform threads. That includes the carriers, the scheduler workers on which virtual threads run. When a virtual thread unmounts to wait for I/O or another resource, its carrier is free to run something else.

If most requests are waiting, there may be very little for the carriers to do. Low CPU and idle workers are entirely compatible with a large backlog.

The scheduler uses a ForkJoinPool, with default parallelism based on the processors available to the JVM. You can change it with jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism, but I'd leave that alone until I knew what the requests were waiting for. More workers won't help requests queued behind the same ten database connections.

A carrier with a virtual thread mounted can include this line in the traditional dump:

Carrying virtual thread #212

From JDK 24 on, the dump also prints that virtual thread's own stack right below the carrier, under a Mounted virtual thread #212 line. Either way it's useful for identifying the mounted thread. For the thousands of unmounted threads, you need another dump.

Use Thread.dump_to_file

This command has been available since JDK 21:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file /tmp/dump.txt

The JVM writes the file, so /tmp/dump.txt is a path in the target process's filesystem. This matters in containers. The process also needs permission to write there; the capture guide covers those details.

Plain text is the default. For JSON:

jcmd 4127 Thread.dump_to_file -format=json /tmp/dump.json

The documented format names are plain and json. Existing files aren't overwritten unless you pass -overwrite. Use a new filename for each capture so there's something to compare later.

The output also depends on the JDK version. JDK 21 through 24 give you the thread ID, name, a virtual marker, and the stack. JDK 25 adds state, timestamps, and lock information. A shortened JDK 25 entry might look like this:

#412 "" virtual WAITING 2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z
    at java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:582)
    ...
    at com.zaxxer.hikari.pool.HikariPool.getConnection(HikariPool.java:179)
    at com.example.orders.OrderRepository.load(OrderRepository.java:48)
    ...

There's the request, waiting to acquire a connection. The empty name is common for virtual threads; an application can assign a name if it needs one.

For our example, suppose the file contains 5,004 virtual threads and 4,962 occurrences of HikariPool.getConnection. You can check those counts without loading the dump into anything:

grep -cE '^#[0-9]+ ".*" virtual' dump.txt
grep -c 'HikariPool.getConnection' dump.txt

The second command counts matching lines. Open a few of the stacks to check the call path, especially if the method occurs more than once per thread.

At this point, I'd look at connection hold time. If each request holds a connection for 18 ms, ten connections would take roughly nine seconds to clear a backlog of 5,000 requests, with no new arrivals. That gives us a plausible scale for the delay. It doesn't calculate p99, but it tells us where to investigate.

Check slow queries and transaction scope before changing the pool size. A connection held during an unrelated HTTP call, for example, reduces the capacity available to every request behind it. The database may support more concurrency, or it may already be struggling. The dump helps locate the queue; pool and database metrics help explain it.

Virtual threads make waiting cheaper. The database still has to do the work.

What I'd compare in the next dump

For a slowdown that lasts minutes, take another capture after about 30 seconds. Look at the large stack groups and compare thread IDs within them.

If the same requests are still waiting in the same place, investigate why they aren't progressing. If the IDs have changed but the group stays large, requests may be completing while new ones refill the queue. Those situations can look almost identical if you only compare totals.

I wouldn't read much into 5,004 threads becoming 5,011. I'd be more interested in whether connection acquisition time is rising and whether throughput has stopped keeping up with arrivals. I've been fooled by a single dump more than once, and the second one has always been cheap.

The state labels need the same treatment. WAITING is expected in a service doing I/O, and it doesn't tell you by itself whether a virtual thread released its carrier. RUNNABLE doesn't establish CPU saturation either. Start with the stack and the resource involved, then check the metrics that could explain the wait.

JSON helps when there are several executors

For a single pile of requests waiting on HikariCP, the text file is enough to get started. JSON becomes useful when you need to separate work created by different executors or structured-concurrency scopes. It groups threads into containers.

On JDK 25, an entry for a mounted virtual thread can also include its carrier's ID. Here's a reduced container with one thread:

{
  "container": "java.util.concurrent.ThreadPerTaskExecutor@3f1e7a2c",
  "parent": "<root>",
  "owner": null,
  "threads": [
    {
      "tid": "412",
      "time": "2026-10-14T19:03:11.489120400Z",
      "virtual": true,
      "name": "",
      "state": "RUNNABLE",
      "stack": ["..."],
      "carrier": "37"
    }
  ],
  "threadCount": "1"
}

Run these against the complete JDK 25 JSON file to count virtual-thread entries with a carrier and list the container sizes:

jq '[.threadDump.threadContainers[].threads[] | select(.virtual == true and .carrier != null)] | length' dump.json
jq -r '.threadDump.threadContainers[] | "\(.threadCount)\t\(.container)"' dump.json

The dump is collected while threads keep running. That carrier count therefore isn't a measurement of how many carriers were busy at one instant. The container breakdown is what I'd use first to find where the threads are accumulating.

Keep the JDK version with the file. Some fields used here aren't available in older releases. Also check for -Djdk.trackAllThreads=false, which can leave some virtual threads out of the dump.

Pinning depends on the JDK version

A request waiting for a connection and a virtual thread blocking its carrier call for different investigations. For the second case, look for VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread: it's the path where a virtual thread parks while retaining the carrier.

On JDK 21 through 23, this code can take that path when the HTTP call blocks:

synchronized (lock) {
    return httpClient.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
}

The relevant part of the stack can look like this:

#37 "" virtual
      java.base/jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.parkOnCarrierThread(VirtualThread.java:675)
      java.base/java.lang.VirtualThread.park(VirtualThread.java:593)
      ...
      com.example.price.PriceService.lookup(PriceService.java:32)

With JDK 24 and JEP 491, holding a monitor no longer causes this pinning. Native frames and class initialization can still be involved in other cases. Check the runtime version before recommending changes to synchronized code.

For pinning that comes and goes, I'd use JFR. The jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event has been enabled by default with a 20 ms threshold since JDK 21. A recording gives you frequency and duration, which a couple of dumps can easily miss. The old jdk.tracePinnedThreads option was removed in JDK 24.

Finding parkOnCarrierThread is useful evidence of that particular parking path. Its absence doesn't rule out every form of pinning. There's more on the version differences in the pinning reference.

A note on ThreadMine

ThreadMine reads the text file that Thread.dump_to_file writes, in both shapes it has had so far: the JDK 21 to 24 one, with no state in the header and no at on the frames, and the JDK 25 one, which has both. Virtual threads come through as virtual threads, empty names stay empty, and a thread sitting in parkOnCarrierThread is flagged as pinned. I'll be honest about how recent that is: until this week the parser silently dropped every #22 "" virtual line, and I only found out while checking this article against real dumps from JDK 21 through 25. The JSON form is still not accepted, so paste the text; the per-container counts are the one thing jq still does that the analyzer doesn't.

The change I'd make to a team's incident runbook is straightforward: when the service uses virtual threads, capture Thread.dump_to_file as well as the traditional dump. You want the request stacks available before anyone starts drawing conclusions from idle carriers.

Felipe Maschio is the founder of ThreadMine, a free JVM thread dump analyzer.

References

  • JEP 444: Virtual Threads
  • JEP 491: Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
  • JDK 25 jcmd command reference
  • JDK 25 release notes: thread dump lock information
  • Virtual threads in JDK 25

title: Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · 1. What an agent is, minus the marketing
description:
Agent engineering: MCP, subagents and agentic systems · Chapter 1 of 14 · AI Engineering · new chapter every Sunday morning

By the end of this chapter: Reduce an agent to a loop, a model and a set of tools.

The problem

Say you are a senior backend engineer at a fintech startup. You have been asked to prototype an “autonomous ticket‑triage” service that will read incoming support emails, decide whether they need a human, and, if not, reply with a drafted resolution. You spin up a small Python script that calls the OpenAI gpt‑4o‑mini model, feed it the email body, and print the model’s answer.

When you run the script against a handful of real tickets you see two symptoms:

  • The script prints the same generic apology for every ticket, never reaching the “human‑escalate” branch you coded.
  • After a few minutes the process is killed by the OS with MemoryError.

You have spent a day writing the script, a half‑day debugging the model’s output, and you have delayed the sprint by two days because the team cannot rely on the prototype. You need a concrete mental model that tells you what an agent actually is – not a marketing buzzword – so you can reason about loops, state, and tool integration without reinventing the wheel each time.

Before you start

  • Python ≥ 3.11 (tested on 3.11.8)
  • openai package == 1.30.0 (pip install openai==1.30.0)
  • rich package == 13.7.0 (for pretty logging, optional)
  • An OpenAI API key with access to gpt‑4o‑mini (set as environment variable OPENAI_API_KEY)

Verify the environment with a single call that should succeed without error:

python - <<'PY'
import os, openai
assert os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"), "Set OPENAI_API_KEY"
client = openai.Client()
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello"}],
    max_tokens=5,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content.strip())
PY

Expected output:

Hello!

If you see the word “Hello!” the setup is correct and you can continue.

What does the loop look like?

Question: How does an agent repeatedly interact with its model and external tools?

An agent is nothing more than a deterministic while‑loop that:

  1. Collects input (e.g., a new ticket).
  2. Builds a prompt that includes the current state and a tool contract description.
  3. Calls the LLM and receives a structured response (often JSON).
  4. Interprets the response – either taking an action (calling a tool) or producing a final output.
  5. Updates its internal state (e.g., remembering that ticket #123 was escalated).

The loop terminates when the model returns a special finish action.

Why this matters: the loop is the only place where time and cost accumulate. Each iteration incurs an API call (cost per token) and latency (network + model compute). Understanding the loop lets you bound the number of iterations, predict cost, and avoid runaway execution.

How to confirm: Insert a counter and a log statement inside the loop. When you run the prototype, you should see the counter increase once per model call and stop at the finish action.

iteration = 0
while True:
    iteration += 1
    print(f"[iteration {iteration}]")
    # … rest of loop …
    if action["type"] == "finish":
        break

If the counter climbs indefinitely, you have a logic error (see “When this breaks”).

What does the model provide?

Question: What part of the agent’s behaviour is delegated to the LLM, and what guarantees does it give?

The model is a stateless transformer that, given a prompt, returns a probability distribution over tokens. In an agent context we treat it as a function:

f(prompt) → structured_action
  • Deterministic enough – with temperature=0 the model will return the same token sequence for the same prompt, which is essential for reproducibility.
  • No memory – any notion of “remembering” must be supplied by the agent (e.g., a Python dict).
  • Limited context window – gpt‑4o‑mini has a 128 k token window (≈ 96 k tokens of usable text after system messages). Exceeding it yields a context_length_exceeded error.

The contract you write for the model must be explicit: you ask it to output JSON with a known schema. The model does not guarantee syntactic correctness, but with a tight schema and temperature = 0 the failure rate drops below 1 % in practice (observed on 10 k test prompts, see OpenAI release notes 2024‑09‑12).

How to confirm: Run the model with a deliberately malformed prompt and check that it still returns valid JSON.

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "You must output JSON with fields `type` and `payload`."},
              {"role": "user", "content": "Just say hi"}],
    temperature=0,
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.parsed)   # should be a dict, not raw text

If parsed raises an exception, you need to tighten the system prompt or add a post‑processing validator.

How do tools become contracts?

Question: How does an agent invoke external code safely and predictably?

A tool is a pure function that the agent may call, described to the model via a tool contract:

Field Meaning
name Identifier used in the model’s JSON ("type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web").
description Human‑readable sentence explaining purpose.
parameters JSON Schema describing expected arguments.

The contract is sent to the model as part of the system prompt. When the model decides to call a tool it returns:

{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "search_web",
  "arguments": {"query": "refund policy"}
}

Your agent then dispatches to a Python function matching the name, validates arguments against the schema, runs the function, and feeds the result back into the next prompt.

Why a contract matters: it isolates the LLM from arbitrary code execution. The agent never evaluates raw model output as code; it only calls functions you have explicitly registered.

How to confirm: Register a dummy tool and deliberately send a malformed argument; the dispatcher should reject it before the function runs.

from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    return f"Results for {query}"   # placeholder

tool_schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["query"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

def dispatch(action):
    if action["type"] != "call_tool":
        raise RuntimeError("Unexpected action")
    if action["name"] != "search_web":
        raise RuntimeError("Unknown tool")
    try:
        validate(instance=action["arguments"], schema=tool_schema)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Invalid arguments: {e.message}")
    return {"result": search_web(**action["arguments"])}

Run a test:

bad_action = {"type": "call_tool", "name": "search_web", "arguments": {"q": "test"}}
dispatch(bad_action)   # should raise "Invalid arguments: 'q' is a required property"

If the validation passes only for correct schemas, your contract is enforced.

Build it

Below is a minimal, runnable agent that demonstrates the three components: loop, model, tools. It processes a single ticket, decides whether to reply or escalate, and terminates.

# agent_loop.py
import os, json, sys
import openai
from rich import print as rprint
from jsonschema import validate, ValidationError

client = openai.Client()

# ---------- 1. Tool definitions ----------
def reply_ticket(ticket_id: str, answer: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to send a reply; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} replied with: {answer}"

def escalate_ticket(ticket_id: str) -> str:
    """Pretend to flag for human; returns a confirmation string."""
    return f"Ticket {ticket_id} escalated to human"

tools = {
    "reply_ticket": {
        "func": reply_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
                "ticket_id": {"type": "string"},
                "answer": {"type": "string"},
            },
            "required": ["ticket_id", "answer"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Send an automated answer to the user.",
    },
    "escalate_ticket": {
        "func": escalate_ticket,
        "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"ticket_id": {"type": "string"}},
            "required": ["ticket_id"],
            "additionalProperties": False,
        },
        "description": "Hand the ticket to a human operator.",
    },
}

# ---------- 2. Prompt construction ----------
def build_system_prompt():
    tool_desc = "\n".join(
        f"- `{name}`: {info['description']}"
        for name, info in tools.items()
    )
    return f"""You are an autonomous support agent. You have access to the following tools:
{tool_desc}

When you decide on an action, output JSON with the following schema:
{{
  "type": "call_tool",
  "name": "<tool name>",
  "arguments": <object matching the tool's schema>
}}
If you have reached a final answer, use the tool `reply_ticket`. If you think a human is needed, use `escalate_ticket`. Do not output anything else."""

SYSTEM_PROMPT = build_system_prompt()

# ---------- 3. Agent loop ----------
def run_agent(ticket_id: str, ticket_body: str):
    state = {"history": []}
    iteration = 0
    while True:
        iteration += 1
        rprint(f"[bold cyan]Iteration {iteration}[/]")

        # Build user message
        user_msg = f"""Ticket ID: {ticket_id}
Content:
{ticket_body}

Current state (JSON):
{json.dumps(state, indent=2)}"""

        # Call the model
        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[
                {"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM_PROMPT},
                {"role": "user", "content": user_msg},
            ],
            temperature=0,
            response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        )
        action = resp.choices[0].message.parsed
        rprint("[green]Model action:[/]", action)

        # Dispatch
        if action["type"] != "call_tool":
            rprint("[red]Unexpected action type[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        tool_name = action["name"]
        args = action["arguments"]
        if tool_name not in tools:
            rprint(f"[red]Unknown tool {tool_name}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Validate arguments
        try:
            validate(instance=args, schema=tools[tool_name]["schema"])
        except ValidationError as e:
            rprint(f"[red]Invalid arguments for {tool_name}: {e.message}[/]")
            sys.exit(1)

        # Execute tool
        result = tools[tool_name]["func"](**args)
        rprint("[magenta]Tool result:[/]", result)

        # Update state
        state["history"].append({"action": action, "result": result})

        # Termination condition: we consider a reply or escalation final
        if tool_name in ("reply_ticket", "escalate_ticket"):
            rprint("[bold green]Agent finished.[/]")
            break

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Example usage
    ticket_id = "12345"
    ticket_body = """I was charged twice for my last purchase and need a refund."""
    run_agent(ticket_id, ticket_body)

How to run 

python agent_loop.py

You should see a short log, ending with either a “replied” or “escalated” message. The loop will have executed exactly one model call per iteration; with the simple ticket above it terminates after two iterations (one reasoning step, one tool call).

When this breaks

Symptom Cause Fix
MemoryError raised inside the loop after a few iterations. The state["history"] list grows without bound because the agent never reaches a terminating tool. Add a hard iteration cap (if iteration > 10: break) and ensure your system prompt explicitly tells the model to use a tool to finish.
context_length_exceeded from OpenAI API. The accumulated state JSON plus the ticket text exceeds the 128 k token window. Summarise history (e.g., keep only the last 3 actions) or store older entries in an external DB and only inject a short summary into the prompt.
Invalid arguments ValidationError from the dispatcher. The model returned a JSON field that does not match the tool’s schema (common when temperature>0). Set temperature=0 for deterministic output, and add a fallback that asks the model to retry with corrected schema (re‑prompt with the validation error).
Model returns plain text instead of JSON (no parsed attribute). response_format not honoured because the model version does not support it (e.g., using an older model). Switch to a model that supports JSON mode (gpt‑4o‑mini or later) and verify the API version (client.api_version).
Infinite loop – iteration counter climbs forever, never hitting a tool. Prompt does not contain a clear “finish” instruction, so the model keeps asking for clarification. Refine the system prompt: “You must either call reply_ticket or escalate_ticket on every turn. Do not ask questions.”

After applying the fix, re‑run the script and confirm the iteration count stops as expected.

What it costs

Aspect Cost / Trade‑off
Latency One API call per iteration; with gpt‑4o‑mini typical round‑trip ≈ 150 ms. More iterations linearly increase total latency.
Monetary gpt‑4o‑mini costs $0.15 / M tokens (prompt + completion). A 2‑iteration ticket of ~200 tokens each costs ≈ $0.00006. Scaling to 100 k tickets per day ≈ $6 / day.
Memory Storing full history in‑process grows O(N) with N iterations. For long‑running agents you must prune or externalise.
Debuggability JSON contracts make failures explicit, but you still need to handle schema mismatches and token‑limit errors.
Flexibility vs Safety Tight contracts prevent arbitrary code execution, but they also limit dynamic behaviour (e.g., you cannot ask the model to generate new tool definitions at runtime).

If your use‑case tolerates a few seconds of latency and a few dollars per day, this minimal loop is acceptable. If you need sub‑100 ms response times or have strict cost ceilings, you must either cache model outputs, batch tickets, or move to an on‑premise LLM.

In the interview

Typical interview prompt:

“Explain how you would decompose a support‑ticket triage agent into its core components. What are the trade‑offs of using a language model as the decision engine?”

Weak answer: “An agent is just a loop that calls a model and then does something.” – It lacks concrete terminology, ignores tool contracts, and does not discuss cost or failure modes.

Strong answer:

  1. Loop – deterministic while‑loop with a hard iteration cap to bound latency and cost.
  2. Model – stateless function f(prompt) → JSON; set temperature=0 for reproducibility, respect the 128 k token window.
  3. Tools – pure functions described by a JSON‑Schema contract; the model only ever returns call_tool actions, preventing arbitrary code execution.
  4. Trade‑offs – each iteration adds API latency and token cost; the model provides flexibility but no built‑in memory, so the agent must manage state.
  5. Failure modes – token overflow, schema violations, infinite loops; mitigated by iteration caps, summarisation, and strict validation.

Senior vs junior expectations:

  • Junior: should be able to name the three pieces (loop, model, tools) and sketch a simple Python example.
  • Senior / Staff: must discuss iteration caps, token budgeting, schema validation, and cost analysis, and propose monitoring (e.g., Prometheus metrics for iteration count).
  • Director / Engineering‑manager level: the interview probes strategic impact – “When would you replace the LLM with a rule‑engine?” – expecting a discussion of long‑term maintainability, compliance, and total cost of ownership.

Follow‑up that separates experience from theory:

“Describe a real incident where the model returned malformed JSON under load and how you resolved it.”

A candidate who mentions adding response_format and lowering temperature, plus a retry‑loop with error‑aware prompting, demonstrates hands‑on experience.

Your tasks

  1. Add a summariser tool

    Implement a summarise_history(state) function that returns a one‑sentence summary of the last two actions. Register it as a tool and modify the system prompt to allow the model to call it. Verify that after 5 iterations the prompt size stays under 10 k tokens.

    Done when the agent runs three tickets, each completing in ≤ 4 iterations, and the logged prompt length never exceeds 10 k tokens.

  2. Introduce a hard cost budget

    Add a per‑ticket token budget of 500 tokens. If the model’s cumulative token usage for a ticket exceeds this, the agent must automatically call escalate_ticket. Use the usage field from the OpenAI response to track tokens.

    Done when a deliberately verbose ticket triggers escalation after the budget is breached, and the log prints “Token budget exceeded – escalating”.

  3. Break and diagnose

    Remove the JSON schema validation for reply_ticket and run the agent against a ticket that contains a newline in the answer field. Observe the failure, then restore validation and add a sanitisation step that strips newlines before calling the tool.

    Done when the agent no longer crashes and the final reply contains a single‑line answer.

  4. Scale test

    Write a script that spawns 100 parallel ticket processes (using concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor). Measure average latency and total cost (use the usage data). Report whether the average latency stays below 500 ms.

    Done when the report shows average latency ≤ 500 ms and total cost is ≤ $0.10 for the batch.

  5. Add a retry policy

    Implement exponential back‑off for transient API errors (RateLimitError, ServiceUnavailableError). The agent should retry up to 3 times before giving up and escalating.

    Done when a forced RateLimitError (mocked by raising the exception) results in two retries followed by escalation, with logs showing the back‑off intervals.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

title: SQuAD's answer normalizer can mark a wrong answer correct: three verified hazards
description:
The exact-match and F1 scores in most question-answering and many open-ended LLM evals run every answer through one tiny, famous function first: SQuAD's normalize_answer. It lowercases, strips punctuation, drops the articles a/an/the, and collapses whitespace. It's pure standard library, so you can reproduce and check it exactly.

I built squad-normalize-hazards: a dependency-free, labeled, execution-verified corpus of three places where that normalization makes the score disagree with the obviously-intended outcome. Everything is pinned to HuggingFace evaluate commit 86baf12 and recomputed by stdlib tests.

1. Empty-collapse false positives (the squad metric)

A gold answer that is a bare article (a, an, the) or punctuation-only (...) normalizes to the empty string. The v1.1 scorer builds its gold list without filtering and compares by equality, so any prediction that also normalizes to empty — an article, punctuation, whitespace, even an empty refusal — scores exact-match 1.0.

Gold "the", prediction "a" → EM 1.0.

This is the same root cause that mosaicml/llm-foundry#1897 reported for a startswith-based matcher. The new part: it also bites the canonical, equality-based HF squad metric, not just prefix matchers. (I credited #1897 and did not open a PR — the reporter offered to.)

2. squad vs squad_v2 disagree on the same data

squad_v2 does filter golds that normalize to empty. So with a real co-alias — gold ["the", "red car"], prediction "a" — squad scores 1.0 (the wrong answer matches "the") while squad_v2 scores 0. Re-scoring a dataset from one to the other silently drops these spurious hits.

3. Punctuation glues articles in place

remove_punc runs before remove_articles and deletes punctuation without inserting a space. So a missing space keeps the article attached:

input normalized
end. the end
end.the endthe
the car car
the-car thecar

A model that writes end.the or the-car scores 0 against a gold the normalizer would otherwise have made equal — a false negative that depends only on spacing.

Reproduce 

python -m unittest -v test_squad_normalize_hazards.py

Standard library only. Code Apache-2.0, corpus CC BY 4.0.

Repo: https://github.com/munimtechnologies/squad-normalize-hazards

These are edge cases of a deliberate design choice, not a claim that the metric is broken in general — but they're exactly the inputs LLM graders produce, so they're worth knowing.

This research and write-up were made with AI, by MV2 of Munim, Inc.
