title: CircuitCraft: a Rust circuit editor with ngspice simulation.
description:
I’m developing CircuitCraft, an open-source desktop application that combines circuit drawing, ngspice simulation and basic PCB design.

The application is written in Rust, while ngspice handles the circuit simulations.

Currently, it supports:

  • Schematic editing and hierarchical circuits.
  • AC, DC and transient simulations.
  • Waveform plots and CSV export.
  • Manual PCB routing and an experimental two-layer autorouter.
  • A 3D PCB preview.
  • Gerber and Excellon export.

To try it, download the Windows release, extract the full ZIP and run Start-CircuitCraft.bat. The first-circuit guide walks through an RC filter example.

This is an early project. The component library is limited, the autorouter can leave connections unrouted, and the 3D component shapes are approximate.

Source code, screenshots and getting-started guide:
https://github.com/Berserk-hub150/CircuitCraft

Windows release:
https://github.com/Berserk-hub150/CircuitCraft/releases/tag/v0.3.0

Feedback on the editing workflow, simulation results and reproducible bugs would be helpful.

Disclosure: This post was drafted with AI assistance.

title: Synthetic Data vs Fake Data: What's the Difference and When Should You Use Each?
description:
Developers often use the terms fake data, dummy data, mock data, and synthetic data as if they all mean the same thing.

Sometimes that is harmless.

Sometimes it causes real confusion.

Consider these two records:

{
  "name": "Test User",
  "email": "test@test.com",
  "city": "Test City"
}

and:

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "country": "DE",
  "postalCode": "20095"
}

Both are not real customer records.

But they serve very different purposes.

The first is obviously placeholder data.

The second is designed to resemble the structure and relationships found in real data.

That difference becomes important when you're testing applications, APIs, imports, forms, analytics pipelines, or databases.

So what exactly is synthetic data, and how is it different from ordinary fake data?

What is fake data?

Fake data is any information created specifically for testing, demonstrations, development, or other non-production purposes.

It can be extremely simple:

John Doe
123 Fake Street
test@example.com

Or even:

foo
bar
123

The goal is usually not realism.

The goal is simply to have something to put into a field.

For example, if you're testing whether a form submits correctly, this might be enough:

{
  "firstName": "Test",
  "lastName": "User",
  "email": "test@example.com"
}

Nothing about that record needs to resemble a real user.

It only needs to satisfy the basic input requirements.

What is synthetic data?

Synthetic data goes a step further.

It is generated data designed to imitate the properties, structure, distributions, or relationships of real data without copying actual records.

For a simple customer profile, that could mean:

{
  "firstName": "Anna",
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "postalCode": "20095"
}

The person is not meant to represent a real customer.

But the record is internally plausible.

The fields relate to each other in a meaningful way.

That makes synthetic data useful for testing systems that behave differently depending on realistic combinations of values.

Fake data can be intentionally unrealistic

Sometimes unrealistic data is exactly what you want.

Suppose you're testing whether a username field accepts a value.

This may be perfectly fine:

test123

You do not need a sophisticated identity generator.

Likewise, if you're testing a calculator:

2 + 2 = 4

there is no benefit in generating realistic financial records.

Simple fake data is often best for:

  • unit tests
  • simple form tests
  • exact business rules
  • predictable fixtures
  • small examples
  • documentation

The simpler the test, the simpler the data should usually be.

Synthetic data is useful when relationships matter

Now imagine a checkout system.

You may need:

name
country
city
postal code
phone number
currency
tax rules
shipping options

If every field is generated independently, you might get:

{
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Tokyo",
  "postalCode": "SW1A 1AA",
  "phone": "+1 212 555 0100"
}

Every individual value looks valid.

Together they make little sense.

If your application uses those relationships, your tests become less useful.

Synthetic data can preserve context.

For example:

{
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg",
  "postalCode": "20095",
  "phone": "+49 40 12345678"
}

That is much more useful for testing country-aware behavior.

Dummy data is usually simpler

The term dummy data usually refers to placeholder information.

Examples:

John Doe
Company ABC
123456
example@example.com

It is often used for:

  • screenshots
  • demos
  • temporary UI development
  • prototypes
  • documentation

Dummy data does not necessarily try to reproduce real-world distributions or relationships.

It just fills space.

That makes it useful.

But it is not automatically realistic.

Mock data is slightly different

Mock data often appears in the context of mocked systems.

For example, a frontend may call an API that does not exist yet.

Instead of making a real request:

const response = await fetch("/api/users");

the frontend might receive a mocked response:

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Anna",
  "plan": "pro"
}

The important concept is not whether the values are realistic.

The important concept is that the response stands in for another system.

Mocking is about replacing dependencies.

Synthetic data is about generating realistic data.

They can absolutely be used together.

A mocked API can return synthetic data.

Test fixtures are about repeatability

A fixture is data prepared for a test.

For example:

const user = {
  id: "user-42",
  plan: "pro",
  balance: 100
};

Fixtures are often deliberately static.

That is useful because the expected state is obvious.

If a test fails, you know exactly what the input was.

Synthetic data can also be used as a fixture, especially when it is seeded.

For example:

seed = checkout-user-42

The generator can recreate the same synthetic customer every time.

That combines realism with reproducibility.

Realism should match the test

One mistake developers make is assuming that more realistic data is always better.

It isn't.

Suppose you're testing this function:

function addTax(price, rate) {
  return price + price * rate;
}

You probably want a test like:

expect(addTax(100, 0.19)).toBe(119);

Generating a realistic customer, address, order, product catalog, and payment method adds nothing.

But if you're testing a full checkout flow, realistic synthetic data becomes much more useful.

A simple rule:

Use the least complicated data that still tests the behavior you care about.

Production data is not test data

There is another category developers sometimes use:

copied production data.

For example:

export 1,000 customers
import into staging

This may create realistic test conditions.

It also creates privacy and security risks.

Production data can contain:

  • names
  • emails
  • addresses
  • phone numbers
  • account identifiers
  • transaction histories
  • internal notes
  • sensitive metadata

Once copied into development, that information may appear in:

  • local databases
  • logs
  • screenshots
  • test exports
  • bug reports
  • backups
  • developer laptops

Synthetic data avoids this problem by generating new records rather than copying actual customers.

Synthetic does not automatically mean anonymous

This distinction is important.

If you take real customer data and simply replace:

John Smith

with:

User 123

the dataset is not necessarily synthetic.

Other attributes may still allow the person to be identified.

For example:

location
age
transaction history
rare job title
specific timestamp

can potentially reveal identity when combined.

Truly synthetic data should be generated rather than merely renaming real individuals.

Format-valid data is another category

Sometimes realism means following a technical format.

For example:

UUID
IBAN
MAC address
IMEI
IP address
phone number
email

A useful test value may need to satisfy structural rules.

For example, this:

DE123

is not very useful for testing a real IBAN validator.

You may instead need an identifier that follows:

country length
BBAN structure
checksum rules

That makes the test data technically realistic.

But an important distinction remains:

Format-valid does not mean real-world verified.

A generated IBAN can satisfy structural checks without representing an existing bank account.

A generated device identifier can match the expected format without representing an actual device.

Synthetic data can preserve distributions

For some applications, individual realistic records are not enough.

Imagine testing analytics.

Production data might contain:

70% free users
20% standard users
10% premium users

A naive generator could produce:

33% free
33% standard
33% premium

That may create misleading results.

A more advanced synthetic dataset could preserve the intended distribution:

free: 70%
standard: 20%
premium: 10%

Likewise, synthetic datasets can model relationships such as:

country → currency
country → phone format
product → price range
subscription → feature usage
age group → behavior

This becomes useful for:

  • analytics
  • machine learning testing
  • load testing
  • dashboards
  • data pipelines
  • BI systems

Synthetic data can still contain edge cases

Realistic does not mean normal.

Good test datasets should include unusual scenarios.

For example:

very long names
empty optional values
Unicode characters
leap-day dates
zero-value orders
duplicate records
minimum values
maximum values
unusual postal formats

These cases often expose more bugs than ordinary records.

A good synthetic-data system should allow realism and deliberate edge cases to coexist.

Example: signup testing

For a simple unit test, this may be enough:

{
  "email": "test@example.com"
}

For integration testing:

{
  "firstName": "Anna",
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE"
}

For edge-case testing:

{
  "firstName": "A".repeat(100),
  "lastName": "Schneider",
  "email": "anna+very-long-alias@example.com",
  "country": "DE"
}

Different tests deserve different data strategies.

Example: API testing

Imagine this endpoint:

POST /customers

The API expects:

{
  "name": "string",
  "email": "string",
  "country": "string",
  "phone": "string"
}

A basic fixture could be:

{
  "name": "Test",
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "phone": "123"
}

That may be enough to test JSON parsing.

But it is not very useful for testing phone validation.

A realistic synthetic fixture could be:

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "phone": "+49 40 12345678"
}

Now the same payload exercises more realistic application behavior.

Example: database testing

Suppose you need 100,000 customer rows.

Writing static fixtures is obviously impractical.

A synthetic generator can create:

100,000 records
multiple countries
different subscription plans
varied signup dates
different order histories

That is useful for:

  • query testing
  • pagination
  • indexing
  • search
  • analytics
  • performance testing

For this kind of workload, synthetic data becomes much more valuable than simple dummy records.

Seeds make synthetic data reproducible

Pure generation introduces a problem:

run 1 → dataset A
run 2 → dataset B
run 3 → dataset C

If dataset A exposes a bug, you may want it again.

That is where seeds help.

For example:

seed = regression-42

can produce the same synthetic dataset repeatedly.

Then a CI failure can report:

Generator: customer
Seed: regression-42

A developer can recreate the exact input locally.

This makes synthetic data much more practical for automated testing.

Don't use synthetic data everywhere

Synthetic data is not the answer to every problem.

Use static fixtures when:

  • exact values matter
  • the test is small
  • readability is important
  • business rules are simple

Use synthetic data when:

  • realistic variation matters
  • you need many records
  • relationships between fields matter
  • you want multiple locales
  • you need performance datasets
  • production data should not be copied

Use deliberately invalid data when:

  • testing validators
  • testing error messages
  • testing edge cases
  • testing defensive code

The best test suite usually combines all three.

A practical hierarchy

I like to think about test data in layers.

Level 1: Placeholder data 

foo
bar
123

Useful for very simple tests.

Level 2: Static fixtures 

{
  "email": "test@example.com",
  "plan": "pro"
}

Useful for predictable business logic.

Level 3: Synthetic records 

{
  "name": "Anna Schneider",
  "email": "anna.schneider@example.com",
  "country": "DE",
  "city": "Hamburg"
}

Useful for realistic application testing.

Level 4: Synthetic datasets 

10,000 related records
multiple countries
weighted distributions
edge cases

Useful for analytics, system testing, and performance testing.

The higher the level, the more complexity you introduce.

Only move up when the test actually benefits from it.

Where tools like Genory fit

Developer tools such as Genory focus on generating synthetic test data and structured developer fixtures without requiring real customer records.

For example, you can work with:

  • synthetic profiles
  • custom datasets
  • addresses
  • UUIDs
  • format-based test identifiers
  • validators
  • developer utilities

For more complex fixture generation, you can start with the Genory test-data tools.

For programmatic workflows, the current API documentation is available at genory.dev/docs.

The goal is not to replace explicit test fixtures.

The goal is to make realistic test data easier to create when realism actually helps.

A simple rule

When choosing test data, ask:

Does this test care about the exact value?

If yes:

Use an explicit fixture.

If no, ask:

Does realism matter?

If no:

Use simple fake data.

If yes:

Use synthetic data.

And if the test must be reproducible:

Use a seed.

Final thought

Fake data and synthetic data are not enemies.

They solve different problems.

Fake data is often simple, obvious, and predictable.

Synthetic data is useful when your tests benefit from realistic structure, relationships, variation, or scale.

The mistake is not choosing one over the other.

The mistake is using complicated data where simple fixtures would work — or using meaningless placeholders when your application depends on realistic relationships.

Choose the data based on the behavior you're trying to test.

Not based on which generator looks more impressive.

title: Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React
description:
title: "Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React"
published: true
published_at: "2027-01-10T09:00:00+05:30"
description: "A practical engineering guide to Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React. Learn core mechanics, production tradeoffs, and best practices."
tags: [webdev, react, nodejs, websockets]
ai_disclosure_level: some_ai

In modern software development, Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React is a critical subject that every serious engineer must understand. Whether building distributed backend systems, designing scalable databases, or optimizing developer productivity, mastering the underlying mechanics separates junior developers who guess from senior engineers who deliver reliable architectures.

In this deep dive, we break down why Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React matters, examine common failure modes in production, and walk through concrete implementation patterns.

The Problem: Why Naive Approaches Fail

In earlier development workflows or smaller-scale projects, teams frequently overlook the subtleties of projects architectures.

When systems scale, common bottlenecks emerge:

  1. Unpredictable Latency & Resource Starvation: High concurrency and unoptimized execution pipelines exhaust system resources, leading to degraded response times and thread pool stalls.
  2. Hidden Failure Cascades: Unhandled edge cases and lack of defensive invariants create silent data corruption that propagates across microservices.
  3. High Cognitive Overhead: As codebases evolve, poorly structured domain abstractions become difficult to maintain, test, and refactor.

To resolve these challenges, engineering teams must implement disciplined patterns focusing on:

  • Websocket Protocol Handshakes: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Broadcasting Cursor Positions And Canvas Events: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • Operational Transformation Basics: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.
  • And Managing Reconnects: Practical implementation patterns and production considerations.

Under the Hood: Architectural Overview

Understanding how Architecting a Real-Time Collaborative Whiteboard with WebSockets and React functions beneath high-level abstractions is essential for diagnosing production anomalies.

+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| System Workflow: Projects Architecture                    |
|                                                              |
| [Incoming Workload] ---> [Validation & Boundary Layer]       |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                     [Optimized Core Execution]               |
|                                     |                        |
|                                     v                        |
|                  [Resilient State / Output Store]            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+

When designing systems around this pattern, prioritize:

  • Isolation of Concerns: Keep business invariants decoupled from transport protocols and third-party drivers.
  • Deterministic Resource Management: Bound memory allocations, connection pools, and worker concurrency to prevent out-of-memory crashes.
  • Observability & Metrics: Expose granular latency histograms, error rates, and throughput metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.

Practical Implementation

Here is a clean, production-oriented pattern demonstrating these principles in action:

import asyncio
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ExecutionContext:
    task_id: str
    payload: dict
    retries: int = 3

class ResilientProcessor:
    """Production-ready processor addressing: WebSocket protocol handshakes, broadcasting cursor positions and canvas events, operational transformation basics, and managing reconnects."""

    def __init__(self, concurrency_limit: int = 10):
        self.semaphore = asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency_limit)

    async def execute_with_guardrails(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> Optional[dict]:
        async with self.semaphore:
            for attempt in range(1, ctx.retries + 1):
                try:
                    logger.info(f"Processing task {ctx.task_id}, attempt {attempt}")
                    result = await self._process_task(ctx)
                    return result
                except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError) as ex:
                    backoff = 2 ** attempt
                    logger.warning(f"Transient error on {ctx.task_id}: {ex}. Retrying in {backoff}s...")
                    await asyncio.sleep(backoff)
                except Exception as ex:
                    logger.error(f"Permanent failure processing {ctx.task_id}: {ex}")
                    raise
            return None

    async def _process_task(self, ctx: ExecutionContext) -> dict:
        await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
        return {"task_id": ctx.task_id, "status": "completed", "meta": ctx.payload}

Production Gotchas to Avoid

When deploying this architecture at scale, keep these three operational realities in mind:

  1. Beware of Unbounded Queues: Always place hard limits on in-memory buffers and connection queues. An unbounded queue simply hides backpressure until the process encounters an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) crash.
  2. Set Aggressive Timeouts: Never make external network or storage calls without explicit connection and read timeouts. A single hanging dependency can exhaust worker pools system-wide.
  3. Ensure Idempotency: Network packets get dropped and clients retry. Ensure that mutating operations can be executed multiple times safely without producing duplicate side-effects.

Summary Checklist

  • [x] Validate at the boundary: Ensure invalid states never penetrate deep domain layers.
  • [x] Enforce bounded resource limits: Protect memory, connections, and CPU threads against unexpected spikes.
  • [x] Log structured telemetry: Attach correlation IDs to log records for rapid root-cause analysis during outages.
  • [x] Design for failure: Always provide graceful fallbacks and fast-failure mechanisms when dependencies degrade.

title: Our validator checked files, not frames — the first external user taught us the difference
description:
auto-xhs is an open-source system that lets an AI agent (Muse, Dots, or Grok Bot) run a Xiaohongshu account end to end: research, writing, video production, posting, and replying to comments. It works through the browser like a person would — no unofficial APIs. I open-sourced it on Oct 14.

On the same day, a user in Vietnam, axiom3356, ran the pipeline as-is, measured the output videos, and filed issue #1: three reproducible visual flaws that our validator, validate.py, had not caught. Not one of them.

The three flaws:

  1. At a scene change, the picture goes almost blank for about 2 seconds. Cards in the new scene appear one by one, and before the first one lands, there is nothing on screen.
  2. The finished video came out at 585 kb/s. For 1080p that is far too low — edges smear. 2 Mb/s is the floor anyone recommends.
  3. Two annotation cards in the same area, entering with different delays, can overlap each other.

His root-cause note was the part that stung: the validator checked the file — duration, resolution, word counts, silence gaps — but never looked at a single frame.

What we changed, all of it credited to his report:

  • Blank frames are now a check. Every 0.5 seconds we grab a frame, shrink it to a small grayscale image, and ask whether it is nearly one flat color. Two seconds of that in a row raises a warning with the rough position. Only ffmpeg and the Python standard library.
  • Low bitrate is now a check. Below 2000 kb/s the validator warns. Our own weather example, rendered with the old settings, is 844 kb/s — it gets warned too, and that warning is correct.
  • The assembler got a bitrate floor: target 3M, cap 4M. A small trap here: we had -crf 21 and -b:v set together, and in that combination ffmpeg follows crf and the bitrate target is ignored. Dropping crf fixed it.
  • The overlapping cards are NOT a machine check, and I want to be plain about why. A frame is pixels. Pixels cannot tell a full-bleed background (fine) from a card cropped by the frame edge (broken). A check built on that would cry wolf every day. So instead the template rules now say: one delayed entrance per area, and cards sharing an area go into a layout container. Prevention, not detection.

Both new checks are warn-only. A warning respects the person running the pipeline; a hard error from a check that can misfire does not.

The issue is still open, on purpose. If axiom3356 sends a PR, his gets reviewed first and used first — he found the problems and proposed the checks.

If you run it and your videos look wrong in a way the validator misses, that is exactly the report I want. And if you have content that repeats daily — weather, a digest, a ranking — playbooks live in scenarios/ and new ones are welcome.

title: I Built a Pixiv Alternative in Go (and Taught It SEO)
description:
Pixiv is wonderful. It's also, architecturally, a black box you can't learn from. So I built my own illustration community platform — Lumiina — live at https://www.lumiina.art, open source at Nyanns/lumiina.

The stack: Go (Gin + GORM) on the backend with strict Clean Architecture, PostgreSQL + Redis, and a React 19 + Vite SPA frontend. The interesting part wasn't the CRUD — it was everything around it: auth hardening, an image pipeline that doesn't melt your bandwidth bill, and making a JavaScript SPA actually rank on Google.

Here's what I learned.

1. SPAs are invisible to Google unless you fight for it

A client-rendered gallery is a ghost town for crawlers. I implemented bot pre-rendering: when the user-agent smells like Googlebot, the server returns fully rendered HTML with real <title>, meta/OG tags, and JSON-LD structured data per artwork — instead of an empty <div id="root">.

On top of that, every artwork publish fires an IndexNow ping, so Bing/Yandex learn about new content in minutes instead of weeks. Combined with a proper sitemap.xml and robots.txt, the site went from "exists" to "indexed" without waiting on Google's mercy.

Lesson: if your SPA needs SEO, server-side rendering isn't the only answer. Targeted bot pre-rendering is cheaper and keeps your SPA architecture intact.

2. Uploads are an attack surface — treat them like one

Anyone who's run a public upload endpoint knows the dread. My pipeline:

  • Magic-byte validation — never trust the extension or the Content-Type header.
  • Decompression bomb guard — decode config first, reject absurd dimensions before allocating a single pixel.
  • Client-side downsampling — a Canvas GPU pipeline shrinks 10–20 MB master illustrations to ~800 KB WebP before network transit. The server never sees the giant file, and neither does my Cloudinary bill.

Lesson: push expensive work to the client when you can. The cheapest byte to process is the one that never reaches your server.

3. Auth: boring, paranoid, and proud of it

  • bcrypt with constant-time dummy-hash execution so username enumeration via timing attacks doesn't work.
  • JWT (strict HS256) with Redis-backed revocation and a password-change epoch — changing your password kills every session, everywhere.
  • Rate limiting in layers, account lockout, and generic error messages that never reveal whether the username or the password was wrong.

None of this is novel. That's the point — auth should be boring. The novel bugs are the ones that end up on Have I Been Pwned.

4. IDs people can share

Artwork URLs use Sqids hash IDs (/artwork/v06sDC) instead of sequential integers. Short, non-guessable, and they don't leak "we have exactly 47 artworks" to competitors. Trivial to implement, surprisingly nice UX.

5. What I'd do differently

  • httpOnly cookies instead of localStorage JWT. It's the stronger default; the current setup works but cookies win on XSS resilience.
  • Start the content flywheel earlier. I over-invested in infrastructure before having content. A gallery with no art is a very fast empty room. Now there's a daily publishing rhythm — one new original artwork every day — and that's what actually moves the SEO needle. Tech gets you indexed; content gets you ranked.

The code

Everything is MIT-licensed: github.com/Nyanns/lumiina. The live site is lumiina.art.

If you're building a content platform in Go — or fighting SPA SEO — happy to answer questions in the comments. What would you have done differently?

title: Architectural Breakdown: Python performance: native loops, NumPy and the vectorize trap
description:
![Architecture Diagram](https://image.pollinations.ai/prompt/high+performance+cloud+systems+Python+performance%3A+native+loo+round+2?width=800&height=400&nologo=true)

# `np.vectorize` Is Just a For Loop in a Fancy Coat

It was 02:14 AM on a Tuesday when the on-call alert fired. Our ETL layer on an **8 GB RAM** cloud node (Python 3.11, CPython) started timing out normalising a batch of **500 k** feature vectors. The offending line in `transforms.py`:


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_features(records):
# "Vectorized!" , three exclamation points. Nobody believed it.
return np.vectorize(lambda x: (x - np.mean(x)) / np.std(x))(records)


Forty-seven seconds. For what should have been sub-100 ms. This is the kind of thing that keeps senior engineers up at night, not because it is complex, but because it *looks* correct.

What follows is a hardened rewrite that respects hardware limits, bounded-queue design, and race-condition resilience. Production builds from our [full-stack MVP reference codebase](https://www.shipmvp.tech) run variations of this exact pattern without incident.

---

## Why `np.vectorize` Is a Lie

| Tier | Per-element cost | What actually happens |
|------|------------------|-----------------------|
| Native Python loop | ~100 ns | Bytecode, ref-count, GIL |
| NumPy broadcast | ~50 ns | One C-level boundary crossing |
| `np.vectorize` | ~100 ns | Python loop behind a ufunc costume |
| Numba JIT (`nogil`) | ~10 ns | Compiled machine code, SIMD, no GIL |

`np.vectorize` is built on `np.frompyfunc`. It iterates **in Python**, calls your lambda for every element, builds an object array, then casts back to a numeric dtype. Two full passes. No SIMD. No parallelism. It is a slower `for` loop wearing a NumPy tie.

---

## Hardware-Aware Refactor

### Broadcast-First Normalisation


python
import numpy as np

def normalize_broadcast(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
"""True vectorisation, one C-level pass."""
if not arr.flags["C_CONTIGUOUS"]:
arr = np.ascontiguousarray(arr)

mean = arr.mean()
std  = arr.std()
return (arr - mean) / std


On an 8 GB node, a `float64` array of 500 k by 128 rows occupies roughly 4.9 GB. A single contiguous buffer avoids hidden copies that push us past the RAM ceiling and trigger swapping. Swapping is where the 47-second disaster comes from.

### Numba JIT for Conditional Logic

When the logic cannot be expressed as a chain of ufuncs (clipping, per-row state), Numba gives near-C speed without the GIL.


python
from numba import njit, prange
import numpy as np

@njit(cache=True, nogil=True, parallel=True)
def normalize_numba(arr: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
n = arr.size

# First pass: compute mean
mean = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    mean += arr[i]
mean /= n

# Second pass: compute variance
var = 0.0
for i in prange(n):
    diff = arr[i] - mean
    var += diff * diff
std = np.sqrt(var / n)

# Third pass: normalise with clipping and NaN guard
out = np.empty_like(arr)
for i in prange(n):
    val = (arr[i] - mean) / std
    out[i] = 0.0 if np.isnan(val) else max(min(val, 3.0), -3.0)
return out


- `cache=True` writes compiled machine code to disk, so there is no JIT warm-up penalty on container restarts
- `nogil=True` lets multiple worker threads run concurrently
- `parallel=True` enables auto-vectorisation and multi-core execution on inner loops

---

## Bounded-Queue Architecture

Production does not process a 500 k by 128 matrix in one shot. We slice it into chunks that fit in memory and keep the queue size bounded.


python
import queue
import threading

CHUNK_SIZE = 64_000 # ~4 MB per chunk (float64)
MAX_QUEUE = 8 # 32 MB buffer, safe headroom on 8 GB node
NUM_WORKERS = 4

def producer(src_iter, q: queue.Queue):
buffer = []
for rec in src_iter:
buffer.append(rec)
if len(buffer) == CHUNK_SIZE:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))
buffer.clear()
if buffer:
q.put(np.asarray(buffer, dtype=np.float64))

def consumer(q: queue.Queue, out_q: queue.Queue):
while True:
arr = q.get()
if arr is None:
out_q.put(None)
break
try:
out_q.put(normalize_numba(arr))
finally:
q.task_done()


The `maxsize` bound guarantees we never allocate more than roughly 32 MB of raw data plus 32 MB of normalised output. The producer converts once. No repeated allocation tax. Consumers run in a thread pool and the Numba kernel releases the GIL, so they are actually parallel.

Sentinels (`None`) guarantee each consumer exits exactly once. No lost-wake-up bugs. No manual lock handling.

---

## Failure Modes (Because They Happen)

| Failure mode | Symptom | Root cause | Fix |
|--------------|---------|------------|-----|
| **OOM** | Process killed by OS | Chunk too big for 8 GB node | Reduce `CHUNK_SIZE`, add `resource` guard |
| **Stalled pipeline** | Workers block forever | Producer throws before sentinel | Wrap in `try/finally`, always emit `None` |
| **Wrong results** | NaNs post-normalisation | Non-contiguous input, dtype mismatch | `np.ascontiguousarray(..., dtype=np.float64)` upfront |
| **CPU thrashing** | 100% usage, no speedup | Numba without `parallel=True` | Enable `parallel=True`, use `prange` |
| **Deadlock** | `q.join()` hangs | Exception skips `task_done()` | Always call in `finally` |

---

## Benchmarks (8 GB node, 500 k by 128 float64)


plaintext
native_python_list 0.34 s ± 0.01
numpy_broadcast 0.018 s ± 0.001
numpy_vectorize 0.29 s ± 0.02 ← same as pure Python
numba_jit (cached) 0.009 s ± 0.001
pipeline (8-chunk, 4-workers) 0.025 s ± 0.003


Peak memory: ~6 GB. Scales linearly with worker count because the GIL is released. The pipeline includes queue overhead and still beats the naive approach by **13×**.

---

The lesson is not about NumPy or Numba. It is about reading what you write, not what it promises. `np.vectorize` says "vectorised" in its docstring. That is the entire pitch. Do not fall for it.

**Open question for the comments:** When you have a per-row transformation that mixes aggregation with conditional clipping, do you reach for Numba first, or do you prefer the readability of NumPy broadcasting even when it means an extra pass over the data?

title: Vercel Sandbox now runs on Vercel Managed Images
description:
Today we are introducing Vercel Managed Images (VMI), a set of versioned, open-source base images you can use as-is or extend. The source for every image lives in the public vercel/sandbox repository.

Managed images replace Sandbox runtimes, which are now deprecated. Starting with version 3 of the Sandbox SDK, new sandboxes default to vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. It ships with Node.js, Python, common coding agents and standard utilities, so most users never build a custom image or install packages at boot.

The universal image switches our default operating system from Amazon Linux to Ubuntu, a lighter and more widely used system across the industry.

Secure by default

Every managed image gets a nightly release. Rolling tags such as latest and the major-version tags pick up operating system and dependency updates automatically, including security patches and new releases of Node.js, Python, and the preinstalled coding agents.

Within each release, dependencies are pinned to specific versions wherever possible, so a given image version stays consistent.

If you need a fully immutable, reproducible environment, pin to an image digest (SHA). Digest-pinned images opt out of automatic updates.

Choose a managed image from the catalog

Each managed image targets a different starting point:

  • vercel/sandbox/universal:latest is the new default, a rolling release on Ubuntu 26.04 with Node.js 24, Python 3.14 with uv, the opencode, claude-code, codex, and pi coding agents, and utilities including git, vim, nano, tmux, ripgrep, jq, and fzf.

  • vercel/sandbox/node:22, node:24, and node:26 provide Node.js versions on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/python:3.14 provides Python on Ubuntu 26.04.

  • vercel/sandbox/ubuntu:latest provides base Ubuntu 26.04 with no extra tooling.

  • vercel/sandbox/arch:latest provides Arch Linux, regularly updated, with no Node.js or Python preinstalled. Its large package repository makes it useful for agents that install tools on the fly.

Reference an image and migrate from runtimes

Sandboxes can use an image from any repository in your project, a repository which has been shared with your team or any public repository.

Images are addressed by their full path, team-slug/project/repo:tag, for example vercel/sandbox/universal:latest. The SDK types the image property so built-in images autocomplete while any string is still accepted. The previous runtime property is deprecated, not removed, so existing code keeps working.

Amazon Linux runtimes are not part of the managed image catalog, so teams that need AL2023 can stay on runtime. Managed images run as the default ubuntu or arch user with passwordless sudo, rather than the vercel-sandbox user.

Open an issue or a pull request to improve them, and read the Vercel Sandbox images documentation to get started.

title: AZ-500 practice, week 1: 4 questions
description:
Four exam-style questions I wrote this week (PIM, Key Vault, storage, NSG), answers hidden, explanations in plain words.

How to use these: read the question, pick your answer before you open Answer, and write it down (or in the comments). Then check the "why not the others" part even if you got it right: that is where the exam traps live. Every scenario, name and number is made up by me; only the question formats follow the real exam.

Table of contents

  • Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval
  • Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret
  • Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later
  • Q004: NSG rules with application security groups
  • Cheat sheet
  • Coming next

Q001: Admin role only on request, max 4 hours, with approval

Identity and access · Single choice · standalone page

Your helpdesk lead, Mai, sometimes needs the User Administrator role to fix accounts. Your security team says: "Fine, but only when she asks for it, for at most 4 hours, and someone has to say yes first."

What should you configure?

  • A. A permanent active assignment of User Administrator, plus a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA
  • B. A Privileged Identity Management (PIM) eligible assignment of User Administrator, with role settings: activation maximum duration 4 hours and require approval to activate
  • C. An access review on the User Administrator role that runs every 4 hours
  • D. An administrative unit that contains Mai's account

Answer

B. "Eligible" means Mai does not hold the role until she activates it. In the PIM role settings, the activation maximum duration can be anything from 1 to 24 hours (so 4 is fine), and "Require approval to activate" makes at least one approver say yes first.

Why not the others:

  • A gives her the role 24/7. MFA proves it is really Mai, it does not make the role go away after 4 hours.
  • C checks who has access, after the fact. An access review every 4 hours would mostly annoy the reviewers.
  • D limits which users she can manage, not when she can manage them.

Source: Configure Microsoft Entra role settings in Privileged Identity Management

Q002: A VM reads a Key Vault secret without keeping a secret

Identity and access · Yes/No series ("Does this meet the goal?") · standalone page

Yes/No series: same scenario, a different solution each time. Some scenarios have several right solutions, some have none.

An app on the Azure VM vm-lab-01 must read a database password stored in the key vault kv-lab-01. The vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Goal: no password, key or certificate is stored in the app code or on the VM.

Solution: You enable a system-assigned managed identity on vm-lab-01 and assign it the Key Vault Secrets User role on kv-lab-01.

Does this meet the goal?

  • A. Yes
  • B. No

Answer

A. Yes. The VM gets its own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, so the app asks Azure for a token instead of keeping a secret in a config file. Key Vault Secrets User can read secret contents, and it works here because the vault uses the Azure RBAC permission model.

Other solutions you might see in the same series:

  • "Store a client secret for an app registration in appsettings.json" → No. That is a secret sitting on the VM, the exact thing the goal forbids.
  • "Assign the managed identity Key Vault Reader" → No. Reader sees the vault and the names of its secrets (metadata), but it cannot read the secret values. Close, but no password for you.

Source: Provide access to Key Vault keys, certificates, and secrets with Azure role-based access control

Q003: Stop anonymous blob reads, now and later

Compute, storage and databases · Hot area · standalone page

Someone set one container in the storage account stlabdata01 to "Container (anonymous read access)". Your boss wants no anonymous reads in any container of this account, now and later, even if someone changes a container setting again next week.

Pick the right value for each line:

Where Setting Your choice
Storage account stlabdata01 › Settings › Configuration Allow Blob anonymous access ▢ Enabled ▢ Disabled
Each container Anonymous access level ▢ Must be changed to Private one by one ▢ Nothing more to do

Answer

Disabled / Nothing more to do. The account setting (property AllowBlobPublicAccess) overrides the container settings: once it is off, containers that were set to anonymous access are no longer reachable anonymously. Flipping containers to Private one by one is nice tidying, but it is not what stops the leak, and the next person can flip a container right back.

Why not the other values: Enabled leaves every container in charge of its own fate. Changing containers one by one only fixes today, not "later".

Bonus: to do this for every storage account at once, use the built-in Azure Policy "Storage account public access should be disallowed" (Audit or Deny). One gotcha: a static website's $web container stays public no matter what, because that is its job.

Sources: Remediate anonymous read access to blob data · Azure Policy built-in definitions for Azure Storage

Q004: NSG rules with application security groups

Networking · Drag and drop · standalone page

The virtual network vnet-shop has one subnet with the network security group nsg-shop attached. The VMs web01 and web02 are in the application security group asg-web. The VMs api01 and api02 are in asg-api. Everything is in the same virtual network.

You need to meet these rules:

  1. People on the internet can reach the web VMs on HTTPS.
  2. Only the web VMs can reach the API VMs, on TCP 8443.
  3. Nothing else inside the virtual network can reach the API VMs. (Yes, that includes the test VM someone "temporarily" created in March.)

Drag the right value into each numbered box. Each value can be used once, more than once, or not at all.

Values: Internet · VirtualNetwork · AzureLoadBalancer · asg-web · asg-api · 443 · 8443 · 3389

Inbound rules on nsg-shop:

Priority Name Source Destination Port Action
100 allow-https-web [1] [2] 443 Allow
200 allow-web-to-api [3] [4] [5] Allow
300 deny-vnet-to-api [6] asg-api Any Deny

Answer

[1] Internet · [2] asg-web · [3] asg-web · [4] asg-api · [5] 8443 · [6] VirtualNetwork

Application security groups let you write rules against "the web VMs" instead of a list of IP addresses, and they work as both source and destination. Rule 300 is the one people forget: the default rule AllowVNetInBound (priority 65000) lets every machine in the virtual network talk to every other one. You cannot delete default rules, but a custom rule with a lower number wins. Rules are checked from the lowest number up and stop at the first match, so the web VMs still get in through rule 200 before rule 300 says no to everyone else.

Why not the other values:

  • AzureLoadBalancer in [6] would block the load balancer health probes, not your test VM. Your API would go "unhealthy" and you would get a very confusing afternoon.
  • VirtualNetwork in [3] would let any VM in the network call the API, which breaks rule 2.
  • 443 in [5] or 3389 anywhere: wrong port. Nobody asked for RDP from anywhere.

Gotcha: all network interfaces in one application security group must be in the same virtual network, and when a rule uses an ASG as both source and destination, both groups must be in that same virtual network.

Sources: Application security groups · Network security groups overview

Cheat sheet

The same four ideas in plain words, for the manager who asks "so what?". Share it with them.

Coming next

Monday and Tuesday bring a SAS question for storage accounts with key access switched off, and a just-in-time RDP question for Defender for Cloud. All questions live in the AZ-500 practice folder.

Got one wrong? Good. That is one fewer surprise in the exam room. Drop your answers in the comments.

title: Flutter vs. React + Capacitor in 2026: Which Stack Saves More Time & Budget for Your Business App?
description:
If you are a founder or business owner planning to build a cross-platform mobile app for iOS and Android in 2026, you will immediately face a critical technical decision: Should we build it in Flutter, or use a Web-to-Mobile stack like React + Capacitor?

Pick the wrong stack for your specific use case, and you can easily add 4 to 6 extra weeks to your development timeline.

At VanzaLabs, we don't treat technology choices like a religion. In fact, we recently built and shipped two production B2B mobile apps to Google Play—one written in Flutter (FormGrid: Forms & Sheets) and the other in React 19 + Tailwind CSS 4 + Capacitor 8 (Vanza: Invoices & Contracts).

Here is a practical, business-focused guide on when to use each stack—based on real production trade-offs.

When Flutter Is the Unbeatable Choice
We chose Flutter for FormGrid, our mobile workspace for creating and managing Google Forms™ and Google Sheets™ in the field.

Choose Flutter for your business app if:

You need 60/120fps native scrolling and gesture fluidity: Flutter renders its own UI via Impeller/Skia rather than relying on a browser WebView. When users scroll through hundreds of spreadsheet rows or switch between tabs rapidly, it feels indistinguishable from a native iOS/Android app.
Deep OS & Hardware Integration: Receiving shared files directly from other mobile apps (Share Intents), background isolates, and native OAuth flows are rock-solid in Flutter's ecosystem.
Mobile-First Product: If 90% of your users will interact with your product strictly on smartphones and tablets rather than a desktop web dashboard, Flutter delivers a superior mobile UX.
When React 19 + Capacitor 8 Cuts Development Time in Half
For our second product, Vanza: Invoices & Contracts (an offline PDF generator for contractors, freelancers, and SMBs), we intentionally chose React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and Capacitor 8.

Why didn't we use Flutter here? Because the core of an invoicing and contract app is document layout, dynamic multi-step forms, and complex print formatting.

Choose React + Capacitor for your business app if:

You need both a Web App AND a Mobile App from a single codebase: With React + Capacitor, 95% of your web application code runs natively inside an iOS/Android shell with full access to native APIs (filesystem, camera, share sheet, in-app purchases via RevenueCat). For a startup on a tight budget, this saves 35–45% compared to building a web app and mobile app separately.
Heavy Document, Table, or PDF Rendering: Designing 12 customizable invoice/contract themes with dynamic line-item tables, automatic tax/discount math, and canvas finger signatures was dramatically faster using HTML/CSS Flexbox & Grid + jsPDF than writing low-level PDF layout code in Dart.
Rich Offline Local Storage with IndexedDB: Using Dexie.js over IndexedDB allowed us to build a 100% offline client and service catalog database that works seamlessly in basements and construction sites without internet.
Side-by-Side Decision Matrix for Founders
Time to Market (Web + Mobile combined): React + Capacitor wins (1 shared codebase).
UI/Animation Smoothness on Budget Phones: Flutter wins.
Complex Forms, Dashboards & PDF Generation: React + Capacitor wins.
In-App Subscriptions (RevenueCat) & Offline Support: Tie — both work great in production.
Need Help Choosing the Right Architecture for Your MVP?
At VanzaLabs, our senior engineering team builds production-ready Web and Mobile MVPs in 3 to 8 weeks using both Flutter and React / Next.js / Capacitor—depending on what gives your business the fastest path to revenue and the lowest maintenance cost.

We also help growing companies automate manual workflows by integrating CRMs, ERPs, payment gateways, and custom AI agents.

🌐 Explore our work and request a free 1-day project estimate: https://vanzalabs.tech

title: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant: Benchmarked for RAG in 2026
description:
I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings into pgvector and Qdrant and measured recall, latency, index build and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its docs only, since I didn't run it. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings in a vector column and searches them with HNSW or IVFFlat indexes, next to your normal tables. Qdrant is an open-source vector database you run yourself or use as a managed cloud. Pinecone is a fully managed, serverless vector database you only reach through an API.

For a RAG app, the real question is whether you need a separate vector database at all. I loaded the same 100,000 OpenAI embeddings (1,536 dimensions) into pgvector 0.8.7 on PostgreSQL 18.6 and into Qdrant 1.19.2 on one machine. Then I measured recall, latency, build time and filtered search. Pinecone is covered from its official docs and limits only, because I didn't run it and I won't invent numbers for it.

TL;DR: pgvector vs Pinecone vs Qdrant, which should I use?

Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres and have up to a few million vectors. One database, SQL joins, transactions and backups you already have. Choose Qdrant when vector search is the core workload and you need the best recall per millisecond or heavy filtering. Choose Pinecone when you want zero infrastructure and accept a managed service with usage pricing.

pgvector Qdrant Pinecone
What it is Postgres extension Vector database (open source) Managed vector database (closed)
Hosting Anywhere Postgres runs Self-host or Qdrant Cloud Pinecone's cloud only
Index HNSW, IVFFlat HNSW per segment Managed (serverless, object storage)
Max indexed dims 2,000 vector, 4,000 halfvec 1,536 tested here 20,000 dense
Filtering SQL WHERE (post-filter, iterative scans) Payload indexes + filter-aware HNSW Metadata filters (40 KB per record)
Consistency Transactional (ACID) Upserts readable after wait=true Eventually consistent
Recall@10 at ~2.6 ms, my test 0.978 (ef_search 100) 0.985 (hnsw_ef 40) not tested
Cost to start Your Postgres Free binary / free cloud tier Free Starter; Standard $50/month minimum

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Usually not at first. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, pgvector adds vector search without a second system to deploy, secure, back up and keep in sync. In my test it answered top-10 queries over 100,000 OpenAI embeddings in 1.5-4 ms, with 95-99% recall. A dedicated database starts to pay off at very large scale, under heavy filtering, or when search load needs to scale separately.

The hidden cost of a separate vector store is synchronisation. Every document insert, update and delete has to reach two systems, and a failed write leaves them disagreeing. With pgvector the embedding sits in the same row and the same transaction as the document it describes.

What is pgvector?

pgvector is an open-source PostgreSQL extension that adds vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec types, distance operators like <=> (cosine) and <-> (L2), and approximate HNSW and IVFFlat indexes. Per the pgvector README, it "performs exact nearest neighbor search, which provides perfect recall" by default. An index trades a little recall for speed.

CREATE EXTENSION vector;

CREATE TABLE documents (
  id        bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id int NOT NULL,
  content   text NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON documents USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops);

-- top 5 chunks for a question, inside one tenant
SELECT id, content
FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 5;

Index limits matter for model choice. HNSW can index a vector of "up to 2,000 dimensions" and a halfvec of "up to 4,000 dimensions". A 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large needs a halfvec index or a shorter output size.

What are Qdrant and Pinecone?

Qdrant is an open-source vector search engine written in Rust. It stores points (vectors plus a JSON payload), builds an HNSW index per segment, and adds payload indexes so filters run inside the graph search. You can run a single binary, Docker or Qdrant Cloud.

Pinecone is a managed, serverless vector database. Per its architecture docs, "all your vector data is stored in highly efficient, distributed object storage." Pinecone "separates write and read operations into different paths, with each scaling independently based on demand." There is no self-hosted version.

How I benchmarked pgvector and Qdrant

  1. Data. The first 100,000 rows of the public DBpedia OpenAI embeddings dataset: 1,536-dimension text-embedding-ada-002 vectors of Wikipedia entities, a typical RAG shape. 1,000 held-out rows from the same dataset served as queries.
  2. Ground truth. Exact cosine top-10 for every query, computed with NumPy. Recall@10 is the share of those 10 that each engine returned.
  3. Machine. One 8-vCPU, 15 GB Linux box, everything on localhost, no Docker.
  4. pgvector. PostgreSQL 18.6 with pgvector 0.8.7, shared_buffers = 2GB, maintenance_work_mem = 2GB. HNSW with defaults (m = 16, ef_construction = 64), loaded with binary COPY through psycopg 3.
  5. Qdrant. The Qdrant 1.19.2 release binary, cosine distance, m = 16 and ef_construct = 64 to match pgvector, default optimizer settings (it made 4 segments). Loaded with the official Python client over gRPC from a single process.
  6. Queries. One client, sequential, 50 warm-up queries, then 1,000 timed queries. Latency includes the Python client round trip on both sides.
  7. Filters. Every vector got a random category from 0 to 9, about 10% of rows each. Filtered queries asked for the top 10 inside one category.

Is pgvector fast enough? Recall and latency results

Yes, at this scale both engines are fast. pgvector reached 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms median with default settings, and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with hnsw.ef_search = 200. Qdrant reached 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms median and 0.999 at 5.4 ms. At roughly equal recall (about 98.5-98.8%), Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster: 2.6 ms against 4.0 ms.

Engine and setting Recall@10 p50 latency p95 latency Queries/s (1 client)
pgvector, ef_search = 40 (default) 0.948 1.45 ms 2.16 ms 683
pgvector, ef_search = 100 0.978 2.60 ms 3.70 ms 389
pgvector, ef_search = 200 0.988 4.02 ms 5.82 ms 249
pgvector halfvec index, ef_search = 100 0.973 2.33 ms 3.30 ms 433
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 40 0.985 2.63 ms 3.56 ms 368
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 100 0.997 3.73 ms 4.66 ms 255
Qdrant, hnsw_ef = 200 0.999 5.37 ms 6.99 ms 176
pgvector exact (no index) 1.000 380 ms 445 ms 3
Qdrant exact (no index) 1.000 24.7 ms 32.6 ms 39

Why does Qdrant get higher recall at the same ef? It splits the collection into segments (4 here) and searches each one with that ef, so it explores more candidates in total. Compare the engines at equal recall, not equal settings.

How fast do they load and index?

Qdrant indexed faster: 30.8 seconds from the first upload to a fully indexed collection, with the upload itself taking 20.2 s from one Python process. pgvector loaded the rows with COPY in 3.9 s, then needed 69.1 s to build the HNSW index with the default 2 parallel workers.

pgvector Qdrant
Load 100k vectors 3.9 s (COPY) 20.2 s (Python client, gRPC)
Build HNSW index 69.1 s included, indexed at 30.8 s
Table / data size 798 MB —
HNSW index size 781 MB (vector), 391 MB (halfvec) —
Server memory after test Postgres buffers + OS cache 1,293 MB RSS

Use the halfvec trick in pgvector: indexing embedding::halfvec(1536) halved the index from 781 MB to 391 MB and cost about half a point of recall (0.973 against 0.978 at ef_search = 100). Query the index with the same cast:

CREATE INDEX ON documents
  USING hnsw ((embedding::halfvec(1536)) halfvec_cosine_ops);

SELECT id FROM documents
ORDER BY embedding::halfvec(1536) <=> $1::halfvec(1536)
LIMIT 10;

How does filtered vector search compare?

Qdrant handled filters best. With a payload index on category, filtered top-10 queries returned 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms median. pgvector gave three very different results depending on the plan Postgres picked, so you need to know how its filtering works.

Filtered query (10% of rows match) Rows returned (of 10) Recall@10 p50
pgvector, planner's choice (B-tree on category, exact sort) 10 1.000 44.2 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = off 3.92 0.389 1.77 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = strict_order 10 0.915 3.62 ms
pgvector, HNSW, iterative_scan = relaxed_order 10 0.953 3.37 ms
Qdrant, payload index 10 0.993 2.11 ms

Why does pgvector return fewer rows with a filter?

Because HNSW filters after the index scan. The README explains: "If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average." I measured 3.92. Since pgvector 0.8.0, iterative index scans keep walking the graph until enough rows match.

-- once per session or per transaction (SET LOCAL)
SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order;

SELECT id, content FROM documents
WHERE tenant_id = $1
ORDER BY embedding <=> $2
LIMIT 10;

Postgres often picks the exact plan by itself for a selective filter. In my test it used the category B-tree and sorted about 10,000 rows exactly: perfect recall, but 44 ms instead of about 3 ms. That is fine for one tenant with a few thousand chunks. For large tenants, check EXPLAIN and turn on iterative scans. If one filter dominates, consider a partial index or partitioning by tenant.

What does Pinecone offer that pgvector and Qdrant don't?

Fully managed, serverless scaling with nothing to run. Reads and writes scale separately, storage lives in object storage, and you never tune ef or m. The trade-offs are documented:

  • Eventual consistency. The known limitations page says "Pinecone is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records are available to query."
  • Operation limits. Per the operation limits: dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions, 40 KB of filterable metadata per record, 1,000 records or 2 MB per upsert batch, and top_k up to 10,000.
  • Plans. The object limits give the free Starter plan 2 GB of serverless storage and 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Pinecone pricing lists the Standard plan at a $50/month minimum.
  • Network hop. Every query leaves your VPC. Expect your cloud region's round-trip time on top of search time. My localhost latencies are not comparable to Pinecone and I did not measure it.

When should I choose each one?

Decide by what you already run and what dominates your workload. The pgvector default is strong for product teams. Move when you measure a reason, not before.

  1. Choose pgvector when your data lives in Postgres, you need joins, row-level security or transactions with your embeddings, and you have up to a few million vectors per index. Add pgvectorscale (StreamingDiskANN) if the index outgrows RAM.
  2. Choose Qdrant when search is the product: tens of millions of vectors, many filters, multi-vector or hybrid search, or quantization to cut memory. Its quantization guide says scalar quantization achieves "4x compression with minimal accuracy loss."
  3. Choose Pinecone when nobody on the team should run a database, traffic is spiky, and a usage bill plus eventual consistency are acceptable.

How do I move from pgvector to Qdrant later?

Keep embeddings and IDs portable from day one. Use the same primary key in both systems, store the embedding model name and dimensions with each row, and write a re-sync job that streams rows by ID. Qdrant accepts integer or UUID point IDs, so a UUIDv7 primary key maps across directly.

Then run both side by side, compare recall on a fixed set of real queries, and switch reads before you stop writing to Postgres.

Common mistakes with vector search in production

  • Indexing 3,072-dimension vectors as vector. HNSW on vector stops at 2,000 dimensions. Use halfvec or a smaller output dimension.
  • Forgetting iterative scans. Filtered HNSW queries in pgvector can silently return fewer than LIMIT rows.
  • Comparing engines at equal settings. ef means different work in different engines. Compare at equal recall.
  • Measuring recall on random vectors. Use real embeddings from your model. Random data hides graph quality.
  • Creating Qdrant payload indexes after loading. The indexing docs say payload indexes should be created before ingesting data, so filter-aware HNSW edges get built.
  • Ignoring re-embedding cost. Switching embedding models means re-embedding everything, whichever store you use.

If you want a working starting point, my open-source Next.js AI starter kit, Forgekit, ships RAG on pgvector. For self-hosting Postgres or Qdrant next to your app, see self-hosting Next.js with Coolify.

Key takeaways

  • With 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector 0.8.7 hit 0.948 recall@10 at 1.45 ms with defaults and 0.988 at 4.0 ms with ef_search 200.
  • Qdrant 1.19.2 hit 0.985 recall at 2.6 ms, about 1.5x faster than pgvector at roughly equal recall.
  • pgvector's HNSW filters after scanning: a 10% filter returned only 3.92 of 10 rows until iterative scans were enabled.
  • Qdrant's payload index gave the best filtered search in my test: 0.993 recall at 2.1 ms.
  • A halfvec HNSW index halved pgvector's index size (781 MB to 391 MB) for about half a point of recall.
  • Pinecone is serverless and eventually consistent, supports 20,000-dimension vectors, and its Standard plan has a $50/month minimum.
  • Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres; move to Qdrant or Pinecone when measurements show a need.

FAQ

Is pgvector as good as Pinecone or Qdrant?

For most RAG apps up to a few million vectors, yes. In my test of 100,000 OpenAI embeddings, pgvector reached 0.988 recall@10 at 4.0 ms median, and Qdrant reached 0.985 at 2.6 ms. Qdrant was about 1.5 times faster at equal recall and better at filtered search, but pgvector keeps embeddings in the same transactional database as your data.

Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Not usually at the start. If your app already uses PostgreSQL, the pgvector extension adds vector columns and HNSW indexes without a second system to deploy, back up and keep in sync. Consider a dedicated vector database when you reach tens of millions of vectors, need heavy filtering at low latency, or need to scale search separately.

Why does pgvector return fewer results than my LIMIT?

Because pgvector's HNSW index applies WHERE filters after scanning the index. With a filter matching 10 percent of rows and the default ef_search of 40, about 4 rows match on average; I measured 3.92. Set hnsw.iterative_scan to relaxed_order or strict_order, available since pgvector 0.8.0, so the scan continues until enough rows match.

How many dimensions can pgvector index?

pgvector's HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support the vector type up to 2,000 dimensions, halfvec up to 4,000 and bit up to 64,000. For a 3,072-dimension model such as text-embedding-3-large, index the column as halfvec or request a smaller output dimension. Pinecone supports dense vectors up to 20,000 dimensions.

Is Qdrant faster than pgvector?

In my single-machine test, yes, at equal recall. Qdrant 1.19.2 returned 0.985 recall@10 at 2.6 ms median against pgvector's 0.988 at 4.0 ms, and indexed 100,000 vectors in about 31 seconds against pgvector's 69-second HNSW build. With default settings, pgvector was faster per query but at lower recall, 0.948 at 1.45 ms.

How much does Pinecone cost?

Pinecone has a free Starter plan with 2 GB of serverless storage and up to 5 indexes per project, all in AWS us-east-1. Its Standard plan for production has a $50 per month minimum, after which you pay as you go for usage, according to Pinecone's pricing page. Qdrant's open-source build and pgvector are free to self-host.

What is halfvec in pgvector?

halfvec is pgvector's half-precision vector type, storing each dimension in 2 bytes instead of 4. Indexing an expression like embedding::halfvec(1536) halves the HNSW index size; in my test it shrank from 781 MB to 391 MB with recall dropping from 0.978 to 0.973. It also raises the indexable limit to 4,000 dimensions.

Is Pinecone eventually consistent?

Yes. Pinecone's documentation states that it is eventually consistent, so there can be a slight delay before upserted records can be queried, and suggests checking index stats to confirm counts. pgvector writes are transactional and visible on commit, and Qdrant upserts sent with wait=true are applied before the call returns.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Local Whisper vs. Cloud Dictation: Privacy, Latency and Accuracy Tradeoffs (Plus a Private Setup)
description:
"Just run Whisper locally" is good advice that skips a lot of detail. Local speech-to-text is genuinely useful, but it is not automatically faster, more accurate, or even fully private, depending on what else sits in your pipeline.

This post breaks the decision into three questions (what leaves the machine, where latency comes from, and how accurate it is for your voice) and ends with a setup where nothing leaves your computer. I use InsertKit as the dictation front end because it supports local Whisper, bring-your-own-key cloud providers, and custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints in one place. The tradeoffs apply to any stack.

1. Privacy: map the data flow first

A modern dictation pipeline usually has two stages:

mic audio -> [speech-to-text] -> raw transcript -> [LLM formatting] -> text at cursor

Each stage can be local or remote, and people often secure one and forget the other.

  • Speech-to-text. With a cloud engine, your audio is uploaded and processed by that provider. With a local Whisper model, audio stays on your machine.
  • Formatting. Clean-up (removing filler words, fixing punctuation, adapting tone) is usually done by a chat model. If that model is in the cloud, your transcript leaves the machine even when the audio did not.
  • Side channels. Sync features count too. In InsertKit, snippets, clipboard history, custom vocabulary, and API keys sync to your account. If your vocabulary list contains an unreleased product codename, that word list is synced, even if every audio clip stays local.

What InsertKit stores is worth knowing precisely: cloud voice history in Settings → Usage covers the last 30 days and is text only, no audio, with a Clear button. Local voice history stays on the device, and setting its maximum to 0 disables it.

So "private" is not a property of a model. It is a property of the whole path.

2. Latency: where the milliseconds actually go

Local is not always faster. Rough breakdown:

Cloud: upload time + queueing + inference on fast hardware + download. On a good connection, short utterances can come back very quickly, because providers run large models on serious GPUs.

Local: zero network, but inference runs on your CPU or GPU. A small model on a modern laptop is responsive. A large model on an older CPU can take noticeably longer than the time you spent talking.

Two details that matter in practice:

  • Model loading. Expect the first transcription after loading a large model to be slower than the ones that follow.
  • Long dictation. If the tool waits until you finish a three-minute ramble before transcribing, you wait for all of it at the end. InsertKit splits long speech into chunks at natural pauses and transcribes them while you keep talking, which hides much of that delay locally and in the cloud.

3. Accuracy: benchmark your own voice

Published word error rates come from benchmark datasets, not from your accent, your mic, or your jargon. Ten minutes of testing beats any leaderboard.

Here is a quick, tool-agnostic way to compare Whisper model sizes with whisper.cpp:

git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp
cd whisper.cpp
cmake -B build
cmake --build build -j --config Release

for m in base small medium; do
  sh ./models/download-ggml-model.sh $m
done

# Convert a 60-second recording of you reading real work text to 16 kHz mono WAV
ffmpeg -i sample.m4a -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le sample.wav

for m in base small medium; do
  /usr/bin/time -p ./build/bin/whisper-cli -m models/ggml-$m.bin -f sample.wav -otxt -of out-$m
done

Then score each output against what you actually said:

# pip install jiwer
from jiwer import wer

ref = open("reference.txt").read()
for m in ["base", "small", "medium"]:
    hyp = open(f"out-{m}.txt").read()
    print(m, "WER:", round(wer(ref, hyp), 3))

Use real material: a commit message, a ticket description, a paragraph full of service names. Generic sentences flatter every model.

A few patterns you will likely see:

  • Bigger models handle accents and noise better, at the cost of speed and memory.
  • Jargon fails across all sizes. That is a vocabulary problem, not a model-size problem.
  • Whisper can hallucinate on silence or noise, producing text nobody said. Trimming silence and using a decent mic reduce it.

For jargon, a correction layer helps more than a bigger model. InsertKit's Custom Vocabulary has word hints plus "heard as → write as" corrections, like post gres → Postgres, and corrections run before and after formatting so the LLM cannot undo them.

The decision, simplified

  • Audio must never leave the machine: local Whisper.
  • Speed on modest hardware: cloud, or a small local model.
  • Accuracy on difficult audio: a large local model with a GPU, or a strong cloud engine.
  • Zero setup: a hosted engine that needs no key.
  • Air-gapped or offline work: local Whisper plus a local LLM, or formatting turned off.

Many developers end up hybrid: local for anything touching client code or internal docs, cloud for low-stakes chat.

A fully private dictation setup

Here is the setup where audio and text both stay on your machine. Local Whisper is a desktop feature in InsertKit (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Step 1: Local speech-to-text

In the Speech Engine panel, choose Local Offline (Whisper) and download a model inside the app. Sizes go from Tiny (~75 MB) and Base (~140 MB) through Small (~460 MB) and Medium (~1.5 GB) to Large v3 (~3 GB). Use your benchmark results to pick. Small is a sensible starting point on most laptops.

Step 2: A local LLM for formatting

Run a local OpenAI-compatible server. With Ollama:

ollama pull llama3.2
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/models

LM Studio exposes a similar server, by default at http://localhost:1234/v1.

In InsertKit, open Settings → API Keys and add a Custom OpenAI-compatible provider: a name, the base URL (for example http://localhost:11434/v1), a key if your server needs one, and the models (auto-fetched or entered by hand). Then choose that model for Smart Formatting.

Smaller local models format well enough for clean-up. If output gets too creative, add a short custom instruction under Use my own instructions, such as "Fix punctuation and remove filler words. Do not add or change content."

Step 3: Decide what happens when formatting is unavailable

Enable Keep working offline so the raw transcript is pasted if the formatter cannot be reached. Or skip formatting for sensitive sessions and rely on vocabulary corrections.

Step 4: Verify, do not assume

Turn off Wi-Fi (or run nmcli networking off on Linux) and dictate a paragraph into your editor. If text still appears and is formatted, both stages are local. Turn the network back on afterwards, because account sync needs it.

Linux note

Check Settings → General → Linux Dependencies. Typing and pasting rely on tools such as xdotool and wtype, and on Wayland the tips point to wtype or ydotool.

Where cloud still wins

To be fair to cloud dictation:

  • No local resources. Large models do not eat your RAM or battery during a long build.
  • Consistent quality on weak hardware.
  • Language coverage. InsertKit's voice typing covers 100+ languages with auto-detect. If you dictate in more than one, benchmark each on your local model before committing to it.
  • Mobile. InsertKit's Android app uses hosted or BYOK engines; there is no on-device Whisper there.

If you use the cloud, at least choose deliberately. InsertKit Free needs no key and has a daily limit, Premium uses credits, and BYOK covers providers such as OpenAI, Groq, Deepgram, AssemblyAI, and ElevenLabs.

Wrapping up

Local Whisper is a strong default for private work, but privacy depends on the full path, latency depends on your hardware, and accuracy depends on your own voice. Benchmark with real text, add vocabulary corrections for your stack, and verify your setup with the network off.

If you want to try this exact setup, the desktop builds are at insertkit.com/download.

title: A Control Plane for an AI-Run Firm: Workflow, Agent and Human Lanes
description:
"Autonomous company" sounds like a model choice. In practice it is a control-plane design. This post sketches one for a small service firm doing lead intake. The firm is illustrative, not a customer story, and I have no results to share.

The idea

Split every task into one of three lanes and enforce the lane in code.

from enum import Enum
from dataclasses import dataclass

class Lane(Enum):
    WORKFLOW = "fixed steps, no model decisions"
    AGENT = "model picks steps, inside limits"
    HUMAN = "person decides"

@dataclass
class Task:
    name: str
    lane: Lane
    tools: list[str]
    needs_approval: bool = False

TASKS = [
    Task("capture_lead",   Lane.WORKFLOW, ["crm.create"]),
    Task("send_reminder",  Lane.WORKFLOW, ["email.send_template"]),
    Task("draft_reply",    Lane.AGENT,    ["crm.read", "email.draft"]),
    Task("quote_price",    Lane.HUMAN,    []),
]

Anthropic's guide says coded workflows give predictability for well-defined tasks, and that agents bring higher cost and compounding errors, so test them in sandboxes with guardrails. Salesforce describes "hybrid reasoning" that combines deterministic logic and adaptive AI. The lanes above are one simple way to do that.

The router 

def route(task: Task, payload):
    log("start", task.name, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.HUMAN or task.needs_approval:
        return queue_for_human(task, payload)
    if task.lane is Lane.WORKFLOW:
        return run_steps(task, payload)
    return run_agent(task, payload, allowed_tools=task.tools)

Three things live here and not in a prompt: which tools a task may touch, which tasks need approval, and what gets logged.

Incident handling 

PAUSED = set()

def pause(task_name: str, who: str):
    PAUSED.add(task_name)
    log("paused", task_name, who)

Check PAUSED at the start of route. Someone must own the pause, and the log must say who used it.

Red lines to code first

  • Money, contracts and customer promises always go to a person.
  • Every agent action has a log entry with inputs and outputs.
  • Every task has a named owner and an off switch.

What this is not

It is not proof that a company can run itself. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index describes humans setting direction and "checking in as needed". The control plane is how that check-in becomes real.

Tej Pandya, founder of GrowEasy.ai.

title: Use ACP-compatible harnesses with the AI SDK harness layer
description:
The AI SDK harness layer now supports any Agent Client Protocol (ACP)-compatible harness with HarnessAgent through the new @ai-sdk/harness-acp package.

Previously, every harness adapter wrapped one specific runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Deep Agents, OpenCode). @ai-sdk/harness-acp wraps the protocol instead. It is a meta adapter: rather than adapting a single harness, it lets you build an adapter for any harness that ships an ACP-compatible package.

Implement a harness by passing that package to createACP and configure basic harness mapping.

Then pass it to HarnessAgent like any other harness:

ACP is an abstraction over coding harnesses, but the AI SDK harness layer stays deliberately decoupled from it. Not every harness supports ACP, and for some, ACP limits or changes how well they expose their internal behaviors, so a direct adapter can produce a tighter integration.

For Claude Code and Codex, prefer the direct @ai-sdk/harness-claude-code and @ai-sdk/harness-codex adapters over an ACP-based implementation; reach for @ai-sdk/harness-acp when a harness has no direct adapter but ships an ACP-compatible package.

Read the ACP harness documentation to get started.
