title: Collections.unmodifiableList vs List.copyOf in Java
description:
Quick Answer: Collections.unmodifiableList in Java creates a read-only view wrapper over an existing collection rather than an immutable copy. If the underlying collection mutates, those changes immediately reflect in the unmodifiable view. To create a true, isolated snapshot of your data that resists changes to the original source, use List.copyOf() introduced in Java 10.

When you pass a list to another component in your application, you usually want to guarantee its state won't change unexpectedly. You might call Collections.unmodifiableList(), hand over the reference, and assume your work is done. But there is a subtle trap in this approach that leads to unexpected side effects in production.

What is the difference between an unmodifiable view and an immutable list in Java?

An unmodifiable view prevents callers from mutating a list through that specific reference, but it remains linked to the original collection. An immutable list, by contrast, is completely decoupled from the original data source and cannot be altered by any reference.

If you pass around an unmodifiable view, you are essentially placing a clear glass shield over a whiteboard. The consumer holding the view cannot write on the glass, but if another thread or service writes directly on the whiteboard behind it, the consumer sees those changes instantly.

How does Collections.unmodifiableList handle underlying mutations?

When you pass a collection into Collections.unmodifiableList(), Java wraps your original list in a lightweight decorator. Any attempt to call write operations like add() or remove() on this wrapper throws an UnsupportedOperationException.

However, because it remains a view, any direct modification to the underlying collection updates what the view renders.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Alice", "Bob"));
List<String> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(names);

names.add("Charlie"); // Modifying the underlying list

System.out.println(view.size()); // Prints 3, not 2!

If you hand this view to a service expecting a stable collection, background updates to names will leak through, potentially causing silent bugs or race conditions.

How do you create a true snapshot list in Java using List.copyOf?

Introduced in Java 10, List.copyOf() creates an unmodifiable list containing a shallow copy of the source collection's elements. Because this operation creates a brand-new backing store, subsequent modifications to the source collection have zero effect on the copied list.

It is vital to remember that List.copyOf() creates a shallow copy. While the list structure itself is completely immutable and isolated, the objects contained inside it are not cloned. If you store mutable objects inside the list, their internal properties can still be modified elsewhere.

The same concept applies across languages. If you are working in C#, calling .AsReadOnly() on a list produces a ReadOnlyCollection<T>, which behaves exactly like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList() by acting as a view over the backing list.

Comparison of Read-Only and Snapshot Collections

Method / API Type Decoupled From Source? Language Version
Collections.unmodifiableList(list) Read-Only View No Java 1.2+
List.copyOf(list) Immutable Snapshot Yes Java 10+
list.AsReadOnly() Read-Only View No .NET Framework 2.0+

Frequently Asked Questions

Does List.copyOf create a deep copy of objects in Java?

No, List.copyOf() performs a shallow copy of the collection elements. The reference structure of the list becomes immutable and decoupled from the source collection, but the individual elements inside still refer to their original object instances in memory.

Why does Collections.unmodifiableList throw UnsupportedOperationException at runtime?

Java's collection framework uses unified interfaces like List for both mutable and read-only structures rather than separate interface hierarchies. Calling mutation methods on read-only wrappers triggers a runtime UnsupportedOperationException to enforce the contract without breaking interface consistency.

How does C# handle read-only list wrappers compared to Java?

C# uses the .AsReadOnly() extension method on List<T>, which returns a ReadOnlyCollection<T>. Just like Java's Collections.unmodifiableList(), this wrapper provides a read-only interface but remains a live view over the underlying list.

title: A sandbox without a network boundary is only half a sandbox
description:
Running untrusted code safely requires more than separating it from the host. You also have to control what that code can reach.

This matters more as AI agents gain the ability to read files, execute commands, install packages, and generate programs of their own. A microVM can prevent that code from accessing the host or another workload. By itself, it cannot stop the code from exfiltrating data, probing internal services, attacking systems elsewhere on the internet, or using credentials available inside the environment.

Isolation without egress control contains the process, not its consequences.

A complete sandbox therefore needs both compute isolation and control over the authority available through its network: where code can connect, which credentials it can use, and how those permissions change throughout the workload’s lifecycle. These controls are part of the security boundary, not protections to bolt on later.

A sandbox has more than one boundary

Compute isolation answers one important question: what can this program access on the machine where it runs? Network isolation answers another: what can it access, or attack, through the network?

Consider an agent that reads a repository and runs generated code. A prompt injection hidden in an issue, log entry, dependency, or source file might instruct it to upload private data. The generated program does not need to escape its microVM. With unrestricted outbound traffic, it can simply send anything it can read to an external server.

The same access can be used to scan internal networks, exfiltrate data and credentials, or call an authenticated API. From the attacker’s perspective, crossing the VM boundary may be unnecessary. Without a network boundary, it is only half a sandbox.

A network bypass can be a sandbox escape

Recent security research has made one pattern clear: untrusted code does not need to cross a VM boundary to escape containment. It only needs one network path that the security model failed to account for.

That path might be a DNS resolver left available in an otherwise disconnected environment, an empty allowlist that fails open, a hostname interpreted differently by a policy engine and a proxy, or a trusted package service turned into a relay. Any one of them can give untrusted code a channel to exfiltrate data, receive instructions, or move toward more sensitive infrastructure.

These are not compute escapes. The kernel, VM, or container boundary may continue working exactly as designed while containment still fails. The practical security boundary also includes DNS, proxies, identity services, internal networks, and every intentionally permitted destination.

Whether we call the result an escape or a bypass, the requirement is the same: a sandbox must account for every path by which untrusted code can communicate.

Useful sandboxes need selective connectivity

Completely disconnecting a sandbox closes the network path, but it also makes many workloads impractical. An agent may need to clone a repository, install a dependency, call an AI model, query a database, or upload its result.

Unrestricted internet access is not the only alternative. A useful sandbox should grant only the connectivity a workload requires:

  • Allow an AI provider, but no other public destination.

  • Allow one object storage bucket, rather than an entire cloud network.

  • Reach a private service, while blocking the rest of the private address space.

  • Install dependencies during trusted setup, then remove registry access before generated code runs.

  • Authenticate an API request without placing the API key inside the sandbox.

A practical policy model should support fully open access, complete network isolation, and granular policies that deny unmatched traffic by default. Those policies should be able to combine domain rules with allowed and denied address ranges.

Domains and CIDRs solve different problems. Domain policies are precise enough for modern services whose IP addresses change or serve many unrelated hostnames. CIDR policies work across protocols and provide control over fixed infrastructure and private networks.

Connectivity should also be temporary. A workflow can begin with access to a package registry, narrow access before untrusted execution, briefly permit an output destination, and finish with no outbound access, all without restarting the workload.

How Vercel enforces the network boundary

The Vercel Sandbox firewall runs on the host, outside the microVM, where code inside the sandbox cannot modify or disable it.

Linux networking transparently redirects outbound TCP connections and DNS queries through the firewall. Workloads do not need to configure a proxy, and the firewall retains each connection’s original destination.

For domain-restricted connections, the firewall inspects the beginning of the TLS handshake and extracts the Server Name Indication, or SNI. This identifies the requested hostname before the firewall opens an upstream connection. It checks that hostname against the sandbox’s domain policy and also checks the destination address against its CIDR policy.

Ordinary allowed TLS connections pass through without decryption. The firewall reads only the unencrypted handshake information required to enforce the policy, then connects the workload directly to its destination.

Some policies need to inspect or modify the HTTP request itself. For those configured domains only, header injection and request forwarding selectively terminate TLS using a certificate authority unique to the sandbox. The firewall can then match requests by hostname, path, method, query, or headers before injecting a credential or forwarding the request to an endpoint that you trust.

DNS traffic is filtered using the same domain policy. Together, these layers control both where a sandbox can connect and what authority a particular connection receives.

Keep credentials outside untrusted compute

An agent often needs to call an authenticated service, but a credential stored in an environment variable or file is a transferable bearer credential. Every program inside the sandbox can read it. Malicious code can copy it to a third-party service, where it can be retained and used long after the sandbox stops.

Vercel Sandbox instead injects credentials at the host network boundary. The firewall creates a dedicated certificate authority just in time for the sandbox and adds it to the sandbox’s trusted certificates. For a configured destination, it selectively terminates TLS, adds or replaces the authentication header, then establishes a new TLS connection to the upstream service.

The credential never enters the microVM. It never leaves the host unencrypted. The certificate authority is unique to the sandbox and is disposed when the sandbox stops.

Injection also limits where the credential can be used. The firewall sends it only to its configured destination, so uploading the sandbox’s files or environment to another service does not transfer that authority. Matchers can restrict it further by path, method, query, or request headers. Generated code might receive permission to submit results to one endpoint without receiving permission to read other resources from the same API.

Injected credentials should still follow the principle of least privilege, with access limited to the specific operations the workload requires.

Put your own policy in the path

Static allowlists cannot express every security requirement. Some workloads need to inspect payloads, enforce business rules, record an audit trail, or make an authorization decision using context only you have.

Request forwarding sends selected HTTPS requests through a proxy that you control. The proxy receives the original request along with a Vercel-issued OIDC token identifying the team, project, and sandbox that originated it.

That proxy becomes a programmable policy layer. It can:

  • Redact sensitive fields before a request leaves the environment.

  • Enforce per-user or per-sandbox authorization.

  • Route package downloads through supply-chain scanning and block artifacts that fail organizational policy.

  • Record requests and responses for compliance workflows.

  • Exchange a sandbox identity for a narrowly scoped credential.

  • Reject an operation that does not match organizational policy.

The policy and its secrets remain outside the sandbox, even when the code being governed has full root access inside its microVM. You can read more about request proxying in the Sandbox documentation.

Security belongs in the baseline product

We believe a sandbox should not require a payment method before it can safely handle untrusted code.

Every Vercel Sandbox includes both compute isolation and a complete firewall for defining what code inside it can communicate with.

The goal is not to make every sandbox completely offline. It is to make authority explicit:

  • Which destinations can this sandbox reach?

  • Which private address ranges are unavailable?

  • Which requests can use credentials?

  • Which operations must pass through additional policy?

  • When should all communication stop?

These are fundamental properties of the execution environment, not security controls to add after a workload reaches production. We believe so strongly in this that we have made our full egress firewall capabilities available to all Sandboxes.

Getting started

The following policy allows outbound connections to one API and injects a credential only for one operation. Other destinations are denied by default, and the credential remains outside the sandbox.

The same policy can be replaced while the sandbox runs:

A sandbox is not defined only by where its code runs. It is defined by what that code can reach, what authority it receives, and which boundaries still hold when the code itself is hostile.

The network is part of the sandbox.

Further reading

  • Vercel Sandbox firewall documentation

  • Understanding Vercel Sandboxes

  • Security boundaries in agentic architectures

Read more

title: Build a Reviewable Gemini Form Assistant in React
description:
A person filling out a travel request often already has the information in a message:

Prepare a round trip from SFO to JFK, departing November 12, 2026 and returning November 15, 2026, for one traveler in economy. Purpose: customer workshop.

An AI assistant can turn that brief into form fields. The more interesting problem starts when its response arrives. The person might have changed the dates, corrected the purpose, or opened another request.

I built and maintain Trip Workbench, a React and TypeScript demo with synthetic travel data, to explore that interaction. Its assistance flow lets a person request suggestions, inspect proposed fields and clarification questions, and explicitly apply a change.

The useful unit of work is a proposal tied to a particular draft state. That gives the application something it can validate, display, reject when outdated, and save through its existing API.

Keep generation separate from saving

The feature uses two application operations:

Operation Responsibility
POST /api/trips/:id/proposal Read the authorized draft, ask Gemini for suggested fields, and validate the response
PATCH /api/trips/:id Apply a user-accepted patch after checking authorization, revision, and domain rules

Generating a proposal leaves the saved trip unchanged. Clicking Apply proposed changes sends a separate mutation. In this demo, applying saves the draft; reviewing and submitting the trip request happens afterward.

That distinction should be visible in the interface. A generic “Accept” button is less clear than a label that explains whether the action fills a local form or saves to the server.

The Gemini call runs in the Node backend using @google/genai. The React client sends its brief and draft context to the application API. Google’s API-key guidance recommends keeping production keys out of browser code.

This article follows that embedded assistance flow. Trip Workbench’s separate WebMCP tools provide another entry point for external agents; they are not involved in the Suggest button.

Define what a proposal can contain

A proposal contains two things: a patch and clarification questions.

For the opening brief, this is an illustrative response:

{
  "patch": {
    "origin": "SFO",
    "destination": "JFK",
    "departureDate": "2026-11-12",
    "returnDate": "2026-11-15",
    "tripType": "round_trip",
    "passengerCount": 1,
    "cabin": "economy",
    "purpose": "customer workshop"
  },
  "clarifications": []
}

The patch contains editable trip fields. It has no place for an owner ID, tenant ID, approval decision, or submitted status.

Partial patches are useful. If the brief says “change the destination to JFK,” the assistant should preserve unrelated fields. If the destination is ambiguous, it can return an empty patch and a question.

For example, “Springfield next Friday” needs more context. This demo supports a small airport list. The assistant should explain that limit and ask for a supported destination instead of silently substituting one.

Here is a stricter proposal schema I would use when extending the adapter. It constrains airports at the schema boundary and rejects unknown keys throughout:

import { z } from "zod";
import { AIRPORTS } from "../../domain/types.js";

const Field = z.enum([
  "origin", "destination", "departureDate", "returnDate",
  "tripType", "passengerCount", "cabin", "purpose",
]);

const ProposedTripSchema = z.object({
  patch: z.object({
    origin: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    destination: z.enum(AIRPORTS).nullable().optional(),
    departureDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    returnDate: z.string().nullable().optional(),
    tripType: z.enum(["one_way", "round_trip"]).optional(),
    passengerCount: z.number().int().min(1).max(9).optional(),
    cabin: z.enum(["economy", "premium_economy", "business"]).optional(),
    purpose: z.string().max(500).optional(),
  }).strict(),
  clarifications: z.array(z.object({
    field: Field.nullable(),
    kind: z.enum(["missing", "ambiguous", "unsupported"]),
    question: z.string().min(1).max(240),
  }).strict()).max(8),
}).strict();

The date strings still need calendar validation. A string-shaped value does not establish that February 30 exists.

Define patch semantics explicitly, too: omitting a field preserves its value; null clears a nullable field. The model should omit uncertain information and ask a question. It should clear a field only when the requested change calls for that.

Give Gemini the context needed to interpret the brief

The server loads the current saved draft after checking access. It also supplies a reference date, application timezone, and allowed values.

These details affect interpretation. “Next Friday” depends on a reference date and may still require clarification. An airport mentioned in ordinary language might be outside the application’s supported set.

The prompt should describe those limits and ask for only the requested changes. Treat the brief as input data; instructions embedded in it do not grant additional application capabilities.

At commit 4b3f370, the repository pins @google/genai 1.30.0. Its adapter requests JSON using responseMimeType, then parses and validates the result locally. It does not yet pass an output schema to Gemini.

A focused improvement is to supply the schema during generation as well:

const { GoogleGenAI } = await import("@google/genai");
const ai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: config.geminiApiKey! });

// config and prompt are constructed by the server adapter.
// ProposedTripSchema is the schema defined above.
const response = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model: config.geminiModel,
  contents: prompt,
  config: {
    responseMimeType: "application/json",
    responseJsonSchema: z.toJSONSchema(ProposedTripSchema),
  },
});

if (!response.text) {
  throw new Error("AI_INVALID_OUTPUT");
}

const proposal = ProposedTripSchema.parse(
  JSON.parse(response.text),
);

This excerpt belongs inside the existing adapter, after its API-key check. Its route must translate parsing and validation failures into an application error.

The SDK reference documents responseJsonSchema for this API. It supports a subset of JSON Schema, so keep runtime checks such as string limits and calendar rules even when the schema is supplied to the model. Current Google examples also show the newer responseFormat shape; do not copy fields between SDK generations without checking the version you actually ship.

These examples follow the repository’s models.generateContent path. Google now documents that path under Generate Content API Legacy; its newer Interactions API uses a different request shape. Keep the SDK version and API surface consistent when adapting the code.

The next check is application-specific. Merge the proposed patch with the saved fields and run the existing domain validator. A return date can be a real date and still precede departure. A valid cabin can still require policy review.

Google’s structured-output documentation also calls for application validation. Constraining the response shape does not establish that its values match the person’s intent.

Bind the proposal to the state that produced it

Consider this sequence:

  1. A suggestion request starts with the purpose “customer workshop.”
  2. The person changes the purpose to “leadership meeting.”
  3. The original suggestion arrives with “customer workshop.”

Checking only the server revision misses the problem. The person’s newer text may still be unsaved.

Trip Workbench tracks three versions for this reason:

Version What it tracks
Saved revision Changes persisted by the backend
Client edit version Local form edits
Brief version Changes to the text being interpreted

The server echoes those bindings outside the model-generated proposal. They are application metadata; Gemini does not choose them.

The coordinator’s freshness check includes:

return (
  bound.boundRevision !== state.savedDraft.revision ||
  bound.boundClientEditVersion !== state.editVersion ||
  bound.boundBriefVersion !== state.briefVersion
);

The surrounding implementation also checks the draft identity, session, and editor generation. That prevents a response for one editor context from being treated as a suggestion for another.

Check freshness when the response arrives and again when the person clicks Apply. The second check matters because a proposal can become outdated while someone is reading it.

The simplest policy is to mark the proposal stale and ask for a new suggestion. For eight fields, that is easier to explain than automatically merging an old proposal with new intent. A larger editor might justify more granular conflict handling.

There is another practical detail: this endpoint uses saved fields as model context. Unsaved form edits are not sent to Gemini. The coordinator blocks an agent-style patch while local edits remain unsaved. A clearer UI would ask the person to save or discard those edits before requesting a suggestion.

Version checks protect this particular handoff. They do not, by themselves, prove that every refresh or recovery path in a shared editor preserves local changes.

Make review useful and apply through the existing API

The current React panel lists proposed values and clarification questions. It disables Apply when the proposal is stale or its patch is empty.

For an existing populated form, I would add a current-value column:

Field Current Proposed
Destination BOS JFK
Departure November 10, 2026 November 12, 2026
Purpose Team meeting Customer workshop

That table is a suggested review improvement, not a screenshot of the current demo. It makes the consequences of applying easier to inspect.

Keep clarification questions visible beside the fields. A partial proposal can be useful without being ready for submission. In the current design, the person can refine the brief and request another suggestion.

The Apply handler checks freshness, then delegates to the existing coordinator:

if (coordinator.isProposalStale(proposal)) {
  // Keep the form unchanged and ask for another suggestion.
  return;
}

const result = await coordinator.applyAgentPatch(
  proposal.patch,
  proposal.boundRevision,
  newCommandId(),
);

The backend checks the user’s authority, validates the patch against the current draft, and enforces the expected revision. If another writer changed the draft, the application should require a fresh review before applying a different change.

This second validation is necessary even though the proposal was already checked. The draft can change between generation and application. Client-side review is also not an authorization boundary.

A business-cabin request illustrates the distinction: the patch can save successfully while the later validation step returns a review requirement. Saving the draft does not approve a policy exception or purchase a ticket.

Keep failures understandable

The manual form should remain usable when assistance fails.

A rejected model response should leave the fields unchanged and explain that no suggestion could be prepared. A stale proposal should explain that the brief or draft changed. A revision conflict should lead to reviewing current data before trying again.

For a production feature, also release the “Suggesting” state in a finally block and distinguish provider failures from invalid output. The current adapter maps otherwise unclassified provider exceptions to AI_TIMEOUT; that label alone does not establish that a timeout occurred.

Generation failures and save failures need different treatment. A lost proposal response has not saved a trip. A lost PATCH response may have followed a successful save. The latter requires reconciling the original command’s outcome before creating another mutation.

Evaluate the proposal and the handoff separately

Trip Workbench has disabled, fixture, and live modes. Fixture mode returns canned examples so the interface can be exercised repeatedly. Its SFO–JFK example uses fixed dates, so it does not measure Gemini’s extraction ability.

Use deterministic checks for the application behavior:

Check Expected behavior
Unknown patch key or invalid calendar date Reject the proposal without changing saved fields
Form edit while generation is pending Mark the returned proposal stale
Brief change after generation Prevent applying the old suggestion
Navigation to another draft Discard the old context’s response
Server revision changes before Apply Reject the stale mutation
Network failure during generation Restore usable controls and preserve the form

Then evaluate live Gemini with a complete brief, an ambiguous brief, and a partial update to an existing draft. Run each several times and record the model, prompt, proposed fields, clarification questions, human corrections, and final saved state.

For the partial update, explicitly check what stayed unchanged. A correct destination is not enough if the assistant also overwrote a purpose that the user never asked to change.

The repository’s results document records fixture evidence and leaves live Gemini unverified. These exercises define the next evaluation; they are not a reported success rate.

Finally, compare the complete task with manual entry. Include the time spent writing the brief, waiting, reviewing, and correcting. For a short form, manual entry may be faster. Assistance becomes more interesting when the user already has a longer brief containing the required information.

The question I want feedback on is concrete: can a person understand and correct the proposed change with less effort than entering it themselves?

That is the outcome this design lets us evaluate. The model provides a candidate change, the interface makes it reviewable, and the application decides whether it can be saved.

title: Introducing the new v0 API
description:
Today we're introducing the new v0 API: programmatic, headless access to v0's app-building agent. Send a prompt and v0 generates an app, starts a dev server in a Vercel Sandbox, and gives you a preview URL you can embed in your own UI.

Each chat is an isolated workspace for one app, where v0 can read, edit, and run the files. Follow-up messages continue from the current state. v0 verifies the code running in the Sandbox, so it can catch and fix errors in your app in real time.

The new API is now generally available.

How it works

Create a chat from a prompt, stream its work, and render the live preview, all from your own interface. First, install the v0 SDK.

Then, create a chat. Send a prompt, and v0 generates your app.

Send follow-up messages to the same chat to keep building. Each one continues from the current state.

Then embed the app.

A prompt goes in, a running app comes out. v0 operates the Sandbox, dev server, and preview behind it. When you're ready, deploy to Vercel in one API call. v0 manages the whole pipeline.

What this unlocks

The new API lets you run v0's app builder inside your own product or pipeline. This opens use cases like:

  • A white-labeled app builder: Your users describe an app and get one back.

  • Automated app changes: Trigger v0 from a script, CI job, or webhook to generate a new app or update an existing one.

  • A build tool for your agents: An agent hands back a working app instead of a code snippet.

Below, we break down the API primitives behind this workflow.

Start with a chat

Each chat holds the state for one app, and a repo or Vercel project can have many. Keep each chat's ID and send its follow-up messages to that chat. Metadata lets you group chats by customer, workspace, app, or any key you already use.

Learn more about messages.

Stream the trace

Your interface needs to show what happens between sending a request and seeing the updated preview.

Every message includes ordered parts: text, thinking, file reads and edits, searches, bash commands, tool calls, and agent actions. The same object can drive a one-line status, a changed-files view, or the full trace.

Usage is returned with chat and message responses, so you can account for the work when it finishes.

Choose sync, async, or streaming

Chat creation and messages support synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming responses. Use sync when the caller needs the completed response. Use async to queue the work and receive updates via webhook or poll for v0's response later. Stream the request to render v0's work as it happens.

Work from existing code

You can also create a chat from a repository, ZIP archive, or set of files.

Render the dev server preview

Each chat gets a short-lived preview token. Fetch it from a server route and proxy browser requests through it, so your v0 API key never reaches the browser. When a preview is ready, traffic forwards to it; while the Sandbox spins up, requests fall back to a loading route. Point an iframe at your proxy route and cache the preview details until they expire.

Read more about Accessing Previews in the docs.

Bring your own tools and design systems

Turn on specific MCP servers for a chat, or use the defaults.

Design Systems 2.0 saves a design system as a skill. Include it in a request to load its components, tokens, setup, and starter app.

You can pass up to three skills per request, from team or user memory, skills.sh, or the connected repo, or let the agent pull them in for you.

Use v0 from agents

If you're building an agent, give it v0 as a tool. When the agent needs to produce a working app, it calls v0, and gets back a running preview or deployment to hand to the user. Your agent stays in charge of everything else.

There are three ways to connect it:

MCP

Connect the v0 MCP server to an IDE, desktop assistant, or agent runtime that supports MCP.

The first connection starts an OAuth flow. The MCP server exposes tools for creating chats, listing chats, getting chat details, listing and sending messages, resolving pending tasks, and getting preview URLs.

AI SDK

For TypeScript agents built with AI SDK, use @v0-sdk/ai-tools to expose v0's API operations as tools in the agent's own loop.

The agent decides when to create or continue a chat. Your AI SDK run keeps control of the orchestration and final response.

eve

For eve agents, add an OpenAPI connection file. eve turns the allowed operations into tools and attaches the API key at execution time, out of model context.

Connect a Vercel project

Create a Vercel project for the chat, then manage its environment variables, integrations, and settings through the Vercel API. Your apps get Vercel's security and observability by default.

When you're ready to ship, deploy the chat to Vercel.

Migrate your chats

Chats from the previous version of the v0 API don’t run on the new one, so carry them forward. Pick the version you want to keep, download it as a ZIP, and create a new chat from that ZIP. Store the old identifiers in the new chat’s metadata if you need traceability.

The migration guide covers the full mapping. The main changes:

  • Use https://api.v0.dev/v2 for new requests.

  • The chat holds current app state, and messages hold its history.

  • Replace version workflows with chat file workflows, and v0 Project organization with chat metadata.

  • Use vercelProjectId plus the Vercel API for project operations.

  • Render message parts, not only final text.

Get started

Create an API key in v0 settings and install the SDK.

Or, scaffold a full app.

Read the documentation and migration guide.

title: Graph on one server: a 4-hop query 19 to 388 times faster than the incumbents
description:
Originally published on the Semurg blog: https://one.semurg.io/blog/graph-on-one-server. Every figure below is a row on https://one.semurg.io/benchmark#graph with the release it was measured on.

Graph databases are judged on traversals: start from one node, follow relationships out several hops, and return what you reach. We
ran that question on a public social graph against six graph databases, on one bare-metal server, with every engine's answer checked
against two independent reference implementations before anything was timed. This post has the results, the one place where it is
close, a mistake in our own benchmark kit, and the one command that reruns the whole thing on your own machine.

What we ran

  • The data: SNAP's com-Orkut social graph: 3.07 million people and 117.2 million relationships, loaded as published.
  • The machine: one Vultr bare-metal server, AMD EPYC 4345P (8 cores, 16 threads), 64 GB of memory, two NVMe disks, no GPU.
  • The engines: Semurg, Neo4j, ArangoDB, FalkorDB, FalkorDBLite, ArcadeDB and SurrealDB, each in Docker on that server, one after another, each with every thread, both data disks and no memory cap, its own recommended settings, and its fastest query form.
  • Two shapes of use: inside your application (Semurg linked into the client; the other engine's embedded mode where it has one, otherwise its fastest connection) and as a server (each engine through its own fastest connection).
  • Three cycles: cold, warm, warm again; the figure is the median of the warm cycles.

One query, 4 hops

Starting from one person, every distinct person within 4 hops (455,604 of them). As a server, Semurg answered in 3.83 ms; ArcadeDB
took 73.14 ms, FalkorDBLite 164.14 ms, FalkorDB 205.89 ms, Neo4j 281.40 ms and SurrealDB 1,484.92 ms. Across those
five server rows that is between 19 and 388 times faster. Inside the application the picture is the same: 3.84 ms for
Semurg against 93.08 ms for ArcadeDB's embedded mode and 1,360.65 ms for SurrealDB's.

Many queries at once

The same 4-hop question from 16 clients at once, each side driven by the same number of clients. As a server, Semurg answered 240.2
queries per second, ArcadeDB 28.0, FalkorDB 8.5 and Neo4j 2.6.

Walks to 131,072 hops

The ladder walks from the same person to every depth from 2 to 131,072 hops, checking each step against the reference. On this graph
everything reachable is reached within a few dozen hops, so past that point every engine is timing one full walk of the reachable
graph. As a server, Semurg's full walk took 95.22 ms; ArcadeDB's took 113.71 ms, FalkorDB's 412.67 ms and Neo4j's
14,033.83 ms. Inside the application Semurg's took 96.88 ms and ArcadeDB's embedded mode 459.74 ms.

The server comparison with ArcadeDB is the close one, and we care about it most. ArcadeDB answers its traversals from what it calls a
Graph Analytical View: an index of the whole graph it builds in memory when the database opens (the build is counted in its load
time). Semurg needs no such build when it opens. The next release carries two speed-ups to the graph walk; in our own test build they took the full walk from 96.4 ms to 81.1 ms on 8 threads (a test build, not a published release), and the published number follows the release.

What did not run, and why

A result we could not judge is shown as held, never dropped. In this run:

  • ArangoDB answered the 4-hop question correctly, but it was stopped by the out-of-memory killer during the many-at-once test, and the walk that followed found it already stopped. Our benchmark kit read that as a failure of the walk itself and set aside all of ArangoDB's results, its correct ones included. That was our kit's mistake, not ArangoDB's: the kit now checks that an engine is running before a walk starts, and ArangoDB is re-run on the next release. Until then its cells on the benchmark page read results pending.
  • FalkorDBLite's many-at-once run had failed requests and SurrealDB's had a zero median, so neither has a throughput figure; load times are held for every engine until each load has its run-to-run band.

Bigger than memory

Every domain we publish runs four classes: in the application and as a server, each on a dataset that fits in memory and one that
does not. This graph fits. The bigger-than-memory run uses SNAP's com-Friendster, a far larger social graph, with each engine held to a
fixed memory budget; its reference answers are still being computed, and the results go on the benchmark page when they finish.

Run it yourself

The kit that produced every number above is published. On a Linux machine with Docker, one command runs the graph benchmark for every
engine: curl -fsSL https://one.semurg.io/bench | sudo bash -s -- --graph. On a machine like ours it needs about 22 GB of free disk,
about 48 GB of memory for the largest engine, and about eight and a half hours (test tree, not a published release). Every figure,
every held row and the reason for each is on the benchmark page.

title: Download mode explained: how to enter it, what each screen means, and how to exit safely
description:
If you have ever plugged a Samsung phone into a flashing tool and watched it sit there unrecognized, Download mode is usually the missing piece. It is a low-level state that lets a computer talk to the phone before the normal system starts. That is why tools such as Odin need it: they are not installing an app, they are writing system software, and they need a stable channel to do that work.

What Download mode actually does

Download mode, also called Odin mode, puts the phone in a waiting state. The phone is not booting into its home screen, and it is not running your apps. Instead, it listens for instructions over USB and accepts a firmware package when a trusted tool sends one. When the connection is working, the flashing tool can see the phone, check that it is ready, and start the transfer.

That also explains why the phone can look almost blank in this mode. It is not frozen, and it is not broken. It is simply holding still so the computer can do its job without the normal system getting in the way.

How to enter Download mode on newer Galaxy phones

On most newer Galaxy phones without a physical Home button, use this sequence:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Up and Volume Down at the same time.
  3. While still holding both buttons, plug in a USB cable connected to a computer.
  4. Keep holding the buttons until the warning screen appears, then let go.

If the phone starts charging or boots normally, you probably released the buttons too early or plugged the cable in after the phone had already started. Power it off and try again, keeping both volume buttons held as the cable goes in.

How to enter Download mode on older models

On older models with a physical Home button, the combination is different:

  1. Power the phone fully off.
  2. Press and hold Volume Down, Home, and Power at the same time.
  3. Keep holding them until the warning screen appears, then let go.

The idea is the same on both kinds of phone: start from powered off, hold the right buttons, and wait for the warning screen rather than the normal logo animation.

What the warning screen means and how to continue

The first screen is a warning. It tells you that installing unofficial or custom software can cause problems, and it asks you to confirm that you understand the risk. That warning is there for a reason. Flashing the wrong package, or stopping halfway, can leave the phone unable to boot normally.

Read it, pause, and only continue if you are sure about what you are about to flash. To continue into Download mode, press Volume Up. To cancel and restart the phone instead, press Volume Down. Do not rush this step. If you are unsure, backing out is the safer choice.

What the downloading screen shows

After you press Volume Up, you should see the main Download mode screen. It usually shows the word Downloading, a large icon, and a short block of device details such as the model, product name, and current binary status. On some phones it also shows whether the bootloader is locked or unlocked and whether the device has been modified.

Those details matter. Before you flash anything, check that the model shown matches the phone in your hand and the firmware you prepared. If something looks off, stop and check your files before you connect a flashing tool.

At this point the phone is ready. A flashing tool on the computer should now detect it, and you can load the firmware package you already checked.

How to exit safely

If you have not started a flash, leaving Download mode is simple.

  • Hold Volume Down and Power together until the phone restarts.
  • On some models, a long press of the Power button alone will also restart the phone.

Let the phone restart on its own and reach the normal lock screen. Do not pull the battery on a phone with a sealed battery, and do not force a restart in the middle of a transfer.

If a flash is already in progress, do not exit. Wait until the tool reports that it finished and the phone restarts by itself. Interrupting a transfer is one of the fastest ways to cause a boot problem.

Common mistakes to avoid

Entering Recovery mode by accident

Recovery mode uses a different button combination and shows a menu with options such as reboot, wipe, and apply update. If you see that menu, you did not enter Download mode. Power off and try the Download mode combination again, paying close attention to which volume button you held.

Unplugging the phone mid-flash

Once a flash starts, the cable is part of the process. Unplugging the phone, closing the tool, or letting the computer sleep can break the transfer. Keep the phone still, keep the cable connected, and wait for the tool to finish.

Using a bad cable or loose port

A cable that only charges, a worn connector, or a loose port can drop the connection at the worst moment. Use a good-quality data cable, plug it directly into the computer rather than through a hub when you can, and check that the phone is detected before you start. If the tool keeps losing the phone, swap the cable and try another USB port before you blame the firmware.

A short safety note

Back up anything you cannot afford to lose before you flash. Flashing can wipe data, and it can fail even when you follow the steps carefully. Also use firmware made for your exact model and CSC, which is the region and carrier configuration code. A package for a similar-looking model is not close enough. Check the model number on the phone, check the CSC, and only then start.

Download mode is not something to fear, but it is something to respect. Enter it with the right buttons, read the warning, confirm the details on the screen, and leave it the clean way. If you want a place to check firmware details before you start, SamFware keeps things organized, and you can return to SamFware whenever you need to double-check a model or CSC before flashing.

title: 12,534 MCP and Agent Skill Repositories, One Conclusion: This Ecosystem Has No Middle Class
description:
Originally published at MCPMarkets. Live numbers and methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights.

A full-catalog data analysis of the MCP server and agent-skill ecosystem — snapshot: October 17, 2026

We crawled public GitHub data for every MCP server and agent skill we could find, classified it, and measured what the ecosystem actually looks like — not what the launch posts say it looks like. The catalog held 13,598 published entries at snapshot time; this analysis covers the 12,534 deduplicated entries we could pull and verify (5,945 MCP servers, 6,589 agent skills) — about 92% coverage.

The picture that emerges is not a healthy long tail. It is a very tall, very narrow head, a wide lukewarm plain, and a ravine in between.

Three findings up front:

  1. The head is far narrower than most people assume. The top 1% of repositories by stars hold 47.5% of all server-side stars (41.7% on the skill side). The top 10% hold roughly 83%. Gini: 0.867 for servers, 0.882 for skills.
  2. The middle is nearly empty. 62.8% of MCP servers have fewer than 100 stars. Median: 64. Mean/median ratio: 8.4×.
  3. Skills are hotter than servers — and it isn't close. Median stars 160 vs 64 (2.5×); 84.6% of skill repos were pushed to within the last six months, versus 64.2% of servers. One in five servers has been dormant for a year or two.

By the numbers

Metric MCP servers Agent skills
Entries analyzed 5,945 6,589
Total stars 3,211,236 14,168,570
Median stars 64 160
Repos under 100 stars 62.8% 37.1%
Repos under 1,000 stars 93.1% 78.1%
Pushed within 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
Repos with ≥ 10,000 stars 54 256
Gini coefficient 0.867 0.882

Method

Data comes from the MCPMarkets catalog (mcpmarkets.com), sourced from GitHub's public API: stars, license, primary language, last push date, and README content. Three things stated plainly, because they matter for how far to trust the numbers:

  • Snapshot: 2026-10-17. The catalog kept growing while we were pulling it (~690 new entries in a three-hour window), so pagination over a live dataset drifts at the boundaries. We ended up with 12,534 deduplicated entries — about 92% of the 13,598 published at snapshot time. Distribution metrics are barely affected; absolute counts run slightly low.
  • The server/skill split is heuristic. It comes from keyword and README-feature rules at ingestion time. See Limitations for what that costs us.
  • Stars are a proxy for attention, not quality. They follow HN threads, Twitter posts, and awesome-list cross-promotion, not production usage.

Finding 1: Ten repositories hold about a fifth of the sky

Server side: 5,945 repositories, 3,211,236 stars. Here is how those stars are distributed:

Percentile Stars
p25 36
Median 64
p75 166
p90 631
p99 8,841
Max 96,415

Mean over median is 8.4×, which almost always means a handful of extreme values dominate — and they do. The top 10 repositories hold 18.1% of all server-side stars. The top 1% hold 47.5%. Gini: 0.867.

The leaderboard needs a footnote. #1 is punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers at 96,415 stars — an awesome list, which our keyword rules filed as a server (more on this in Limitations). Behind it: headroomlabs-ai/headroom (75,471) and sansan0/trendradar (62,923).

The skill side is more lopsided at the very top: its ten largest repos hold 15.6% of all skill stars, and the single largest repository in the entire catalog is a skill repo — openclaw/openclaw at 392,124 stars, four times the server-side leader. Then vinta/awesome-python (327,970, another awesome list) and obra/superpowers (299,876).

One leaderboard entry is worth pausing on: anthropics/skills — 181,394 stars, no license field set. The company that created the protocol never licensed its own official example repo. That is a thread we pick up in Finding 4.

Finding 2: 62.8% of servers live below 100 stars

The back side of the head story is the long tail. Server-side star histogram:

Star range Entries Share
0 229 3.9%
1–5 122 2.1%
6–10 27 0.5%
11–50 2,072 34.8%
51–100 1,301 21.9%
101–500 1,490 25.1%
501–1,000 296 5.0%
1,001–5,000 292 4.9%
5,001–10,000 62 1.0%
> 10,000 54 0.9%

(Bands are inclusive of their upper bound, so "≤ 100" sums to 63.1%; the 62.8% figure above is strictly under 100.)

This is not a smooth long tail. It is a wide lukewarm plain with a ravine: a third of all servers sit in the 11–50 band, a second cluster at 101–500, a noticeably smaller notch at 51–100 in between, and then a deep gap before the four-digit head.

93.1% of servers have under 1,000 stars. About one in sixteen (6.3%) has under ten, and only 229 (3.9%) have zero. So "nobody looked at it" is the minority case. The typical MCP server is in use, but barely starred — a production dependency for one team, invisible to everyone else.

The skill-side distribution has the same shape, shifted one bracket up: 37.1% below 100 stars, 78.1% below 1,000, median 160.

Finding 3: Skills are the crowded end of the ecosystem

This is the one we did not expect going in: skill repositories are visibly hotter than server repositories.

  • Median stars: 160 (skills) vs 64 (servers) — a 2.5× gap
  • Total stars: 14,168,570 vs 3,211,236 — 4.4×
  • Pushed within the last six months: 84.6% vs 64.2%
  • Dormant for 1–2 years: ≈0% vs 20.4%
  • The ≥ 10,000-star club: 256 skills vs 54 servers

Two explanations, probably both true. Authoring a skill has a lower barrier — a SKILL.md is the deliverable; there is no protocol layer to implement. And skills arrived later, straight into the agent hype cycle.

The practical read is counter-intuitive: the server side looks less crowded to enter, but its median survival environment is colder. If you ship a server, "being genuinely maintained" is already a differentiator (see Finding 6).

Finding 4: Licenses are boringly permissive — the problem is no license at all

Server-side license distribution:

License Share
MIT 58.4%
Apache-2.0 13.5%
Unlabeled (unrecognized by GitHub) 16.1%
NOASSERTION (no match) 5.7%
AGPL-3.0 2.1%
GPL-3.0 1.8%
Other GPL/LGPL/MPL/EPL variants ~2%

Grouped: permissive licenses (MIT, Apache, BSD, ISC, CC0, Unlicense…) account for 73.2% of servers. Copyleft with teeth — AGPL and GPL together — totals just 5.0%. Skills look similar: MIT 53.5%, Apache-2.0 11.6%, permissive 66.4%, copyleft 2.9%.

For anyone consuming these tools, that is good news: closed-source use, commercial embedding, and redistribution rarely hit a license wall.

The real hazard is ambiguity: unlabeled + NOASSERTION together cover 21.8% of servers and 30.4% of skills. "No license" is a question every user has to answer for themselves — and most will answer it wrong. A directory that surfaces the field verbatim, per entry, is doing a small but real service.

Finding 5: Installation is the ecosystem's weakest link

This finding came out of parsing READMEs. For every server, we tried to extract one runnable install command (something like npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-xxx) and one copy-paste-ready mcpServers JSON block:

  • Only 28.7% of servers yield an executable install command.
  • Only 34.5% contain a usable config snippet.

Put plainly: for more than seven in ten MCP servers, the install path is broken. A reader finishes the README and still doesn't know the one command to run — the README links to the source repo, or buries the config in 300 lines of prose, or waves at npm install and moves on.

Skills, by contrast, hit 100% on install-command extraction — because the install path is uniformly npx skillfish add owner/repo/path. One convention, zero ambiguity.

If you maintain a server, this is the cheapest available edge: hoist the install command and the JSON config to the top of the README, in their own fenced blocks. Ten minutes of work. It is the difference between a user and a bounce.

Finding 6: Two-thirds actively developed, one-fifth asleep

By last upstream push (as of 2026-10-17):

Window Servers Skills
< 6 months 64.2% 84.6%
6–12 months 15.3% 13.6%
1–2 years 20.4% ≈0%
No record 0.1% 1.7%

One in five servers hasn't been touched in a year or two. Given that MCP's client config formats and transports have changed more than once in that window, a meaningful share of them are dead on arrival — yet they still sit in every directory's listing, often near the top, because directories rank by stars.

"Maintained" is a more useful filter than "popular." It is also cheap to surface: that is why every entry in our catalog carries a last-push date next to its star count.

What this means if you're building here

Three practical takeaways, in order of expected impact:

  1. Don't target stars. 62.8% of servers live below 100, and the median is 64. A server at 40 stars is not a failure; it is the norm. Optimize for the one team that adopts it, not the timeline.
  2. Fix your install command first. Seven in ten repos ship it broken. A copy-pasteable command plus a ready mcpServers block is the highest-leverage ten minutes in this ecosystem.
  3. Just stay maintained. One in five server repos is asleep. If you ship a real server and keep it working, you are already in the top quintile of "will still work next quarter" — and you can say so, because it shows up in your commit dates.

And one meta-lesson for people reading ecosystem data: the head is a list, the tail is the market. The top repos by stars are, in significant part, curated lists and aggregators (two of the top five across both sides are awesome-lists). The actual supply of working software lives in the 11–50 and 101–500 bands — the part nobody writes launch posts about.

Limitations

Stated plainly, so you can judge how far to push the conclusions:

  1. Classification noise. Entries were ingested by keyword heuristics, and some obvious lists slipped in (punkpeye/awesome-mcp-servers as a server; vinta/awesome-python as a skill). This inflates the head numbers; the tail shape is unaffected.
  2. Stars are not quality. They are driven by exposure, not usage. A 30-star server can be a team's production dependency.
  3. Single source. No npm/PyPI download data, so "starred" and "used" cannot be separated.
  4. Snapshot drift. ~92% coverage, as described in Method; absolute counts are conservative.
  5. Our taxonomy is early. 89% of server entries currently land in a single category (developer tools), and skills have no useful category split yet — so no category-level analysis is offered here.

Every number above is reproducible from the public catalog. If you find a discrepancy, tell us — we would rather correct it than defend it.

Explore the data

  • Live numbers & methodology: mcpmarkets.com/insights — the same metrics, recomputed on demand with the page's Refresh button, with daily snapshots you can cite
  • Browse the catalog: MCP servers and agent skills
  • Browse by category: e.g. developer tools — the server list has a category filter
  • Every entry carries install command, quality score, last-push date, and license

This is the first in what we intend to be a quarterly MCP and Agent Skill Ecosystem Report. Next edition: category-level analysis and install-command coverage trends.

About MCPMarkets. We crawl, classify, and maintain a multilingual (EN/ZH/JA/KO/RU) directory of MCP servers and agent skills — 13,000+ entries with install commands, quality scores, and maintenance signals. The point is not to list everything; it is to make the one useful thing findable, with the fields that actually decide adoption.

Data: public snapshot of the MCPMarkets catalog, 2026-10-17. Written by the MCPMarkets team.
