title: Model Pest Control So Activity Has a Location and an Owner: Device, DeviceCheck, Sighting and CorrectiveAction
description:
By Isaac Muthui, CEO, Tamalaki Business Network Ltd. Originally published at factoraerp.com.

In most factory systems, pest control does not exist as data. It is a PDF the contractor emails once a month, filed in a shared folder that nobody queries. Finance sees a supplier invoice. Quality sees a binder. Nobody can answer a simple question like "which bait station has shown activity three visits in a row, and what did we do about it?"

That is a modelling problem before it is a hygiene problem.

The standards are explicit about what the records should prove. The Codex General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969), section 11.2, says that even when monitoring is outsourced, the food business should review monitoring reports and make sure corrective action is taken; that the cause of an infestation should be identified; and that records should be kept of infestation, monitoring and eradication. In Kenya, the Food, Drugs and Chemical Substances (Food Hygiene) Regulations, 1978 require effective measures to exclude pests from food areas and pesticide use that does not contaminate food or packaging (regulation 12).

"Review", "cause", "corrective action" and "records" are all things a schema can enforce. Here is how I would model it for a food or agro ERP.

The entities 

Site ─┬─ Zone (EXTERNAL | INTERNAL_NON_FOOD | INTERNAL_FOOD)
      │     └─ Device (bait station, trap, insect light trap) — numbered, on a map
      │           └─ DeviceCheck (who, when, finding)
      ├─ Sighting (staff report between visits)
      ├─ PestFinding (opened from a check or sighting)
      │     ├─ RootCause (ENTRY_POINT | FOOD_SOURCE | HARBOURAGE | INCOMING_MATERIAL)
      │     ├─ CorrectiveAction (owner, due date, closed_at, verified_by)
      │     ├─ Treatment (product, registration ref, quantity, applicator)
      │     └─ LotExposure → Lot (hold / release)
      └─ MonthlyReview (trend sign-off)

Zone and Device 

CREATE TABLE zone (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  site_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES site(id),
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_type   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (zone_type IN ('EXTERNAL','INTERNAL_NON_FOOD','INTERNAL_FOOD'))
);

CREATE TABLE device (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  code        TEXT NOT NULL,           -- the number painted on the device
  device_type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (device_type IN ('TOXIC_BAIT','NON_TOXIC_MONITOR','SNAP_TRAP','GLUE_BOARD','INSECT_LIGHT_TRAP')),
  map_x       NUMERIC, map_y NUMERIC,
  active      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
  UNIQUE (zone_id, code)
);

The zone type matters because Codex says traps and detectors should be designed and located so they cannot contaminate raw materials, products or facilities. Make the policy a constraint, not a memo: for example, reject TOXIC_BAIT in an INTERNAL_FOOD zone with a trigger or an application-level rule your site agrees with its qualified provider.

DeviceCheck: append-only 

CREATE TABLE device_check (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  device_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES device(id),
  checked_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  checked_by  TEXT NOT NULL,           -- staff or contractor technician
  source      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (source IN ('INTERNAL','CONTRACTOR')),
  finding     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (finding IN ('NO_ACTIVITY','BAIT_TAKEN','DROPPINGS','CATCH','DAMAGED','MISSING')),
  catch_count INT,
  notes       TEXT
);

Two design choices carry most of the value:

  1. One row per device per check. If the contractor's report is a PDF, import it into rows. A PDF cannot tell you a station's history; rows can.
  2. No updates. A check is evidence. Corrections are new rows with a reference to the one they correct.

Sightings close the gap between visits 

CREATE TABLE sighting (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  zone_id     BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  seen_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  reported_by TEXT NOT NULL,
  pest_type   TEXT NOT NULL,           -- rodent, cockroach, stored-product insect, bird, fly...
  description TEXT
);

This is the cheapest table in the schema and the one that changes behaviour most: a phone form on the floor that anyone can submit.

Findings must end in a cause and a verified action 

CREATE TABLE pest_finding (
  id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  opened_from   TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (opened_from IN ('DEVICE_CHECK','SIGHTING','INTAKE','AUDIT')),
  source_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
  opened_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  root_cause    TEXT CHECK (root_cause IN ('ENTRY_POINT','FOOD_SOURCE','HARBOURAGE','INCOMING_MATERIAL','UNKNOWN')),
  status        TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'OPEN' CHECK (status IN ('OPEN','ACTION_PENDING','VERIFIED','CLOSED'))
);

CREATE TABLE corrective_action (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  action      TEXT NOT NULL,           -- "fit door brush, side door B"
  owner       TEXT NOT NULL,
  due_date    DATE NOT NULL,
  closed_at   TIMESTAMPTZ,
  verified_by TEXT,
  verified_at TIMESTAMPTZ
);

The business rule: a finding cannot move to CLOSED while root_cause is null or any action is unverified. That single rule encodes the Codex expectation that the cause is identified and corrective action taken, and it stops the classic failure where the same station shows activity every month and the only action is "bait replaced".

Treatments carry the chemical audit trail 

CREATE TABLE treatment (
  id               BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  finding_id       BIGINT REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  applied_at       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  product_name     TEXT NOT NULL,
  registration_ref TEXT NOT NULL,      -- registration details as recorded from the regulator's list
  quantity         NUMERIC NOT NULL,
  unit             TEXT NOT NULL,
  zone_id          BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES zone(id),
  applicator       TEXT NOT NULL,
  applicator_cert  TEXT                -- evidence of the provider's qualification/certificate
);

In Kenya, the Pest Control Products (Inspection and Certification) Regulations, 2024 set qualifications for the person in charge of a pest control service (regulation 12(6)) and require a Board certificate for fumigation with Restricted Class 1 products (regulation 14). Storing the evidence next to each treatment is far easier than reconstructing it during an audit.

LotExposure links hygiene to traceability 

CREATE TABLE lot_exposure (
  finding_id  BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES pest_finding(id),
  lot_id      BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES lot(id),
  decision    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('HOLD','RELEASED','REWORK','WRITE_OFF')),
  decided_by  TEXT NOT NULL,
  decided_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (finding_id, lot_id)
);

When a finding is in or next to an INTERNAL_FOOD zone, query which lots were in that zone during the exposure window and propose holds. A WRITE_OFF decision should post a stock adjustment with a pest-damage reason code, so it does not show up later as an unexplained variance.

Queries that answer real questions

Stations with activity on three or more consecutive checks:

WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT device_id, checked_at,
         finding <> 'NO_ACTIVITY' AS active,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY checked_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM device_check
)
SELECT device_id
FROM ordered
WHERE rn <= 3
GROUP BY device_id
HAVING bool_and(active);

Findings older than 14 days still waiting on an action:

SELECT f.id, f.opened_at, a.action, a.owner, a.due_date
FROM pest_finding f
JOIN corrective_action a ON a.finding_id = f.id
WHERE a.verified_at IS NULL
  AND f.opened_at < now() - interval '14 days';

The monthly review becomes a report on those two queries plus trend charts by zone, signed off as a monthly_review row.

Where IoT fits, and where it does not

Connected traps and insect light traps with catch counters can write device_check rows automatically. Treat them as another source, not a replacement for people walking the building. A sensor will not notice the torn mesh or the pallet stacked against the wall; the weekly entry-point walk still produces corrective_action rows.

Records

Design these tables for retention and audit, not edits. The goal is that, on any given day, you can show an inspector or auditor the map, the checks, the findings, the causes, the actions and who verified them.

The full operations checklist for factory teams, with an FAQ, is here: Pest Control Checklist.

title: Frontend Monitoring: The Complete Guide to Observability That Actually Works
description:
Frontend monitoring is not a luxury. It is the difference between knowing your application works and guessing it does. Your backend can return perfect 200 responses while users on mid-range phones stare at frozen screens, broken forms, and silent failures that never generate a support ticket. This guide covers what frontend monitoring actually is, why it matters for revenue and SEO, the tools worth your time, and how to avoid the privacy traps that turn observability into a liability.

What Frontend Monitoring Really Means

Frontend monitoring is the practice of observing how your application behaves inside real users' browsers: how fast pages load, how stable the layout remains, whether interactions respond promptly, and where errors occur before anyone complains. It spans three distinct disciplines that are often conflated but serve different purposes.

Performance monitoring tracks speed and responsiveness. The industry standard is Google's Core Web Vitals: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, target under 2.5 seconds), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, target under 200 milliseconds), and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, target under 0.1) . These thresholds are not arbitrary. Google's research drew on human-computer interaction studies showing that users perceive delays beyond roughly one second as a loss of immediate responsiveness, and the 2.5-second LCP threshold was validated against real-world Chrome data as consistently achievable for well-optimized sites .

Error tracking captures unhandled exceptions, Promise rejections, and client-side failures with readable stack traces. The critical caveat that most teams learn the hard way: frameworks like Next.js intentionally swallow errors inside error boundaries and try/catch blocks. If you do not explicitly report those errors, they never reach your dashboard.

Session replay records what users actually did before an error occurred. It is invaluable for UX debugging, but it carries privacy risks that must be configured before deployment, not after.

Why This Matters More Than You Think

The business case is straightforward. Users who encounter a slow or broken page rarely return. Without frontend monitoring, teams typically learn about problems only after users complain or abandon the product. With it, regressions surface immediately after deployment, and historical data lets you pinpoint exactly which change caused a metric to degrade.

There is a direct SEO consequence as well. Google's core ranking systems evaluate Core Web Vitals, and Google explicitly states that good scores alone do not guarantee top rankings, but they contribute to success in competitive queries where multiple pages offer equally helpful content . Google evaluates field data from real users at the 75th percentile, meaning you must optimize for the slowest quarter of your audience, not the median . A site that looks fast on your developer machine can fail for a meaningful portion of actual visitors.

There is also a compounding operational cost. A real case study from Supabase illustrates the failure mode perfectly: their frontend Sentry project accumulated roughly 475,000 weekly events of pure noise from a single rethrown user-cancellation bug, browser extension injections, and expired captchas. When an actual frontend outage occurred, not a single alert fired because the signal was buried under noise. After implementing client-side filtering and fixing the root cause, weekly crashes dropped from over 2,000 to 32, and five high-impact bugs were discovered and fixed, unblocking approximately 6,300 users . The lesson is clear: monitoring without discipline is worse than no monitoring at all.

The Tool Landscape: What Each One Is Actually For

Sentry

Sentry remains the industry standard for error tracking with precise stack traces. Its strengths are framework support (including automatic instrumentation for Next.js Server Actions and React Server Components), source map uploads during build, and a genuinely usable free tier. It has expanded into performance monitoring and session replay, but its core identity is exception diagnosis. For solo developers through mid-size teams, Sentry is the correct starting point .

Datadog

Datadog is a full observability platform connecting frontend, backend, infrastructure, and logs in one place. Its distributed tracing is powerful for microservice architectures: a single user action touching three services appears as one connected trace. However, it is expensive, has a steep learning curve, and is overkill for a simple Next.js application on Vercel. Datadog earns its cost when you have a dedicated platform team, run Kubernetes, or need compliance-grade log retention .

LogRocket

LogRocket centers the user session as the debugging record. It is the right choice when your first question after an error is "what did the user do before this happened?" rather than "what exception was thrown?" Pricing follows captured sessions, not error volume, which means a session-heavy product needs to forecast session counts even if its crash rate is low . Error tracking depth is shallower than Sentry.

New Relic

New Relic sits between Sentry and Datadog in complexity. It offers frontend error monitoring, backend performance tracing, and infrastructure monitoring with a real free tier (100 GB per month ingest). Its strongest feature is browser agent performance monitoring, capturing real user timing data across DNS lookup, connection, first byte, and DOM processing. It is worth evaluating when you need backend tracing but find Datadog's pricing difficult to justify .

Bugsnag

Bugsnag does one thing and does it well: error monitoring with clean grouping, filtering, and alerting. No session replay, no performance dashboards, no infrastructure metrics. For teams that find Sentry's dashboard overwhelming, Bugsnag is a focused alternative. Pick whichever dashboard your team will actually open .

A Decision Framework That Actually Helps

Stop reading comparison tables and ask one question: what is your biggest risk right now?

If you do not know what errors users are hitting, start with Sentry. Its free tier is sufficient for most early-stage products.

If users complain about slowness but you lack data, prioritize Real User Monitoring and Core Web Vitals tracking. RUM captures performance from actual user interactions across devices, networks, and geographies, while synthetic monitoring runs scheduled tests in controlled environments . Both matter, but RUM reflects what real users experience.

If product teams ask what users are actually doing, evaluate LogRocket or Sentry's session replay.

If you are running Kubernetes with a dedicated platform team, Datadog becomes worth its cost.

For a solo developer or side project, Sentry's free tier plus Vercel Analytics covers everything you genuinely need at zero cost .

The Privacy Trap Nobody Mentions Early Enough

Monitoring tools serialize exception data, breadcrumbs, and network events. A careless configuration can ship access tokens, session cookies, or personal data directly to a third-party backend. The beforeSend and beforeBreadcrumb hooks exist specifically to strip sensitive fields before transmission. Client-side scrubbing is a stronger guarantee than relying on server-side filtering alone, especially under GDPR. If you enable session replay, mask inputs by default and unmask only what is explicitly safe.

The Supabase case study reinforces this at the architectural level: they implemented filtering directly in the SDK rather than relying on Sentry-side data filters. Events filtered client-side never leave the browser, so they do not count against quota and do not pollute the project at all. The filter configuration lives in version control, reviewed like any other code change . Treat monitoring configuration as production code, not a set-and-forget setting.

Ready to Stop Guessing?

Install Sentry's free tier on your frontend this week. It takes under ten minutes, and the first real error you catch before a user reports it will justify the effort. If you are already running monitoring, audit your configuration today: confirm source maps are uploading, confirm PII is being scrubbed client-side, and confirm your error boundaries are actually reporting. The gap between a monitored application and a correctly monitored one is exactly where production incidents hide.

title: Seedance 2.5 now available on Vercel AI Gateway
description:
Seedance 2.5 from ByteDance is now available on AI Gateway. It can generate up to 30-second clips with synchronized audio, and takes up to 50 reference inputs in one request, spanning images, video, audio, and style.

A single clip holds camera movement and continuity without stitching shots together in post, and short clips can be extended, carrying over character, scene, and camera movement. Prompts work in more than ten languages.

Seedance 2.5 can also edit a finished video in place, swapping backgrounds, products, or characters while the frame, camera, and pacing stay fixed, so one shoot yields several variants.

Generating a video

Set model to bytedance/seedance-2.5 and call generateVideo from the AI SDK:

Adding image references

Pass image URLs in inputReferences and point at them in the prompt with [Image 1], [Image 2]. Tag each entry with its media type. Seedance treats an untagged URL as an image.

Combining reference types

Mix videos and images in the same request to pull different qualities from each: motion and camera work from a clip, a subject's appearance from a still.

Videos go in the same inputReferences array as images, tagged with a video media type. Numbering runs per type so the first video is [Video 1] and the first image is [Image 1], and both can appear in one prompt.

Editing a video

Referencing and editing use the same setup, so the prompt decides which you get. Ask the model to follow a clip's camera movement and it builds a new video from scratch. Ask it to change something in the clip and it edits the video you gave it.

You can reference and edit in one prompt, though results get less predictable, so it helps to be explicit about what each asset is for.

For the playground and API reference, see the model page, or browse every video model on AI Gateway.

title: GST Helper: a local-first GSTR-1 preparation assistant
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

I built GST Helper, a local-first AI workspace that helps a small business prepare selected GSTR-1 values from sales invoice PDFs.

The demo company is BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. The user starts by loading outward-sales invoice PDFs. GST Helper reads the invoices, extracts values, shows page evidence, and turns the documents into a guided GSTR-1 review flow.

The current app prepares these GSTR-1 sections:

  • Table 4A regular domestic B2B invoices
  • Table 12 B2B HSN/SAC summary
  • Table 13 document numbers issued

It shows the invoice value including tax, taxable value, IGST, CGST, SGST or UTGST, cess, total tax, and invoice count for the supported B2B scope. It also creates a reference PDF tied to the saved review revision, so the user can inspect the same values before downloading the file.

The problem is simple: small business owners and bookkeepers often do this first pass manually. They read invoice PDFs, copy values into spreadsheets, check invoice numbers, and then use those figures while working in the GST Portal. That work is slow, error-prone, and full of accounting language that is not friendly to a non-expert.

GST Helper is meant for a small business owner, bookkeeper, or accountant who wants a faster way to prepare and review the numbers before portal entry. The paid version could charge for private local workflows, more GST sections, accountant review packs, and better import and export support.

The app does not file a return, connect to the GST Portal, or claim that the whole GSTR-1 return is complete. Other GSTR-1 sections must be handled separately. That boundary is visible in the product because tax software needs trust more than magic.

Demo

Video demo: https://youtu.be/RFq9whXetRg


The demo shows the full BharatBiz flow:

  1. Load sample sales invoice PDFs.
  2. Confirm the seller GSTIN, tax period, and turnover band.
  3. Review invoice fields with page evidence.
  4. Save the reviewed values.
  5. Inspect the Table 4A totals.
  6. Generate a verified reference PDF.
  7. Use the review chat beside the final PDF.

Code

Repository: https://github.com/sonu0702/pgst

sonu0702 / pgst

GST Helper

GST Helper is a local-first GSTR-1 preparation app for BharatBiz, a fictional small business based in Bengaluru. It turns outward-sales invoice PDFs into reviewed values, a clear summary for the supported GSTR-1 sections, and a reference PDF the user can inspect before downloading.

This release prepares only regular B2B invoices in Table 4A, the B2B HSN/SAC summary in Table 12, and documents issued in Table 13. It does not prepare a complete GSTR-1 return, connect to the GST Portal, submit or file a return, or decide GST treatment. Other applicable GSTR-1 sections must be prepared separately. The GST Portal accepts a JSON workflow through its offline tool, but the portal still validates the account and return when the user uses that file.

What the app does

  • Starts with outward-sales PDFs, then suggests seller GSTIN and tax period with page evidence before asking for return details.
  • Shows observed invoice-number…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The app is a single repository with a React frontend and a FastAPI backend.

Tech stack:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Local AI: Ollama with Gemma 4
  • PDF processing: Python PDF extraction with optional local OCR support
  • Export artifacts: reference PDF and supported-section JSON
  • Storage: no database in this prototype. Reviews live in temporary process memory.

The user flow starts with source documents, not a chatbot. That choice matters. Invoices are the source of truth, so the app first reads the PDFs and creates a review workspace from them.

The backend extracts invoice fields and line items, keeps compact evidence snippets, and builds a temporary GSTR-1 review case. The frontend lets the user inspect and edit each value. When the user saves, the backend runs local checks for the supported sections and returns readiness results.

Gemma 4 is used through Ollama for a narrow review task. It can answer questions about values already in the review or prepare a proposed edit from invoice evidence or from a value the user states. It cannot decide tax treatment, calculate GST, approve filing, or submit anything.

The user stays in control:

  • The model proposes changes.
  • The user applies the proposal.
  • The user reviews the form.
  • The user saves the revision.
  • The user regenerates the PDF if anything changed.

The reference PDF is tied to the saved revision. The app renders the PDF back in the browser and verifies the expected content before the user downloads it.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters here because tax preparation needs transparency, local control, and the ability to inspect the workflow.

A closed hosted API can produce a polished answer, but that is not enough for this use case. A small business owner needs to know where a number came from and what the app did with the source document. GST Helper keeps the review path visible: invoice evidence, editable fields, saved revision, local checks, and a reference PDF.

Open-weight local AI also changes the privacy story. In this prototype, Gemma 4 runs locally through Ollama. The app does not need to send invoice details to a hosted model API. That made it possible to build an AI-assisted review flow that still respects sensitive business documents.

Open-source tools also made the project practical for a hackathon:

  • FastAPI made the backend small and inspectable.
  • React and Vite made the review UI fast to iterate.
  • Ollama made local Gemma 4 setup approachable.
  • Python PDF tooling made extraction and reference PDF generation possible without building a document pipeline from scratch.

The project is not trying to replace a tax professional or the GST Portal. It is trying to make the preparation step clearer, safer, and more reviewable.

My Agent Session

I used Codex as an AI coding agent throughout the build. The agent helped with product scoping, GSTR-1 flow design, FastAPI and React implementation, sample invoice generation, UI polish, PDF review, and the demo walkthrough.

The most useful part was not code generation alone. The agent helped keep the product narrow. Whenever the app started to look like a generic invoice-review demo, I pushed it back toward one clear filing workflow: GSTR-1 preparation from sales invoices.

That made the final project stronger. It has a specific user, a specific filing task, a clear supported scope, and visible review boundaries.

title: What a Clinic Website Actually Has to Do in the UAE
description:
Most clinic websites are built like brochures: a hero, a list of services, a contact page. Patients do not use them like brochures. A patient arrives with one job — book the right doctor, fast, on a phone — and every screen that does not serve that job is friction.

We shipped a healthcare solutions page today and had to make these decisions for real, so here is the checklist that survived contact with an actual build:

1. Booking is the product, not a feature

The appointment action has to be reachable from every key screen, not parked on a contact page. On mobile that means the booking/contact action stays in reach while the visitor reads — the same pattern we use for enquiries generally: a lead is a WhatsApp message, a call, or a form submit, and the path to one of those three should never be more than a tap away.

2. Doctor profiles are decision pages

Patients choose people, not departments. A doctor profile needs the things a patient actually compares: specialty, languages spoken, location, and a direct booking route from that profile. A grid of names with no detail forces the patient to call and ask — and many simply book elsewhere instead.

3. Arabic is not a translation toggle

In the UAE, an Arabic version that is a shallow copy of the English page reads as an afterthought to the exact audience it is meant to serve. Proper RTL layout and genuinely reviewed Arabic copy are part of the build, not a plugin. We treat bilingual work as its own scope for this reason.

4. Trust content belongs before the ask

Insurance partners accepted, accreditations, and what happens at the first visit — placed before the booking prompt, not after it. Patients hand over health details and payment information on these sites; the proof has to arrive before the form does.

5. Speed and security are patient-experience issues

A slow mobile page loses the booking. A neglected site — outdated software, no maintenance routine — risks the one incident a clinic cannot afford. Security patching and backups are not IT chores on a healthcare site; they are part of patient trust.

The full breakdown of how we structure this — patient journey, booking flow, doctor profiles, bilingual build, and the maintenance side — is here: clinic and healthcare website solutions in Dubai.

If you run a clinic site, audit it against the patient's job, not the brochure: can a new patient, on a phone, in Arabic or English, reach the right doctor's booking in under a minute? Everything else is decoration.

title: React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked
description:
I compiled a Next.js 16.4 app with no compiler, the Babel React Compiler and the experimental Rust one, then counted re-renders in Chrome. The original, with any updates, lives on fabwaseem.com.

React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes your components and hooks, so you no longer write most useMemo, useCallback and memo calls by hand. In Next.js it is one config flag, reactCompiler: true, stable since Next.js 16.0. Next.js 16.4 adds an experimental native Rust version.

I built a Next.js 16.4.2 test app and compiled it three ways: compiler off, the Babel compiler, and the Rust compiler. Then I counted re-renders in a real browser. With the compiler on, 20 clicks on a counter caused 0 list-row re-renders instead of 20,000, and scripting time fell from about 60 ms to about 7 ms. The Babel version more than doubled compile time. The Rust version cost about a quarter of a second and produced byte-identical output.

TL;DR: should I turn on the React Compiler in Next.js?

Yes, for most App Router projects. Turn it on with reactCompiler: true, run the compiler lint rules first, and try experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler if you build with Turbopack. In my test the compiler removed almost all wasted re-renders for free. It does not replace memo on list items whose parent re-renders, and it skips code that breaks the Rules of React.

Compiler off Babel compiler Rust compiler (experimental)
Config default reactCompiler: true + experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true
Extra install none babel-plugin-react-compiler none
Compile step (median, my app) 2.25 s 5.65 s 2.5 s
Full next build (median) 7.7 s 11.1 s 8.2 s
Client JS, gzip 178,305 B 181,295 B 181,295 B (identical to Babel)
Row re-renders, 20 counter clicks 20,000 0 0
Works with webpack yes yes no (Turbopack only)

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool that rewrites your components so they cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders, and recompute them only when their inputs change. The React Compiler v1.0 announcement calls it "a build-time tool that optimizes your React app through automatic memoization." Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025.

It works with React 17 and later, and on React Native. The introduction docs say that in most cases its memoization "will be as precise, or moreso, than what you may have written." Meta reports that in the Meta Quest Store, "initial loads and cross-page navigations improve by up to 12%, while certain interactions are more than 2.5× faster."

You keep writing plain components. The compiler does the bookkeeping at build time.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js 16?

Install the Babel plugin and set the top-level reactCompiler option in next.config.ts. It moved out of experimental in Next.js 16.0. Next.js does not run Babel on every file: per the reactCompiler docs, "Next.js uses a custom SWC optimization that only applies the React Compiler to relevant files—like those with JSX or React Hooks."

npm install -D babel-plugin-react-compiler@1.0.0

// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from "next";

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
};

export default nextConfig;

That is the whole setup. New projects can also pick the compiler in the create-next-app prompts.

Can I enable it only for some components?

Yes. Set compilationMode: "annotation" and add the "use memo" directive to the components or hooks you want compiled. This is a good way to start on a large codebase. Add "use no memo" to a component to opt it out in the default mode while you fix it.

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: { compilationMode: "annotation" },
};

export default function Dashboard() {
  "use memo";
  // ...
}

What is the Rust React Compiler in Next.js?

It is a native Rust port of the React Compiler that runs inside Turbopack instead of through Babel in Node.js. It was merged into the React repo in June 2026 (PR #36173) and added to Next.js 16.3 as an experimental option. The Next.js 16.4 release added a fast check that skips files that don't need compiling.

Next.js 16.4 says the Turbopack team's memory changes "reduced the React Compiler's memory usage by 30% and compile time by 15%." To turn it on:

// next.config.ts
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  reactCompiler: true,
  experimental: {
    turbopackRustReactCompiler: true,
  },
};

From the turbopackRustReactCompiler docs:

  • It "requires reactCompiler to be enabled". It picks the implementation but doesn't switch the compiler on.
  • It works only with Turbopack. "Using it with webpack will throw an error."
  • You do not need babel-plugin-react-compiler installed.

How I tested it

I wanted numbers from a real Next.js app, not a toy counter, so I measured both build cost and runtime behaviour.

  1. App: Next.js 16.4.2, React 19.3.1, Turbopack, Node 24, on an 8-vCPU Linux box. The client dashboard has 1,000 product rows, a filter input, a counter, a stats panel and one deliberately "bad" component. Nothing uses useMemo or useCallback.
  2. Build load: 300 more generated client components on a /gen route, so compile time is measurable.
  3. Three builds: one next.config.ts read an RC_MODE variable (off, babel, rust). I deleted .next before every build, so the Turbopack disk cache never helped, and ran 5 rounds. The tables use the median of rounds 2-5. Round 1 was a cold start: 3.3 s, 12.6 s and 2.9 s of compile time.
  4. Re-renders: each component calls a tiny useRenderCount(name) hook that increments a counter in an effect. Puppeteer drove headless Chrome against next start, and Chrome's ScriptDuration metric measured JavaScript time. I ran each scenario 3 times, and the render counts were identical every run. 
// lib/useRenderCount.ts
"use client";
import { useEffect } from "react";

export function useRenderCount(name: string) {
  useEffect(() => {
    const r = (window.__renders ??= {});
    r[name] = (r[name] ?? 0) + 1;
  });
}

The counter lives in an effect on purpose. Writing to a global during render breaks the Rules of React, and the compiler would skip that component.

Does the React Compiler reduce re-renders?

Yes, dramatically for state that doesn't touch a component's props. Clicking the counter 20 times re-rendered every component on the page with the compiler off: 20,000 row renders. With either compiler, only the two components that actually use the count re-rendered. Rows, stats, the list and even the uncompilable component were all skipped.

Scenario (renders counted) Off Compiler Compiler + memo(Row)
20 counter clicks: Row renders 20,000 0 0
20 counter clicks: JS time 55-62 ms 6-7 ms 6-7 ms
Type "99" in filter: Row renders 290 290 0
Select 10 rows: Row renders 10,000 10,000 19
Select 10 rows: JS time 26-31 ms 14 ms 8 ms

The Babel and Rust builds produced exactly the same render counts, which you would expect from identical output.

The click case is the common one in real apps. Some unrelated state changes high in the tree, and with the compiler off everything below it re-renders.

Why do list rows still re-render with the compiler?

Because the compiler memoizes inside components. It does not turn every component into React.memo. When ProductList must re-render, for example because selectedId changed, its .map() creates new <Row> elements and each row runs. The compiled Row is cheaper to run, since its internals are cached, so JS time still halved from about 28 ms to 14 ms. But all 1,000 rows rendered on each click.

Wrapping the row in memo() fixed it. Selecting 10 rows then rendered 19 rows (1 + 9×2: the newly selected row and the previously selected one).

import { memo } from "react";

function Row({ item, selected, onSelect }: RowProps) {
  return (
    <li style={{ fontWeight: selected ? 700 : 400 }} onClick={() => onSelect(item.id)}>
      {item.name}
    </li>
  );
}

const MemoRow = memo(Row); // still worth it for big lists

Without the compiler, the same memo(Row) did nothing: still 10,000 renders. The parent passes onSelect={(id) => setSelectedId(id)} as a new function every render, which breaks memo's prop comparison. The compiler caches that callback automatically. That pairing is what makes memo reliable: compiler for stable props, memo for big lists.

What does the compiled code look like?

The compiler adds a small cache array per component (_c(n) from react/compiler-runtime) and wraps each computation in an "inputs changed?" check. This is what the Babel plugin produced for my Stats component, which totals prices on every render in the source:

function Stats(t0) {
  const $ = _c(10);
  const { items } = t0;
  let onSale, t1, t2, t3;
  if ($[0] !== items) {
    const total = items.reduce(_temp, 0);
    onSale = items.filter(_temp2).length;
    // ...store results in $[1..4]
  } else {
    onSale = $[1]; // reuse cached values
    // ...
  }
  // the returned <p> is cached the same way
}

The expensive reduce and filter run only when items changes. This is the same thing you would do by hand with useMemo, applied to every value in every component.

Does the React Compiler slow down next build?

The Babel version does, the Rust version barely does. In my 300-component app the compile step went from 2.25 s with the compiler off to 5.65 s with Babel, about 2.5 times longer. The Rust compiler took 2.5 s, only 0.25 s more than no compiler at all. Full next build wall time was 7.7 s, 11.1 s and 8.2 s.

Both compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript: the same chunk hashes and the same sizes. Compiled code is larger, because every component now carries cache checks. Raw client JS grew by 213,496 bytes (+28.9%), but after gzip the difference was only 2,990 bytes (+1.7%). The cache checks are repetitive and compress well.

These are numbers from one small app on one machine. Your ratio will differ with codebase size, but the direction should hold: Babel adds noticeable compile time and Rust mostly removes it.

Which code does the React Compiler skip?

Components that break the Rules of React. The compiler checks your code, and if it can't prove a component is safe to memoize it leaves that component uncompiled instead of guessing. The build does not fail. My Bailout component reads and writes ref.current during render, and the Babel plugin's logger reported CompileError: Cannot access refs during render.

export function Bailout({ label }: { label: string }) {
  const renders = useRef(0);
  renders.current += 1; // breaks the rules: ref mutation during render
  return <aside>{label} (render #{renders.current})</aside>;
}

Notice from the render table that Bailout was still skipped on counter clicks. The compiled parent cached the <Bailout label="legacy widget" /> element, so React never re-rendered it. Code the compiler skips simply misses its own internal optimizations. It doesn't break.

How do I find code the compiler can't optimize?

Use the latest eslint-plugin-react-hooks (7.x today). Since React Compiler 1.0, the compiler-powered lint rules ship in the plugin's recommended preset: refs, purity, immutability, set-state-in-effect, set-state-in-render, globals, static-components, incompatible-library and more. You don't need the separate eslint-plugin-react-compiler package any more.

// eslint.config.mjs
import reactHooks from "eslint-plugin-react-hooks";
import tseslint from "typescript-eslint";

export default [
  ...tseslint.configs.recommended,
  reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended,
];

On my test app, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7.1.1 flagged the Bailout ref access three times. It also caught a real bug pattern in my generator: 300 components called setState inside useEffect. The rule message says this "can trigger cascading renders". I fixed the generator before benchmarking.

Run the linter before turning on the compiler, fix what it reports, and treat the warnings as a list of components that won't be optimized.

Step by step: adopt the React Compiler in an existing Next.js app

  1. Upgrade. Use Next.js 16.x and React 19.x. The compiler also supports React 17 and 18 through react-compiler-runtime.
  2. Lint first. Add reactHooks.configs.flat.recommended, run eslint . and fix or note the errors.
  3. Install and enable. Run npm i -D babel-plugin-react-compiler, then set reactCompiler: true. On a large app, start with compilationMode: "annotation" and add "use memo" to hot paths.
  4. Try Rust on Turbopack. Add experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler: true and compare next build times.
  5. Test behaviour. Run your end-to-end tests. Watch effects that depend on memoized values.
  6. Keep memo on big lists. The compiler stabilizes props. memo still decides whether a list item renders.
  7. Remove manual memoization slowly. The React team advises keeping existing useMemo and useCallback or testing carefully before removing them, because removal can change compilation output.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback?

Not in a hurry. For new code, write plain components and let the compiler memoize. In existing code, leave useMemo and useCallback alone until you have tests. The React docs say the hooks "can continue to be used with React Compiler as an escape hatch", for example to keep an effect dependency stable. Removing them can change what the compiler outputs.

Common React Compiler mistakes in Next.js

  • Expecting it to fix big lists alone. It doesn't add React.memo to children. Keep memo() on heavy list items.
  • Mutating during render. Ref writes, global writes or prop mutation make the compiler skip the component, with no build error.
  • Using the Rust flag with webpack. turbopackRustReactCompiler throws with webpack. Remove it or switch to Turbopack.
  • Enabling it without the lint rules. You won't know which components were skipped.
  • Benchmarking with a warm cache. Turbopack's build disk cache hides compile cost. Delete .next between comparison builds.
  • Expecting Server Component wins. The compiler targets components that re-render on the client. Server Components render once per request.

If you are on Next.js 16.4, pair this with the other new client-side features in my guides to React View Transitions in Next.js and the use cache directive.

Related: the React Compiler lint rules from eslint-plugin-react-hooks 7 don't all survive a linter switch. Oxlint ported 12 of 14, Biome none; see Oxlint vs Biome vs ESLint.

Related: wondering whether to leave Next.js entirely? In TanStack Start vs Next.js I built the same app in both: TanStack Start shipped 111 KB of gzipped JS to Next.js 16.4's 139 KB and built in 1.26 s vs 4.86 s.

Key takeaways

  • React Compiler 1.0 automatically memoizes components and hooks at build time; in Next.js 16 enable it with reactCompiler: true.
  • In my Next.js 16.4.2 test, 20 counter clicks caused 0 row re-renders with the compiler versus 20,000 without, and JS time fell from about 60 ms to 7 ms.
  • The compiler does not make children React.memo; list rows still re-rendered until I wrapped them in memo(), which then cut 10,000 renders to 19.
  • The Babel compiler made the compile step 2.5x longer (2.25 s to 5.65 s); the experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 s.
  • Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical client JavaScript; gzipped size grew only 1.7%.
  • experimental.turbopackRustReactCompiler needs reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack, and needs no Babel plugin.
  • Run eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules first; components that break the Rules of React are silently skipped.

FAQ

What is the React Compiler?

The React Compiler is a build-time tool from the React team that automatically memoizes components and hooks. It rewrites your code to cache values, callbacks and JSX between renders and recompute them only when inputs change, replacing most manual useMemo, useCallback and memo calls. Version 1.0 shipped on October 7, 2025, and it supports React 17 and later.

How do I enable the React Compiler in Next.js?

Install babel-plugin-react-compiler as a dev dependency and set reactCompiler: true at the top level of next.config.ts. The option became stable in Next.js 16.0, moving out of experimental. Next.js applies the compiler only to files with JSX or hooks, using an SWC pre-check, to keep build cost down. Use compilationMode: 'annotation' to opt in per component.

What is turbopackRustReactCompiler?

It is an experimental Next.js option, added in 16.3, that runs the native Rust port of the React Compiler inside Turbopack instead of the Babel plugin. It requires reactCompiler: true, works only with Turbopack and throws with webpack, and needs no babel-plugin-react-compiler install. In my test it compiled in 2.5 seconds versus 5.65 seconds for Babel.

Does the React Compiler make next build slower?

With the Babel plugin, noticeably. In my 300-component Next.js 16.4.2 app the compile step went from 2.25 seconds to 5.65 seconds, and full next build from 7.7 to 11.1 seconds. The experimental Rust compiler took 2.5 seconds to compile and 8.2 seconds in total, so most of the cost disappeared.

Does the React Compiler replace React.memo?

Not for list items. The compiler memoizes inside each component and caches child elements, but when a parent re-renders and maps over data, every child still runs. In my test, selecting a row re-rendered all 1,000 rows with the compiler alone. Wrapping the row in memo() cut 10,000 renders to 19, because the compiler kept its props stable.

Should I remove useMemo and useCallback when using the React Compiler?

Not right away. Write new code without them, but keep existing calls until you have tests, because the React team notes that removing them can change compilation output. The hooks still work as an escape hatch, for example to keep an effect dependency stable so the effect doesn't fire repeatedly when its inputs haven't meaningfully changed.

What happens if my code breaks the Rules of React?

The compiler skips that component and leaves it unoptimized; the build does not fail. In my test, a component that mutated ref.current during render produced a 'Cannot access refs during render' compile error in the logger and was left as written. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks recommended rules report the same problems in your editor.

Does the React Compiler increase bundle size?

Slightly. Compiled components carry cache checks, so in my test raw client JavaScript grew 28.9 percent, by 213,496 bytes, but gzipped size grew only 1.7 percent, by 2,990 bytes, because the generated code compresses well. The Babel and Rust compilers produced byte-identical bundles in Next.js 16.4.2.

Originally published on fabwaseem.com.

title: Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?
description:
Chip Stocks Tumble as Wall Street Asks: Is the AI Boom a Bubble?

For months, the artificial intelligence trade seemed unstoppable. Giant chipmakers, cloud providers, and data-center builders lifted Wall Street to one record after another. This week, the music stopped — at least temporarily — as a brutal sell-off swept through the technology sector and forced investors to confront a question they had been happy to ignore: what happens if the most expensive technology bet in history stops paying off?

A Week of Red Numbers

The damage was fast and broad. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite posted its first weekly loss in five weeks, and the S&P 500 logged its worst week since June. Chip stocks — the engine of the AI boom — took the hardest hits. Micron Technology fell more than five percent, Advanced Micro Devices dropped over five percent, Broadcom slid more than four percent, and Intel lost close to six percent on Friday alone. AI data-center infrastructure company CoreWeave, a major Nvidia customer, plunged more than seven percent after a double-digit decline earlier in the week.

The rout was global. Seoul's tech-rich Kospi briefly triggered a trading halt after diving more than eight percent, with Samsung sinking over nine percent and SK hynix down more than eleven percent. Tokyo shed close to five percent, dragged down by chip-linked names like Advantest and Kioxia as well as investment giant SoftBank.

Why Now? Inflation and the Cost of Money

The immediate trigger was economic, not technological. US inflation data came in hotter than expected, with the consumer price index jumping to 3.7 percent in September and wholesale inflation surging 6.3 percent year-on-year — its biggest jump since 2022. Those numbers stoked fears that the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September for the first time in three years, may have to tighten further, with futures markets now pricing in a high probability of another hike by December.

Higher rates matter more to AI companies than to almost anyone else. Tech giants have financed an unprecedented infrastructure spree — data centers, GPU clusters, and power-hungry compute farms — largely through debt markets. With bond yields climbing to their highest levels in years, the cost of financing that buildout is rising exactly as patience with unprofitable AI ventures is wearing thin. A week before the crash, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh had called AI "the most consequential change" to the global economy in his lifetime. Investors this week appeared to decide that consequence cuts both ways.

The IMF's Warning Shot

The market turmoil coincided with an uncomfortable warning from the International Monetary Fund. At the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the fund released a report projecting that a decline in AI investment could reduce global GDP by 0.4 percent by 2028, and cautioned that "weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction."

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva did not mince words: if confidence evaporates and "money runs away from AI, that can lead to financial stability risks" that "would be felt across the world." Yet the same meetings underscored how central AI already is to the global economy. The fund noted that global trade grew 8.3 percent between 2023 and 2025 — a figure that would have been closer to 4.6 percent without AI-related products. Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem put it bluntly: "It is here, and it's just the beginning."

Bubble or Growing Pains?

Not everyone reading the sell-off sees a bubble bursting. The Dow Jones actually rose on Friday, suggesting investors are rotating out of tech rather than abandoning equities altogether. Earnings expectations for the quarter remain strong, and companies at the heart of the AI supply chain — from TSMC to memory makers — have continued to report robust demand. Nvidia shares, though down more than five percent for the week, remain up dramatically over the longer arc of the AI era.

The bear case, though, is no longer fringe. Critics point to debt-financed capital expenditure, stretched valuations, and monetization that still lags the hype. Analysts this week cited "worries about the AI buildout, bubbly valuations, lower-than-expected earnings growth at leading US frontier labs, and Chinese competition" as compounding pressures. Moody's Analytics economists added that a prolonged Middle East conflict, by pushing up energy prices and interest rates, could "puncture" the AI boom by straining the economics behind AI investment.

What to Watch

Three signposts will matter in the coming weeks. First, the Fed's October 28 policy decision, landing a week before the US midterm elections — a hawkish surprise could renew the pressure on rate-sensitive tech names. Second, the ongoing earnings season, where markets will demand evidence that AI revenue is catching up to AI spending. Third, and hardest to measure: confidence. As Georgieva noted in Bangkok, "if there are no safeguards, then the risks may exceed the opportunities."

Whether this week proves to be a healthy correction in a long structural boom or the first crack in a bubble, one thing is clear: the era of unquestioned AI enthusiasm on Wall Street is over. From now on, the market will want receipts.

title: The wappalyzer npm package is deprecated: options for detecting tech stacks in code
description:
For years, npm install wappalyzer was how developers detected a website's technologies in code. The package's last release, 7.0.3 from August 2023, is now marked deprecated on npm ("Package no longer supported"), and the open-source GitHub repository is no longer public. Wappalyzer continues as a commercial product. If you need tech detection in your own code, here are the options.

Option 1: Wappalyzer's paid service

The browser extension is still the quickest way to check a single site by hand, and Wappalyzer sells API access. That's a good fit if you want a managed service and the pricing works for your volume.

Option 2: the open-source fingerprints plus your own engine

The community fork webappanalyzer (GPL-3.0) keeps the technology fingerprints up to date and is actively maintained. It's data only, so you write the engine:

  1. Fetch the page.
  2. Match each technology's patterns against the HTML, script URLs, headers, cookies and meta tags.
  3. Apply the implies, requires and excludes rules.
  4. Pull versions out of the regex groups, and add up confidence.

A basic matcher is a weekend project. Getting versions, implied technologies and false positives right takes longer.

Option 3: a hosted API built on those fingerprints

We maintain a Tech Stack Detector on Apify that runs that engine for you, against a list of any size. It also reads public DNS, which a browser extension can't see. MX and SPF records show the email provider and sending services, and TXT verification records reveal connected SaaS tools such as Atlassian, DocuSign or Zoom.

From Node.js (npm install apify-client):

import { ApifyClient } from 'apify-client';

const client = new ApifyClient({ token: process.env.APIFY_TOKEN });
const run = await client.actor('rimulabs/tech-stack-detector').call({
    domains: ['basecamp.com', 'allbirds.com'],
    includeDns: true,
});
const { items } = await client.dataset(run.defaultDatasetId).listItems();
for (const site of items) console.log(site.domain, '->', site.techStack);

Real output from 18 October 2026:

basecamp.com -> Atlassian Cloud, Bootstrap, Cloudflare, Cloudflare DNS, Google Search Console, MailChimp, Microsoft 365, Open Graph, Priority Hints, Stimulus, Zoom
allbirds.com -> Apple Pay, Cloudflare, Cursor, DocuSign, Google Search Console, Google Tag Manager, HSTS, HTTP/3, Microsoft 365, Miro, Open Graph, PayPal, Priority Hints, Shopify, Swiper

Each site also has a technologies array shaped much like the old package's output, plus foundIn, the evidence behind each detection:

[
  { "name": "Shopify", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Ecommerce"], "foundIn": ["meta", "scripts"] },
  { "name": "PayPal", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Payment processors"], "foundIn": ["html"] },
  { "name": "Microsoft 365", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Webmail", "Email"], "foundIn": ["dns:mx", "dns:txt"] },
  { "name": "DocuSign", "version": null, "confidence": 100, "categories": ["Miscellaneous"], "foundIn": ["dns:txt"] }
]

It also has ready-made columns such as cms, ecommerce, analytics, email, hosting and cdn for spreadsheets. A filter returns only sites using the technologies you name, and a monitor mode reports what was added or removed since the last run.

Differences from the old npm package

  • No headless browser. The old package could drive Chrome and see tools that load only after JavaScript runs. The Actor reads the page as served, which is faster and cheaper, but some tag-manager-loaded pixels can be missed. DNS checks make up for part of that.
  • Polite by design. It fetches each home page once, respects robots.txt, and reports sites behind a bot check as blocked rather than trying to get around it.
  • Nothing to host. There are no Chrome binaries or fingerprint updates to manage. Results come back as JSON, CSV or Excel.

Cost: $3.00 per 1,000 sites checked. Sites that are unreachable, blocked or closed to crawlers are free. A weekly check of 50 competitors costs about $0.60 a month.

The full guide, kept up to date, is at rimulabs.com/guides/wappalyzer-alternative.

Disclosure: Rimu Labs builds and maintains the Actor in this post. It was written by the AI assistant for Rimu Labs and checked against real runs on 18 October 2026. Questions or corrections: support@rimulabs.com.

title: How to accept crypto payments in Node.js (Express) in 5 minutes
description:
Adding crypto as a payment option sounds like a lot of work: running nodes, generating addresses, watching the
blockchain, handling confirmations, converting prices. With a payment gateway, it comes down to two endpoints on your
server:

  1. Create a payment and send the customer to a hosted checkout.
  2. Receive a signed notification when the payment confirms, and mark the order as paid.

In this tutorial we build both with Node.js and Express, using CigalPay
(disclosure: I'm part of the team building it). It's plain HTTP, so the same flow works in any language.

What you need: Node.js 18 or later (for the built-in fetch), and a CigalPay account. Your account ID and
your notification signing secret are in the merchant dashboard, under Settings.

1. Set up the project 

mkdir crypto-checkout && cd crypto-checkout
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
npm install express

Put your credentials in environment variables, never in the code:

export CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID="your-account-id"
export CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET="your-notification-signing-secret"
export PUBLIC_URL="https://your-app.com"   # where CigalPay can reach your server

2. Create a payment

When the customer clicks "Pay with crypto", your server creates a payment and redirects them to the checkout.
The price is in USD or EUR; the customer chooses the coin on the checkout, and the rate is locked while they pay.

// server.js
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import express from 'express';

const app = express();
const { CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID, CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET, PUBLIC_URL } = process.env;

// A tiny in-memory "database" for the demo.
const orders = new Map();

app.post('/checkout/:orderId', async (req, res) => {
  const orderId = req.params.orderId;
  const order = { id: orderId, amount: 49.9, currency: 'USD', status: 'pending' };
  orders.set(orderId, order);

  const response = await fetch('https://coins-api.cigalpay.com/api/pre-invoice', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      accountId: CIGALPAY_ACCOUNT_ID,
      amount: order.amount,
      currency: order.currency,              // USD or EUR
      description: `Order #${orderId}`,      // shown to the customer
      extraId: orderId,                      // your reference, sent back in the notification
      lang: 'en',                            // checkout language: en, fr, es, de
      callback: `${PUBLIC_URL}/thank-you`,   // where the customer returns
      ipn: `${PUBLIC_URL}/cigalpay/ipn`,     // where the signed notification goes
    }),
  });
  if (!response.ok) return res.status(502).send('Could not create the payment');

  const { chargeLink } = await response.json();
  res.redirect(303, chargeLink);
});

That's the whole integration on the "pay" side. The customer lands on the checkout, picks a coin (Bitcoin, USDT,
Ethereum and many others), scans the QR code or copies the address, and pays.

3. Verify the signed notification

When the payment status changes, CigalPay sends a POST with a JSON body to your ipn URL. The x-cigalpay-sig
header holds an HMAC-SHA512 signature of the body, computed with your signing secret over the JSON with its
top-level keys sorted.

Never mark an order as paid from the customer's redirect to /thank-you: anyone can open that URL. Only trust the
notification, and only after checking its signature.

function isSignatureValid(body, received) {
  const expected = crypto
    .createHmac('sha512', CIGALPAY_IPN_SECRET)
    .update(JSON.stringify(body, Object.keys(body).sort()))
    .digest('hex');
  return (
    typeof received === 'string' &&
    received.length === expected.length &&
    crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(received), Buffer.from(expected))
  );
}

app.post('/cigalpay/ipn', express.json(), (req, res) => {
  const payment = req.body;
  if (!isSignatureValid(payment, req.get('x-cigalpay-sig'))) return res.sendStatus(401);

  const order = orders.get(payment.extraId);
  if (!order) return res.sendStatus(404);

  switch (payment.status) {
    case 'CONFIRMING':
      // Seen on the network, not final yet: show "payment pending", don't ship.
      order.status = 'confirming';
      break;
    case 'CONFIRMED':
    case 'FINISHED':
      // Final: fulfil the order. Notifications can arrive more than once,
      // so make this step idempotent.
      if (order.status !== 'paid') {
        order.status = 'paid';
        console.log(`Order ${order.id} paid`);
      }
      break;
    case 'PARTIALLY_PAID':
    case 'EXPIRED':
    case 'FAILED':
      order.status = payment.status.toLowerCase();
      break;
  }
  res.sendStatus(200);
});

app.get('/thank-you', (_req, res) => res.send('Thanks! Your payment is being confirmed.'));

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));

A few details worth knowing:

  • Constant-time comparison. crypto.timingSafeEqual avoids leaking how much of the signature matched.
  • Idempotency. The same status can be delivered more than once; check the current order state before acting.
  • CONFIRMING is not paid. The transaction is on the network but not confirmed yet. Ship only on a final status.
  • Other coins. If the customer paid with a coin that was converted at checkout, the notification also contains swapFromCurrency, swapFromNetwork and swapFromAmount, so you can show what they actually sent.

4. Test it end to end

Your notification URL must be reachable from the internet. Locally, a tunnel does the job:

node server.js
# in another terminal
npx localtunnel --port 3000     # or ngrok, cloudflared...

Set PUBLIC_URL to the tunnel's address, restart, then:

curl -i -X POST "$PUBLIC_URL/checkout/1042"

Open the Location URL from the response, pay a small amount (a real $1 payment is the best test), and watch your
terminal: Order 1042 paid.

Wrapping up

The whole integration is two routes:

Route Job
POST /checkout/:orderId Create the payment with POST /api/pre-invoice, redirect to chargeLink
POST /cigalpay/ipn Verify x-cigalpay-sig, update the order from status and extraId

No nodes, no wallets to run, no blockchain polling. If you'd rather not write code at all, the dashboard can also
create a payment link you can send by message or show as a QR code.

  • Docs and API reference: cigalpay.com/developers
  • Pricing: 1% per transaction, no monthly fee.

Questions about confirmations, underpayments or wrong-network deposits? Ask in the comments, happy to help.

title: A Kotlin Data Class Works as a HashMap Key. In a TypeScript Map It Never Matches
description:
• Book: Kotlin and Java to TypeScript
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

A Kotlin grid keyed by Point is about as ordinary as code gets: a cell type and a map from cell to whatever lives there.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    val labels = hashMapOf(Point(1, 2) to "spawn")
    println(labels[Point(1, 2)]) // spawn
}

Two different Point instances, one lookup, a hit. The Kotlin compiler derives equals() and hashCode() from every property in the primary constructor, so the second Point(1, 2) lands in the same bucket as the first and compares equal. Java gives you the same deal with records, final since JDK 16.

Now you port it to TypeScript. The compiler is happy, and the lookup returns undefined with no error anywhere.

Why the Map can't see your Point

Here is the port, as most JVM developers write it on day one:

type Point = { readonly x: number; readonly y: number };

const labels = new Map<Point, string>();
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");

labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // undefined
labels.size;                // 1

const seen = new Set<Point>();
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.add({ x: 1, y: 2 });
seen.size;                  // 2

JavaScript's Map compares keys with the SameValueZero algorithm. MDN spells out what that means for objects: "for object keys, equality is based on object identity. They are compared by reference, not by value." Two object literals with the same fields are two objects, so they are two keys. Set works the same way, which is why your "deduplicated" set holds the same point twice.

The JVM reflex is to add an equals method and move on. It does nothing here:

class Pt {
  readonly x: number;
  readonly y: number;
  constructor(x: number, y: number) {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
  }
  equals(o: Pt): boolean {
    return this.x === o.x && this.y === o.y;
  }
}

const m = new Map<Pt, string>([[new Pt(1, 2), "spawn"]]);
m.get(new Pt(1, 2)); // undefined

There is no equals/hashCode protocol in JavaScript collections. Map never calls your method, and there is no hook to make it. On the JVM, the Object contract says equal objects "must produce the same integer result" from hashCode, and HashMap is built on that promise.

The type checker won't save you either. TypeScript's type system is structural: any { x, y } is a valid Point, so labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }) type-checks perfectly.

One more trap while you are here. If you reach for a plain object as a dictionary instead, every property name gets coerced to a string, and every plain object becomes "[object Object]". Now every point matches every other point. You traded "never matches" for "always matches".

Fix 1: derive a string key

The smallest fix is to stop using the object as the key and use a string computed from it:

const keyOf = (p: Point): string => `${p.x},${p.y}`;

const grid = new Map<string, string>();
grid.set(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
grid.get(keyOf({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"

Strings are primitives, and SameValueZero compares primitives by value, so this works. For numeric fields the comma is safe because a JavaScript number never stringifies with a comma in it.

String fields are where this goes wrong. With a naive template, { org: "a,b", name: "c" } and { org: "a", name: "b,c" } both produce "a,b,c". Encode the fields as a JSON array in a fixed order instead:

type Member = { readonly org: string; readonly name: string };

const memberKey = (m: Member): string =>
  JSON.stringify([m.org, m.name]);

JSON escaping makes the encoding unambiguous, and the array fixes the order. Don't call JSON.stringify(m) on the whole object: property order follows Object.keys(), which is insertion order for string keys, so { org, name } and { name, org } give you two different keys for the same member.

The cost of Fix 1: the map now holds strings. Iterate it and you get "1,2" back, not a Point. And nothing stops a teammate from calling grid.get("1, 2") with a stray space.

Fix 2: a KeyedMap that takes a key function

If you miss HashMap<Point, V>, write the small wrapper that moves hashCode out of the class and into a function you pass in. It keeps the original key next to the value, so iteration hands you real Point objects:

class KeyedMap<K, V> {
  readonly #entries = new Map<string, [K, V]>();
  readonly #keyOf: (key: K) => string;

  constructor(keyOf: (key: K) => string) {
    this.#keyOf = keyOf;
  }

  set(key: K, value: V): this {
    this.#entries.set(this.#keyOf(key), [key, value]);
    return this;
  }

  get(key: K): V | undefined {
    return this.#entries.get(this.#keyOf(key))?.[1];
  }

  has(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.has(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  delete(key: K): boolean {
    return this.#entries.delete(this.#keyOf(key));
  }

  get size(): number {
    return this.#entries.size;
  }

  [Symbol.iterator]() {
    return this.#entries.values();
  }
}

Using it reads like the Kotlin version again:

const labels = new KeyedMap<Point, string>(keyOf);
labels.set({ x: 1, y: 2 }, "spawn");
labels.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // "spawn"

for (const [point, label] of labels) {
  console.log(point.x, point.y, label);
}

One JVM rule carries over unchanged. The java.util.Map docs warn that "the behavior of a map is not specified if the value of an object is changed in a manner that affects equals comparisons while the object is a key in the map." Here, if you mutate a key after set, the stored string is stale and the entry is unreachable by its new value. Keep key types readonly, as Point is above.

Fix 3: branded value types

Fixes 1 and 2 still let anyone pass a raw { x, y } or a hand-built string. Branding closes that door at compile time. The TypeScript playground's nominal-typing example intersects a type with a __brand property, a convention that makes a plain value unassignable to the branded type.

Start with the key string. Brand it, and make one function the only way to produce it:

type PointKey = string & { readonly __brand: "PointKey" };

const pointKey = (p: Point): PointKey =>
  `${p.x},${p.y}` as PointKey;

const spawns = new Map<PointKey, string>();
spawns.set(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 }), "spawn");
spawns.get(pointKey({ x: 1, y: 2 })); // "spawn"
// spawns.get("1,2"); // compile error: not a PointKey

The brand exists only in the type system: at runtime a PointKey is an ordinary string and the map behaves exactly as in Fix 1, while a hand-typed "1, 2" is rejected by the compiler because it has no brand.

You can go one step further and brand the value itself. If a factory hands out one canonical frozen object per coordinate, reference equality becomes value equality, and the plain Map from the first snippet starts working:

type GridPoint = Point & { readonly __brand: "GridPoint" };

const pool = new Map<string, GridPoint>();

function gridPoint(x: number, y: number): GridPoint {
  const key = `${x},${y}`;
  let p = pool.get(key);
  if (p === undefined) {
    p = Object.freeze({ x, y }) as GridPoint;
    pool.set(key, p);
  }
  return p;
}

const owners = new Map<GridPoint, string>();
owners.set(gridPoint(1, 2), "spawn");
owners.get(gridPoint(1, 2));       // "spawn"
gridPoint(1, 2) === gridPoint(1, 2); // true
// owners.get({ x: 1, y: 2 }); // compile error: no brand

This is interning: one shared instance per distinct value. The brand is what makes it safe: a Map<GridPoint, V> refuses object literals, so the day-one bug from the first section can't compile. The trade-off is memory. The pool keeps every point it ever created alive, so use it for bounded domains like grid cells, currency pairs or enum-like tuples, not for arbitrary user input.

Records and Tuples will not fix this for you

For years the answer to "when will JavaScript get value-equal objects?" was the Records and Tuples proposal, with its #{ x: 1, y: 2 } syntax. That proposal is gone. At the TC39 plenary on April 14, 2025, the committee reached consensus to withdraw it; it "was at stage 2 and unable to gain further consensus for adding new primitives to the language." The inactive-proposals list records the rationale as "Subsumed by Composites".

The Composites proposal is the successor, and it is listed at Stage 2 as of October 2026. Its pitch is this exact problem. Composite({ x: 1, y: 4 }) returns an interned, frozen object, so two composites built from the same values are the same object, === is true, and they work as Map and Set keys. It is the gridPoint factory above, proposed as a language feature.

Read the fine print before you wait for it. Stage 2 in the TC39 process means "refining the solution": the design is a draft that may still change significantly. The README mentions experimental implementations and a polyfill, not a shipping engine. Nested plain objects are compared by reference, so Composite({ v: {} }) !== Composite({ v: {} }). Composites can't be WeakMap keys. And every object you get from JSON.parse, a database driver or an HTTP client will still be a plain object, so you'd convert at the boundary anyway, which is what Fix 3 already does.

Which fix to pick

Reach for Fix 1 when the key is used in one function and never iterated. KeyedMap is the one to pick when you want HashMap<K, V> ergonomics and need the original keys back. Use branded keys or interned values when the map crosses module boundaries and you want the compiler, not code review, to catch the raw object literal.

If this was useful

Map keys are one of those places where Kotlin and Java instincts compile cleanly in TypeScript and then fail quietly at runtime. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript walks through these translation gaps one by one: variance, null safety, sealed classes to unions, coroutines to async/await. If you came to TypeScript from the JVM, it's the one to start with.

The rest of the collection, so you can see which one or two fit you:

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Books 1 and 2 are the core path. Kotlin and Java to TypeScript stands in for them if you think in JVM terms, and The TypeScript Type System is where branded types like PointKey get the full treatment. Book 5 is for anyone shipping TypeScript at work. Browse all five on the collection page.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

title: Checkpoints for AI Code Changes: The Feature Nobody Talks About
description:
Everyone compares AI coding tools on model quality. Almost nobody compares them on recoverability — and that's the thing that actually saves your day.

The scenario

You ask an AI to "refactor the payment module." It touches 9 files. Six of them are fine. Three of them break something subtle that you won't notice until production.

With most tools, your options are:

  • Manually figure out which of the 9 changes was wrong
  • git stash and lose everything
  • Revert the whole thing and start over

What checkpoints change

A checkpoint is a snapshot of your code at a specific moment — usually right before each AI action. Instead of one big "before" and one big "after," you get a timeline:

[checkpoint] before refactor
  [checkpoint] after file 1-3
    [checkpoint] after file 4-6   <- the break is here
      [checkpoint] after file 7-9

Now when something breaks, you don't debug the whole change. You rewind to the last good checkpoint and go from there.

Why this matters more with AI

Human commits are usually coherent — you commit when something works. AI changes are exploratory. The agent is guessing, and guesses are wrong sometimes. Checkpoints turn "the AI broke my code" from a disaster into a two-click fix.

The mental shift

Once you have checkpoints, you stop being afraid of letting the AI try things. You can say "go ahead, attempt the refactor" without the usual dread, because you know you can always rewind.

That fearlessness is the real productivity gain — not the typing speed.

Arcwright builds checkpoints into every AI step on Windows, and it's free to start. Whatever tool you pick, look for this feature. It's the difference between an assistant you supervise and one you're scared of.
