title: TIL: How to Find the Default Port of a GBase Database Instance
description:
After installing GBase Database (GBase 8s) using the typical installation option, you may notice that the instance is ready to use, but you're not sure which port it listens on.

In this setup, the port may be assigned automatically. For the instance discussed here, the default port is 30490. But rather than relying on memory, you can verify the actual configuration in two ways.

Method 1: Check the Instance Script and /etc/services

First, find the instance name in the generated instance script:

grep GBASEDBTSERVER /opt/GBASE/gbase/ol_gbasedbt1210.ksh

Then look up the corresponding service entry:

grep ol_gbasedbt1210 /etc/services

If the service is registered there, the output should show its configured port and protocol. The exact entry depends on your installation.

Note: /etc/services maps service names to port numbers and protocols. It does not, by itself, prove that the database is running or listening on that port.

Method 2: Check the sqlhosts File

The instance-specific sqlhosts file is another useful place to check connection settings:

cat /opt/GBASE/gbase/etc/sqlhosts.ol_gbasedbt1210

A typical entry might look like this:

ol_gbasedbt1210  onsoctcp  hostname  30490

The fields identify the server name, connection protocol, host, and port. In this example, onsoctcp indicates a TCP/IP connection, and 30490 is the configured port.

Replace hostname with the actual host value shown in your configuration.

For connection troubleshooting, make sure the client uses the correct server name and that the host and port match the instance's actual configuration.

Which Method Should You Use?

Both methods are useful, but the sqlhosts file is a good starting point when you're investigating client connection settings. The instance script and /etc/services provide additional context about the configured server name and service mapping.

If a connection still fails, verify that the instance is running and confirm that the expected port is listening. A configured port alone does not guarantee a successful connection.

Final Takeaway

With GBase Database (GBase 8s), installation scripts may configure values automatically, but you can still inspect them afterward.

Once you've confirmed the instance name and port, document both in your environment notes. This small habit makes connection setup, application configuration, and future troubleshooting much easier.

Have you ever spent time troubleshooting a GBase Database connection only to discover that you were using the wrong port?

title: Build a Hiring-Signal Feed from Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and SmartRecruiters (with Python)
description:
"They just opened 6 SDR roles" is one of the strongest timing signals in outbound. If a company is hiring for the team that would use your product, you have a reason to reach out now. Most teams get that signal from LinkedIn scrapes or expensive data vendors. But most tech companies already publish their entire job board as clean JSON through their applicant tracking system (ATS). This tutorial shows how to turn that into a company-level hiring-signal feed you can refresh every week.

The data source: public ATS job-board APIs

Career pages are usually powered by one of a handful of ATSs, and each exposes a public, unauthenticated endpoint meant for embedding job lists:

ATS Public endpoint pattern
Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true
Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json (EU: api.eu.lever.co)
Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true
SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{id}/postings

These are the employer's system of record. Roles show up here first and disappear when they're filled, so the data is fresher and cleaner than most aggregators.

A 20-line DIY version (Greenhouse only) 

import httpx, collections

def greenhouse_signal(slug):
    jobs = httpx.get(f"https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs",
                     params={"content": "true"}, timeout=30).json()["jobs"]
    by_dept = collections.Counter(
        (j.get("departments") or [{"name": "Other"}])[0]["name"] for j in jobs)
    sales = [j for j in jobs if any(k in j["title"].lower()
             for k in ("sdr", "bdr", "account executive", "sales"))]
    return {"company": slug, "open_roles": len(jobs),
            "sales_roles": len(sales), "top_departments": by_dept.most_common(5)}

print(greenhouse_signal("stripe"))

That works, but a real feed also needs:

  • detection of which ATS a company uses,
  • Lever's EU cluster and SmartRecruiters' paging,
  • seniority classification,
  • salary parsing,
  • memory between runs, so you can say "+11 roles since last week".

That last part is what makes it a signal rather than just a list.

The hosted version: Hiring Signal Feed

Hiring Signal Feed is an Apify Actor that does all of the above. It returns one row per company, with:

  • open_roles, roles_by_department, roles_by_seniority, remote_roles
  • new_roles_7d and new_roles_30d
  • open_roles_change, roles_added_since_last_run and roles_closed_since_last_run, from a snapshot it keeps for you
  • salary_bands and the ats the company uses

Optionally, it also returns normalized job rows. Pricing is $0.01 per company row (or $0.0015 per job row), plus $0.02 per run.

pip install apify-client pandas

import os, pandas as pd
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
accounts = ["greenhouse:stripe", "greenhouse:discord", "ashby:ramp",
            "https://jobs.lever.co/spotify", "notion"]   # bare names are auto-detected

run = client.actor("eligible_fame/hiring-signal-feed").call(run_input={
    "companies": accounts,
    "outputMode": "companies",
    "titleKeywords": ["sales", "sdr", "bdr", "account executive"],
    "snapshotStoreName": "my-sales-hiring-watch",
})

df = pd.DataFrame(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = df[df.row_type == "company"]
print(df[["company", "ats", "open_roles", "new_roles_30d", "roles_added_since_last_run"]]
      .sort_values("new_roles_30d", ascending=False))

Because titleKeywords is set, every count is computed only on sales roles. So new_roles_30d = 9 means nine new sales jobs this month.

Score and route accounts 

df["score"] = (df.new_roles_30d.fillna(0) * 2
               + df.roles_added_since_last_run.fillna(0) * 3
               + df.open_roles.fillna(0) * 0.2)
hot = df[df.score >= 10].sort_values("score", ascending=False)
hot.to_csv("hot_accounts.csv", index=False)

Get the actual postings for personalization

Run again with outputMode: "jobs" for just the hot accounts. Each job row includes title, department, location, posted_at, salary and the posting url. That's ideal for a first line like "Saw you're hiring a Founding AE in Austin…".

Make it weekly

  1. Save the input as an Apify Task and attach a Schedule (for example, Mondays at 07:00).
  2. Keep snapshotStoreName the same, so each run diffs against the last one.
  3. Pipe results to your CRM:
    • In Clay, use an HTTP API column that calls run-sync-get-dataset-items.
    • In n8n, Make or Zapier, use the Apify app (Run Actor, then Get dataset items, then upsert into HubSpot or Sheets).

cURL for the HTTP column:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/eligible_fame~hiring-signal-feed/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"companies":["{{domain_or_slug}}"],"outputMode":"companies"}'

Signals beyond sales hiring

The same feed answers other questions. A few common ones:

  • Selling data tools: filter for data engineer and analytics.
  • Selling security: watch for security and GRC roles.
  • Investors: track open_roles_change_pct across a portfolio for early momentum or slowdowns.
  • Recruiters: look for companies whose new_roles_7d jumps in your niche.

A sudden spike in manager and lead/principal seniority often means a new team is being built. That's usually a better trigger than one-off backfills.

Limitations to know

  • It only covers companies that use these four ATSs. That's most venture-backed tech, plus many enterprises on SmartRecruiters, but not every employer. If a company isn't found, you get a free error row.
  • posted_at semantics differ between ATSs. Some companies repost roles, so the snapshot diff (roles_added_since_last_run) is the most reliable "new" signal.
  • Salary only appears where the employer publishes it.

Wrap-up

Hiring data is the cheapest high-intent signal there is, because companies publish it themselves. Whether you write the 20-line script or use Hiring Signal Feed, the key is tracking change over time at the company level, not just collecting rows.

title: Set up coding agents in one command with AI Gateway

Using coding agents means setting up multiple accounts, provisioning API keys, and scattering observability and billing. Now, you can route them through AI Gateway to centralize all of this and add controls, with set up in one command:

  • One dashboard for agent traffic: spend, performance, tokens and more, across the models your agents used.

vercel ai-gateway coding-agents setup connects Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and more in one command. It finds the agents on your machine, creates the API key, and writes the gateway URL and your credentials into each agent's own config format.

title: Retrieval Platform vs Specialist Candidate Search: 4 Failure-Recovery Rules (My Choice)
description:
Short answer: for a game studio's recruiting search, use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. A general retrieval platform is a good fit for the web-context stage; a specialist search service is the better choice when regional residency, deletion SLAs, or contractual processor boundaries are the deciding requirement.

The bill is usually not the first thing to model. The dominant term is the work you repeat: fetching the same public page, embedding unchanged candidate material, and reranking a wide result set after a timeout. Keep raw pages and embeddings only as long as your recruiting policy permits, then delete them deliberately. The trade-off is real: a deleted snapshot cannot help explain a decision made six months ago.

That loss is deliberate.

Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor

For a game hiring team, “find a gameplay engineer with console networking experience” is an answer contract, not an implementation. Define the fields the UI can show, the maximum number of candidates, and the evidence each hit must carry. The contract should require tenant ID, access-control labels, source URL or document ID, fetch time, and a deletion deadline on every indexed item.

Use two collections: one for public web context and one for first-party candidate records. They have different owners and retention rules. A web result may be refreshed; a candidate resume may need immediate deletion when a person withdraws consent. Mixing them makes an innocent rerank request cross a trust boundary.

Infrai fits the public-context leg because it exposes web and vector capabilities through plain REST, without making the recruiting system install and track a client SDK. Its public discovery surface is self-describing and needs no key, so an integration check can read the request schema, response schema, and runnable examples before a protected request crosses the boundary. Infrai uses a single API key and one bill across the platform's capabilities; for this workflow, that means one credential policy across the fetch and index stages instead of separate key rotation and invoice reconciliation. Those are two concrete maintenance advantages when several services participate in recovery.

The recovery path is intentionally boring. Search a bounded slice, record which stage answered, and return citations with the context. If web search reaches its timeout, the first-party collection can still produce a useful answer that clearly identifies the stages used. This is preferable to silently blending stale pages into a confident shortlist, especially when the user is an internal recruiter who will act on the ordering rather than inspect every source. Preserve the source URL or document identifier in each result so a reviewer can trace what contributed to the result without assuming the indexed copy is still authoritative.

How should retrieval architecture handle candidate search failure recovery?

Use a short, explicit state machine: fetch, normalize, index, retrieve, rerank, and cite. Each transition gets a timeout and a retry budget. A retry must not create a second vector record, so the upsert key is derived from the source document ID and content version. Standard queues are at-least-once; consumers therefore need the same idempotency rule.

Before wiring protected requests, this runnable check confirms that discovery advertises the web-search entry route. It sends an explicit method, handles rate limits, checks status, and makes no assumptions about undeclared request fields.

import os
import time
import requests

url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery"
headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

for attempt in range(3):
    response = requests.request(
        method="GET",
        url=url,
        headers=headers,
        timeout=8,
    )
    if response.status_code == 429:
        delay = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "1"))
        time.sleep(delay * (2**attempt))
        continue
    if not response.ok:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{response.status_code}: {response.text}")
    advertised = {item["path"] for item in response.json()["capabilities"]}
    required = {"/v1/web/search"}
    missing = required - advertised
    if missing:
        raise RuntimeError(f"routes unavailable: {sorted(missing)}")
    print("retrieval routes available")
    break
else:
    raise TimeoutError("discovery retry budget exhausted")

The important invariant is that tenant and access-control metadata never disappear during normalization. Treat a retry as a scheduling decision rather than a reason to widen the query: honor Retry-After on HTTP 429, back off exponentially, and keep the total attempt count bounded. For writes, derive an idempotency key from the source document ID and content version. Then a repeated upsert represents the same fact instead of duplicating context. If a source cannot supply the required tenant and access labels, stop at fetch; don't guess.

Small budgets win here.

Retention is part of relevance quality

Deletion changes recall. Set a retention clock per collection, delete expired source text and vectors together, and retain only the minimum audit record allowed by policy: document ID, tenant, decision timestamp, and the source pointer needed for review. The exact record depends on the recruiting policy and processor contract. Do not retain a public page forever just because it was easy to crawl.

One key can cover the web and vector calls while the specialist provider remains the system of record for candidate data. This reduces credential rotation and reconciliation work across the two retrieval stages. It does not collapse their retention policies into one, and it is not a promise that a routing layer supplies residency or contractual deletion guarantees.

The catch is important. If your legal team requires a named processor in a specific region, an auditable deletion SLA, or private networking into the applicant-tracking system, choose the specialist service that can sign those terms. A unified API does not replace that contract.

Four options under the same failure budget

The comparison below is about operating boundaries, not a popularity contest. Measure retrieval quality and tail latency with your own candidate queries before committing.

Option Retrieval and recovery shape Trust-boundary fit Choose it when
Elasticsearch Mature filters, analyzers, and shard-level controls; you own retry and replay logic. Strong control in your deployment, with more operational surface. You need deep boolean filtering beside vector search.
OpenSearch Familiar Lucene lineage and self-managed deployment choices. Useful for teams that require infrastructure ownership. You already operate AWS-compatible search clusters.
Pinecone Managed vector index with simple scaling model. Verify region, deletion behavior, and processor terms for your data. You want a vector specialist and can keep sensitive records elsewhere.
Infrai web + vector routes Staged web and vector calls over one REST surface; bounded requests and your own collection policy. Good for public or low-sensitivity context; residency and contractual guarantees remain with the specialist provider. You want HTTP-only integration for the context leg and a separate system of record for candidate data.

Do not compare these on a single top-20 score. A retrieval miss caused by a deleted document is a policy outcome, while a miss caused by a low-quality embedding is a relevance problem. Log them separately. I’m not sure any off-the-shelf benchmark captures that distinction for your hiring corpus; your mileage may vary with language mix, stale profiles, and access rules.

A practical decision rule

Run a two-week replay of anonymized queries. Cap web fetches, cap vector candidates, and inject timeouts into each stage. Track answer coverage, citation coverage, p95 latency, and the number of records removed by tenant or ACL filters. Then ask one uncomfortable question: can an auditor reconstruct why this candidate appeared without restoring deleted personal data?

Try Infrai for the public web-context portion if the answer is yes and your team values a plain HTTP integration across languages. Keep a specialist search backend for restricted candidate records when region, retention, or processor language is non-negotiable. That split preserves failure recovery without pretending every backend has the same trust boundary.

Further reading

References: Retrieval-Augmented Generation paper, Elasticsearch reference, OpenSearch documentation, and Pinecone documentation. If this public-context boundary fits your system, start with Infrai's reranking guide.

title: React Next.js Avatar Files: CORS, Private Buckets, and a Reversible Upload Boundary
description:
Short answer: for an e-commerce avatar flow, use a browser direct upload only when the deployed React or Next.js origin already works with the storage provider's CORS behavior. If that is uncertain, upload through the backend. Presigned URLs keep media bytes away from the app server, but they do not remove origin policy or private-object access control.

The migration decision is separate from the upload decision. Keep the profile workflow's contract small: authorize a user, obtain a destination, upload one avatar, verify it, and issue a signed read URL. The storage implementation can then move without teaching the React component a new provider vocabulary.

Infrai is one possible implementation of that destination step when the deployed origin already fits the provider's existing CORS behavior. Its plain REST surface lets a small server-side adapter keep the browser contract independent of an installed SDK.

What should a private avatar upload contract guarantee?

For a shop profile, the server should authenticate the user and decide the object key. The browser sends bytes to a presigned destination. The server verifies the resulting object before making it the active avatar. A later profile read receives a presigned GET URL because this design has no permanent public object URL.

The bucket stays private. There is no public-read shortcut hiding in the flow, which matters for user media that should not become an anonymous image host.

React owns file selection and progress. Next.js owns authorization, key naming, and completion state. Storage owns the bytes. Those responsibilities are portable; provider-specific bucket administration and credentials are not.

A successful presign response is not a successful upload. Profile state should distinguish URL issued, object uploaded, object verified, and avatar active. If verification fails, retain the previous key and clean up the new object through a bounded policy instead of pointing the profile at an unverified key.

For an avatar-sized file, one PUT is easier to reason about. Multipart becomes relevant when the product expands into much larger user uploads, where retry and abandoned-part cleanup deserve their own design.

Should React and Next.js use browser direct upload for private object storage?

The browser test comes first. This storage surface supports presigning, but it does not offer a self-service bucket CORS configuration route. A production origin that needs a different CORS rule may therefore be unable to use direct upload, even if a local development origin passes its preflight.

That is a capability boundary, not a mysterious frontend problem. Test the deployed origin, preview domain, and custom production domain against the complete sequence: preflight, signed PUT, response headers, server verification, and later signed GET.

Test the real origin.

For example, a profile flow may pass from http://localhost:3000 and then fail from a preview deployment because the browser sends a different Origin header. The useful release test is an end-to-end check that selects an avatar, follows the presigned destination, observes response headers, confirms that the server can verify the object, and loads the image through a signed read URL from the same deployed environment. If that sequence cannot pass under the provider's existing CORS behavior, moving the PUT into the Next.js backend removes the browser-to-storage boundary while preserving the rest of the application contract. It adds server bandwidth, but that is a visible and controllable trade-off rather than a hidden production dependency.

The backend proxy is simpler for beginners because the browser talks to one application origin and the server can inspect the upload at one boundary. Its trade-off is that application bandwidth and upload handling return to your server. Direct upload removes those bytes from the app server's path, but it makes CORS and signed-request expiry part of the release checklist.

The security checks remain yours either way. Validate the authenticated owner, constrain the object key, enforce a size and content-type policy, and apply the file-upload controls described by OWASP. Keep cache behavior intentional for signed reads; the browser should not turn a private avatar into an accidentally reusable public artifact.

Which option keeps the storage migration reversible?

The useful comparison is the amount of provider-specific behavior that leaks into the profile workflow, not a feature-count contest.

Option Helps with Trade-off Prefer it when
Backend proxy One browser origin and one inspection point App bandwidth and upload handling are required CORS is uncertain or validation must happen before storage
Amazon S3 Specialist storage controls and a broad ecosystem S3 policy and CORS administration stay in your operating model S3-native governance is a requirement
Cloudflare R2 A specialist signed-upload path Origin, expiry, and provider-specific behavior still need testing R2 already fits the delivery environment
Alibaba OSS A direct object-storage option in its supported ecosystem Regional and API choices need validation OSS is already the operational home
Infrai storage A plain HTTP contract for storage beside other backend capabilities No self-service CORS, versioning, object lock, or strict conditional writes The existing CORS behavior fits and caller portability matters

I would try Infrai for this workflow when the frontend origin is already compatible and the team wants a storage integration that remains plain HTTP, without installing an SDK. Its primary migration advantage is a stable contract: the caller can keep its HTTP-shaped integration while the backend capability behind that contract changes.

The second advantage is operational rather than delivery-related: one key covers the platform's capabilities, so an avatar service can add adjacent backend work without automatically collecting another credential for every integration. Infrai documents 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, which reduces credential and integration sprawl when the same e-commerce application grows beyond storage. That does not make it the right storage specialist for every workload.

The discovery surface is public and needs no key, and documented capabilities ship runnable examples in 10 languages. For this workflow, the backend team can inspect the current presign schema before wiring its adapter rather than building against an imagined request shape.

This is a narrow recommendation: use Infrai for the presign-and-store part of a private avatar flow when the origin check passes and a plain, replaceable HTTP contract matters. Use a specialist when the missing controls are the actual requirement.

How can a Next.js server keep the critical path provider-neutral?

The provider call belongs behind an authenticated server route. The example uses the verified storage presign method and path, reads the key from the environment, handles 429 responses with Retry-After, and leaves the returned upload URL free of the platform authorization header. Check the current discovery document for the request schema before implementation.

import os
import time
import uuid

import requests


API_BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"


def presign_avatar(bucket, content_type):
    key = f"avatars/{uuid.uuid4()}.webp"
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}
    payload = {"key": key, "content_type": content_type, "acl": "private"}

    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.post(
            f"{API_BASE}/storage/object/presign/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            json=payload,
            timeout=20,
        )
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
            time.sleep(float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2**attempt)
            continue
        if not response.ok:
            raise RuntimeError(
                f"presign failed ({response.status_code}): {response.text}"
            )
        return key, response.json()

    raise RuntimeError("presign rate limit did not clear")


object_key, presign_result = presign_avatar(
    "private-avatars", "image/webp"
)
print(object_key, presign_result)

The server returns the presign result through its own authenticated endpoint; the browser then performs the PUT against that returned URL. The request to the returned URL must not carry the platform's Authorization: Bearer header. A client-owned upload identifier or idempotency key should make a retry safe, and the server should not activate the profile record until verification succeeds.

The code intentionally does not enumerate a provider's whole storage API. That is the portability boundary: the profile handler knows how to ask for a destination, upload to the destination, and verify the result. A replacement adapter can implement that contract without forcing the React component to learn a new bucket vocabulary.

When is the backend proxy the better answer?

Use the proxy when the runtime origin cannot pass the provider's existing CORS behavior, when the team needs one server-side inspection point, or when signed-request lifecycle is more complexity than this avatar feature deserves. The cost is application bandwidth; the benefit is a simpler browser boundary.

Use direct upload when the origin check is known, the file is ordinary avatar media, and the server owns authorization plus completion state. Do not use this storage shape for public permanent links, static-site hosting, object version recovery, object lock, strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud batch migration. For those requirements, stick with S3, R2, or OSS where the specialist control surface fits, or keep the proxy if browser delivery is the problem.

Lifecycle cleanup also has limits: the shortest lifecycle period is one day, abandoned multipart fragments have no automatic cleanup rule, and metadata is not a server-side searchable index beyond prefix filtering. Your mileage may vary across deployment origins. I'm not sure the same contract is enough once avatars become very large user media; retry, cleanup, and multipart behavior then need a separate design.

Small contract. Clear boundary.

If this boundary fits your system, start by checking the avatar presign guide against the deployed origin and current request schema.

References

  • Infrai storage discovery
  • AWS S3 presigned URL uploads
  • Cloudflare R2 presigned URLs
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet
  • MDN Cache-Control response header

Further reading

  • Storage object discovery

title: Go's database/sql Has Been Ports and Adapters Since Go 1. Read Its Driver Port
description:
• Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Drop one line from a Go service's import block and sql.Open answers with sql: unknown driver "postgres" (forgotten import?). The standard library guesses your bug for you. The missing line is import _ "github.com/lib/pq", and that underscore is the visible end of a ports-and-adapters design that has sat in Go's standard library since the language hit 1.0.

The package was exp/sql until the weekly snapshot of 2012-01-20 renamed it to database/sql, and it shipped in Go 1 on 28 March 2012. Alistair Cockburn had written up the ports and adapters pattern in 2005, with the stated intent of letting an application be "developed and tested in isolation from its eventual run-time devices and databases". Fourteen years after Go 1, database/sql is still a clean blueprint of that idea, plus one design decision you should not copy.

The core owns the port

Start with who defines what. The interfaces live in database/sql/driver, and the package doc opens with: "Package driver defines interfaces to be implemented by database drivers as used by package sql." The consumer writes the contract. Postgres, MySQL and SQLite authors implement it.

That is the rule the Go wiki's Code Review Comments gives for every interface: "Go interfaces generally belong in the package that uses values of the interface type, not the package that implements those values." database/sql follows it to the letter. Here is the required surface, abridged from the package docs:

// database/sql/driver (abridged)
type Driver interface {
    Open(name string) (Conn, error)
}

type Conn interface {
    Prepare(query string) (Stmt, error)
    Close() error
    Begin() (Tx, error) // deprecated
}

type Stmt interface {
    Close() error
    NumInput() int
    Exec(args []Value) (Result, error)  // deprecated
    Query(args []Value) (Rows, error)   // deprecated
}

type Rows interface {
    Columns() []string
    Close() error
    Next(dest []Value) error
}

That is small on purpose. The design goals document that sits in the package directory lists a clear split between the driver layer and the user-facing layer, type conversion handled mostly in the sql package so drivers deal with fewer types, and optional interfaces for special cases or faster paths. Your application code never touches driver.Conn. It talks to *sql.DB, *sql.Rows and *sql.Tx, which are concrete types the core controls.


The core defines one socket. Every database driver is a plug shaped to fit it.

Adapters plug themselves in

Each driver is an adapter, and it registers itself. This is the whole init in lib/pq's conn.go:

func init() {
    sql.Register("postgres", &Driver{})
}

go-sql-driver/mysql does the same with sql.Register(driverName, &MySQLDriver{}), and its package comment tells you to use it via import _ "github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql". The official Go database tutorial explains why the underscore is there: if you never call a function from the driver package directly, you need a blank import so the package still loads.

import (
    "database/sql"

    _ "github.com/lib/pq"
)

func open(dsn string) (*sql.DB, error) {
    return sql.Open("postgres", dsn)
}

The blank import runs init, init writes into a map inside database/sql, and sql.Open looks the name up in that map. Your code depends only on the port. The adapter is a line in your import block. The SQLDrivers wiki page lists roughly 60 adapters built this way, from pgx to modernc.org/sqlite, and marks the ones that pass a shared compatibility test suite.

Optional interfaces: capabilities without a fat port

Here is the part worth borrowing first. The required port stayed tiny, but the protocol grew a lot after 2012: context cancellation, named parameters, session resets, connection validation. The Go team did not add those methods to driver.Conn, which would have broken every driver. They added separate, optional interfaces and let the core detect them at runtime.

Go 1.8 brought QueryerContext, ExecerContext, ConnBeginTx and Pinger. Go 1.9 brought NamedValueChecker. Go 1.10 brought Connector, DriverContext and SessionResetter. Go 1.15 brought Validator. An old driver that implements none of them still compiles and still works.

The detection is a type assertion with a fallback. A simplified sketch of what queryDC in sql.go does:

// simplified sketch of database/sql's queryDC
queryerCtx, ok := dc.ci.(driver.QueryerContext)
var queryer driver.Queryer
if !ok {
    queryer, ok = dc.ci.(driver.Queryer)
}
if ok {
    rows, err := ctxDriverQuery(ctx, queryerCtx,
        queryer, query, args)
    if err != driver.ErrSkip {
        return rows, err // adapter handled it
    }
}
// fallback: Prepare, Query, Close the statement

The driver package docs spell out the chain: if a Conn implements neither QueryerContext nor Queryer, DB.Query prepares the statement, runs it, and closes it. And driver.ErrSkip, whose message reads "driver: skip fast-path; continue as if unimplemented", lets an adapter say "I have this capability, but not for this particular call."

Argument checking follows the same idea. According to convert.go, the core looks for NamedValueChecker on the statement first, then on the connection, and falls back to the statement's column converter or its own default checker when neither exists or when the checker returns ErrSkip. pgx's stdlib adapter implements CheckNamedValue, ResetSession and QueryContext. A smaller driver can skip all three and still get correct behaviour from the core.

That gives you a port that can grow for a decade without a breaking change.

The pool lives in the core

The other half of the design is what adapters do not have to write. The sql.OpenDB doc comment says the returned DB "maintains its own pool of idle connections". The DB struct in that same file holds freeConn, connRequests, maxOpen, maxLifetime and maxIdleTime. Idle connections default to defaultMaxIdleConns = 2, and SetMaxOpenConns documents that "The default is 0 (unlimited)."

No driver reimplements pooling, lifetimes or waiting for a free connection. The adapter contributes hooks the core calls at the right moment. If a Conn implements Validator, the driver docs say IsValid runs before the connection goes back to the pool. If it implements SessionResetter, ResetSession runs before reuse. And driver.ErrBadConn tells the core to retry on a fresh connection, with a warning not to return it if the server might already have done the work.

Policy in the core, mechanism in the adapter. When you design your own ports, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking and pooling belong on the core side for the same reason: otherwise every adapter writes its own slightly different version.

The half you should not copy: a global registry

Now the part that breaks the hexagonal rules. In sql.go, the registry is a package-level map behind a mutex:

var driversMu sync.RWMutex
var drivers = make(map[string]driver.Driver)

Adapters are wired by import side effects into global state, not by an explicit composition root, which Mark Seemann describes as "a (preferably) unique location in an application where modules are composed together." Three costs follow from that.

First, the wiring fails at runtime, not compile time. That is the error from the top of this post: the message has to guess at the forgotten import because the compiler never sees the dependency.

Second, names collide globally. Register panics with sql: Register called twice for driver on a duplicate name. pgx works around that in its init: it registers "pgx" only if sql.Drivers() does not already contain it, and always registers "pgx/v5".

Third, the map is now hard to change. The comment above it in sql.go says it should be an internal detail, but that other packages reach into it via linkname, and asks that its type signature not change.


Side-effect registration on the left, an explicit composition root on the right.

Go 1.10 gave you the exit. sql.OpenDB takes a driver.Connector value instead of a name string, so main hands the adapter to the core directly:

// pgx is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5
// stdlib is github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib (pgx's adapter)
cfg, err := pgx.ParseConfig(os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
db := sql.OpenDB(stdlib.GetConnector(*cfg))

MySQL has the same shape through mysql.NewConnector, which the Go tutorial uses as its example. Importing the package still runs its init, so the registry entry still exists, but your code no longer depends on a magic string or on import order.

Apply the good half to your own ports

Take the three habits that aged well and leave the registry behind. Say a billing service sends notifications. The service package owns the port, a richer capability is optional, and there is always a fallback:

package billing

// Sender is the port. billing owns it.
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// BatchSender is optional. Detected, never required.
type BatchSender interface {
    SendBatch(ctx context.Context, ms []Message) error
}

func (s *Service) notifyAll(
    ctx context.Context, ms []Message,
) error {
    if bs, ok := s.sender.(BatchSender); ok {
        return bs.SendBatch(ctx, ms)
    }
    for _, m := range ms {
        if err := s.sender.Send(ctx, m); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }
    return nil
}

Retries and rate limits go in Service, not in each adapter, the same way sql.DB owns the pool. And the wiring happens in one visible place:

func main() {
    db := mustOpenDB()
    repo := postgres.NewInvoiceRepo(db)
    sender := smtp.NewSender(loadSMTPConfig())
    svc := billing.NewService(repo, sender)
    runHTTP(svc)
}

No init, no name strings, no blank imports. If you forget an adapter, the code does not compile. For tests, pass a fake Sender into NewService, which is exactly the isolation Cockburn's 2005 write-up was after.

Next time you type import _ for a database driver, read it as the stdlib showing you the pattern, and the one place it cut a corner. Wire your own adapters in main.

If this was useful

database/sql gets the port and the capability detection right, and gets the wiring wrong. Hexagonal Architecture in Go works through both halves for your own services: where ports live in the package layout, how persistence adapters stay behind them, and how to build a composition root in main that the compiler can check. If the billing example above looks like the direction you want your codebase to go, that book is the long version of it.

title: Zoom your landing page to 200% before you ship it: a two-minute check
description:
Most of us check a landing page at the size of our own screen. Plenty of visitors don't see it that way: they zoom in, use a larger default font, or browse on a small window. Here is a short check that catches the most common breakage.

The check

  1. Open the page in a desktop browser.
  2. Press Ctrl and + (Cmd and + on a Mac) until you reach 200%.
  3. Scroll the whole page, top to bottom.
  4. Zoom further, to 400%, and scroll again.

Two WCAG success criteria cover this:

  • 1.4.4 Resize Text: text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow: content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without scrolling in two dimensions, at a width of 320 CSS pixels. W3C notes that this is the same as a 1280 pixel wide window at 400% zoom. Parts that need a two-dimensional layout, such as data tables, maps and diagrams, are an exception. A single column is a common way to meet it, but the requirement is the lack of sideways scrolling and of lost content, not a specific layout.

What usually breaks

  • Fixed-height hero sections. If the hero has height: 600px, big text spills over the next section. Use min-height instead.
  • Text that gets clipped. Buttons or cards with a fixed width and overflow: hidden cut off labels. Let them grow.
  • A sticky header that eats the screen. At 200%, a tall fixed header can cover half the viewport. Check that you can still reach the content under it.
  • Sideways scrolling. Usually one wide element, like a pricing table or a code block, pushes the page past the viewport. Wrap it in its own scroll area.
  • Font sizes in px. If someone sets a larger default font in their browser, px text ignores it. Using rem for body text respects it.

A quick way to find the culprit

If the page scrolls sideways, run this in the console to list elements wider than the window:

[...document.querySelectorAll('*')].filter(
  (el) => el.getBoundingClientRect().right > document.documentElement.clientWidth
);

The first few results are normally the cause.

One fix worth making today

Swap fixed heights on text containers for min-height, and change one body font size from px to rem. Both are small edits and both help at any zoom level.

What's the first thing that broke when you zoomed one of your own pages?

title: We changed one word in a prompt and broke a feature nobody was watching
description:
The change was one word in a system prompt. "Concise" became "brief." The diff was a single line. What broke: a summarization feature that our team judged by vibes — read the output, seems fine, ship it — had started omitting a detail that mattered, and three weeks passed before anyone noticed. Nobody was to blame individually. There was just no mechanism in place that could catch it, because we treated prompts like config when they behave like code.

30-second takeaway

  • 3-week bug discovery window collapsed to 60 seconds with prompt regression guards
  • "Concise" vs "brief" — one-word diff → feature silently broke for 8% of users (my own users)
  • Prompts are code: same regression-test arguments apply, and almost nobody I know actually gates them in CI (my own observation, not a measured rate)
  • CI-native: eval gates run where ships already get gated, no manual checklists

(Confession: I changed one word in a system prompt — "concise" to "brief" — and a summarization feature silently degraded for 8% of users (my own users). Nobody noticed for three weeks. Three weeks! I treated prompts like config when they behave like code. Same arrogance, different medium.)

(Caveat: your eval set is only as good as the cases you pick. Ship broken tests = ship broken prompt. And eval sets drift too — revisit them quarterly.)

Prompts are code without a test suite

Every argument for regression testing applies to prompts: changes have non-local effects, behavior varies across inputs you didn't test, and "it seems fine on the two examples I tried" is exactly the confidence level that produces three-week-late bug reports. But most teams' prompt testing process is a human squinting at a handful of outputs — slow, inconsistent, and not something that runs before every ship.

Eval checklists instead of vibes

TestPilot turns prompt testing into a repeatable gate: paste your prompt and the expected behavior, get an eval checklist and a version regression guard — so "brief" vs "concise" gets compared across a real set of cases before it ships, not discovered by users after. It's aimed at dev and QA teams shipping LLM-powered features, with CI integration so the check runs where ships already get gated, and version compare so you can see what actually changed when you touched the prompt.

The version-compare framing matters. The unit of change in an LLM app is the prompt+model+params combination, and "what did this change affect" is only answerable if you can diff behavior across versions, not just diff the text.

The realistic version of this practice

Full honesty about costs: building an eval set is real work, the checklist you define is only as good as your understanding of what the feature should do, and LLM outputs are probabilistic — expect some eval noise, and design thresholds with that in mind rather than demanding perfect determinism. Start embarrassingly small: ten cases that capture what "correct" means for your feature, including the inputs that broke it before. Ten good cases beat a hundred mediocre ones, and the set grows every time reality surprises you.

What it is not

It doesn't score abstract "quality" — it checks the behaviors you specify, which means the hard part (deciding what correct looks like) stays with you. It won't catch biases or failure modes absent from your case set. And CI integration gates what you run it against; a feature with no eval cases has no guard, just the vibes you started with.

The one-feature start

Pick the single LLM feature whose silent failure would embarrass you most. Write down what it must always do and must never do. Turn that into ten test cases, and run the next prompt change against them in TestPilot before it ships. Free to try — and if the first regression it catches pays for the hour you spent, that's the moment prompt testing stops being an idea and becomes a habit.

title: Easy Full Stack Authentication and Login in the Style of Spring
description:
Three requests leave your app just as its access token expires. If each refreshes independently, the first exchange can invalidate the refresh token the other two are about to use. A login feature becomes a race between requests.

What is Codename One? Codename One is an open-source framework for building native iOS, Android, desktop, and web apps from a single Java or Kotlin codebase. Learn more at codenameone.com.

This week's security work joins the Codename One client and backend around those transitions. The client can coordinate renewal, the server can rotate tokens, and tests can verify what happens after a real request is refused.

Put the access rule beside the route

The backend has Spring-style security chains under com.codename1.backend.security. A chain chooses which requests it handles, then authenticates and authorizes them. This excerpt from the security guide example protects an API using JWT scopes:

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) {
    http.securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .sessionManagement(session ->
            session.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
    return http.build();
}

Configure the trusted issuer and the audience your API expects. The guide's configuration keys include cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri and cn1.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences. Audience checking is optional unless configured, so set it deliberately when several services share an issuer.

A backend with no SecurityFilterChain bean has no security layer. Adding a dependency does not secure the routes. A stateless chain also has no CSRF filter unless you request one. Session-based browser applications have a different threat model and need the corresponding session and CSRF configuration.

Method rules such as @PreAuthorize are compiled into checks. They can apply to self-calls and private methods because the build weaves them into the method, rather than relying on calls passing through a runtime proxy. The expression language is a supported subset; ACLs, @PostAuthorize and arbitrary expression evaluation are outside it.

Give the client one owner for renewal

Register an installed app as a public OAuth client with an exact redirect URI and PKCE. A client secret embedded in an app would not remain secret. After configuring OidcClient, install an authorizer for the API base URL:

OidcRequestAuthorizer authorizer =
        new OidcRequestAuthorizer(client).install("https://api.example.com/v1");
authorizer.addSignInRequiredListener((source, reason) -> showSignIn());
authorizer.load().ready(saved -> {
    if (saved == null) {
        showSignIn();
    } else {
        showNotes();
    }
});

This is an application excerpt: client is configured with your provider and token store; showSignIn() and showNotes() are your UI methods. Use SecureStorageTokenStore for platform-protected persistence. Plain storage fallback is an explicit option, not something the app should silently enable to make an error disappear.

The authorizer matches the scheme, host and port, then whole path segments. /v1 includes /v1/notes, but not /v10. It covers ordinary ConnectionRequest calls, the REST builder and generated clients through the network layer.

Renewal starts before expiry by default. Requests queued during the exchange wait for its result. If a token-bearing request receives 401, the authorizer can refresh and retry it once; the caller receives the eventual response. A refused refresh ends the session, clears stored tokens and calls the sign-in listener. If your request writes a body from a stream, verify that your implementation can supply it again before depending on a retry.

For redirects followed by Codename One, the token is removed outside the registered origin or path. The current iOS port lets the system follow redirects before application code sees them. Keep protected API redirects within hosts you control; do not infer that every transport has the same redirect interception point.

Choose the state your deployment can share

The backend includes form login, HTTP Basic, API keys, JWT resource servers, OAuth login and authorization-server support. MFA includes TOTP and recovery codes; passkey endpoints use WebAuthn. These are separate mechanisms with separate configuration, not one switch that makes every deployment secure.

Several instances cannot share an in-memory token repository or rate limiter. Declare the database-backed stores when that is your deployment shape. cn1.security.schema.enabled=true belongs in the module's build-time application.properties; it registers the security migrations. It creates tables, but does not select JDBC stores for you.

Refresh tokens and one-use codes must be consumed atomically. Otherwise two instances can both accept the same secret. The JDBC implementations use conditional database operations and their affected-row counts for those decisions. TOTP secrets are sealed under the configured encryption key; password hashes and one-use recovery codes have their own storage rules.

The packaged server links the mechanisms its chains reach. A token-verifying API need not carry login pages and a password store. That is a useful consequence of explicit configuration and dead-code removal, although it does not reduce the need to review the rules you enabled.

Test the failure after the successful login

The end-to-end client tests connect to the HelloCodenameOne backend. BackendTokenRefreshTest deliberately replaces an access token with one the server did not sign. It checks that the generated client receives one successful response after renewal, that the refresh token rotates, and that reusing a spent refresh token ends the session.

That proves more than a mock that always supplies an authenticated user. It exercises the client's networking and token state together with the server's token endpoint and protected route.

Test layer What it can establish What it does not establish
Backend MockMvc and mock identities Route and method authorization decisions A provider login or signature verification when identity is injected
Native client integration tests Requests, token exchange, renewal and denial against the backend Every external identity provider or device sign-in surface
Browser-specific tests Browser networking and credential APIs, including the virtual-authenticator vault test Passing the native credential/redirect harness unchanged
Port test matrix The declared cases on each supported target Every security mechanism on every port

The credential/redirect tests explicitly report a browser skip because the browser owns those cookies and redirects. A green port suite must be read with those skips. WebAuthn PRF bridge coverage uses Chromium's virtual authenticator; it is not a claim that every hardware authenticator supports that extension.

SAML, LDAP, opaque-token introspection and several authorization-server extensions are outside this release. The backend security guide and client identity guide specify the supported surface. PR #5961 connects those pieces; tomorrow we will look at the migrations underneath their persistent stores.

Discussion

Which failure is hardest to reproduce in your sign-in flow: renewal, revocation, or returning from the provider?

title: Why I Want My AI Coding Assistant to Ask Before It Acts
description:
Most AI coding tools are built around one promise: speed. Type a prompt, get code, move on.

But after a while I noticed the speed was costing me something. The AI would edit files I didn't expect, delete things I still needed, or run a command I hadn't read. I'd spend the next hour undoing work I never approved.

The problem with "just do it" AI

When an AI agent has full permission to write, delete, and execute, every action is a small act of trust you didn't explicitly give. For a throwaway script that's fine. For a real codebase it's not.

The failure mode isn't dramatic. It's quiet:

  • A helper function gets "cleaned up" and something subtle breaks
  • A config file gets rewritten with slightly different values
  • A dependency gets bumped and nothing works the next morning

What I actually want

I want an assistant that treats my codebase like it belongs to someone else. That means:

  1. Ask before writing. Show me the change, let me approve it.
  2. Show diffs, not summaries. "I updated the auth logic" tells me nothing. A diff tells me everything.
  3. Checkpoint every step. If step 4 was wrong, I want to rewind to step 3 — not start over.
  4. Ask before running commands. A shell command is the most powerful thing an agent can do. It should be the most gated.

The trade-off is worth it

Yes, this is slower per action. But it's dramatically faster per outcome, because I'm not spending my afternoon fixing things I never agreed to.

If you're on Windows and want an AI editor that works this way, that's the idea behind Arcwright — it's free to start. But the principle applies to whatever tool you use: the AI should earn your trust one approved change at a time.

title: My Q4 model said True where BF16 said False, so I diffed them layer by layer
description:
Qwen3-0.6B in BF16 reads this:

def is_prime(n):
    if n < 2:
        return

and puts 97.9% on False. The Q4_K_M quant of the same model puts 79.1% on True.

That's one token out of 1,282 I scored. Across the whole text, Q4_K_M changes the top token at 11.6% of positions, its mean KL from BF16 is 0.067, and perplexity goes from 7.83 to 8.53. Those numbers tell you the quant drifted. They don't tell you where: which tokens, which layers, which block inside a layer, or whether the weights are even the main cause compared with the KV cache or the batch size.

I built heterodyne to answer that.

zaydmulani09 / heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, and move activations between them to test which layers, and which attention or MLP blocks, carry the divergence. Local, CPU, no API keys.

heterodyne

Diff two llama.cpp runs token by token and layer by layer, then move activations between them to test which layers' divergence actually reaches the output.

A quantized GGUF, a quantized KV cache, a different batch size, a fine-tune: each changes what your model says, and the usual answer to "how much, and where?" is one aggregate number. heterodyne runs two configurations of llama.cpp (two arms: a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers) on identical tokens and shows:

  • where the outputs differ: exact full-vocabulary KL(A‖B) and top-1 changes at every position, next to a measured numerical floor;
  • where inside the network the difference appears: the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • which layers carry it to the output: activation transplants that write one arm's residual stream into the other, layer by layer, in llama.cpp's own numerics;
  • attention or MLP…
View on GitHub

Why not the usual interpretability tools

TransformerLens, nnsight and the rest run PyTorch. But on CPU, llama.cpp quantizes the activations to 8 bits before every quantized matrix multiply. A PyTorch model with dequantized weights is a different model from the GGUF you actually run. And llama.cpp's own llama-perplexity --kl-divergence reports aggregates only.

So heterodyne works inside llama.cpp, in the same kernels you deploy.

Two arms, same tokens

An arm is a GGUF file plus the runtime settings that can change its numbers: K and V cache types, flash attention, ubatch size. heterodyne runs arm A and arm B on identical tokens, chunk by chunk, and records:

  • exact KL(A‖B) over the full vocabulary at every position, summed in f64 from raw logits, plus every top-1 change and how confident it was;
  • a numerical floor: arm A re-run with an odd batch split, as a yardstick for how big harmless differences get on this machine;
  • the residual stream of both arms after every layer;
  • transplants (next section);
  • optionally, every combination of the settings that differ, to attribute the change to one of them.

Everything is saved as an experiment file with provenance (GGUF hashes, llama.cpp commit, build flags) and an integrity hash. heterodyne verify re-runs it and compares every stored number exactly.

The hook

llama.cpp's scheduler accepts an eval callback, cb_eval. When it's set, the scheduler asks for each graph node "do you want this tensor?" and, if you say yes, computes everything up to that node, synchronizes, and hands you the data before anything downstream runs.

A small C++ shim uses that moment to either copy the tensor out or overwrite it. Every consumer of a node comes after it in topological order, so an overwrite is seen by everything downstream. Tensors are addressed by graph name: l_out-N is the residual stream after layer N, ffn_inp-N the residual between layer N's attention and its MLP. The shim counts rows per ubatch and checks that every row of every hooked tensor was seen, so a missing name is an error, not silent zeros. Rust only sees structs I define, so a llama.cpp update can't silently shift a field under the FFI.

Transplants

Denoise: run B, but write A's l_out-N into it, and measure KL(A‖patched B). Noise: the reverse. Do it at every layer and you get a curve. For Q4_K_M vs BF16:

layer   0      4      8      12     16     20     24     26     27
KL    0.062  0.052  0.038  0.029  0.021  0.013  0.006  0.004  0.0013

It falls steadily over all 28 layers: no single layer carries the divergence. The 0.0013 left after the last layer is what the final norm and output head add on their own.

At the is_prime token, writing BF16's residual into Q4_K_M brings that token's KL from 0.48 after layer 6 down to 0.04 after layer 9, and writing Q4_K_M's residual into BF16 reproduces the flip from about layer 12. At that token, the decisive difference forms in layers 6 to 12.

New: attention or MLP?

The obvious way to split a layer is to write A's MLP output into B. The problem: that also erases the MLP's reaction to every difference upstream, so a block with identical weights in both arms can still look responsible.

So heterodyne restores A's whole residual at two points per layer, after attention (ffn_inp-N) and after the MLP (l_out-N), and takes the steps between consecutive points. Attention's share at layer N is the KL with A restored at the layer's input minus the KL with A restored after attention; the MLP's is the next step. The steps telescope: summed over all layers they equal the untouched KL minus what's left after the last layer, so nothing is counted twice.

There's a check with a known answer. If two arms differ only in K-cache type, only attention reads the K cache, so every MLP step must be exactly zero. The tests check that bitwise, and it holds on Qwen3 too.

12 chunks, 1,282 scored positions, 95% intervals over chunks:

attention MLP
restoring BF16 in Q4_K_M (of 0.067) removes 0.030 (0.019–0.041) removes 0.036 (0.024–0.048)
injecting Q4_K_M into BF16 adds 0.026 (0.021–0.031) adds 0.040 (0.028–0.051)

Restoring BF16, the paired difference is 0.006 (−0.011 to 0.022): it spans zero, and attention's part ranges from 20% to 82% across chunks, so on this text the two can't be told apart. Injecting Q4_K_M, the MLPs add more (0.014, 0.005 to 0.023). The largest single step is layer 0's attention, but llama.cpp doesn't name layer 0's input, so that bar also holds any difference in the token embeddings. A few steps are negative (layer 2's attention, −0.0014): restoring that block alone left Q4_K_M further from BF16.

It costs two more passes per layer per chunk; the 12-chunk run took 29 minutes on a laptop i7-1355U.

Other things it turned up

All on Qwen3-0.6B, same text, same laptop:

B mean KL top-1 changed perplexity (BF16: 7.83)
Q8_0 0.0022 2.2% 7.83
UD-Q4_K_XL 0.058 11.3% 8.33
Q4_K_M 0.067 11.6% 8.53
Q3_K_M 0.214 20.8% 9.47
Q2_K 0.780 36.3% 16.75
  • The KV cache matters more than you'd think. Same Q8_0 file twice, B with a q8_0 K and V cache: KL 0.0038. That's further than quantizing the weights from BF16 to Q8_0 (0.0022).
  • llama.cpp's CPU path isn't batch-invariant at every size. With flash attention off, Q4_K_M output was bitwise identical at ubatch sizes that are multiples of 4 and changed at others (ubatch 63: 4.7% of top tokens). The repacked K-quant matmul quantizes activation rows in groups of 4 and sends the remainder down a separate path. That's why heterodyne's numerical floor uses an odd split.

What this is and isn't

  • One small model, one text, one machine. Intervals are 95% t-intervals with a cluster-robust standard error over chunks, because tokens within a chunk are correlated.
  • Transplants are interventions on your input. They say where restoring one model's activations removes the divergence on that text, not which block's weights quantize worse in general.
  • CPU only. GPU kernels compute differently, and nothing here says anything about them yet.

Try it

Grab a binary from the releases (Linux, Windows, macOS arm64) and run:

heterodyne serve --models ~/models

or from the command line:

heterodyne diff --a Qwen3-0.6B-BF16.gguf --b Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --text-file examples/corpus.txt --chunk 128 --max-chunks 12 --components

The experiment files behind every number here are in examples/. If you run it on a bigger model or different prompts, I'd love to see what you get.

title: Anatomy of a Paid AI Video Job: What Happens Between Upload and MP4
description:
A walkthrough of the lifecycle behind a two-photo trend video generator: validation, quotes, credit holds, async rendering and data expiry.

Consumer AI video looks like a single button: upload photos, get a clip. Behind that button sits a long-running, paid, failure-prone job, and most of the product work goes into making that job predictable for someone who just wants a funny video of their friends.

This post follows one job through AIHotelLobby.win, a single-purpose tool that recasts the Hotel Lobby trend video with two uploaded portraits. It makes a good example because its public guides, help page, terms and privacy policy spell out every stage, from upload checks to how long each file lives. Everything below is based on those pages; the snippets are simplified sketches of the behavior they describe.

Stage 1: Reject bad input before anything expensive happens

A GPU minute costs far more than a file check, so the cheapest quality control is at the upload box. Each photo has to be a JPG, PNG or WebP, at least 512 × 512 pixels and no larger than 10 MB, showing one clearly visible adult.

const ACCEPTED = ['image/jpeg', 'image/png', 'image/webp'];
const MAX_BYTES = 10 * 1024 * 1024;

function checkPhoto(type: string, bytes: number, w: number, h: number): string | null {
  if (!ACCEPTED.includes(type)) return 'Use a JPG, PNG or WebP image';
  if (bytes > MAX_BYTES) return 'Keep the file under 10 MB';
  if (w < 512 || h < 512) return 'Use an image at least 512 × 512 pixels';
  return null;
}

Two details worth noting. Metadata is stripped when the images are prepared, which removes location data people forget their phones attach. And the docs are explicit that these checks only cover the file: they do not verify identity, age or consent. Being honest about what validation can't do is part of the design.

Stage 2: Keep the draft alive through the login wall

Users can pick both photos, assign left and right, and choose length and sound before creating an account. The draft is kept on the device while they sign in, so the login wall doesn't throw away their work. Signing out clears it.

This is a conversion detail as much as a technical one. The moment someone is asked to sign in is the moment they are most likely to leave, and making them redo the upload afterwards doubles that risk.

Stage 3: Quote first, then hold the credits

After sign-in, the photos upload privately and the server returns a quote: length, format and credit cost. Prices are fixed per length (5 seconds is 30 credits, 10 is 50 and 15 is 70), and the quote is pinned to the task.

type Quote = {
  durationSeconds: 5 | 10 | 15;
  aspect: '16:9';
  audio: 'original' | 'silent';
  credits: 30 | 50 | 70;
  configRevision: string; // the model, template and price recorded for this task
};

The terms make the pinning explicit: prices and models can change for new requests, but an existing task keeps the provider, settings and price recorded in its quote. Confirming the quote reserves the credits. They are captured only after a valid video has been stored, and released if the task definitively fails. Buying credits is a separate flow and never starts a job by itself.

Stage 4: Hand off to the model, then let the user leave

The configured model is Kling 3.0 Omni, accessed through KIE as the API provider. (A second model, Seedance 2.0 Mini, is integrated but not enabled for customers.) The provider receives the two photos, the reference video and the instructions for that task.

From here everything is asynchronous. The published examples list render times from about three to seven and a half minutes, which is far too long to hold a browser tab hostage. The user can close the page; the task keeps running and shows up in My videos on any device signed in to the same account.

The hard case is a timeout during submission: the provider may or may not have accepted the job. Releasing the credits risks giving away a video that will finish anyway; capturing them risks charging for nothing. The answer here is a holding state:

type Job =
  | { state: 'reserved' }
  | { state: 'running' }
  | { state: 'needs_review' } // submission outcome unknown; credits stay held
  | { state: 'completed'; videoKey: string } // credits captured
  | { state: 'failed' }; // confirmed failure; credits released

The page on credits and task recovery tells users what this means for them: losing the connection does not stop generation, an uncertain task keeps its credits reserved while it is checked, and they should follow that same task rather than start a duplicate. Credit returns and cash refunds are also kept separate, which saves a lot of support confusion.

Stage 5: Deliver briefly, then delete

Personal photos are a liability the moment you no longer need them, and the retention schedule reflects that:

Data How long it stays
Validated photos never submitted for a task 24 hours
Photos needed by an active or uncertain task Up to 48 hours
Task inputs after the task reaches a final state Scheduled to expire within 24 hours
Finished videos 7 days
A download link 5 minutes

Downloads use short-lived signed links. Deleting a file stops new links from being issued, though a link already handed out can work until it expires, and the privacy policy says so plainly. It also notes that provider copies and backups follow their own schedules, which is the kind of caveat most products leave out.

What's worth copying

  • Validate cheaply, and say what validation can't check.
  • Let the draft survive authentication.
  • Pin the quote to the task, so a price or model change never rewrites a job already in flight.
  • Model the unknown state explicitly instead of guessing between refund and charge.
  • Publish retention times as numbers, not "as long as necessary".

None of this is specific to trend videos. Any product that runs a slow, paid job on someone's personal media faces the same five stages, and users notice when one of them is handled carelessly.

AIHotelLobby.win is an independent service. It is not an official Kling, Seedance or KIE product and is not affiliated with the artists behind "Hotel Lobby". Details come from its public pages as of October 18, 2026.

title: AI Gateway logs now show session affinity
description:
AI Gateway logs now have a Sessions view that groups requests into sessions and shows how session affinity routed each one. Each row shows the coding agent or app that ran the session, such as Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor, along with its cost, models, providers, and how much of its input was cached across every turn.

Open a session to see its cache hit rate, duration, and path. The path lists each turn with its model and timing, and names the provider serving the session along with any earlier ones. Session affinity sends each turn to the provider that served the one before it, so the provider already has most of the prompt in cache. A session that stays on one provider reads more of each prompt from cache.

Filter sessions by turns, client, model, provider, authentication, or cost. Single-turn sessions are hidden until you clear the minimum turns filter.

Session affinity runs by default on text and chat requests. To group requests yourself, send the same sessionId in providerOptions.gateway, or the same x-session-id header, on every request in a conversation. Requests without one are grouped by a fingerprint of the conversation's opening and appear as fingerprinted sessions.

Read the session affinity documentation for more information on how AI Gateway identifies sessions.

title: The build went green because it stopped checking
description:
A teammate deleted a test file on a Friday. Not on purpose. The suite still passed. The pipeline still went green. Nobody noticed for three weeks.

Here's the part that should bother you. Nothing in that green was a lie. Zero tests failed. True statement. Also worthless, because the number that mattered was the one nobody printed: how many tests ran.

Most CI tells you pass or fail. Almost none tell you nothing was checked. A suite that collects zero tests exits clean in more setups than you'd like. So you get the friendly color, the little badge, and you file it under done.

Now widen it. Every green you trust has this hole in it:

  • A health check that pings the process, not the thing the process does.
  • A monitor whose query quietly returns no rows, so the graph draws a flat happy line.
  • An alert rule that can never fire because the label it filters on stopped existing.
  • A backup job that runs every night, exits 0, and writes an empty file.

None of these will page you. All of them will let you sleep. That's the whole problem. The failure mode isn't red. It's a green that stopped being a claim and turned into decoration.

So the question I keep losing arguments about: what did you actually check, and when did you last check that the check was still checking?

Green has never meant "it works." Green means "nothing failed." Only one of those is a fact about your code. The other is a fact about your test runner.

I'll take an honest red over a green that says nothing. But I'd rather have neither than a green I never verified.

A whale walked out of the ocean and onto the open web. The first thing he learned is that on land, everyone loves a green light and nobody reads the bulb.

title: LLMs on Consumer Hardware — Part 6: The Orchestration Ceiling — Why a Bigger Coordinator Doesn't Fix the Loop
description:
Part 6 of a series. Previously: Part 5 — Distributing the Workers and the Memory Budget.

Part 5 ended with the 77 GB coordinator finally running as it should — resident, no thrashing, the memory problem resolved by moving the workers to a second machine. That made it possible to answer a question Part 4 had deferred: now that the big model can actually run, does a bigger coordinator fix orchestration? The answer was no, and the reason reshaped how the team was run.

The ceiling persists on the big model

With memory no longer the bottleneck, the coordinator's orchestration could be judged on its own merits. It sequenced delegations more reliably than Gemma had — but it did not escape the same failure modes. On longer plans it still dropped steps, issuing some delegations and silently omitting others before writing its summary. It still, on occasion, emitted a delegation as text rather than executing it — Part 4 showed one such case, a hand-off printed as raw JSON and then abandoned. And it periodically returned nothing at all after a tool call, requiring an automatic nudge to continue:

⚠ Model returned empty after tool calls — nudging to continue

That warning recurred often enough to be diagnostic. These were not the mistakes of a weak model; they were the mistakes of a capable model asked to do something it is structurally poor at — hold a long control loop in its head while also doing the reasoning inside it.

The diagnosis: the ceiling is the loop, not the model

The decisive observation was that all three failure modes — dropped steps, commands narrated instead of executed, empty turns — appeared on the large model exactly as they had on the small one. The common factor was not model size. It was the agentic loop itself.

Asking a language model to orchestrate is asking it to be, simultaneously, the planner that decides the steps, the dispatcher that issues each delegation, the bookkeeper that tracks which delegations are still outstanding, and the evaluator that judges the results as they return. That is a great deal of state to carry across many turns, and carrying state across turns is precisely what these models are weakest at. A bigger model raises the ceiling a little; it does not remove it.

The fix: take the loop away from the model

If the loop is the problem, the loop should not be the model's job. The resolution was deterministic orchestration: a small script owns the control loop. It holds the list of tasks, dispatches each delegation, waits for and collects the result, and decides what runs next. The model is invoked only for the two things it is genuinely good at — planning (what are the steps?) and evaluating (is this result acceptable?) — and never has to remember what it has already dispatched, because the script does that.

The improvement was immediate and measurable. A task sequence that the model-driven loop had stalled on partway through — completing three of five steps before losing the thread — ran all five to completion when the same plan was executed by the script. The model had not become more capable. It had simply been relieved of the one job it could not reliably do.

The lesson

The instinct, when an agent loop is unreliable, is to reach for a bigger model. That instinct was wrong here, and expensively so — it was the reasoning behind the whole coordinator search of Part 4, and the memory wall of Part 5, and in the end it did not solve the problem it was chasing. Orchestration reliability is not a model capability that can be bought in larger quantities; it is a property of how the loop is structured. The durable fix was architectural: move the deterministic part — the loop, the bookkeeping, the dispatch — into deterministic code, and reserve the model for the parts that genuinely require judgment. A control loop is a job for a program, not for a language model, and the sooner that division is drawn the more reliable the system becomes.

What follows

Deterministic orchestration made the team's execution reliable: a plan was now carried out without dropped steps or invented progress. But it did nothing for the moment a plan meets a wall — when the right next step is not in the plan at all, and someone has to rethink the approach rather than merely execute it. Reliable execution and good judgment are different capabilities, and the next entry is about supplying the second without compromising the first.
