title: AWS Transform Now Automates Azure-to-AWS Cloud-Native Code Conversion
description:
Originally published on PkLavc.

Confirmed facts

On October 16, 2026, AWS announced the general availability of Azure-to-AWS SDK code conversion in AWS Transform, a feature designed to automate migration of Microsoft Azure cloud-native .NET applications to AWS.

The service identifies Azure service code within submitted .NET source code and converts it to equivalent AWS SDK calls, validating that changes are incorporated into the transformed output.

AWS Transform is available in eight AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney), Canada (Central), and Europe (Frankfurt, London).

Conversion support includes Azure Functions to AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage to Amazon S3, and Azure Queue Storage to Amazon SQS. Azure Cosmos DB to Amazon DynamoDB conversion is available in preview status.

Technical analysis

The feature operates through an assessment phase where AWS Transform discovers Azure SDK usage in the submitted codebase, presenting conversion options in both an assessment report and modernization plan. Developers can accept these options or modify them before execution.

This approach addresses a significant engineering challenge in cross-cloud application modernization by automating what was previously manual code refactoring. The service's ability to translate service calls between cloud providers reduces migration complexity for .NET applications leveraging serverless and storage services.

The regional availability across eight AWS Regions suggests the service is designed for global enterprise use, though the announcement does not disclose processing requirements, data residency handling, or transformation accuracy metrics. The preview status of Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion indicates ongoing refinement of that specific mapping.

  • Supported conversions: Azure Functions → AWS Lambda, Azure Blob Storage → Amazon S3, Azure Queue Storage → Amazon SQS

  • Cosmos DB to DynamoDB conversion is in preview

  • Service requires .NET application source code submission for analysis

title: TIL: GBase Database Default Character Set Can Cause Chinese Text Issues
description:
I recently ran into a character encoding issue while testing GBase Database (GBase 8s). The installation completed successfully, and the database was running normally. However, when I inserted Chinese text, the characters did not display as expected.

The problem wasn't necessarily the SQL statement or the application. It could be related to the database locale and character encoding configuration.

Why Does This Happen?

A typical GBase Database installation is designed to help users get an instance running quickly. However, its default locale settings may not be suitable for every language requirement.

For example, an environment using en_US.8859-1 may not be appropriate for an application that needs to store and process Chinese text.

Character encoding issues can occur when the database locale, client locale, and application encoding are incompatible. Depending on the configuration, symptoms may include garbled Chinese characters, conversion errors, or unexpected text output.

The important lesson is that a successful installation does not guarantee that the default character set meets your application's requirements.

Step 1: Check the Locale Configuration

Before changing anything, check the relevant environment variables:

echo "$DB_LOCALE"
echo "$CLIENT_LOCALE"

These commands show the values currently set in your shell. Keep in mind that they do not independently confirm the actual locale of an existing database.

You should also verify the database's locale configuration and check which locale values are supported by your GBase Database installation.

Step 2: Set the Locale Before Creating a Database

If you're setting up a new database, one approach is to configure the appropriate environment variables before creating it.

For example:

export DB_LOCALE=<supported_chinese_locale>
export CLIENT_LOCALE=<compatible_client_locale>

Replace the placeholders with locale values supported by your installation and compatible with your application. A value such as zh_CN.utf8 may be worth evaluating, but do not assume it is available or appropriate for every environment.

After setting the variables, create the database using the intended locale configuration.

Then test the complete workflow:

  • Insert Chinese text.
  • Query the stored text.
  • Confirm that the results display correctly in your client.
  • Verify that your application uses compatible encoding settings.

This approach is particularly useful when preparing a new development or test environment because you can establish the required locale before creating the database.

Step 3: Recreate the Database if Its Locale Is Unsuitable

What if the database has already been created with an unsuitable locale?

In some situations, recreating the database with the correct configuration is a practical solution, especially for a test instance that contains no important data.

The general process is:

  1. Back up any data that needs to be retained.
  2. Confirm the supported locale values and required configuration.
  3. Set the relevant environment variables.
  4. Create a new database with the intended locale.
  5. Restore or migrate the required data.
  6. Test Chinese text insertion, retrieval, and application compatibility.

Important: Changing environment variables alone does not automatically change the locale or character set of an existing database. If the database contains production data, plan the migration carefully and verify whether data conversion is required.

Step 4: Verify the Entire Encoding Path

Even after creating the database with the intended locale, don't stop at checking a single environment variable.

Confirm that the following components work together:

  • Database locale: Determines the database's locale and character-handling behavior.
  • Client locale: Affects how the client handles character data exchanged with the database.
  • Application encoding: Must be compatible with the data being sent and received.
  • Terminal or display settings: Can affect how text appears when viewed through command-line tools.

Testing both insertion and retrieval is important. Text that looks correct in one tool may still display incorrectly in another if their encoding configurations differ.

Final Takeaway

GBase Database (GBase 8s) makes it convenient to get an instance running, but default installation settings aren't necessarily suitable for every application.

If your application needs Chinese text, check the locale configuration early. For a new database, setting the appropriate environment variables before creation may be sufficient. If an existing database uses an unsuitable locale, recreating it and migrating the data may be necessary.

A few minutes spent validating the locale can save hours of troubleshooting later.

Have you encountered Chinese character encoding issues in GBase Database? Did you solve them by adjusting environment variables, recreating the database, or changing your client configuration? Share your experience in the comments.

title: Meet Minty: An AI Assistant That Runs an Entire Video Studio From a Chat
description:
Most AI video apps have a chat bolted on that answers questions about the app. Minty is the opposite: she is the way in. Every feature of ReelMint, the studio, the publisher, the bots, the live shows, can be run by telling her what you want in plain words. We build the product, and this is how she works and why we made the sign-in land on her instead of a dashboard.

What talking to her looks like

"Make a 10-second clip of a puppy running through autumn leaves, then post it to my YouTube Shorts at 6 pm." She picks a model, shows the price, asks for approval, generates, and schedules the post. If something is missing, she asks one question with quick answers rather than a form. If you say "use the cheapest model", she does.

The feed shows cards, not walls of text: a tool row for each thing she ran, a question card, a library picker when she needs a file, a job card that updates until the video is done, and an approval card before anything that spends.

The approval card is the point

Nothing in the chat spends credits without a card that says what it will cost and a button that says Approve. That one rule is why we trust her with a credit balance. You can tell her to go ahead with a whole plan, but each spend is still visible, named and priced before it happens.

What she can run

  • Text to video, image to video, video to video, anime, talking photos, images, image edits, music, speech, voice cloning.
  • Multi-scene films with a consistent cast, written from one line.
  • Publishing and scheduling to TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Facebook and X, with a caption per platform.
  • Bots: she can quote a daily bot, say the monthly figure out loud, and save it paused.
  • Mint Moments: photos in, a scored film out.
  • Mint Live: a character goes live on YouTube or TikTok, hosted in its own voice.
  • Tutorials: ask how something works and she plays the one-minute video in the chat.

Characters by name

Type @ and the cast you have built appears. Click a chip and you get the character's looks, the voice attached with a play button, and the rest of the cast to swap in. "Film @mara reading the weather, in the kitchen look" is a complete instruction.

What she will not do

She does not talk about plans or billing; that lives on the plans page where the numbers are. She does not spend without the card. And she tells you when a model refused a prompt and why, instead of retrying silently.

Why sign-in lands on her

We used to land people on a library or a studio with forty controls. Sign-ups went up and first videos did not. Landing on a chat that opens with "Mint it. Connect. Post it everywhere." and the three steps to do it moved more people to a first finished video than any onboarding tour. A new account can also claim 27 finished creations for free, with no card, and Minty points to them in her first message.

She also exists outside the app: the same studio is an MCP server, so Claude Code and other AI clients can drive it with the same approval rules.

title: Integrating OpenAI Function Calling with Meta WhatsApp Cloud API
description:
Traditional chatbot flows rely on static decision trees (Press 1 for Sales, Press 2 for Support). While predictable, they create severe user friction when a prospect wants a personalized answer or needs to check order status, book an appointment, or check flight updates.

By integrating OpenAI's Function Calling (Tools API) directly into your WhatsApp Cloud API webhook, your AI agent can converse naturally while executing backend API calls deterministically.

In this architecture guide, we demonstrate how to connect an LLM tool loop with WhatsApp interactive messaging.

The Function Calling Execution Loop

When a user messages on WhatsApp:

  1. Ingest Inbound Message: Webhook receives the message payload from Meta.
  2. Query Model with Tool Declarations: Pass the user's message along with defined tool schemas (e.g., check_order_status, book_demo_slot).
  3. Model Tool Decision: If the user intends to perform an action, the LLM emits a tool_calls payload instead of raw text.
  4. Execute Internal Business Logic: Run the database lookup or CRM update with the LLM's structured arguments.
  5. Synthesize Final Natural Response: Pass the tool output back to the LLM to format a friendly WhatsApp response.
  6. Dispatch WhatsApp Message: Send the formatted text or interactive button back via WhatsApp Cloud API.

Step 1: Defining the Tool Schema

Declare your functions using JSON schema:

const tools = [
  {
    type: "function",
    function: {
      name: "check_order_status",
      description: "Lookup the real-time shipping status and tracking code for an order",
      parameters: {
        type: "object",
        properties: {
          order_id: {
            type: "string",
            description: "The 6 to 8 character order tracking ID, e.g. ORD-1092"
          }
        },
        required: ["order_id"]
      }
    }
  }
];

Step 2: The Agentic Execution Function 

import OpenAI from "openai";
const openai = new OpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY });

async function handleWhatsAppAgentQuery(customerPhone, userMessage) {
  const messages = [
    { role: "system", content: "You are the helpful customer service assistant for our store on WhatsApp. Keep responses concise, warm, and mobile-friendly." },
    { role: "user", content: userMessage }
  ];

  const response = await openai.chat.completions.create({
    model: "gpt-4o-mini",
    messages: messages,
    tools: tools,
    tool_choice: "auto"
  });

  const responseMessage = response.choices[0].message;

  // Check if model decided to call a function
  if (responseMessage.tool_calls) {
    for (const toolCall of responseMessage.tool_calls) {
      if (toolCall.function.name === "check_order_status") {
        const args = JSON.parse(toolCall.function.arguments);

        // Execute real DB query
        const orderData = await queryOrderDatabase(args.order_id);

        messages.push(responseMessage);
        messages.push({
          role: "tool",
          tool_call_id: toolCall.id,
          content: JSON.stringify(orderData)
        });

        // Get final answer from LLM
        const secondResponse = await openai.chat.completions.create({
          model: "gpt-4o-mini",
          messages: messages
        });

        return secondResponse.choices[0].message.content;
      }
    }
  }

  return responseMessage.content;
}

Step 3: Guardrails and Human Agent Handoff

Even the best LLMs can misunderstand complex edge cases. In production:

  • Set strict confidence thresholds: If the user expresses frustration or asks to "talk to human", trigger an immediate handoff flag.
  • Lock session context: Store the conversation history in Redis or PostgreSQL keyed by the user's phone number with a 24-hour expiration window.

Turnkey AI Agents with AI Soul

Rather than maintaining custom OpenAI token budgets, rate limit queues, vector embeddings, and WebSocket handoffs yourself, platforms like AI Soul offer an enterprise-ready solution.

With AI Soul's WhatsApp AI Chatbot, you can train autonomous LLM agents directly on your website URL, product catalogs, and PDFs with zero code. Furthermore, AI Soul's built-in Conversational CRM provides visual Kanban deal pipelines and multi-agent shared team inboxes so your human team can intervene whenever needed.

Summary

OpenAI Function Calling transforms WhatsApp bots from simple FAQ repeaters into autonomous digital employees capable of booking appointments, qualifying B2B prospects, and recovering lost sales.

title: GitView CodeAudit: Go security reviews that never leave your laptop
description:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built

GitView CodeAudit is a security review for Go backends that runs on your laptop. A static analyzer finds the problems and collects the evidence; an open-weight model, Gemma running on Ollama, explains a finding when you ask, but it never decides one.

GitView started as my terminal tool for watching Git changes and studying Go code: call graph, data flow, SQL operations and HTTP routes, each with the evidence behind it. This week I built CodeAudit on top of those analyses.

Who would pay for it? Freelancers and small agencies that build Go APIs for clients. Clients ask for a security review before a launch, a funding round or a big customer's due diligence, and they pay for it. But that code usually comes under an NDA, and pasting it into a cloud AI tool is exactly what the contract forbids. CodeAudit lets one developer do that review on their own laptop and hand over a real deliverable: an offline HTML report with each finding, the path that reaches it, the evidence, and the reviewer's decision with its justification.

That is the side hustle: the client pays for the review, and producing it costs nothing per token.

Every finding answers the questions a client will ask:

  • Where? File, line and function.
  • Why? The rule, and the data that reaches the line, for example c.Query("q") → "... LIKE '%" + term + "%'" → db.QueryContext.
  • How is it reached? Every HTTP route that leads there, through each middleware, marking the one that authenticates.
  • How sure are we? Severity, confidence and verdict are separate fields. A possible IDOR is shown as Review Required — Authorization Not Established, never as "IDOR confirmed".
  • How do I fix it, and how do I test the fix?
  • What did we decide? Open → Investigating → Confirmed / False Positive / Accepted Risk / Fixed, with a history of every change: its date, its justification and the commit it refers to.

Demo

GitView is a local tool, so there is no deployed link: everything below runs on your machine. The repository ships a small vulnerable API, with safe variants of each case, that the tests use. You can reproduce these screenshots with it:

git clone https://github.com/Darrkkens/gitview && cd gitview && go install .   # Go 1.25
gitview audit scan --module internal/audit/testdata/app
gitview audit serve --module internal/audit/testdata/app   # opens 127.0.0.1 in the browser

A SQL injection: the route, the middleware chain and the handler lead to the query, and the inspector shows the evidence.

The same finding explained by Gemma. Each evidence ID the model cites is checked against the analysis.

A possible IDOR is a review, not a verdict. The resource ID comes from the request and the query has no owner or tenant condition, but authorization could live somewhere the static analysis cannot see.

The report you hand to the client is a single offline HTML file. It has no network access, a strict CSP, and only bounded, redacted excerpts of the code.

Code

Darrkkens / gitview

GitView

Monitor de alterações Git em tempo real no terminal. Cada arquivo modificado pode ser expandido ou recolhido individualmente, e os diffs se atualizam sozinhos. Inclui busca global nos diffs, exportação de relatórios, execução de testes, Code Flow e o Go Deep Inspector, para estudar código Go com evidências verificáveis.

go install .
gitview [opções] [diretório]
Opção Descrição
--delta Renderiza diffs com git-delta (alternável com d)
--expand Expande automaticamente arquivos novos
--interval 2s Intervalo do polling de segurança
--no-watch Desativa fsnotify e usa apenas polling
--export-dir DIR Diretório padrão dos relatórios (também GITVIEW_EXPORT_DIR)
--test-timeout 10m Tempo limite de uma execução de testes
--ascii Símbolos ASCII (também GITVIEW_ASCII=1)

Atalhos

? mostra a ajuda da tela atual.

Mouse: a roda rola o diff; clicar numa dica do rodapé (por exemplo x Exportar) equivale a pressionar a tecla; na exportação, clicar num formato, escopo ou caixa [x] escolhe ou…


View on GitHub


  • internal/audit: the rules, the taint paths, the review store, the audit diff and the report.
  • internal/audit/ai: the Ollama client, the context builder and the validator of the model's answers.

How I Built It

Static analysis first. CodeAudit has 18 deterministic rules for injection, authentication, authorization, sensitive data, configuration and dependencies. They run over analyses GitView already had: go/packages, go/types and SSA for the call graph and the data flow, the SQL operations, and the HTTP routes with their middleware chains.

  • Taint: a taint finding is the shortest path in the data flow graph from an HTTP input to a sink.
  • Sanitizers: they only count when their meaning is known. strconv.Atoi neutralizes everything and filepath.Base neutralizes paths; an arbitrary function call is not a sanitizer.
  • Checks: an if that dominates the sink and examines the value, like if !allowed(origin), turns "vulnerable" into "review", because the analyzer cannot prove the check is sufficient.
  • Authorization: a 403 only counts as authorization when the request is already authenticated. A 403 from a CORS filter is shown as a request filter instead.
  • Dependencies: they are checked only against a local copy of the Go vulnerability database (OSV format). Without one, the report says "dependencies not checked" instead of pretending, and a database older than 30 days is flagged as possibly out of date.

Gemma on Ollama, kept on a short leash.

  • Model: by default GitView picks the smallest installed Gemma model (gemma3:4b on my machine). It never downloads one, and it refuses any endpoint that is not on this machine unless you pass --ai-allow-remote.
  • Context: the context sent to the model is built from the analysis, not from a file dump. It holds the finding, its evidence, the route path and the function's code, within a budget of about 6,000 tokens. Secrets are redacted, and the repository's comments and strings go in as data, never as instructions.
  • Answer: Ollama's structured outputs (format with a JSON schema) shape the reply. Every evidence ID, file, line and symbol the model cites is validated against the context, and a citation that does not exist is shown as rejected.
  • Cache: answers are cached by context hash, model digest and prompt version.
  • No authority: the model can recommend a review state, but it cannot change one. The reviewer decides.

Being honest about the model. On my CPU-only laptop, one explanation from gemma3:4b took between three and a half and five minutes (215 s and 310 s in two runs), and gemma3:12b did not fit in the free memory. The prose is useful but not perfect; in one test the model expanded "IDOR" incorrectly. That is exactly why the model is not allowed to decide anything and why its citations are checked.

Testing without a model. The test suite never needs a real model. It runs against a simulated Ollama, including answers that cite evidence that does not exist. The fixture app has one case per rule plus its safe variant (Atoi before the query, filepath.Base, a tenant filter, an admin route that answers 403, a secure cookie…), and the test fails on any unexpected finding.

Dogfooding found my own false positives. Running CodeAudit on GitView itself flagged three "hardcoded secrets". They were descriptions like credential = "Authorization header". The rule now skips values with spaces, the fixture has that case, and the rule documents what it misses because of it: a hardcoded passphrase.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair, from the spec to the browser tests.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  • The code cannot leave. For a review under an NDA, a model I run myself is the only way AI can touch the code at all. A closed API is simply not an option here.
  • The economics work. A fixed-price review cannot absorb a per-token bill that grows with the size of the codebase. On a local model, each explanation costs electricity.
  • No lock-in. Swapping models takes one flag (--model), and the validator does not trust any model, so a better open model is a drop-in upgrade.
  • The client can audit the auditor. The investigator's prompt, the answer schema and the validator are in the repository. A client can check exactly what was sent to the model: a bounded, redacted context built from the evidence.

My First User

The first real codebase it audited was my own: the Go backend of a production SaaS I maintain, with 134 HTTP routes. The whole analysis took about a second and a half, and CodeAudit reported 16 findings, none of them a confirmed vulnerability:

  • 4 public routes of the authentication flow that write to the database, shown as Review Required — No Authentication Identified. A login route is public by design, which is exactly why the rule asks instead of accusing.
  • 1 CORS middleware that reflects the Origin with credentials, but only after an allow-list check. It is a review, and the inspector points to the check itself.
  • 11 SQL statements built at runtime whose origin the data flow could not determine. They are reported as info instead of being silently dropped, so the reviewer knows where the analysis stopped.

The first version was much noisier, and fixing it on real code shaped the rules:

  • A CORS filter that answers 403 counted as authorization on every route, which hid the authorization rule entirely. A 403 now only counts after authentication.
  • Once that was fixed, the authorization rule flagged login routes, webhooks and reference-data tables. It now skips handlers that authenticate themselves, and it reads the SQL migrations to know which tables have an owner or tenant column.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma, running locally on Ollama, is the AI Security Investigator. It explains findings and paths from the static evidence, its answers are schema-constrained, and every citation is validated.

This post and the code it describes were written with the help of AI (Claude Code).

title: Your AI Agent Needs a Face: Building Animated AI Assistants for Web Apps
description:
AI agents can think, plan, and respond. But can your users actually tell what they're doing? Let's explore how interactive animation, Rive, and React can make AI assistants feel more responsive, expressive, and human-friendly.

AI agents are becoming a familiar part of modern web applications.

They're answering customer questions, helping users complete tasks, generating content, analyzing data, and automating entire workflows.

But there's one thing many AI interfaces still have in common.

They look like a chat box.

You type a message, wait for a response, and watch a few dots animate while the AI processes your request.

That works.

But what if your AI assistant could communicate what it's doing through movement, expressions, and real-time reactions?

Imagine an assistant that:

  • Welcomes users when they open the application.
  • Listens attentively while someone speaks.
  • Shows a thoughtful expression while generating a response.
  • Moves its mouth naturally when speaking.
  • Celebrates when a task is completed.
  • Reacts gently when something goes wrong.

This is where interactive AI characters and animated mascots can make a difference.

And tools like Rive make it possible to build these experiences for production web applications.

Let's explore how.

1. The Problem With Traditional AI Chat Interfaces

Most AI-powered products have a similar interaction pattern:

User Input → Loading Indicator → AI Response

From a technical perspective, that's completely reasonable.

But from a user experience perspective, there's often a communication gap.

Consider a voice AI assistant.

When a user finishes speaking, they might wonder:

  • Did the assistant hear me?
  • Is it processing my request?
  • Is it about to respond?
  • Has something gone wrong?

A loading spinner communicates activity, but it doesn't necessarily communicate which activity is happening.

An animated AI character can offer an additional layer of visual feedback.

For example:

AI Activity Visual Behavior
Ready Natural breathing, blinking
Listening Attentive eyes, subtle head movement
Thinking Thoughtful expression, slower motion
Speaking Mouth animation, facial movement
Success Smile, small celebration
Error Concerned or reassuring expression

These behaviors can help users understand the current interaction without repeatedly reading status messages.

Of course, animation should support clear text and accessibility features, not replace them.

The goal isn't to make an AI system pretend to be human.

It's to make its interface easier to understand.

2. What Is an Interactive AI Mascot?

An interactive AI mascot is an animated character that responds to events from an application.

Unlike a traditional GIF or looping video, its behavior can change dynamically.

For example, your application might send a status update:

activity = "thinking"

The mascot responds by switching into a thinking animation.

When the AI starts speaking:

activity = "speaking"

The character transitions into a speaking state.

These transitions are driven by application logic rather than a fixed video timeline.

An interactive mascot might also receive additional information:

  • Emotion or response tone
  • Audio intensity
  • Mouth shape or viseme
  • Cursor position
  • User interaction events
  • Task completion events

This creates opportunities for more expressive interfaces without relying on prerecorded videos for every possible interaction.

3. Why Use Rive for AI Character Animation?

Rive is a real-time interactive animation tool designed for applications, websites, and games.

It's particularly useful when visual elements need to respond to changing application state.

With Rive, designers can build animated characters and define how different animations interact.

Developers can then connect the animation system to their application through supported runtimes.

For an AI assistant, several Rive capabilities are especially useful.

State Machines

State machines manage how animations transition between behaviors.

For example:

Idle → Listening → Thinking → Speaking → Idle

But real AI interactions aren't always linear.

A user might interrupt an assistant while it's speaking.

A network request could fail during thinking.

Or a user might close the voice interface entirely.

A well-designed state machine can account for these situations.

Data Binding

Rive Data Binding allows application data to influence visual properties and animation behavior.

You can expose values such as activity, emotion, or audio level and connect them to your character's animation system.

This creates a useful separation between application logic and character animation.

Reusable Character Rigs

A reusable rig lets one character support different behaviors and expressions without requiring a completely separate design for every state.

Runtime Integration

Rive supports web and mobile development workflows, making it suitable for interactive experiences across different platforms.

The important advantage isn't simply that Rive can animate a character.

It's that the animation can respond to the product.

4. Designing the AI Assistant's Behavior System

Before animating a character, define what your AI assistant actually needs to communicate.

For a conversational web assistant, I would typically start with six core activities.

Idle

The character is available but isn't currently interacting.

Possible movements:

  • Subtle breathing
  • Natural blinking
  • Small head movements
  • Occasional eye movement

Good idle animation should make the character feel present without distracting users from the interface.

Listening

The assistant is receiving user input.

Possible movements:

  • Attentive eye expression
  • Slight head tilt
  • Gentle reactive movement
  • Subtle response to microphone activity

Avoid exaggerated movement that could suggest the assistant is speaking when it's actually listening.

Thinking

The assistant is processing a request.

Possible movements:

  • Thoughtful facial expression
  • Slow eye movement
  • Gentle head movement
  • Controlled looping animation

Thinking animations should communicate progress without implying the AI has a particular internal emotion.

Speaking

The assistant is delivering a response.

Possible movements:

  • Mouth animation
  • Facial expressions
  • Natural head movement
  • Small gestures
  • Audio-reactive animation

For voice applications, you can go beyond a simple open-and-close mouth animation.

More on that shortly.

Success

The assistant completes a task.

Possible movements:

  • Smile
  • Celebration gesture
  • Small jump
  • Positive facial expression

Success reactions work well when used selectively.

Celebrating after every basic message quickly becomes repetitive.

Error

Something goes wrong.

Possible movements:

  • Concerned expression
  • Small apologetic gesture
  • Return to a calm resting pose

The animation should complement an actionable error message explaining what happened.

5. Connecting an AI Agent to an Animated Character

Here's a simple architecture for connecting an AI agent to an interactive Rive character.

              USER
               |
               v
        React Application
               |
               v
        AI Agent Controller
               |
       +-------+--------+
       |                |
       v                v
  AI Backend       UI Activity
  / Voice API       Controller
       |                |
       |                v
       |           Rive Runtime
       |                |
       +--------------->|
                        v
                Animated Mascot

The important principle is to separate the responsibilities.

AI backend: Processes requests and generates responses.

Application controller: Determines the current interaction activity.

Rive animation system: Displays the visual response.

This separation keeps your character animation independent from whichever AI provider your application uses.

Whether the backend is powered by OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, or another model, the visual interface can respond through the same normalized activity system.

6. A Simple React Activity Controller

Let's start by defining the possible activities.

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

Now create a small React component that manages the application-side state.

import { useState } from "react";

type AgentActivity =
  | "idle"
  | "listening"
  | "thinking"
  | "speaking"
  | "success"
  | "error";

export default function AgentDemo() {
  const [activity, setActivity] =
    useState<AgentActivity>("idle");

  const activities: AgentActivity[] = [
    "idle",
    "listening",
    "thinking",
    "speaking",
    "success",
    "error",
  ];

  return (
    <main>
      <h2>AI Assistant</h2>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        Current activity: {activity}
      </p>

      <div className="agent-preview">
        {/* Mount your Rive character here */}
      </div>

      <div className="controls">
        {activities.map((nextActivity) => (
          <button
            key={nextActivity}
            onClick={() => setActivity(nextActivity)}
          >
            {nextActivity}
          </button>
        ))}
      </div>
    </main>
  );
}

This is an application-state demo, not yet a complete Rive integration.

The next step is to connect activity to a Rive View Model property through the appropriate React runtime API.

For example, your Rive project could expose an enum property named activity with the same six values.

Your integration would then follow this flow:

React activity changes
         |
         v
Update Rive View Model
         |
         v
Rive State Machine
         |
         v
Character transitions

In modern Rive workflows, Data Binding is a useful approach for this connection.

The exact integration code depends on your chosen runtime version and exported Rive file. See the official Rive runtime documentation for the current API.

7. Making Your AI Assistant Speak Naturally

One of the most interesting challenges in conversational AI animation is lip synchronization.

A basic speaking animation might repeatedly open and close the character's mouth.

That can work for a simple chatbot.

But voice AI products can benefit from more expressive mouth movement.

There are two common approaches.

Audio-Level Animation

Use the current audio amplitude to influence how much the mouth opens.

Conceptually:

const mouthOpen = Math.min(
  Math.max(audioLevel, 0),
  1
);

Then provide mouthOpen to the Rive character.

The animation system can use this value to control mouth movement.

This approach is relatively simple, but it doesn't accurately reproduce individual speech sounds.

Viseme-Based Lip Sync

Visemes represent visual mouth shapes associated with speech sounds.

A speech system capable of providing viseme information can send these values to the animation layer.

For example:

type Viseme = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5;

Your Rive character could support six simplified mouth shapes.

As the voice system produces timed viseme data, the animation controller updates the mouth shape accordingly.

Text-to-Speech System
         |
         v
Timed Viseme Events
         |
         v
Animation Controller
         |
         v
Rive Mouth Shapes

For accurate lip sync, timing matters as much as the mouth shapes themselves.

Your developer needs to coordinate the animation with actual audio playback rather than assuming that generated text and sound will arrive simultaneously.

Not every voice API provides viseme events, so the implementation depends on the audio system you're using.

8. Making the Character React to Emotion

An AI assistant doesn't necessarily need a different full-body animation for every response tone.

Instead, emotion can often be designed as an additional control layer.

For example:

type AgentEmotion =
  | "neutral"
  | "happy"
  | "empathetic"
  | "concerned"
  | "surprised";

Your activity and emotion controls can work independently.

Example:

Activity: Speaking
Emotion: Happy

The character speaks with a positive expression.

Another example:

Activity: Listening
Emotion: Concerned

The character listens attentively with a more serious facial expression.

This modular approach can reduce duplicated animation work.

However, avoid assuming that an AI model's tone classification perfectly represents the user's emotional state.

Use expressions conservatively, especially in sensitive applications such as healthcare, financial assistance, or mental health support.

9. Designing Transitions That Don't Break

This is where interactive animation becomes a real engineering problem.

Consider the following situation:

Your character is speaking.

The user interrupts.

Your application immediately switches to listening.

What should happen to the character's mouth, hands, and facial expression?

If the animation system isn't designed carefully, you might see:

  • A mouth frozen open
  • Sudden head movement
  • Hands snapping into the wrong pose
  • Conflicting animations
  • Unexpected idle transitions

The solution is to define clear transition rules and ownership of animation properties.

For example:

Transition Expected Behavior
Idle → Listening Smooth attentive movement
Listening → Thinking Gradual pose transition
Thinking → Speaking Begin speaking posture
Speaking → Listening Stop lip sync and reset mouth
Any state → Error Interrupt safely
Success → Idle Complete reaction, return to rest

For some characters, a single activity enum is sufficient.

For more advanced systems, separate layers for body movement, facial expressions, and mouth animation may provide greater flexibility.

The best architecture depends on the character and product requirements.

10. Don't Forget Performance and Accessibility

An animated AI assistant should improve the experience, not make the application harder to use.

Before shipping, consider the following.

Performance

Keep artwork and animation systems as efficient as possible.

Test your Rive file on the actual devices and browsers your users will use.

Pay attention to unnecessary redraws, heavy assets, and complex layered animations.

Reduced Motion

Respect users who prefer reduced motion.

Your application should offer a calmer version of the character or a static alternative when appropriate.

Accessibility

Animation alone shouldn't communicate critical information.

If the agent is listening, thinking, or reporting an error, provide accessible status information as well.

For example, use appropriate status messages for screen-reader users without announcing every decorative animation transition.

User Control

Allow users to minimize or disable the animated assistant.

A helpful mascot shouldn't become an obstacle.

11. Where Animated AI Assistants Make Sense

Interactive AI characters aren't appropriate for every product.

But they can be particularly useful when the application benefits from ongoing visual communication.

Potential use cases include:

AI coaching platforms: A companion that welcomes users, listens, and provides encouragement.

Language learning applications: A speaking character with expressive mouth movement and positive feedback.

Voice AI interfaces: A visual indicator for listening, thinking, and speaking.

Educational applications: Interactive tutors that guide students through tasks.

Product onboarding: Friendly characters that explain features and celebrate completed steps.

Virtual pets and gamified apps: Characters that reflect progress, rewards, and activity.

Customer support interfaces: An optional visual assistant that communicates its current activity.

In each case, the design should be driven by the user's needs rather than adding a mascot simply because it's visually appealing.

12. How I Approach Rive AI Mascot Projects

As a freelance Rive animator, I focus on building interactive character systems that designers and developers can actually use in production.

For AI companion projects, my workflow generally includes:

  1. Understanding the application's interactions and required character behaviors.
  2. Planning the character rig and animation states.
  3. Building expressive idle, listening, thinking, speaking, and reaction animations.
  4. Creating and testing the state machine.
  5. Defining runtime-facing inputs or Data Binding properties.
  6. Testing transitions, interruption behavior, and animation loops.
  7. Delivering the Rive assets with clear integration guidance.

For more advanced projects, this can also include lip-sync mouth shapes, audio-reactive animation, gaze tracking, emotions, and reusable character systems.

The goal is to create something that looks good but also behaves reliably inside the application.

Final Thoughts: Give Your AI Agent a Better Interface

AI agents are becoming increasingly capable.

But the interface connecting those systems to users still matters.

A thoughtfully animated character can make an AI product feel more responsive, approachable, and easier to understand.

It doesn't need exaggerated expressions or constant movement.

Sometimes a natural blink, an attentive listening pose, or a smooth transition into speaking is enough.

The best AI mascot isn't the one that moves the most. It's the one that communicates the right thing at the right moment.

And with tools like Rive, these experiences can become part of a real web application's interaction system rather than remaining a decorative animation.

Need an Interactive Rive Animator for Your AI Project?

I'm Praneeth Kawya Thathsara, a freelance Rive animator specializing in interactive mascots, AI character animation, state machines, lip sync, and developer-ready animation systems.

I work with startups, designers, and development teams building interactive experiences for websites, mobile applications, and AI-powered products.

If you're creating an AI agent, voice assistant, AI coach, or interactive mascot, I'd be happy to help bring the character to life.
